Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 1:

(p-31) Surat al-Baqarah (the Chapter of the Cow)

All of it is Medinan, without disagreement. Its number of verses is two hundred and eighty-six. Several reports about its virtues are authentic. Among them is what is in the Musnad of Ahmad, Sahih Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not make your houses graves, for the house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited, Satan does not enter."

Al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih" (good and authentic).

Ibn Hibban related in his Sahih, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, for everything there is a peak, and the peak of the Qur'an is al-Baqarah. Whoever recites it in his house at night, Satan does not enter his house for three nights, and whoever recites it in his house by day, Satan does not enter his house for three days."

Muslim related from Abu Umamah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Recite the Qur'an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions. Recite the two bright ones (al-Zahrawayn): al-Baqarah and Surat Al 'Imran, for they will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or as if they were two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companions. Recite Surat al-Baqarah, for taking it is a blessing, leaving it is a regret, and the sorcerers (al-batalah) cannot withstand it."

(Regarding his saying al-Zahrawayn: that is, the two luminous ones, either in their inimitability or in the abundance of their rulings. Al-ghayayah is what shades you from above. Al-firq is a portion of a thing. Al-sawaff are those arranged in rows. Al-batalah are the sorcerers. The meaning of "cannot withstand it" is: they cannot gain influence over its reciter, or they cannot memorize it. And Allah knows best.)

(p-32) On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ [1]

Know that people hold two positions regarding this and what is similar to it among the disjointed letters at the openings of chapters (al-fawatih):

The first: that this is a hidden knowledge and a concealed secret, which Allah, blessed and exalted, has reserved for Himself. Therefore it is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters. Many of the careful scholars (al-muhaqqiqin) did not accept this and said: It is not permissible that there should appear in the Book of Allah, Exalted is He, anything that is not understood by creation. They argued with rational and transmitted proofs, which al-Allamah al-Fakhr (al-Razi) expounded.

The second position is that of those who explained them and spoke about what may be intended by them, and this is the position of the majority. Within it there are two views:

(The first), and it is the view of most: that they are names of the chapters.

(The second): that the occurrence of these names in this manner, listed in sequence, is like an awakening and like the striking of a staff for one who is challenged (tuhuddiya) with the Qur'an and its strange composition. It is also like a stirring of reflection, that this recited speech which has been recited to them, and at which they have all been unable, is composed of the very same material from which they compose their own speech. This is so that reflection will lead them to be certain that their capacity has not fallen short of it, and that their miracle (mu'jizah) has not been shown to be beyond their ability to produce its like, after lengthy disputations, and they are the leaders of eloquence, the chiefs of debate, those eager to compete in the composing of concise sermons, and those who are fervently devoted to the refinement of qasidas and rajaz verse. Yet it did not reach in eloquence and beauty of composition the level that surpassed the rhetoric of every speaker and outstripped the dust of every forerunner. It did not exceed the bounds that lie beyond the capacities of the eloquent, nor did it fall beyond the aspirations of the discerning eyes, except because it is not the speech of humans, and that it is the speech of the Creator of powers and capacities. This is what al-Zamakhshari said.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[2] ﴿That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing.﴾

That is, this Qur'an is undoubtedly from God, exalted is He, as He said in Surah al-Sajda: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ [32:1] ﴿The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [32:2]. Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: the restriction of that to the demonstrative for the distant is a conventional (*'urfi*) rule, not a lexical (*wad'i*) one, for the Arabs interchange the two demonstratives, using each of them in place of the other, and this is well known in their speech. The Revelation contains many verses of this. Whoever holds that *dhalika* indicates the distant says: the demonstrative with *dhalika* was used here for something that is not distant, in order to magnify the thing pointed to, implying the loftiness of its rank and its high station and status in guidance and honour.

The *rayb* (doubt) in origin is the verbal noun of *rabani*, meaning that unease (*ribah*) has occurred within you. Its reality is the restlessness and agitation of the soul. Then it was used to mean doubt in general, or doubt accompanied by suspicion, because it disturbs the soul and removes tranquillity.

In a hadith: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

The negation of it from the Book means that it is of such lofty status and such manifest proof that there is no ground for anyone to doubt its reality, and that it is a revelation sent down from God, exalted is He. The matter is indeed so, because the Arabs, despite their attainment of eloquence to its utmost limit, were unable to match even the shortest sura of the Qur'an. This testifies that this proof has reached such a degree of clarity that it is not permissible for a sane person to doubt it, not that no one at all doubts it.

﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾: that is, it guides them and points them to the upright religion that leads to the happiness of both abodes.

Al-Nasir said in *al-Intisaf*: *al-huda* (guidance) is used in the Qur'an in two senses. The first is instruction and clarifying the path of truth, and from this is His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness to guidance﴾ [41:17]. In this sense, guidance applies to the one who has gone astray, insofar as he has been directed to the truth, whether or not he himself attains guidance. The second is God, exalted is He, creating guidance in the heart of the servant, and from this is: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [6:90]. When it is established that the word is used in both senses, then in this verse it may mean both of them together. On the first meaning, restricting guidance to the God-fearing serves to praise them, to make clear that they are the ones who were guided and benefited from it, as He said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾ [79:45], and He said: ﴿You can only warn those who follow the Reminder﴾ [36:11]. The Prophet (ﷺ) was a warner to all people, but He mentioned these because they are the ones who benefited from his warning. This verse is similar to the verse: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing; but for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears and it is blindness for them; those are called from a far place﴾ [41:44], and ﴿We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers, and it adds only loss to the wrongdoers﴾ [17:82], and like His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [10:57], and other verses which indicate that only the righteous attain benefit from it. The meaning of "the God-fearing" here is those whom God described with His saying—

"The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:"

[3] ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.﴾

"Those who believe" means: those who affirm as true. "In the unseen" (al-ghayb): originally it is the verbal noun of ghaba, meaning to be hidden, concealed, or out of sight. It is used in the sense of the active participle (like zawr for za'ir, "visitor"), and is applied to it as an intensive. What is meant by it is that which does not fall under the senses and is not required by the immediate judgment of the intellect, and which is known only through the report of the prophets, peace be upon them. The meaning is: they believe in what their senses do not reach, such as the Essence of Allah, exalted is He, His angels, Paradise, the Fire, the Throne, the Chair (al-Kursi), the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), and the like.

"And establish prayer": that is, they perform it with its limits and obligations, both outward and inward, such as humility (khushu'), vigilance over the heart (muraqabah), and reflection upon what is recited.

Al-Raghib said: "Establishing prayer means fulfilling its limits and maintaining it continuously. The specification of 'establishing' is a reminder that it is not merely the performance of it. For this reason He did not command prayer, nor praise it, except with the word 'establishing,' as in: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾ [al-Isra: 78], and His saying: ﴿those who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Nisa: 162], and: ﴿those who establish the prayer﴾ [al-Anfal: 3]. He did not say 'the one who prays' (al-musalli), except regarding the hypocrites: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'un: 4], ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5]. This is a reminder that those who pray are many, while those who establish it are few, as 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'The pilgrims are few, while the riders are many.' For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'Whoever prays two rak'ahs, turning towards his Lord with his heart, will come out of his sins like the day his mother bore him.' He mentioned, along with his saying 'prays,' turning the heart towards Allah, as a reminder of the meaning of establishing, and by this its reward is greatly magnified. Many of the acts which Allah, exalted is He, urged to fulfil His right, He mentioned with the word 'establishing,' such as: ﴿If only they had established the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], and: ﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ [al-Rahman: 9], as a reminder of preserving its balance." End of quote.

So "iqamah" derives from aqama al-'ud, meaning to straighten a stick when he straightened it. "Salat" is of the pattern fa'lah from salla, meaning to supplicate, like "zakat" from zakka. They are written with a waw (salat, zakat) out of regard for the emphatic pronunciation of the word. The specific act is named salat because it includes supplication (du'a').

"And spend out of what We have provided for them": that is, they give from the wealth We have provided for them to whom it has been prescribed that they give and spend, such as the poor, the needy, relatives, orphans, and those like them, as Allah has explained in many verses.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 4:

(p-37) Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[4] ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾

"And those who believe in what has been revealed to you, and what was revealed before you." What is meant by "what has been revealed to you" is the whole Book that was sent down. He expressed it with the past tense, although part of it was still awaited, giving precedence to what exists over what has not yet existed. Likewise, what is meant by His saying "and what was revealed before you" is all the earlier divine books. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before﴾ [al-Nisa: 136], to the end of the verse. Revelation (al-inzal) means transmission from above to below. The descent of the divine books to the messengers, peace be upon them, takes place by Jibril receiving them from His presence, glorified and exalted is He, and then descending with them to the messengers, peace be upon them. For this reason it is said: The Qur'an is the speech of Allah, not created, from Him it originated.

Imam Ahmad and others said: "To Him it returns," meaning He is the one who spoke it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-An'am: 114]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 102]. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Zumar: 1].

"And in the Hereafter they are certain." Al-Akhirah (the Hereafter) originally is the feminine form of al-akhir (the last), which is the opposite of al-awwal (the first), and it is an attribute of the abode, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Last Abode﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. It was so named because it comes after the worldly life. It was said that the worldly life is called dunya because it is nearer (adna) than the Hereafter. Both are among the attributes that have become predominant, and yet they have taken the course of proper nouns, since the mention of the name of the thing they qualify has commonly been omitted alongside them, as though they were not attributes.

Al-iqan (certainty) is the perfecting of knowledge with the absence of doubt and suspicion regarding it. In placing "al-Akhirah" first and in constructing "yuqinun" upon "hum," there is an allusion to the People of the Book and to what they were upon of affirming matters of the Hereafter contrary to their reality, such as their claim that no one enters Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of counted days; and their disagreement over whether the bliss of Paradise is of the same kind as the bliss of this world or not, and whether it is everlasting or not. Thus their belief concerning the matters of the Hereafter is far from correct, let alone reaching the station of certainty!

The Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[5] ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the successful.﴾

"Ula'ika" (those): that is, those who are characterized by what has preceded. "Upon guidance from their Lord": that is, upon light from their Lord, and proof, and uprightness, and rectitude, by His making them firm and His granting them success.

"And they are the successful": that is, the ones who attain success, who obtain by their faith what they sought from Allah, namely triumph with the reward, eternal abiding in the Gardens, and deliverance from what Allah has prepared for His enemies of punishment.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, had described the attributes of the believers before this, He explained the condition of their opposites, namely the disbelievers, the obstinate rebels, [explaining] that they have gone to such extremes in misguidance and error that warning and reminder do not benefit them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96] ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 97], and like His saying, glorified is He, concerning the obstinate People of the Book: ﴿And even if you brought to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 145], and so on.

"Sawa'" (equal, the same) is a noun meaning "equality" (al-istiwa'), and it is used as a description, as sources are used as descriptions, for emphasis. From this (p-40) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Come to a word that is equal between us and you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 64], meaning: equal.

And "al-Indhar" (warning) is informing together with frightening. What is meant here is frightening them with His punishment and His retribution, and restricting the discussion to it, because they are not worthy of glad tidings, and because warning has a greater effect on hearts; and whoever is not affected by it, then he is all the more not moved by glad tidings at all, and this is more fitting.

His saying "they will not believe" is an independent sentence, emphasizing what precedes it and clarifying what is implicit in the equality mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 7:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering; and for them is a great punishment.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) giving the reason for the judgment that preceded it, or it is an elucidation and emphasis of it. The "khatm" (sealing) upon a thing is securing it by striking a seal upon it. What is meant is the bringing about of a state which makes them—because of their persistence in misguidance, their immersion in blind imitation (taqlid), and their turning away from the method of sound reflection (nazar sahih)—such that the warning has no effect upon them and the truth does not penetrate them at all.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The attribution of bringing about that state in their hearts to Allah, exalted is He, is because, according to us, all events in terms of their creation are ascribed to Him, glorified is He. The noble verse's coming in a manner that censures them for their evil conduct and the grave consequence of their end is because their actions, in terms of acquisition (kasb), are ascribed to them. Its creation by Him, glorified is He, is not by way of compulsion (jabr), but by way of arrangement (tartib) in accordance with the abominations they have committed, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Nay, Allah has sealed it upon them because of their disbelief﴾ [an-Nisa 155] and similar to that, (p-41) meaning like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [as-Saff 5] and His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights away, as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am 110].

As for the Mu'tazilah, they took the path of interpretation (ta'wil) and mentioned in this several sayings.

Among them: that when these people turned away from the truth, and that became firmly rooted in their hearts until it became like a nature for them, it was likened to an innate quality with which they were created.

Among them: that what is meant by it is the depiction of their hearts as the hearts of animals, which Allah, exalted is He, created devoid of understanding, or as hearts upon which Allah's sealing has been decreed. Like the expression: "The valley was carried away with him" (meaning he perished), and "the 'anqa' flew away with him" (meaning his absence was prolonged).

Among them: that their dispositions, when they had taken firm root in disbelief and become entrenched, such that no path remained to bringing about their faith except compulsion and coercion; then He did not do that, out of regard for the wisdom of the obligation (taklif), and this was expressed by the seal, because it blocks the path of their faith entirely. In it is an indication of the far-reaching nature of their affair in error and obstinacy.

Among them: that this is a report of what the disbelievers used to say, such as their saying: "Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you there is a barrier," mocking them.

Among them: that this refers to the Hereafter, and it is mentioned in the past tense only to affirm its certain occurrence. Supporting this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf﴾ [al-Isra 97]. End of the summary.

(Benefit): al-Raghib said: The intended meaning of "heart" (qalb) in many verses is the intellect ('aql) and knowledge (ma'rifah). End.

(p-42) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[8] ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers.﴾

The root of nās (people) is unās. The hamza was dropped for ease of pronunciation, and its dropping together with the definite article (al-) is treated as obligatory. Its original form is supported by insān, unās, anāsī, and inS. They were named for their visibility (ẓuhūr), and because they "yu'nisūn," that is, they perceive (yubṣirūn), just as the jinn were named for their concealment (ijtinān). For this reason they were also called bashar. It has also been said that the derivation is from al-uns (familiarity, the opposite of loneliness), because the human being is naturally social (madanī bi'l-ṭab'). The first explanation is more apparent.

Know that the attributes of the hypocrites (munāfiqūn) were revealed only in the Madinan surahs, because there was no hypocrisy in Makkah. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah, the Ansar of al-Aws and al-Khazraj were there, and in their pre-Islamic ignorance they worshipped idols in the manner of the polytheist Arabs. The Jews, from the People of the Book, were also there, in three tribes: Banu Qaynuqa' (allies of al-Khazraj), Banu al-Nadir, and Banu Qurayza (allies of al-Aws). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, those among the Ansar from the two tribes of al-Aws and al-Khazraj who embraced Islam did so, and few of the Jews embraced Islam, except 'Abd Allah ibn Salam (may Allah be pleased with him). Hypocrisy did not yet exist at that time either, because the Muslims did not yet have a power to be feared. Rather, the Prophet (ﷺ) had made a truce with the Jews and many tribes of the Arabs around Madinah. When the great battle of Badr took place, and Allah made His word supreme and gave might to Islam and its people, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul said, (he was a chief in Madinah, from al-Khazraj, and was the son of the leader of both factions in the pre-Islamic period; they had resolved to make him king over them, but the news came to them and they embraced Islam and turned away from him, so he remained in his heart with resentment toward Islam and its people). When the battle of Badr took place, he said, "This is a matter that has come to pass." So he displayed entry into Islam, and groups joined him, of those who shared his way and creed, and others from the People of the Book. From this point, hypocrisy was found among the people of Madinah and among the Bedouins around it.

(p-43) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿They seek to deceive God and those who believe, but they deceive none but themselves, and they perceive it not.﴾

Al-Qashani said: Deception (al-mukhadaʿah) is the use of tricks from both sides. It is showing good while concealing evil. Deceiving God is deceiving His Messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 80]. Their deceiving of God and of the believers is their display of faith and love while concealing disbelief and enmity. God's deception of them and the believers' deception of them is that they are treated peacefully and the rulings of Islam are applied to them, by preserving their blood and protecting their property and other things. It also means storing up for them a painful punishment, a grim final end, an evil outcome, and their humiliation in this world, because they are exposed by God's informing and by revelation about their state. However, the difference between the deceivers is that their deception succeeds only against themselves, by destroying them, causing their loss, and bringing upon them ruin and retribution, through increased darkness, disbelief and hypocrisy, and the gathering of the causes of perdition, distance and wretchedness upon them. As for God's deception, it has the most powerful effect on them and destroys them most severely, as in His saying: ﴿They schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers﴾ [Al ʿImran: 54]. And they, because of how deeply they are immersed in their ignorance, do not sense this matter, though it is manifest.

Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr read: "wa-ma yukhadiʿuna" with an alif.

Ibn Kathir said: God, glory be to Him, drew attention to the attributes of the hypocrites, lest the believers be deceived by their outward appearance, and thereby great corruption occur, through failing to guard against them and through believing in their faith while they are in reality disbelievers. This is among the things to be feared: that good be assumed of the people of wickedness. Moreover, the saying of whoever claims that the Prophet (ﷺ) (p-44) knew the identities of some of the hypocrites is based only on the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman concerning the naming of those fourteen hypocrites in the expedition of Tabuk, who intended to assassinate the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the darkness of the night at a mountain pass there. They resolved to startle his she-camel so that he would fall from it. God revealed their plan to him, and he informed Hudhayfah of it.

As for others than these, God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy. You do not know them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101], and so on. He also said: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease and the agitators in Madinah do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbours therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60]. In these verses is evidence that he was not given authority over them and did not identify them individually. Rather, their attributes were mentioned to him, and he would discern them in some of them, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognised them by their marks; and you will surely know them by the tone of their speech. And God knows your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. Among the most notorious of them for hypocrisy was ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul.

Many of the imams relied, regarding the wisdom behind the Prophet's (ﷺ) restraint from killing the hypocrites, on what is established in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn, the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim) that he (ﷺ) said to ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him: "I dislike that the Arabs should say that Muhammad kills his own companions." Its meaning is: lest, as a result of that, many of the Bedouins be repelled from entering Islam, since they would not know the wisdom of killing them, namely that it is because of their disbelief. They would simply take what appears to them, and say: "Muhammad kills his companions."

"The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[10] ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.﴾

Al-maradh (disease): sickness, which is the opposite of health, caused by what afflicts the body, taking it out of the balance appropriate to it and causing disorder in its functions. It is used metaphorically here for the lack of soundness of their certainty and the weakness of their religion. Likewise, the hearts of the believers are described as sound (salamah), which is the soundness of certainty and the absence of its weakness, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 89], meaning: not diseased by what we have mentioned. Or it is used metaphorically for their doubt, because doubt is wavering between two matters, and the hypocrite is wavering, as in the hadith: "The example of the hypocrite is like the sheep that wanders between two flocks" (p-46), and the sick person wavers between life and death.

"So Allah has increased their disease" means: by sealing their hearts, since He, exalted is He, knows that reminder and warning will have no effect upon them.

Al-Qashani said: That is, another disease — hatred, envy and rancor — by the elevation of the word of religion and the support of the Messenger and the believers. Then he said: All vices are diseases of the hearts, because they are the causes of their weakness and their affliction in their specific functions, and their ruin in the end.

"And for them is a painful punishment" — that is, painful (mu'lim), with a kasra on the lam — fa'il (ʿalīm) in the sense of fa'il (mu'lim), like samī' and baṣīr.

Ibn Sidah said in al-Muhkam: al-alim (painful) is said of punishment whose infliction reaches the utmost extent of pain. From this the reason for choosing it for the punishment of the hypocrites becomes known — over "al-'izam" (great) mentioned earlier in describing the punishment of the disbelievers. This is supported by: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper﴾ [al-Nisa': 145].

"Because they used to lie" — the ba' is causal (lil-sababiyyah) or of exchange (lil-muqabalah): that is, because of their lying, or in exchange for it. And it is their saying: "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," while they are not believers. In this is an indication of the ugliness of lying and its repulsiveness, and an imagining that the painful punishment befalls them because of their lying — together with the listener's full knowledge that the punishment befalls them from various directions. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ [Nuh: 25] — and the people were disbelievers. The sins were singled out only to magnify them and to deter from committing them."

[p. 47]

**On the Interpretation (ta'wil) of His Words, Exalted is He:**

[11] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."﴾ [12] ﴿Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 11–12]

This begins a enumeration of some of their branching evils, based on what He related about them of disbelief and hypocrisy. "Corruption" (al-fasad) is the departure of a thing from its state of soundness and from being beneficial. Its opposite is "reform" (al-salah), which is attaining the upright, beneficial condition. Corruption on the earth is the stirring up of wars and strife, because in that is the corruption of what is on the earth, the loss of uprightness in people's affairs, in crops, and in religious and worldly benefits. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals; and Allah does not like corruption.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 205] ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30] From this comes the saying about a war that took place between Tayy: "the War of Corruption (Harb al-Fasad)."

The corruption of the hypocrites on the earth consisted in their colluding with the disbelievers against the Muslims by disclosing their secrets to them, inciting them against the Muslims, and taking them as allies, together with what they called for in private: denying the Prophet (ﷺ), rejecting Islam, and casting doubts. This emboldened the disbelievers to openly show enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), to wage war against him, and to hope for victory. Since this conduct of theirs led to corruption, by stirring up strife among them, it was said to them: "Do not cause corruption," just as one says to a man: "Do not kill yourself with your own hand, and do not throw yourself into the Fire," when he is about to do what has such an outcome. God Exalted has said: ﴿And those who disbelieve are allies of one another. If you do not do so, there will be fitnah in the land and great corruption.﴾ [Al-Anfal: 73] (p. 48) Thus He informed that the allegiance of the disbelievers leads to strife and corruption, for the reason already mentioned.

Their saying, "We are only reformers," means: between the believers and the People of the Book. We seek to accommodate both parties and intend reconciliation between them, as God related of them that they said: ﴿We intended only good and reconciliation.﴾ [An-Nisa: 62] Or its meaning is: "We are only reformers on the earth through obedience and submission."

Al-Raghib said: They imagined their corruption in the form of reform, because of the sickness in their hearts, as He said: ﴿Then is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good...?﴾ [Fatir: 8] And His saying: ﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they used to do.﴾ [Al-An'am: 43] And His saying: ﴿while they think they are doing well in work.﴾ [Al-Kahf: 104]

Al-Qashani said: They saw reform in securing livelihood, facilitating its means, and arranging worldly affairs, for themselves alone, because they were absorbed in love of this world and immersed in bodily pleasures, and were veiled, by partial benefits and sensory delights, from universal public welfare and intellectual pleasures. By this their aims were made easy and their objectives facilitated, while they did not perceive their corruption, which is grasped only by the senses.

(p-49) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[13] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" Unquestionably, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.﴾

"And when it is said to them" by way of enjoining what is good, following their being forbidden what is evil, to complete the counsel and perfect the guidance: "Believe as the people have believed," i.e., the complete ones in humanity, for the believers are truly "the people" because they combine what is counted among the distinctive qualities and virtues of humankind. "They say, 'Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?'" is an interrogation carrying the sense of denial. And (al-safah, "foolishness") is lightness and feebleness of judgment, which result in deficiency of intellect and little knowledge of the places of benefit and harm. For this reason God called women and children "foolish" in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property, which God has made a means of support for you﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 5].

They called them foolish—though they were in fact the wise, the preferred ones—because, out of their ignorance, their failure to reflect, and their failure to be fair to themselves, they believed that what they were upon was the truth and that whatever else was other than it was falsehood—and whoever mounts the back of falsehood is foolish. Also, they held leadership among their people and affluence, whereas most of the believers were poor, and among them were freedmen such as Suhayb, Bilal, and Khabbab; so they called them foolish, belittling their station! "Unquestionably, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 14:

The discussion of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[14] ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their shayatin (devils, i.e. their leaders in disbelief), they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾

"And when they meet those who believe, they say, 'We believe'" means: they displayed to them faith, loyalty, and friendship, out of hypocrisy, flattery, and dissimulation (taqiyya), and so that they might share with them in what they gained of good and spoils.

Know that the context of this verse differs from the context in which it was presented at the beginning of the story of the hypocrites. Therefore it is not a repetition, because that passage explains their creed and expresses their hypocrisy, whereas this one explains the divergence of their states and the contradiction of their statements in the course of dealing and address, according to the divergence of those they address!

﴿And when they are alone with their shayatin, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾ It is said: "I was alone with so-and-so" (khalawtu bi-fulan wa-ilayhi), meaning I was in private with him. It may also be that khala (in the sense of "to pass away") is meant, as in "the past generations" (al-qurun al-khaliya). By "their shayatin" is meant their companions, the stubborn and obstinate ones. The shaytan may be from among mankind and jinn, as the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy—devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with decorative speech as deception﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. Their attribution of them to themselves is for partnership in disbelief. The derivation of shaytan is from shatana, meaning he went far away, for his distance from righteousness and good.

The meaning of "Indeed, we are with you" is: in belief, upon the same as what you are upon; we are only, in displaying faith before the believers, mockers, deriding them. Al-istihza' (mockery) of a thing is ridiculing it; it is said: hazi'tu and istahza'tu with the same meaning.

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿Allah mocks them and extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

"Allah mocks them" means He ridicules them as retribution against them. This is how Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) explained it, as related by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

"And extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly" means He increases them by way of respite (imlāʾ), leaving them in their insolence and rebellion, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight away, as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Anʿām: 110].

Al-ṭughyān (transgression) here means excess in disbelief and exceeding the limit in insolence. The root meaning is going beyond a bound in something, as He said: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 11].

Al-ʿamah (wandering blindly) is like al-ʿamā (blindness), except that al-ʿamā is general, applying to sight and to judgment, whereas al-ʿamah is specifically in judgment. It is bewilderment and hesitation, not knowing where to turn.

That is, in their misguidance and disbelief, by which their filth has engulfed them and their uncleanness has overtaken them, they wander bewildered and astray, not finding any way out of it.

The well-known reading is with a fatḥah on the yāʾ in "yamuddahum," and it was read with a ḍammah in an irregular reading (shādh). Both have the same meaning. It is said: madda al-jaysh and amaddahu, meaning he increased it and added to it what strengthens and multiplies it. Likewise, madda al-dawāh and amaddahā, meaning he increased the inkwell with what keeps it in good condition.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[16] ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, so their trade has not profited, nor were they guided.﴾

"Those" (ulā'ika) is a demonstrative referring to those previously mentioned, on account of their being characterized by the abominable qualities mentioned, which distinguish them from others in the most complete distinction, such that they become as though present and witnessing what they are upon. The sense of distance contained in it serves to announce the remoteness of their station in wickedness and the badness of their condition. Its place in i'rab is nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His words, Exalted is He, "those who bought" (alladhina ishtaraw), etc. The sentence is brought to confirm what precedes it and to clarify the completeness of their ignorance, in respect of the statements and actions reported of them, by displaying the extreme ugliness of these, and depicting them in a form that one with even minimal discernment would hardly undertake, let alone rational people.

"Error" (ḍalāla) is deviation from the straight aim; "guidance" (hudā) is turning toward it. The first has been used metaphorically for deviating from what is right in religion, and the second for remaining steadfast upon it. "Purchase" (ishtirā') is the exchange of a commodity for a price, that is, taking it in return for that price. Thus "buying error in exchange for guidance" is a metaphor for taking the former in place of the latter, a taking that is contingent upon desire for it and turning away from the latter.

If it is said: How did they buy error in exchange for guidance, when they were not upon guidance?

I say: They treated their capacity for it, through the facilitation of its means, as though it were in their hands; so when they abandoned it for error, they had rendered it inoperative and exchanged it for that. Thus the attribution of possession to them is used metaphorically for their capacity, by the common factor of sharing in the consequence of benefit. There is no doubt that this degree of capacity was actually theirs, through what they had witnessed of the manifest signs and overpowering miracles from the Prophet ﷺ.

"So their trade has not profited" is a coordination with the relative clause, falling within its scope. The fa' indicates that its content follows from it. "Trade" (tijāra) is the craft of merchants, namely engaging in buying and selling to obtain profit, which is the surplus over capital. The attribution of its absence, which is an expression for loss, to the trade itself is from the metaphorical attribution (al-isnād al-majāzī), in which a verb is attributed to a thing that is clothed in the one to whom it truly belongs, just as the trade is clothed in the buyers. Its benefit is exaggeration in their loss, for it implies the abundance of the loss and its generality, which extends to whatever clings to them.

If you say: Grant that buying error in exchange for guidance is metaphorical in the sense of substitution, what is the meaning of mentioning profit and trade, as though there were a genuine transaction?

I say: This is of the wondrous artifice that carries metaphor to its highest peak: a word is driven in the manner of metaphor, then followed by its related forms and sisters; when they succeed one another, you will not see speech more beautiful in its finery, or fuller in its radiance and brilliance. This is what is called the "nurtured metaphor" (al-majāz al-murashshaḥ). Thus their mention after "buying" depicts the benefits of guidance that they missed in the form of the loss of trade, which every person shuns, for the sake of completeness in describing the loss and the regret. This type is close to what the rhetoricians call "tatmīm" (completion), exemplified by al-Khansā''s saying:

"Indeed Sakhr is one whom the guided take as a model, as though he were a banner with fire upon its top!"

When she likened him, in being guided by him, to a raised banner, she followed that with what suits and confirms it, and was not content with the manifestness of height until she added to it another manifestness, the kindling of fire at its top.

His words, "nor were they guided" (wa-mā kānū muhtadīn), mean: because their readiness has disappeared, and their hearts have been darkened by the rust that necessitates the veil and eternal deprivation.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If it is asked: Why did he join by "and" (wa) the non-guidance of theirs to the absence of profit from their trade, when both were arranged by the fa' upon buying error in exchange for guidance? And what is the wisdom of combining them with that arrangement, given that the non-guidance was already understood from substituting error for guidance, so it would be a repetition of what has passed? The answer: Their capital is guidance, so when they substituted for it what is its opposite and does not combine with it at all, the capital was wholly lost, and when nothing remained in their hands but that opposite, namely error, they were described by the absence of profit and by loss. For the one astray in his religion is lost and ruined, even if he gains worldly benefits; and whoever has not preserved his capital is not described as profiting, but rather as lacking it. Thus they squandered the safety of the capital by substitution, and the squandering of profit followed from that.

As for His words, "and they were not guided," its meaning is not their non-guidance in religion, which would be a repetition of what preceded, but rather: because they were described as losing in this trade, it is indicated that they were not guided to the ways of trade, as shrewd merchants are guided to the matters in which they profit or lose. This returns to the nurturing (tarshīḥ).

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He):**

[17] ﴿Their similitude is like that of one who kindled a fire; then when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing.﴾

When He had stated the reality of their description, He followed it with a parable (*darb al-mathal*), to add clarity and to complete the explanation. So He, Exalted is He, said: "Their similitude" (*mathaluhum*), meaning: their likeness in their hypocrisy and their condition in it, "is like that of one who kindled" (*istawqada*), meaning: lit, "a fire" (*naran*) in darkness. The indefinite form (*al-tankir*) is for magnification. "Then when it illuminated" (*fa-lamma adā'at*), meaning: the fire shone, "what was around him" [p. 54], so he could see, warm himself, and feel safe from what he feared. "Allah took away their light" (*dhahaba Allahu bi-nurihim*), meaning: Allah extinguished their fire, which was the source of their light, so they remained in darkness and fear. The pronoun is in the plural in consideration of the meaning of *alladhi* (the one), as in His saying: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged did﴾ [al-Tawbah: 69]. "And left them in darkness, not seeing" what was around them, bewildered about the way and fearful. Likewise, these people were illuminated briefly by benefiting from the word that was uttered on their tongues, since they felt safe for themselves and for what follows from it. Then, behind their illumination by the light of this word lies the darkness of hypocrisy, which casts them into the darkness of Allah's wrath and the darkness of everlasting punishment. The sum of it is that they benefited from this word during the brief span of their lives, then Allah cut it off by death.

It has been transmitted, from many of the early generations (*al-salaf*), another interpretation: that the parable represents their faith first, then their disbelief afterward. Then the taking away of the light refers to this world, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because they believed, then disbelieved﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 3], and so on. When they believed, faith shone in their hearts, just as the fire shone for those who kindled it. Then when they disbelieved, Allah took away their light: He removed it, just as He took away the brightness of this fire. On this view, the parable is connected to what precedes it. When they were described as having exchanged guidance for error, He presented their guidance, which they sold, as the blazing fire that illuminated what was around the one who kindled it, and their error, which they bought and which was sealed upon their hearts, as Allah's taking away their light and leaving them in darkness.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The Arabs' coining of parables and the scholars' summoning of similitudes and analogies is a matter that is not obscure in bringing out the hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, until He shows you the imagined in the form of the verified, the supposed in the guise of the certain, and the absent as if it were witnessed. In it is also a rebuke to the stubborn opponent and a suppression of the fierce, obstinate one.

For some reason, Allah multiplied His parables in His Clear Book and in all His scriptures, and they spread in the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in the speech of the prophets and the wise. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And these parables We strike for the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

And *al-mathal* (the parable), in the original usage of their speech, means *al-mithl* (the like), which is *al-naẓir* (the equal). It is said: *mithl*, *mathal*, and *mathil*, like *shibh*, *shabah*, and *shabih*. Then the saying that is current, whose referent is compared to its source, was called *mathal*. They did not coin a parable, nor did they regard it as worthy of being circulated and accepted, unless it contained some strangeness in certain respects. For this reason it was preserved and protected from alteration.

For if it were altered, the indication of that strangeness might well be lost. It has been said: the preservation of the parable is only because it is a metaphor (*isti'ara*). It is therefore necessary that it be precisely the very wording of the thing compared to. If alteration occurs, it is no longer a parable, but derived from it and an allusion to it, as in your saying: "In summer you wasted the milk," with the masculine form (*bi-l-tadhkir*).

[p. 56] Some have said: the word *mathal* has been borrowed for a state, or a story, or a description, when it has importance and contains strangeness. It is as if it were said: "Their state is wondrous in its circumstance, like the state of the one who kindled a fire." Likewise His saying: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning: in what We have recounted to you of wonders, the story of the Garden, wondrous in its nature. Then He began to explain its wonders. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest likeness﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], meaning: the description which has importance in greatness and majesty. ﴿Their likeness in the Torah﴾ [al-Fath: 29], meaning: their description and their wondrous condition.

Because the meaning of strangeness is in *mathal*, they said: "So-and-so is a *muthla* in good and evil," and so they derived from it an adjective for something of wondrous importance.

**The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[18] ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind; so they will not return.﴾

"Deaf, dumb, and blind." Al-Samam (deafness) is an affliction that prevents hearing. The term is applied to the loss of the faculty of hearing, because its cause is the blocking of the inner part of the ear canal (al-ṣiṣākh) and the closing of its openings, so that air can hardly enter it, and sound is produced only by its vibration. Al-Bukm (dumbness) is muteness. Al-'Amá (blindness) is the absence of sight in that which is capable of being seen.

They are described with these attributes, despite the soundness of their faculties mentioned above, because they closed their ears against paying heed to the truth, refused to speak it with their tongues, and refused to look and perceive with their eyes. Their faculties were therefore treated as though they had been struck by an affliction, as in his saying:

*They are deaf when they hear good being mentioned about me,*
*but if evil is mentioned about me in their presence, they lend an ear.*

And as in his saying:

*I am deaf to the thing I do not desire,*
*yet I hear every creature of God when I desire to hear.*

"So they will not return," meaning: because of their having these described attributes, they do not return to guidance after having sold it, nor from error after having purchased it. The noble verse thus completes the simile, showing that what has befallen them is not merely the extinguishing of their fire and their remaining in dense, terrifying darkness while their sense of sight remains intact. Rather, all their faculties have been disordered, and they have taken on these attributes, so they remain motionless in their place, unable to return, and not knowing whether they should advance or retreat. And how could they return to the point from which they started?

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 19:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[19] ﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder, and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾

"Or like a rainstorm from the sky" is a simile for their condition following another simile, so that the explanation may cover every minute and grand aspect of it, and fulfil its due of dreadfulness and awe. Their varied forms of disbelief and misguidance deserve that similitudes be coined concerning them. Just as it is incumbent upon the eloquent speaker, in the places of brevity and concision, to be concise and succinct, so it is likewise incumbent upon him, in the places of detail and elaboration, to elaborate and expound.

And *al-sayyib* (the heavy rain-cloud, from *sawb*, "torrent"): the cloud that carries *sawb*, and *sawb* is rain. The intended meaning of *al-sama'* (the sky) is the cloud, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is it you who send it down from the rain-cloud, or are We the sender?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 69]. Originally, *al-sama'* is everything that rises above you, such as a roof and the like.

"In it are darknesses, thunder, and lightning": the tanwin (nunation, the "-un" ending of the nouns) in all of them is for magnification and awe, as if it were said: "In it are thick, pitch-black darknesses, a crashing thunder, and a snatching lightning." "They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts": the *sa'iqah* (thunderbolt) is a violent sound from the thunder, with which there falls a piece of fire that is struck out from the cloud when its bodies collide. It does not reach anything without burning it. "For fear" (*hadhar*, meaning "out of fear"), that is, dread, "of death" from hearing it. "And Allah encompasses the disbelievers": in knowledge and power, so they cannot escape Him.

This clause is parenthetical, drawing attention to the fact that what they did, namely stopping their ears with their fingers, does not avail them anything, for destiny is not warded off by caution, and stratagems do not repel the might of Allah, mighty and majestic. The purpose of placing "the disbelievers" in the position of a pronoun (referring back to the people of the rainstorm) is to signal that what befell them of the great events described is due to their disbelief. Thus the severity of the matter is shown to be deserved by them, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It strikes the tilth of a people who wronged themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117], for destruction arising from wrath is more severe.

The explanation of His words, Exalted is He:

[20] ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it shines for them, they walk in it; but when darkness falls over them, they stand still. And if God willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight. Indeed God is over all things capable.﴾

"The lightning nearly snatches away their sight" is another resumptive statement, coming as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "So how are they with that lightning?" It is said: "It nearly snatches away their sight," meaning: it takes it swiftly. "Whenever it shines for them, they walk in it," meaning: in its light. "But when darkness falls over them, they stand still," meaning: they halt and remain in their place. From this comes "the market stood still" when it became slack and stagnant, and "the water stood," meaning it became solid. This is an illustration of the severity of the matter for the hypocrites, by its severity upon the people of the downpour, and of their extreme bewilderment and ignorance, not knowing what to do or what to leave. When they come upon a flash of lightning, despite fearing that it will snatch away their sight, they seize that flash as an opportunity and take a few small steps. But when it fades and its glare dims, they remain standing, restrained from movement: ﴿And if God willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight﴾, meaning: He could increase the crash of thunder and deafen them, or the brightness of the lightning and blind them. The object of "willed" is omitted, because the answer indicates it. The meaning is: If God willed to take away their hearing and their sight, He would indeed take them away.

The omission of the object of "willed" and "wanted" is very frequent. They rarely state the object except in a remarkable matter, such as the verse: "If I willed to weep blood, I would have wept it," and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If We had wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Ourselves﴾ [al-Anbiya’: 17]. "Indeed God is over all things capable" is a justification of the conditional clause and an affirmation of its content, which expresses His power to remove their faculties, by way of demonstrative reasoning.

Remarks:

The first: The gist of the two illustrations, after describing their possessors as having fallen into the error they exchanged for guidance, is that in the first He likened their confusion and the severity of their situation to the plight of one whose fire has gone out after being kindled in the darkness of night.

In the second, He likened their condition to that of people overtaken by the sky on a night whose darkness is dense, with the piling up of clouds and the gathering of their drops, with terrifying thunder, frightening lightning and destructive, varied thunderbolts repeatedly striking, while they are in the throes of death. Thus it is known that both illustrations are among the compound illustrations, and this is what the grandeur of the meanings requires, because the image of compound forms produces in the soul what the comparison of their individual components does not. For when you picture the state of one whose fire has gone out after being kindled... etc., and the state of those overtaken by the sky... etc., there arises in your soul a wondrous image that leads you to knowledge of the state of the hypocrites, in a way that the comparison of the hypocrite in the first illustration to one kindling a fire, his display of faith as light, and the cessation of his benefit when the fire is gone, falls short of; and the comparison of the religion of Islam in the second to the downpour, and what is connected with it of the doubts of the disbelievers to the darknesses, and what it contains of promise and threat to the thunder and lightning, and what afflicts the disbelievers of terror, calamities and trials from the people of Islam to the thunderbolts. Also, in comparing individual components, the omission of the things compared is an evident artifice. Also, the word "likeness" (mithl) carries a sense of indicating composition, since what is understood from it is a story which, in its strangeness, is like a proverb that circulates, and it is in the compound form, not in each of its individual components. Also, the compound illustration includes a comparison of the components in general, with an added matter: the comparison of form with form, and its indication that the combination of those components entails a wondrous form, truly worthy of being a marvel in its strangeness.

The second remark:

The eminent imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in his book (Ijtima' al-Juyush al-Islamiyya 'ala Ghazw al-Mu'attila wa al-Jahmiyya):

"In this verse, He, glory be to Him, likened His enemies, the hypocrites, to a people who kindled a fire so that it would shine for them and they would benefit from it. When the fire lit up for them, and they saw by its light what benefits and harms them, and saw the path—after having been bewildered and lost—they were like a company of travelers who had strayed from the road, so they kindled a fire to light the way for them. When it lit up for them, and they saw and recognized, those lights went out, and they remained in darknesses, not seeing. The three gates of guidance were closed to them, for guidance enters the servant through three gates: what he hears with his ear, what he sees with his eye, and what he understands with his heart. These have had the gates of guidance closed to them: their hearts hear nothing, do not see it, and do not understand what would benefit them. It was said: since they did not benefit from their hearing, their sight and their hearts, they were placed in the station of one who has no hearing, no sight, and no understanding; and the two statements are mutually implicative.

(p-61) And He said describing them: ﴿So they do not return﴾, because they had seen by the light of the fire and perceived the guidance; when it went out from them they did not return to what they had seen and perceived. And He, Glorified and Exalted, said: ﴿God took away their light﴾, and He did not say: "took away their light" [in the form of the noun], and in this there is a wondrous secret: the severance of the secret of that special companionship—which belongs to the believers—from God, Exalted is He. For God is with the believers, and God is with the patient, and: ﴿Indeed God is with those who are mindful of Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128]. So God's taking away that light is the severing of the companionship with which He distinguished His friends; He cut it off between Himself and the hypocrites, so that nothing remains with them after the going of their light, and nothing is with them; they have no share of His words: ﴿Do not grieve, indeed God is with us﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], (p-62) nor of: ﴿No! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 62].

Reflect on His words: ﴿It lit up what was around it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]: how He made its light separate from it, detached; had its light joined with it and mixed with it, it would not have gone away. But it was a light of proximity, not of close attachment and mixing, and the light was accidental while the darkness was essential; so the light returned to its source, and the darkness remained in its source, and each of the two returned to its proper origin. It is a proof from God established, and a wisdom reaching its goal, by which He made Himself known to the people of understanding among His servants.

Reflect on His words: ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and He did not say "their fire," so as to match the beginning of the verse, for fire contains both illumination and burning: He took away what it contains of illumination, which is light, and left them what it contains of burning, which is its fire-nature. And reflect how He said "their light" and did not say "their radiance," along with His words "when it lit up what was around it"; because radiance is an increase in light. If it were said: "God took away their radiance," it would suggest the taking away of the increase only, not the root; but since light is the root of radiance, taking away light is taking away the thing together with its increase. Also, it is more emphatic in negating them, and that they are of the people of darknesses who have no light. Also, God, Exalted is He, named His Book "light," His Messenger ﷺ "light," His religion "light," His guidance "light," among His names is "the Light," and prayer is "light"; so His taking them away, glory be to Him, is a taking away of all of this.

And reflect on the correspondence of these examples with what preceded, His words: ﴿Those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance, so their commerce did not profit, nor were they guided﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]: how (p-63) it corresponded to this losing trade, which contained the horror of error and contentment with it; and He replaced guidance in its place, and the horror of darknesses—which are error and contentment with it—instead of light—which is guidance and light. So they exchanged guidance and light, and took darkness and error in their place. How wretched such a trade, how ruinous such a bargain!

And reflect on how God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], making it singular, then said: ﴿and left them in darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], making it plural. For the truth is one: it is the straight path of God, to which no path leads except it: His worship alone, with no partner, by what He legislated through His Messenger ﷺ, not by desires, innovations, and the ways of those who deviate from what God sent His Messenger with of guidance and the religion of truth; unlike the ways of falsehood, which are many and branching. For this reason He, glory be to Him, makes the truth singular and gathers falsehood into plurality, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿God is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darknesses into light. And those who disbelieve—their protectors are the Taghut; they bring them out of light into darknesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257]. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the ways, lest they scatter you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. So He gathered the ways of falsehood and made the way of truth singular. This does not contradict His words: ﴿By it God guides whoever follows His pleasure to the ways of peace﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16], for those are the paths of His good pleasure, which are gathered under His one way and His straight path; for all the paths of His pleasure return to one path and one way, and it is His way to which there is no access except through it.

It has been authentically transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ that "he drew a straight line and said: 'This is the way of God.' Then he drew lines to its right and left, and said: 'These are ways; upon each way is a devil calling to it.' Then he recited His words: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the ways, lest they scatter you from His way; that He has enjoined you with, that perhaps you may be mindful﴾ [al-An'am: 153]."

It has also been said: this is a parable for the hypocrites and the fire of sedition they kindle among the people of Islam, and it would be in the position of God's words: ﴿Every time they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]; and His words, "God took away their light," would correspond to His words, "God extinguished it." Their frustration and the nullification of what they sought would be: leaving them in darknesses of bewilderment, not finding the way to free themselves from what they have fallen into, nor seeing a path; rather they are "deaf, dumb, blind." And this interpretation, though true, is questionable as being the intended meaning of the verse, for the context was aimed at something else; and the words "when it lit up what was around it" forbid it, since the kindling of a fire of war never lights what is around it at all; and His words: ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] forbid it, since the hearth of war has no light; and His words: ﴿and left them in darknesses, they do not see﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] forbid it. This implies that they moved from the light of knowledge and insight to the darkness of doubt and disbelief."

(p-65) Al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is the hypocrite who saw and then became blind, who recognized and then denied." Therefore He said: ﴿So they do not return﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18], meaning: they do not return to the light which they abandoned. And He said concerning the disbelievers: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171]. So He removed understanding from the disbelievers, since they were not among the people of insight and faith; and He removed return from the hypocrites, since they believed and then disbelieved, so they did not return to faith.

Section.

Then Allah, glorified is He, set forth for them another parable, related to water, and He said, exalted is He: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky, wherein is darkness, thunder, and lightning; they put their fingers in their ears against the thunderclaps, for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19]. So He likened their share of the light and life that Allah the Exalted sent His Messenger ﷺ with, to the share of one who kindles a fire, which went out from him when he needed it most, and his light departed, and he remained in darkness, bewildered and lost, unable to find the way and not knowing a path. And (He likened) their share to the share of the people of the ṣayyib, which is the rain that is poured down (ṣawwaba), that is, descends from a height to a low place. Thus He likened the guidance with which He guided His servants to the ṣayyib, because hearts are revived by it as the earth is revived by rain. And the share of the hypocrites from this guidance is like the share of one who obtains from the ṣayyib nothing but darkness, thunder, and lightning. He has no share beyond that in what is intended by the ṣayyib, namely the life of the lands, the servants, the trees, and the animals. Those darknesses in it, and that thunder and lightning, are intended for something other than themselves, being a means to the full benefit of that ṣayyib. The ignorant person, through the extremity of his ignorance, confines himself to sensing what is in the ṣayyib of darkness, thunder, and lightning, and the consequences of that, such as intense cold, and the traveller being prevented from his journey, and the craftsman from his craft; and he has no insight that penetrates to what that ṣayyib leads to of life and general benefit. Such is the condition of every person of short sight and weak intellect, whose vision does not pass beyond the apparent disliked matter to what lies behind it of every beloved thing. This is the state of most of creation, except those whose insight is sound. (p-66) So when one of weak insight sees the fatigue, hardships, exposure to the loss of life, severe wounds, the blame of blamers, and enmity from those whom he fears to antagonize in jihad, he does not undertake it, because he has not witnessed the praiseworthy outcomes to which it leads, and the goals toward which the competitors race and in which the rivals compete. Likewise the one who resolves to undertake the pilgrimage to the Sacred House, who knows from that journey only the hardship of travel, leaving family and homeland, enduring hardships, and parting from familiar things, and whose vision and insight do not extend beyond the final end, outcome, and consequence of that journey, does not set out on it and does not resolve upon it. The condition of these is the condition of one weak in insight and faith, who sees in the Qur'an the promise and threat, the admonitions and prohibitions, and the commands that are burdensome upon the souls, which wean them from suckling at the breast of familiar things and desires. Weaning is the hardest and most difficult thing for a child. All people are children of intellect, except one who has reached the level of mature, wise, and discerning men, and has attained the truth in knowledge, action, and recognition. He is the one who looks beyond the ṣayyib and what is in it of thunder, lightning, and thunderclaps, and knows that it is the life of existence.

Third admonition:

Al-Qashani said: "The emphasis in mentioning the group of hypocrites, censuring them, rebuking them, depicting the ugliness of their state, threatening them, distancing them, and disparaging their conduct and customs, is only because of the possibility of their accepting guidance and the removal of their incidental sickness. Perhaps reproach breaks the stalks of their stubbornness, and rebuke uproots the roots of their vices, so that their inner selves become purified and their hearts illumined, and they take the path of truth. Perhaps also the conciliation of the believers, their gentleness toward them, and their sitting together with them stirs their natures, arousing in them some love and longing by which their hearts soften toward the remembrance of Allah, and their souls submit to the command of Allah, so they repent and reform, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper﴾ [an-Nisa': 145] ﴿except those who repent, reform, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those are with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾ [an-Nisa': 146]."

[p. 67]

**On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[21] ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous.﴾

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾: When God mentioned the exalted rank of His noble Book, and people divided into three groups regarding it, the first believing in it and preserving the laws and rulings it contains, the second disbelieving in it and casting it behind their backs through open defiance and opposition, and the third wavering between them through deception and hypocrisy, and given what each group is singled out for, which makes them happy or wretched, brings them favor with God or ruin, He addressed them directly. This is the *iltifat* (shift from third person to second person) mentioned at His saying, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. It is a forceful style of speech that stirs and moves the listener. This is like when you say to your companion, recounting a third person who is involved with you both: "So-and-so, his story is such and such," and you narrate to him what that person did, then you turn your address to the third person and say, "O so-and-so! It is your duty to keep to the praiseworthy way in all your affairs, and to stand firm on the path of rectitude in your going and coming." By turning toward him, you have alerted him to a far greater degree of attention, and you have sought his listening to your guidance with far greater insistence. By shifting from the third person to direct address, you have stirred in his nature what he would not find if you continued using the third person. Such is the artful variation in speech, moving from one category to another, which opens the ears to listen and gladdens souls to accept. The call "O mankind" has been frequent in His Book for its distinct emphatic features and causes of intensity: such as clarifying after ambiguity, choosing the word for distance (*ya*, used for distant address, though the one addressed is near), and emphasizing its meaning with the particle of alerting (*ayyuha*, the vocative particle with "ha" of alerting).

It is known that everything God calls His servants to, whether commands, prohibitions, admonitions, warnings, promises, threats, narratives of the histories of nations that passed before them, and other matters He has made His Book speak of, are great affairs and weighty matters, and meanings that He taught them to awaken to and to incline their hearts and insights toward, while they are heedless of them. Therefore the situation required that they be addressed with the most emphatic and most eloquent form. This was conveyed by al-Zamakhshari.

[p. 68]

The intended meaning of "mankind" is all those who are legally responsible, believer and disbeliever alike. So the demand for worship from believers is a demand for increase in it and steadfastness upon it, while for disbelievers it is a demand to begin it. ﴿Who created you﴾: He has bestowed His favor upon you by bringing you out of non-existence into existence. ﴿And those before you﴾ [He created]. ﴿That you may become righteous﴾: that is, so that you may become righteous (*ka-anna* of purpose), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56], and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He who created death and life to test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Mulk: 2].

In the use of "la'alla" (perhaps / that you may), there is a comparison of His demand, exalted is He, to the hope of one who hopes for something from one whose attainment is easy. For when He placed in the hands of the legally responsible the reins of choice, and demanded obedience from them, and set up for them rational and transmitted proofs calling them to it, and promised and threatened, and showed kindness beyond counting, no excuse remained for the responsible person. His situation, in preferring obedience while being able to disobey, became like that of one who is hoped for by another, in that the other prefers what is hoped for from him while being able to do otherwise. Thus God's demand for worship and piety from His servants takes the place of hope, in what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 22:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿He who made the earth for you a resting place and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to Allah while you know.﴾

"Who made" — created. "For you the earth a resting place (firash)" — a spread-out carpet and a cradle, not rough and rugged. "And the sky a structure (bina')" — binā' is, originally, a verbal noun (maṣdar) used to designate the thing built, whether a house, a dome, or a tent.

Some of the astronomers said regarding the meaning of the verse: that is, like a building in which each part holds the others together. "The sky" is intended as a genus, like "the heavens," and what is meant by it is the wandering planets. He said: So all the heavens (p-69) or the planets are like a building bound together from every direction, firm like the parts of a single body, through the gravitational attraction that preserves their order in their orbits, which is the pull of the sun upon them.

"And sent down from the sky" — that is, the clouds — "water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to Allah" — the prohibition follows from the content of that command, as if it were said: since you are commanded to worship the One whose state is this — singular in these magnificent acts — then do not set up for Him rivals, partners in worship, i.e., equals whom you worship as you worship Him. Rivals (andad) is the plural of nidd, which means an equal, and is used only for an equal who opposes. If it is asked: how is it appropriate to call them rivals when they did not claim that these opposed or contended with Him, but rather they made them intercessors before Him? It is answered: when they drew near to them, glorified them, and named them gods, their state resembled the state of one who believes that they are gods like Him, capable of opposing and contending with Him; so this was said to them by way of mockery. And just as He mocked them with the word "rival," He also condemned them and magnified the enormity of their condition, in that they made many rivals for One for whom it is never proper to have a rival at all.

"And you know" — the disparity between Him and them, and that they do not act as His acts. Compare His saying: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ [al-Rum: 40].
