Or "and you are" people of knowledge and understanding — and the rebuke in this is more emphatic — that is: you are discerning people who recognize, then what you are upon in the matter of your religion, of making idols rivals to Allah, is the utmost ignorance and the extreme feebleness of intellect.

Among what should be noticed in reflecting upon this verse is what al-Zamakhshari said: that He, glorified and exalted, put first among the requirements of His worship and the obligations of the right of thanks to Him: creating them living and capable, first, because that is the precedent of the roots of blessings, its beginning, and the cause of the ability to worship and give thanks and other things. Then He created the earth, which is their place and their dwelling that they cannot do without — it is like the courtyard of a dwelling, its place of movement and its spread. Then He created the sky — which is like a stretched dome and a tent with ropes — over this resting place. Then what He, mighty and majestic, arranged of the likeness of a marriage contract between the one that bears and the one that shades (p-70), by sending down water from it upon it and bringing forth thereby from its belly the likenesses of the offspring produced by animals — of the varieties of fruits — as provision for the children of Adam, so that this would be for them a lesson, and a ladder to contemplation leading to monotheism and acknowledgment, and a blessing that they recognize, so that they respond to it with the obligation of thanks, and reflect on the creation of their own selves, and the creation of what is above them and below them, and that none of these created things is able to bring any one of them into being; so that they become certain, at that point, that these things must have a Creator — unlike them — so that they do not make the created things rivals to Him, while they know that they [do not] have power over the kind of thing He has power over.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Allah is He who made for you the earth a resting place and the sky a canopy, and formed you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. So blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. Its meaning is that He is the Creator, the Provider, the Owner of the abode and its inhabitants, and their Sustainer. By this He deserves to be worshipped alone, and nothing else is to be associated with Him.

When He argued against them with what establishes the oneness of God, confirms it, nullifies association and demolishes it, and taught the way to establish and verify that, and made known to them that whoever associates has defied his intellect and covered over what was bestowed upon him of knowledge and discernment, He followed that with what is the proof for establishing the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and what removes doubt concerning the Qur'an being a miracle, and showed them how they may recognize whether it is from Allah — as he claims — or from himself — as they claim — by guiding them to estimate themselves, and to taste their own natures, for they are the sons of his kind and the people of his skin. Then He, exalted is He, said:

The discussion of the words of His saying, the Exalted:

[23] ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call your witnesses other than Allah, if you are truthful.﴾

"And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down" – that is, of the Qur'an which We have sent down – "upon Our servant" (p-71) Muhammad (ﷺ), [in doubt] that it is from Allah, the Exalted. The expression of their belief concerning him as doubt – although they are certain that it is the speech of humans – is as His saying, the Exalted, "if you are truthful" indicates. Either it is to announce that the utmost that can issue from them – even though they are at the peak of obstinacy and stubbornness – is suspicion regarding his matter (and the certainty mentioned is outside the circle of possibility, just as making it indefinite and introducing it with the word of doubt is to convey that its proper status is weak and of doubtful occurrence). Or it is to draw attention to the fact that their certainty in that matter is in the position of weak doubt, because of the complete clarity of the evidences of inimitability and the utmost strength of those evidences. As for why He did not say, "And if you doubt concerning what We have sent down…" etc., it is because of what has been pointed out earlier of the emphasis on declaring the sanctity of the revelation free from any trace of doubt in it – as His saying, the Exalted, "There is no doubt in it" expresses – and to convey that such doubt, if it occurs, comes from their side and not from His lofty side. Considering their settling in it and its encompassing them does not contradict considering its weakness and scarcity, because what that requires is the continuity of their involvement with it, not its scarcity nor its abundance.

In mentioning him (ﷺ) with the title of servanthood, together with its attribution to the pronoun of majesty, there is honour, exaltation, and an alert to his being specific to Him, Glorious and Exalted, and his submission to His commands, the Exalted – what is not hidden. The imperative in His saying, the Exalted, "then produce a surah," is either by way of challenge and silencing, as in His saying, the Exalted, "then bring it from the west" [al-Baqarah: 258], or by way of accommodation with them according to their own reckoning, since they used to say, "If we willed, we would say the like of this."

And (surah): a portion of the Mighty Qur'an that is distinguished, and its least is three verses; its waw is original, transferred from the "sur" (wall) of a city – because it encloses a portion of the Qur'an that is set apart and enclosed, or contains refined branches of knowledge, the way the walls of a city contain what is within it; or from the surah meaning rank. For the surahs of the Qur'an, although in themselves they are ranks – in terms of excellence and nobility, or in terms of length and brevity – are, in terms of their arrangement with their companions in the Mushaf, stations which the reader ascends little by little. The "min" in His saying, the Exalted, "min mithlihi" is explanatory, related to an omitted element serving as an adjective to "surah," and the pronoun refers to "what We sent down," i.e., a surah of a kind like it in loftiness of rank, sublimity of class, refined composition, wondrous eloquence, and possession of all the qualities of inimitability. It has been said that "min" is extra – according to the view of al-Akhfash – based on His saying, the Exalted, "fa'tu bi-suratin mithlihi" [Yunus: 38] and "bi-'ashri suwarin mithlihi" [Hud: 13].

His saying, the Exalted, "and call your witnesses other than Allah" is guidance for them to rouse a great multitude, so that they may gather in the arena of opposition with their horsemen and their infantry, and cooperate in producing a small amount similar in the attributes of perfection to what was brought in its entirety by one of their own kind. This is like His saying, the Exalted, in Surah Hud: "Or do they say, 'He has invented it'? Say, 'Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful'" [Hud: 13].

"Shuhada'" is the plural of shahid, meaning: the present, or the one who bears witness, or the helper. "Min" denotes the starting point and is related to "ud'u," and the adverbial phrase is stable. The meaning: call, going beyond Allah, the Exalted, for support, whoever is present with you – whoever he may be – or those present in your gatherings and assemblies from your leaders and nobles, whom you turn to in calamities and rely upon in grave matters; or those who bear your testimonies that take place among you – from your trustees who are charged with extracting rights by executing the verdict before the rulers (p-73); or those who stand in your support, in reality or in your claim, from humans and jinn, so that they may help you. His exclusion, glory be to Him and Exalted, from the ruling on calling in the first sense – despite his being included in presence – is to emphasize that the phrase encompasses all besides Him, not to explain His sole possession of the power over what they were charged with; for that would suggest that if they called upon Him, the Exalted, He would respond to them with it. As for the remaining aspects: it is to make explicit from the outset their disavowal of Him, the Exalted, and their being on the edge of hostility and opposition to Him, restricting their support to other than Him. And the turn [to direct address] in "if you are truthful" is to instill awe and cultivate reverence – that is, in your claim that it is from his speech (ﷺ). The implication of the antecedent to the consequent: their truthfulness in that claim requires their capability to bring its like, given their sharing with him (ﷺ) in humanity and in the Arabic language, together with their long practice of sermons and poetry, their frequent exercise of the methods of verse and prose, and their exceptional effort in preserving events and days, especially when they support one another and cooperate. There is no doubt that capability for a thing is among the requirements of bringing it about and the motives for commanding it.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[24] ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared for the disbelievers.﴾

"Fa-in lam taf'alu" (But if you do not): that is, if you do not bring the like of what you were commanded to bring, after exerting your utmost effort in the attempt. "Wa-lan taf'alu" (and you will never do) is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) placed between the two parts of the conditional sentence (al-shartiyyah). It confirms the content of its protasis and emphasizes the obligation to act on its apodosis. It is also a dazzling miracle, because He announced a specific unseen matter, which He taught Him, mighty and majestic is He, and the matter came to pass just as stated. "Fattaqu al-nar" (then fear the Fire) is the answer of the condition. Fearing the Fire is a metonymy (kinayah) for guarding oneself against obstinacy, since through that guarding its causation by obstinacy and its consequence following from it are realized. It is as if it were said: when you are unable to bring the like of it, as is established, then guard yourselves against denying that it was sent down from Allah, glorified is He, for that brings punishment by the Fire. However, the aforementioned metonymy was preferred over this, being based on depicting obstinacy in the form of the Fire, and making being characterized by it identical with being joined to it, in order to exaggerate the magnitude of its affair, to intensify its ugliness, to show complete concern by warning the addressees against it, deterring them from it, and urging them to earnestly pursue what is metaphorically meant. There is in it a wondrous conciseness (ijaz) that is not hidden. The original form was: "If you do not, then its truth has been established for you; and when that is established, your persistence in obstinacy and your abandonment of belief in it becomes a cause of your deserving punishment by the Fire. So guard yourselves against it and fear the Fire." "Allati waquduha al-nasu wa-al-hijaratu" (whose fuel is men and stones) is a qualifier of the Fire, adding to it an increase in terror and horror. May Allah protect us from it by His vast mercy.

"Al-waqud" (fuel) is that with which the fire is kindled and which is raised from the firewood. It is also read with a ḍammah on the waw (wuqud), and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a name for the passive object (maf'ul) for emphasis, as one says: "Fulan fakhr qawmihi" (So-and-so is the pride of his people) and "zayn baladihi" (the adornment of his land).

If it is said: the relative clause of "alladhi" and "allati" must be something known to the addressee, so how did those people know that the Fire of the Hereafter is kindled with men and stones?

I say: it is not impossible that they had previously heard about this from the preceding verses of the Revelation, or from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or from the People of the Book. By "stones" is meant the idols, and by "men" themselves, as stated in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:98], for it explains what we are discussing. The wisdom of their being paired with the stones in the fuel is this: since they believed that their worshipped stones besides Allah were intercessors and witnesses through whom they would seek benefit, and by whose position they would ward off harms from themselves, Allah made them their punishment, joining them with them heated in the Fire of Hell, as an intensification of their suffering and a deep fulfillment of their disgrace. Similar to this is what He does with the hoarders who made their gold and silver a store and a treasure, withholding them and denying the rights due from them, when they will be heated in the Fire of Hell, and their foreheads, their sides and their backs will be branded with them.

"U'iddat lil-kafirin" (prepared for the disbelievers): it was made ready for them and designated as their punishment. The intended meaning is either the category of disbelievers, with the addressees entering among them as a primary entry, or specifically them. The placing of "al-kafirin" in the position of their pronoun serves to censure them, and the ruling is attributed to their disbelief. The sentence is a resumptive clause (mustanafah) confirming the content of what precedes it, clarifying who is meant by "men," and removing the possibility of generality.

(Tanbih) (Note):
This magnificent verse is among the verses that boldly challenged the disbelievers with the noble Revelation. Allah, exalted is He, challenged them in more than one place of it. He said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿Say: Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, that I may follow it, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qasas 28:49]. He said in Surat al-Isra': ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants﴾ [al-Isra' 17:88]. He said in Surat Hud: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful﴾ [Hud 11:13]. He said in Surat Yunus: ﴿And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be invented other than by Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [Yunus 10:37]. ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you should be truthful﴾ [Yunus 10:38]. All these verses are Meccan.

Then He challenged them again in Medina with His saying "And if you are in doubt" through the end of this verse, and they were all unable to meet it. They were the knights of speech and masters of arrangement, and they were granted from eloquence and judgment what was not granted to any other nation, and they were given from sharpness of tongue what was not given to any human being, and from decisive speech what captivates minds. Allah made that natural and innate for them, and in them an instinct and a power by which they produce wonders on the spot, and they lead to every cause through it. They deliver impromptu sermons in the critical moments and in severe addresses, they recite rajaz verse amid spear-thrusting and striking, they praise and they satirize, they plead and they gain access, they raise and they lower, and so they bring lawful magic, and they adorn their descriptions more beautifully than a string of pearls. They deceive minds, they tame difficulties, they dispel grudges, they stir up old enmities, they embolden the coward, they extend the hand of the curly-fingered (generous man), they make the deficient complete and leave the intelligent obscure. Among them is the Bedouin, possessing firm diction, decisive speech, lofty language, a jewel-like nature and a strong disposition. Among them is the townsman, possessing outstanding eloquence, pure words, comprehensive expressions, an easy nature, and mastery of speech that is light in effort, abundant in brilliance, and fine in its margins. Both kinds have, in eloquence, the conclusive argument, the crushing power, the decisive stroke and the sweeping course. They do not doubt that speech is subject to their purpose and eloquence is under their control. They refined its arts, derived its springs, entered every one of its gates, and ascended a lofty edifice to reach its causes. They spoke about the important and the base, they varied in the lean and the fat, they competed in quantity and quality, and they contended in verse and prose. Yet with all this, none of their eloquent men undertook to bring anything equal to it or near to it, and not one of their skilled orators rose up to match even the shortest surah of it. Moreover, they were more numerous than the pebbles of al-Batha' and greater in number than the sands of al-Dahna'. The vein of tribal zeal did not throb in them, despite their being famous for extreme opposition and harm, for casting their whole selves into contention and resistance, and for fighting over their honor with the sword and with precise measures, and for riding every excess they desired. If someone brought them a boast, they brought him boasts; if he struck them with a glory, they struck him with glories. He had presented them the argument first and the sword last, yet they opposed only the sword alone. They did not turn away from opposing the argument except because they knew that the sea had surged and overflowed over the stars, and that the sun had risen and obliterated the light of the stars. By this it becomes clear that in His saying "and you will never do" there is another miracle, for they did not do it, nor were they able to. Whoever among their fools attempted it, such as Musaylimah, exposed his deficiency to all of them.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: They mentioned that 'Amr ibn al-'As visited Musaylimah the Liar before 'Amr embraced Islam. Musaylimah said to him: "What has been revealed to your companion in this period?" 'Amr said to him: "A brief and eloquent surah has been revealed to him." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "By the time, indeed mankind is in loss, except those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised one another to truth and advised one another to patience." Musaylimah thought for a while, then raised his head and said: "Indeed, there has been revealed to me something like it." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "O Wabr, O Wabr! You are only two ears and a chest, and the rest of you is a digging and a scratching." Then he said: "How do you see it, O 'Amr?" 'Amr said to him: "By Allah, you know that I know that you are lying!"

Since the Arabs of that era were unable to do this, anyone else would be even more unable in this matter! More than thirteen hundred years have passed until now, and no eloquent opponent of it has been found except that he became a Muslim or one who submits. This indicates that it is not the speech of humans, but the speech of the Creator of powers and capacities, sent down as confirmation of His Messenger and as verification of what he says. This aspect, I mean its reaching in eloquence and rhetoric a limit beyond human capacity, is by itself sufficient for its inimitability, and other aspects have been joined to it:

(Among them): its announcement of hidden matters which appeared just as it announced.

And (among them): that the hearing never tires of it, however often it is repeated.

And (among them): its gathering of sciences that were not known among the Arabs and non-Arabs.

And (among them): its reporting of past events and the conditions of nations, while he to whom it was revealed (ﷺ) was unlettered, neither writing nor reading, because he was self-sufficient through revelation, and so that the aspect of inimitability would be more fitting for acceptance. By this it is known that the Qur'an is the greatest of miracles, for it is a sign remaining throughout the ages, which every person of insight contemplates at all times with the eye of thought, whereas others among the miracles ended with the end of their time, and nothing of them remains but the report.

Some scholars of the Shi'ah have gone, regarding its inimitability, to: its being overpowering over whoever opposes it, victorious over whoever contends with it, effective in destroying whatever contradicts it, its being influential in the establishment of the community, the continuance of the Shari'ah, the enforcement of judgment, and the permanence of the Word, because of the light, guidance and mercy that Allah placed in it. And his expression is:

The speech of God, exalted is He, is distinguished from other speech by its penetrating power and dominance in guiding creation, by its establishment of an independent nation, and by its preservation of a new law. This is a sufficient sign for recognizing the divine words and the heavenly revelations. Then he said: The summary of the argument is that speech which is presented as a challenge by the one who calls to it, and which is attributed to God, when it manifests a complete effect in guiding receptive and seeking souls and in subduing unbelieving and obstructing nations, produces an independent and growing nation and a new, lasting law. Then there remains no doubt that it is the speech of God sent down from heaven. The power that appears through it is the same power that has appeared from the messengers and prophets since ancient times. To this point God, the Exalted, alluded in His words: ﴿And Allah wills to establish the truth by His words and cut off the roots of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 7]. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who argue about Allah after He has been responded to, their argument is baseless with their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 16]. This sign is found only in the books of God, the Exalted, and every person is able to perceive it and understand it from them, whether he is learned or unlettered, Arab or non-Arab, Eastern or Western. . ! . Who could doubt that the Children of Israel did not emerge from the darkness of ignorance into the light of faith, and from the humiliation of servitude into the honor of independence, except through the Torah? . ? ! And who is unaware that the European nations did not arrive at the worship of God, the Exalted, after the worship of idols, except through the Injil (the Gospel)? . ? ! And who does not know that the great nations, from the farthest borders of the East to the remotest parts of Africa, did not come out of the bonds of paganism and fire-worship to monotheism (tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness) and the worship of God, except through the guidance of the Great Qur'an? And they were not freed from the shackles of corrupt beliefs and evil deeds, and did not reach virtuous morals and sound beliefs, except by the light of this noble Book. . ? ! Then he said: The summary is that this sign, namely the guidance of souls and the establishment of a new religion, by subduing the ancient religions and changing the old customs, is the clear sign that distinguishes the divine words from human compositions! Indeed, the first soul that acknowledged the truth of a messenger's mission and the sincerity of his law, if it had not known this guidance within itself and had not felt in its own essence this state of being overcome, would not have been the first to confirm him, respond to him, follow him, and support him. For love of the inherited ancient religion is firmly rooted in all souls, and fear of changing its pillars and its customs is deeply established in the depths of hearts. Therefore guidance is the most evident sign of the truthfulness of prophethood and messengership, since it is an attribute of the act and is connected with the call, like healing for medicine, knowledge of surfaces for geometry, buying and selling for commerce, and making beds and doors and other things for carpentry. Then he said: If you examine the Glorious Qur'an, you will find that God, the Exalted, argued by this in many places, and He described the Qur'an as a proof, by what He deposited in it of guidance and mercy. And you will not find a single place where He described it as the most eloquent of books and the most expressive of scriptures. Consider His words: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what Moses was given?" Did they not disbelieve in what Moses was given before? They said, "Two sorceries supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ [al-Qasas: 48] ﴿Say, "Then bring a book from Allah that is better guidance than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ [al-Qasas: 49]. Do you think that God, the Exalted, silenced them with His words, "Bring a book from Allah that is more eloquent than these two," or "more expressive than these two"? Likewise, when they criticized the Prophet (ﷺ) for not producing a miracle from himself like the earlier miracles, God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they say, "Why were signs not sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ [al-Ankabut: 50] ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book being recited to them? Indeed in it is mercy and reminder for a people who believe.﴾ [al-Ankabut: 51] So God, the Exalted, made clear the superiority of the Qur'an over all other miracles, and its sufficiency without them, in that it contains reminder and mercy. And He, the Exalted, said at the beginning of this surah: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1] ﴿That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the righteous.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2] He did not say in it "eloquence and rhetoric which all the worlds are unable to match." That is because eloquence and rhetoric are among the hidden, obscure, and subtle attributes, in which tastes differ and opinions and views diverge. But what appeared from the Messenger, peace be upon him, because of the descent of the Qur'an upon him, of knowledge and power to guide nations, to remove the diseases of the people of the world, to establish the divine law, and to bring into being the Islamic nation in defiance of the great nations and in opposition to the great religions, is a manifest and perceptible matter, in which dispute is difficult and with which sophistry is of no use. Who could deny that the great nations, such as the Arabs, the Persians, the Khazars, the Turks, the Indians, the Chinese, and the peoples of Africa, came out of the darkness of polytheism, fire-worship, idolatry, and denial of the prophets, and entered the light of monotheism, the worship of God alone, and faith in His prophets, messengers, and books, by the light of the Clear Book? . . . ! 

—Thus it is in the book "al-Durar al-Bahiyya" by Abu al-Fada'il al-Irani—. It is not hidden that what he mentioned is a sound view, but it is not permissible to negate what is other than it on its account; rather, it is fitting that it be added to it, and that it be at its forefront, and God knows best.

Then, it is among His customs, may He be exalted, in His Book, to mention encouragement together with warning, and to follow good tidings with admonition. This is the meaning of naming the Qur'an "mathani" (oft-repeated verses), according to the most correct view, which is that He mentions faith and follows it with mention of disbelief, or the reverse, or the state of the happy and then the wretched, or the reverse. Its essence is mentioning a thing together with its opposite. The wisdom in this is the desire to stimulate the acquisition of what brings nearness, and to discourage the commission of what destroys. So when He mentioned the disbelievers and their deeds, and threatened them with punishment, He followed it with the good news for His servants who combined belief with righteous deeds, by performing acts of obedience and abstaining from sins. So He, mighty and majestic, said:

(p-81) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a provision of fruit therefrom, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and it is given to them in resemblance. And for them therein are purified spouses, and they will abide therein eternally.﴾

"And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds." Al-bishara (good tidings) is the informing of something that manifests the joy of the one informed. From it comes al-bashara (the skin), for the outer surface of the skin. Tabashir al-subh (the first gleams of dawn) is what appears of the first of its light. As for "So give them tidings of a painful punishment," it is from the reversal in speech that is intended as mockery, increasing the anger, pain and distress of the one mocked. It contains the borrowing of one of two opposites for the other, as sarcasm and derision. "Al-salihat (righteous deeds)" are those actions that are upright, meaning fit for the reward to be bestowed upon them. The predecessors (al-salaf) have agreed that faith is speech and action, it increases and decreases. Then, when it is mentioned absolutely, actions enter into it, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Faith has sixty-some or seventy-some branches; the highest of them is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the lowest of them is removing harm from the road, and modesty is a branch of faith."

When it is conjoined with it, as in this verse, then here it may be said: actions have entered into it, being conjoined as the specific with the general. And it may be said: they have not entered into it, but with conjunction, as in the names "faqir" and "miskin" (p-82). When one of them is mentioned alone it includes the other, and when one is conjoined to the other, they are two categories. This distinction in faith is likewise in the words al-birr (piety), al-taqwa (God-consciousness), and al-ma'ruf (what is known to be good). As for al-ithm (sin), al-'udwan (transgression), and al-munkar (what is disavowed), their indications differ in being mentioned singly or in conjunction, for one who reflects upon the Qur'an.

The hadith of Jibril has made clear that faith has its root in the heart, which is faith in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, as in the Musnad from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart."

The Prophet ﷺ also said in the authentic hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart."

So if faith is in the heart, and the heart has become sound, then it is necessary that the rest of the body become sound; therefore it is the fruit of what is in the heart. For this reason some said: actions are the fruit of faith and its soundness; since they are necessarily tied to the soundness of the heart (p-83), they enter into the name, as the Book and the Sunnah have declared in more than one place. This is what the Imam Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, conveyed.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "that for them are gardens" — the plural of (jannah), which is an orchard of palms and trees, dense and shading with the intertwining of its branches. It is called the abode of reward, though it contains chambers and palaces that cannot be described, because it is the locus of its bliss and the majority of its delights. Its plural with indefiniteness is because it comprises many gardens, in each of which there are degrees and ranks that vary according to the variation of deeds and their doers.

As for His saying, "beneath which rivers flow": it is an attribute of gardens. If by them are meant the trees, the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident; if by them is meant the land containing them, then a possessive must be supposed — i.e., beneath their trees. If by them is meant the whole of the land and trees together, then the beneath-ness is considered in relation to the visible part which validates applying the name "garden" to the whole. The mention of the gardens was accompanied by the mention of the flowing rivers because the most delightful and most honourable of gardens in appearance is that whose trees provide shade and whose rivers run through its midst, and in that is the greatest blessing and the greatest pleasure. The definite article in "al-anhar (the rivers)" is for the genus — as in your saying: "So-and-so has an orchard in which there is flowing water" — or for a specific reference. The indication is to what was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Therein are rivers of water unaltered﴾ [Muhammad: 15], and so on.

"Whenever they are provided with a provision of fruit therefrom" — i.e., they are fed from those gardens "with a provision of fruit, they say, 'This is what we were provided with before'" — i.e., like what we were provided with before this which has been brought to us. So the indication is to what is provided in Paradise, due to the resemblance of its fruits, with the evidence of His saying "and it is given to them" — i.e., the angels and the youths (p-84) bring them the provision of Paradise — "in resemblance," resembling one another in colour and differing in taste, and that is more conducive to joy, more increasing in wonder, more manifest in excellence, and clearer in superiority.

Their repeating this saying and uttering it at every fruit they are provided with is a proof that the matter reaches the utmost perfection in the firmness of resemblance, and that it is what captivates their wonder, calls forth their amazement, and exceeds their delight. If it is asked: how does His saying "and it is given to them in resemblance" fit into the structure of the speech? I say: it is like your saying, "So-and-so is better than so-and-so, and how excellent what he did!" and "He held an opinion, and it was correct." And from it is His saying: ﴿And they make the most honourable of its people abased; and thus do they act﴾ [an-Naml: 34], and what is similar to that of sentences which are inserted in speech as parenthetical confirmation.

"And for them therein are purified spouses" — purified from menstruation and irregular bleeding, and from what is specific to women of filth and defilements; and it is permissible, since the word comes unrestricted, that the purity from the stain of dispositions, bad character, and all their faults and guile be included within it.

His saying, exalted is He, "and they will abide therein eternally" — this is the completion of happiness; for they, along with this bliss, are in a secure station free from death and cessation, so there is no end to it and no termination, but rather in everlasting, perpetual bliss forever. And Allah is the One asked to gather us in their company; indeed He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful.

When, in what preceded, Exalted is He struck two parables for the hypocrites — in His saying: ﴿Their example is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], etc., and His saying: ﴿Or like a rainstorm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19], etc. — along with other parables mentioned before the revelation of this surah, from the Meccan surahs, struck for the polytheists — Exalted is He drew attention to the place of lesson in them and the wisdom in them, and to the misguidance of one who does not appreciate their worth, of one who ignores their secret, who turns away from their light, who stands between himself and being guided by them and taking heed through them. So He, glorified is He, said:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[26] ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it. As for those who have believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieve, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" He causes many to go astray thereby and guides many thereby. And He causes none to go astray except the defiantly disobedient.﴾

"Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it" — that is, He mentions some example. One says "ḍaraba mathalan" (he mentioned an example), and it takes one object. Or it is made to mean "ṣayyara" (made, rendered), in which case it takes two objects.

Abu Ishaq said regarding His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And present to them an example﴾ [al-Kahf: 32]: that is, mention to them. The wording of al-Jawhari: "Allah ḍaraba a mathal" means He described and clarified. In the commentary on Naẓm al-Faṣīḥ: ḍarb al-mathal is presenting it so that one may take heed by it and form in mind what the speaker intends to clarify for the addressee. One says: "al-shay' ḍaraba mathalan," "ḍaraba bihi," "tamaththalahu," and "tamaththala bihi." Then he said: This is the meaning of some people's saying: ḍarb al-mathal is considering a thing by means of something else and representing it by it.

And this "mā" is a nominal, indefinite (ibhāmiyya) "mā," which, when attached to an indefinite noun, makes it vague and adds to it generality and comprehensiveness — like your saying: "give me a book, mā," meaning whatever book it may be. It is as if it were said: "a mathal of whatever kind of examples." So it is an adjective to what precedes it. Or it is a particle (ḥarfiyya) that is redundant, for strengthening and emphasizing the attribution, as in His words, ﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 155]. It is as if it were said: "He is not ashamed to present a true example, or definitively."

"Baʿūḍatan" (a mosquito) is a substitute (badal) for "mathalan." Or both are objects of "yaḍrib" (present), since it includes the meaning of making and rendering. The meaning of the verse: Indeed He, Exalted is He, does not abandon presenting the mosquito as an example, as one who is ashamed to be represented by it because of its lowliness would abandon it. That is, He does not consider it beneath Him to present as an example anything—even if it is as lowly and small as the mosquito—just as He does not disdain to create it, so likewise He does not disdain to present it as an example. Just as He presented as an example the fly and the spider in His words: ﴿O mankind, an example has been presented, so listen to it. Indeed, those you invoke other than Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from it. Weak are the seeker and the sought﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and He said: ﴿The example of those who take other than Allah as allies is like the spider, which takes a house. And indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41], and other examples of the Noble Book. Therefore, what the foolish and the people of obstinacy and disputation found strange and objected to—that lowly things should be made examples—is not a matter warranting objection or astonishment. This is because representation is resorted to only for what it contains of disclosing the meaning, lifting the veil from the intended purpose, and bringing the imagined close to the observed. If the one represented is great, the thing used to represent it is likewise great; and if it is lowly, the thing used to represent it is likewise. So greatness and lowliness in the thing used as an example are only a matter required by the state of the one being represented, which draws it toward itself, and the one presenting the example acts according to that circumstance. Do you not see that when the truth was clear, manifest, and radiant, how it was represented by light and illumination? And when falsehood was contrary to its attribute, how it was represented by darkness? (Recorded by al-Zamakhshari.)

"As for those who have believed" — this begins the detailing of the ruling that follows from presenting the example, after establishing the truthfulness of its issuance from Him, Exalted is He. That is: as for the believers, "they know that it is the truth from their Lord," like all that comes from Him, Exalted is He. "Al-ḥaqq" (the truth) is that which is established and whose denial is not permissible. This is because representation by it is directed according to the matter for which it was struck, and modeled upon what it requires—just as the spider's house was made an example of the deities that the disbelievers made equals to Allah, Exalted is He. They were made lesser than the fly and lower in rank, and the mosquito and what is below it was struck for them as an example, because there is no state more lowly and less than those equals.

So the believers, whose custom is fairness, acting upon justice and equity, and considering matters with the eye of reason—when they hear such a representation, they know that it is the truth, which doubt does not pass by its courtyard, and the correct matter around which error does not roam. "As for those who disbelieve," those whom ignorance has overcome over their intellects and which has covered their insight—so they do not perceive, nor do they apply their minds; or they know that it is the truth, but the love of leadership and the desire for habit and custom do not leave them to be fair—"they say: 'What did Allah intend by this as an example?'" That is: when they hear it, they oppose, are stubborn, judge it to be false, and confront it with denial. There is no concealment in the fact that the representation by a mosquito and by what is lower than it is one whose soundness and correctness are not hidden from anyone who has the least discernment. But the habit of one who is refuted and confounded, who has no remaining hold on proof, nor attachment to any sign or persuasion, is to throw off, out of extreme bewilderment and inability to devise a stratagem, the clear, and deny the straight, relying on obstinacy and sophistry, when he finds nothing else to rely upon.

"He causes many to go astray thereby and guides many thereby" — this is an answer to that false statement and a rejection of it, by explaining that it contains a noble wisdom and a beautiful end: that it is a means to guiding those prepared for guidance and misguiding those immersed in error. He placed misguidance before guidance, although the state of the guided had preceded the state of the misguided in what came before, so that the first thing to strike their ears in the answer is a terrible matter that grieves them and weakens their resolve. This is the secret in singling out this benefit for mention. "And He causes none to go astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient" — that is, by the example or by its being struck — as a completion of the answer and rejoinder, and an increase in specifying those whose misguidance is intended, by explaining their ugly attributes that entail it.

(p-88) The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:

[27] ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth; those are the losers.﴾

"Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification" is an attribute of the defiant (al-fasiqin), given for censure. The "covenant" (al-'ahd) for which they are described as breakers is Allah's injunction to His creation: His command to them to obey Him in what He has commanded, and His prohibition of what He has forbidden them from disobedience to Him, in His Books and through the tongues of His messengers. Their breaking of it is their abandoning of acting upon it. "And sever what Allah has commanded to be joined" is general to every severance that Allah does not approve of, such as severing the ties of kinship, turning away from allying with the believers, distinguishing between the prophets, peace be upon them, and the Books in affirmation, and all else that involves rejecting good or pursuing evil. For it severs the bond between Allah, exalted is He, and the servant, which is the connection that is intended in itself from every joining and separation. "And cause corruption on the earth" by preventing [others] from faith, mocking the truth, and severing the bonds by which the order and welfare of the world are sustained. "Those are the losers" because they have exchanged breaking for fulfilment, severing for joining, corruption for righteousness, and its punishment for its reward.

These attributes described in the verse are the attributes of the disbelievers, which contrast with the attributes of the believers, as Allah, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Ra'd (Al-Ra'd 13:19): ﴿Is he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only those of understanding will remember.﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:20): ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of Allah and do not break the pledge.﴾ (Al-Ra'd 13:21): ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord, and dread an evil reckoning.﴾ — the verses — until He said (Al-Ra'd 13:25): ﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth; for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾

(p-89) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[28] ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then bring you to life again, then to Him you will be returned.﴾

"How can you disbelieve in God" is an iltifat (a shift from speaking about a third party to addressing them directly) to the people previously mentioned. It is based on mentioning their earlier ugly deeds that have been enumerated, because of the increase in anger that calls for addressing them face to face with rebuke and reproach. The interrogative is one of denial, meaning the denial of what has occurred, and its deeming unlikely, and the expression of wonder at it, because they have with them what turns them away from disbelief and calls them to faith. "And you were dead" means bodies without life, consisting of elements, nourishment, drops of semen, and clots of blood, shaped and unshaped. The application of "dead" to those inanimate bodies is either literal, based on the principle that the dead lacks life absolutely, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a dead land﴾ [Qaf 50:11] and ﴿a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:33], or metaphorical (isti'ara, metaphor), following the principle that the application of "dead" to things to which life may apply is because both share the absence of spirit and of sensation. "He gave you life" by creating spirits and breathing them into you. The reason it is connected with the particle fa' (then/so) is that it is directly linked to what precedes it and is not separated from it, unlike the rest. "Then He will cause you to die" when your terms are fulfilled. "Then bring you to life again" by resurrection and rising, for reckoning and recompense. "Then to Him you will be returned" after the gathering, and He will repay you for your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. How wondrous is your disbelief, given your knowledge of this condition of yours!...

If it is said: If they know that they were dead and He gave them life, and then He will cause them to die, they do not know that He will bring them to life and then they will be returned to Him (p-90), so how is what they deny, the final bringing to life and the return, arranged in the same string as what they acknowledge, the first bringing to life and the causing to die?

I say: Enabling them to know both of these, through the proofs He has set up for them, is treated as their knowledge in removing excuse. Especially since the verse contains an indication of what confirms the two, namely that He, Exalted is He, who was able to give them life first, is able to give them life a second time, for the beginning of creation is no easier for Him than its restoration! Or the address is to the People of the Two Books, and the denial of the combining of disbelief with the story that God, Exalted is He, has mentioned, either because it contains clear signs that turn them away from disbelief, or because of great blessings which deserve to be thanked and not denied, or because both are intended together. For what He enumerated are signs, and these, despite being signs, are among the greatest of blessings.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[29] ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth; then He turned to the heaven and made them seven heavens; and He is Knower of all things.﴾

"It is He who created for you all that is on the earth" is a statement of another blessing, ordered after the first, for their creation as living beings capable of existing time after time. This is the creation of what their survival depends upon and by which their livelihood is completed. The meaning of "for you" (lakum) is for your sake and for your benefit. In this is evidence that the original state of created things is permissibility, until there is a proof indicating a transfer from this original state. There is no difference between animals and other things, of what is beneficial without harm. And the emphasis with His saying "all" (jami'an) is stronger in indicating this.

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi said: "istawa ila al-sama'" means irtafa'a (He rose up). Al-Bukhari transmitted it from him in his Sahih, and Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated it in his Tafsir from al-Rabi' ibn Anas. (p-91) Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas and most of the commentators said: "irtafa'a ila al-sama'" (He rose up to the heaven). Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said regarding "thumma istawa ila al-sama'": irtafa'a (He rose up). Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr narrated it in his Sharh al-Muwatta', and al-Dhahabi transmitted it in "Kitab al-'Uluw." Some have used His saying "thumma istawa" as evidence that the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the heaven, and likewise the verse in (Ha Mim al-Sajdah). His saying, the Exalted, in Surah (al-Nazi'at): ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 30] only indicates the lateness of its spreading out, not the creation of its substance, for the creation of the earth and its preparation for what is intended from it preceded the creation of the heaven. Its spreading out is after the creation of the heaven. The "duhw" is spreading, the growing of herbage from it, and other things, which His saying explains: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 31] and it was before that waste and empty. Moreover, "ba'da" comes with the meaning of "ma'a" (with), as in His saying: ﴿Violent, and after that, of doubtful birth﴾ [al-Qalam: 13], i.e., with that; so there is no difficulty. The mention of the earth first here is because it is more indicative, due to its intense closeness and immediacy. ﴿So He made them seven heavens﴾ i.e., He fashioned them, as in another verse: ﴿So He completed them﴾ [Fussilat: 12].

(Note) Some astronomers said: The seven heavens mentioned often in the Qur'an are these seven planets. They were singled out for mention, although the planets are more than that, because they are the largest and greatest of the planets; moreover, the noble Qur'an did not mention them in one place in a restrictive manner, so it does not contradict that they are more than seven.

Some linguists said: The Arabs use the word seven, seventy, and seven hundred for exaggeration (p-92) in multiplicity. Thus the number is not intended. From this is the verse: ﴿seven ears﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261], the verse: ﴿and the sea, with seven seas behind it, replenishing it﴾ [Luqman: 27], and the verse: ﴿seventy times﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80]. And God knows best.

Some astronomers held that the restriction to seven is real, and that what is meant by it is the solar system alone, to the exclusion of anything else. His statement: If it is said that everything that rises above the earth—of the sun, the moon, and the stars—is a heaven, why then did the Exalted specify a number which is seven?

The answer: Without doubt it refers to the solar system, which we now know by knowledge, and the restriction of the number does not indicate the possibility of there being more than seven, because saying so would take the application of the Qur'an to astronomy out of line, since science has established them as seven, just as the Qur'an, in which there is no possibility of addition—because the plural includes all the worlds that have no end—so that it could be said that seven is for exaggeration, like seventy and seven hundred. The number seven cannot be for exaggeration, because it is very few in relation to the worlds that are counted in millions, such as the solar system. The restriction to this number is supported by the verses: ﴿Do you not see how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ [Nuh: 15] ﴿and made the moon in them a light and made the sun a lamp﴾ [Nuh: 16]. So He excluded the sun because it is a center, (p-93) and excluded the moon because it follows the earth, and there remained after that only seven . . . . . !

He said: By this there is now made manifest a clear and evident miracle. For in the age of progress and Arab civilization, when knowledge shone over the earth through the scholars of Islam, astronomers knew of the planets only five—by their Arabic names until today—and they are: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn. They used to interpret them as being the heavens mentioned in the Qur'an. When they could not reconcile seven with five, they added the sun and the moon to complete the number. Yet the Qur'an explicitly states that the seven heavens are other than the sun and the moon. That is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you see; then He istawa upon the Throne and subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. The word "wa-sakhkhara" is evidence separating the enumeration of the sun and the moon from the seven heavens. Therefore, the commentators who did not know the configuration of the heavens did not consider the sun to be counted as a heaven, nor the moon, since they knew that the seven heavens are inhabited, whereas the sun is a burning fire; so they went in their interpretation of the heavens according to those assumptions. When a planet previously unknown was later discovered through the telescope, they called it Uranus, then another planet they named Neptune—the collections of planets became seven. This discovery, which appeared after the Prophet ﷺ by twelve hundred years, indicates the miracle of the Qur'an and the prophethood of the one to whom it was revealed ﷺ.

Then he said: As for the heavens being the seven planets without their satellites, this is not understood from the verse, because the moons which we affirm, and the small stars that are with Mars, must be counted among the seven heavens, since they are above us, and they are in the solar system. In that case, the seven heavens are the collections of the seven planets; that is to say, the system of Saturn—including what is in it, namely itself together with its eight moons—is counted as a heaven, because its orbit is a layer above the orbit of the system of Jupiter. This application is indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and made them missiles against the devils, and prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 5], which points to the fact that the lowest heaven—that is, the heaven next to the earth—is the orbit of Mars; so it and what is around it of the many stars, which are called lamps, are all considered a heaven, and the planet itself is not. . . . ! End.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾ is an interjected concluding remark confirming what came before it—the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them—in this wondrous pattern that contains supreme wisdoms and fitting benefits, for His knowledge, mighty and majestic, of all things requires that He create everything He creates in the most excellent manner.

Since the Exalted mentioned life and death, which are witnessed, as an admonition to the power over what follows them of resurrection, and then indicated that also by the creation of this whole universe in this wondrous order, and concluded that with the attribute of knowledge, He mentioned first the creation of this human species—in which is deposited the attribute of knowledge—by which its excellence appears, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 30:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[30] ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."﴾

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)."﴾ That is: a people, some of whom succeed others, generation after generation. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who has made you successors (khala'if) upon the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 165], and He said (p-95) ﴿and makes you successors (khulafa') of the earth﴾ [al-Naml: 62], and He said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have made from you angels upon the earth succeeding﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], and He said: ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor (khalf)﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]. It is permissible that what is meant is: a successor from among you, since they were the inhabitants of the earth, and Adam and his descendants succeeded them therein. And it is permissible that what is meant is: a successor from Me, since Adam was the khalifah of God on His earth, and likewise every prophet: ﴿Indeed, We have made you a khalifah upon the earth﴾ [Sad: 26]. The purpose of informing the angels of this is that they would ask this question and be answered with what they were answered, so that they would know His wisdom in appointing them as successors before their existence, protecting them from the objection of doubt at the time of their succession. Or the wisdom is: teaching the servants consultation in their affairs before they undertake them, and presenting them to their trustworthy and sincere advisors, although He, by His knowledge and perfect wisdom, is free from need of consultation. Or it is the magnifying of the status of the one appointed and the manifestation of his virtue, by announcing the existence of the inhabitants of His kingdom and mentioning him in the exalted assembly before his creation, and naming him with the title "khalifah."

﴿They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."﴾ This is an expression of wonder that one who causes corruption should be appointed—for the cultivation and reform of the earth—and an inquiry about the wisdom in that. That is: how do You appoint these, when among them are those who cause corruption in the earth and shed blood? (p-96) If what is meant is worship of You, then we exalt You with praise and sanctify You—meaning nothing of that proceeds from us—so why was it not restricted to us...? Then He, exalted is He, answered them: "Indeed, I know that which you do not know," meaning: indeed, I have a wisdom in the creation of the creature that you do not know.

If you say: From where did the angels know that, so that they marveled at it, when it is only unseen? It is answered: They knew it either by special knowledge, or by what they understood from human nature, for He informed them that He would create this kind: ﴿from clay of black mud altered﴾ [al-Hijr: 26]. Or they understood from "khalifah" that it is one who separates people, settling what injustices occur among them, and restraining them from the forbidden and sins.

The scholar Burhan al-Din al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: What is said, that before Adam, peace be upon him, there were creatures on the earth who disobeyed, and the angels analogized the state of Adam, peace be upon him, to them—this is a statement with no basis. Rather, Adam was the first to inhabit it by himself. End.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿we exalt You with praise﴾ means: we declare You free of everything unbefitting Your majesty, while joined with praise of You for what You have bestowed upon us of the various kinds of blessings, among which is Your granting us success in this worship.

His saying: ﴿and sanctify You﴾ means: we describe You with what befits You—of exaltedness and might—and declare You free of what does not befit You. It has been said: the meaning is that we purify our souls of sins for Your sake. As if they were contrasting corruption, the greatest of which is associating partners with God, with glorification; and bloodshed, which is the defiling of the soul with the most hideous crimes, with the purification of the soul from sins. Not as self-praise, nor to display a favor, but as a clarification of the reality.

(p-97) Admonitions

Concerning aspects of benefits from the verse:

The first: The verse indicates that God, in His greatness and majesty, is pleased that His servants ask Him about His wisdom in His action, and about what is hidden from them of His secrets in His creation, especially at times of bewilderment. Asking may be by speech and may be by state, and by turning to God, exalted is He, in seeking the knowledge of the sought matter from its springs, from which His custom, exalted is He, has run that it flows—such as scholarly inquiry, rational reasoning, and divine inspiration.

The second: If among God's secrets and wisdoms there is what is hidden from the angels, then we are more fitting for it to be hidden from us. There is no hope for a human to know all the secrets of creation and its judgments, for he has been given of knowledge only a little... !

The third: God guided the angels in their bewilderment and answered their question by establishing proof—after guidance—toward submission and acceptance. That is because, after He informed them that He knows what they do not know, He taught Adam the names, then presented them to the angels, as will come in its explanation.

The fourth: Consolation of the Prophet ﷺ regarding the denial of people and their disputation about prophethood without evidence, in opposition to what they denied and the falsehood of what they rejected. If the exalted assembly was depicted as disputing, seeking clarification and proof concerning what they did not know, then people are more worthy of being excused, and prophets are more worthy of treating them as God treated the near angels. That is: so upon you, O Muhammad, is to be patient with these deniers, to guide those seeking guidance, and to bring to the people of the call a clear authority. This aspect is what shows the connection of these verses with what precedes them: the discourse is still on the subject of the Book, its being beyond doubt; the Messenger, his conveying the revelation of God and guiding His servants by it; and the people's disagreement concerning it.

(p-98) Among the special features of the Wise Qur'an is the transition from one matter to another that is distinct from it or close to it, while all are within the context of one subject—thus in the tafsir of the Mufti of Egypt.

Since He, glorified and exalted, first clarified to them in general and ambiguous terms that in the khalifah there are virtues hidden from them, so that they would aspire to it, He now displayed to them a portion of it, so that they might witness it openly, and manifest to them the wondrous nature of His creation and wisdom, and that their doubt be entirely removed. So He said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 31:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[31] ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them. Then He presented them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."﴾

"And He taught Adam the names, all of them": either by creating in him a necessary knowledge of them, or by casting them into his heart (ruw', "mind/heart"). Ādam is a Hebrew name derived from adamah, a Hebrew word meaning "earth" or "dust", because he was fashioned from the dust of the earth. Likewise Ḥawwā' (Eve) is a Hebrew word meaning "living", and she was so named because she would become the mother of the living. By "the names" is meant the names of everything. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are these names by which people recognise one another: human, animal, land, plain, sea, mountain, donkey, and similar names of kinds and others. In the Torah there is a confirmation of the verse: namely, that He, may He be exalted, formed from the earth every beast of the field and every bird of the sky, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them, and whatever Adam called every living creature, that was its name. Adam gave names to all the cattle, all the birds of the sky, and all the wild beasts of the earth.

Ibn Jarir said: In these verses there is a lesson for whoever takes heed, a reminder for whoever remembers, and a clarification for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is a witness, concerning what Allah, mighty and majestic, has deposited in this Qur'an of subtle wisdoms whose descriptions tongues cannot encompass. That is because Allah, His praise be exalted, argued in them on behalf of His Prophet ﷺ against those among whom he dwelt, the Jews of the Children of Israel, by informing him of the knowledge of the unseen, which none of His creation had been apprised of except a select few, and which he could not have grasped except through reports and narrations, so that the soundness of his prophethood would be established for them, and they would know that what he brought them was from Him.

Ibn Kathir the Ḥāfiẓ said: This was after their prostration to him. He placed this section before that one because of the connection between this station and their lack of knowledge of the wisdom behind creating the vicegerent when they asked about it. So He, exalted is He, informed them that He knows what they do not know. For this reason Allah mentioned this station after that, to show them the nobility of Adam through the knowledge in which he was preferred over them: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾, that is, He presented the possessors of the names, so the pronoun refers to the named things, implicitly indicated: ﴿and said, "Inform Me of the names of these"﴾, that is, those which I taught Adam. He asked them to inform Him, though He knew their inability to do so, as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of their incapacity to uphold what they had hoped for regarding the matter of the vicegerency, for disposal and management, and the establishment of justice, without understanding the ranks of preparedness and the measures of rights, is almost impossible. ﴿"If you are truthful"﴾, that is: in your claim that you are more deserving of the vicegerency than the one I have appointed, as your statement indicates. Truthfulness, as it applies to speech according to its explicit content, may also apply to it according to what it necessarily entails of information. For the lowest rank of entitlement is to know the names of what is on the earth. When the error of their statement became clear to them, and the slip of their stumbling appeared to them, they turned in repentance to Allah, exalted is He, and this is what the words of His, exalted is He, convey:

"The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:"

[32] ﴿They said, "Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise."﴾

"They said, 'Exalted are You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise'" is a glorification and declaration of God's transcendence by the angels, that anyone should encompass anything of His knowledge except as He wills, and that they should know anything except what Allah the Exalted has taught them. It is also an acknowledgment from them of their inability and deficiency regarding what they were charged with, and that He is the One who knows all the knowables, among which is the readiness of Adam, peace be upon him, for which we are far from being prepared, of the hidden sciences related to the kinds of creatures on earth around which the sphere of the vicegerency of the Wise revolves, who does nothing except what wisdom requires (p-100). Among this is the teaching of Adam, peace be upon him, of what he is capable of receiving of universal sciences and particular knowledge, related to the rulings that apply to what is on the earth, and the establishment of the matter of vicegerency upon it.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[33] ﴿He said, "O Adam, inform them of their names." So when he had informed them of their names, He said, "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing?"﴾

"He said, 'O Adam, inform them'" — that is, teach them — "of their names," which they were unable to know. ﴿So when he had informed them of their names, He said﴾ — mighty and majestic is He — confirming what preceded of the general answer and recalling it: ﴿"Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth"﴾. The mention of what you do not know under the heading of the unseen, attributed to the heavens and the earth, is for the sake of emphasizing the explanation of the comprehensiveness of His all-encompassing knowledge and the extent of its breadth, along with the indication that what appeared of their incapacity and of Adam's knowledge (peace be upon him) is among the matters related to the people of the heavens and the earth. This is a clear proof that what is meant by "what you do not know," in what came before, is what was pointed to there. It is as if it were said: "Did I not tell you that I know in it, of the motives for the caliphate, what you do not know in it? It is this which you have witnessed." And in the verse there is an allusion to rebuking them for leaving what was better, which is that they should have paused, waiting for Him to make it clear to them. ﴿"And I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing"﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿"Did I not tell you"﴾, not to "I know", since it does not fall under the saying. That is: what you make apparent with your tongues, and what you used to hide within yourselves.

(p-101) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[34] ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers.﴾

"And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'" When He had informed them of the names and taught them what they did not know, He commanded them to prostrate to him, in the form of greeting and honoring him, glorifying him, acknowledging his excellence, and apologizing for what they had said about him. This was a great honor from Allah Exalted to Adam, peace be upon him. "They prostrated, except Iblis, who refused," meaning he abstained from prostration. "And he was arrogant," meaning he became proud and said, "I am better than him." The letter sin (in "istakbara") indicates intensification. "And he was among the disbelievers," either in Allah's prior knowledge or he became so.

Points of Caution:

The first: People have various opinions about this prostration. One of them is that it was an honoring of Adam and an act of obedience to Allah, and it was not worship of Adam. It has also been said: the prostration was to Allah, with Adam as a qiblah (direction), or the prostration to Adam was a greeting, or the prostration to Adam was worship by the command of Allah and His obligation upon them. Ibn al-Anbari reported from al-Farra' and a group of imams that the prostration of the angels to Adam was a greeting, not worship; it was a prostration of glorification, submission and greeting, not a prostration of prayer and worship. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya said: The people of knowledge said: the prostration was to Adam by the command and obligation of Allah. And this is the consensus of everyone who hears his words, for Allah Exalted said: "Prostrate to Adam," and He did not say "toward Adam." Every letter has a meaning, and there is a difference between "I prostrated to him" (sajadtu lahu) and "I prostrated toward him" (sajadtu ilayhi). Allah Exalted said: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah who created them﴾ [Fussilat: 37], and ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]. The Muslims agreed that prostration to stones, trees and animals is forbidden. As for the Ka'bah, it is said that the Prophet ﷺ used to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, then he prayed toward the Ka'bah, but one does not say he prayed to Bayt al-Maqdis or to the Ka'bah. The correct view is that humility in the heart and acknowledgment of servitude is never owed in absolute terms except to Allah, the Glorified. As for prostration, it is one of the laws of the sharia and follows the command. So if He, the Glorified, had commanded us to prostrate to one of His creatures, we would have prostrated in obedience and following His command. Therefore the prostration of the angels to Adam was worship of Allah, obedience and a means of drawing near to Him. It was for Adam a distinction, glorification and honor. The prostration of Joseph's brothers to him was a greeting and salutation. It is not reported that Adam prostrated to the angels. Rather, he was not commanded to prostrate except to Allah, Lord of the worlds. In summary, the People of the Sunnah said: it was a prostration of glorification, honor and greeting to him. The Mu'tazila (Mu'tazilites) said: Adam was like a qiblah that they prostrated toward, and they did not prostrate to him. They said this fleeing from the possibility that the noble verse would be a proof against them. The People of the Sunnah said: Iblis was of the angels, and the righteous among mankind are better than the angels, and they argued from the prostration of the angels to Adam. The Mu'tazila disagreed with this and said: the angels are better than humans, and the prostration of the angels to Adam was like a qiblah. What refutes this is what Allah, the Glorified, related about Iblis: ﴿He said, "Have You seen this one whom You have honored above me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely control his descendants, except for a few"﴾ [al-Isra': 62].

The second: They differed about the angels who were commanded to prostrate. It was said: they were those who were with Iblis on the earth. Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya said: this view is not among the views of the Muslims or the Jews or the Christians. It was also said: they were all the angels, including Jibril and Mika'il. This is the view of the majority of the people of knowledge of the Book and the Sunnah. Ibn Taymiyya said: whoever says otherwise has rejected the Qur'an with falsehood and slander, (p-103) because Allah, the Glorified, said: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ [al-Hijr: 30], and this is an emphasis of the generality.

The third: Scholars differ as to whether Iblis was among the angels or not, in two views. One of them is that he was among the angels. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and it was chosen by Shaykh Muwaffaq al-Din, Shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, the imams of the Malikiyya, and Ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Al-Baghawi said: this is the view of most mufassirun (exegetes), because Allah, the Glorified, commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam. He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis﴾. If he were not of the angels, the command to prostrate would not have been directed to him, and if the command to prostrate had not been directed to him he would not have been disobedient, nor would he have deserved disgrace and punishment.

The second view is that he was of the jinn and not of the angels. This was said by Ibn Abbas in one narration, and by al-Hasan and Qatada, and it was chosen by al-Zamakhshari, Abu al-Baqa' al-Ukbari, and al-Kawashi in his tafsir. The basis is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Except Iblis, who was of the jinn and defied the command of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 50]. So he is the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind. Also, he was created from fire, while the angels were created from light. Also, he had descendants, and the angels have no descendants.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: The command was directed to him, though it was specific to the angels, because Iblis was in their company and worshipped Allah in their manner. When they were commanded to prostrate to Adam and to humble themselves before him as an honor to him, the jinni who was with them was more worthy of humbling himself. The first view is the correct one, on which the majority of scholars rely, and al-Baghawi declared it sound. They answered the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], meaning: he was of the angels who are the guardians of Paradise.

(p-104) Ibn al-Qayyim said: The correct view in this matter is a distinction, and the two views are in reality one view. Iblis was with the angels in form but was not of them in substance and origin; his origin was fire, while the origin of the angels was light. So the one who denies that he was of the angels and the one who affirms it do not converge on one locus. Likewise Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya said in al-Fatawa al-Misriyya: It is said that a group of the angels was created from fire. They were called "jinn" because they are hidden from eyes, so Iblis was one of them. The evidence for this is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat: 158], which is their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah. And when Allah removed him from the angels, He gave him descendants.

Al-Sha'bi was asked: Does Iblis have a wife? He said: That is a wedding I did not attend! Then he said: I then recited this verse, and I knew that he would have no descendants except from a wife. So I said: Yes. Others said: He has no descendants or children, and his descendants are his helpers from among the devils.

The fourth: Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾, there are two views. One is that at the time of worship he was a hypocrite. The second is that he was a believer and then disbelieved, and this is the view of the majority. It was said regarding the meaning of the verse: "And he was among the disbelievers" in Allah's knowledge, that is, He knew from eternity that he would disbelieve.
