The view of most is that Iblis was the first disbeliever in Allah. Or it is said: the meaning of the verse is that he became one of those who agreed with him in disbelief after that. People differed as to what cause led Iblis, may Allah curse him, to disbelieve. The Khawarij (Kharijites) said: he disbelieved only by disobeying Allah, and every disobedience is disbelief. This is a false view, refuted by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus of the Ummah (community). Others said: he disbelieved by abandoning prostration to Adam and opposing the command of Allah. Others said: he disbelieved because he opposed a direct oral command from Allah, for Allah addressed the angels and commanded them to prostrate, and opposing a direct oral command is more grievous in ugliness. Most people said: Iblis disbelieved because he refused to prostrate, was arrogant, was stubborn and slandered, (p-105) and believed he was right in his rebellion, and he argued with ﴿I am better than him﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], as will come. So he abandoned prostration to Adam, deeming Allah's command and wisdom foolish. This arrogance was expressed by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his saying: "The one in whose heart there is an atom's weight of arrogance will not enter Paradise." Thus it is reported in the Book of Seeking Refuge (Kitab al-Isti'adhah) by the imam Ibn Muflih al-Hanbali, may Allah have mercy on him.

[p. 106] **The discussion of His words, exalted is He:**

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from it freely wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers."﴾

When God Most High created Adam, peace be upon him, and created his wife for him, and settled them in the Garden, He permitted them to eat from it through His saying "and eat from it freely" (*raghadan*), meaning, eat abundantly. "Wherever" (*haythu*) denotes an indefinite place, meaning: in whatever place of the Garden you wish. He granted them permission to eat from the Garden in a manner of far-reaching ease that removes any cause for complaint, since He did not forbid them any part of the eating or any of the places that contain all kinds of food in the Garden, so that they would have no excuse in partaking of what they were forbidden by His saying: ﴿do not approach this tree﴾, meaning this particular tree among the trees present, that is, do not eat from it. He tied the prohibition to approaching it, as an intensification in forbidding eating and in the obligation to avoid it, because closeness to a thing necessitates familiarity, familiarity leads to affection, and love of a thing blinds and deafens. So one does not see the ugliness of it, nor hears a prohibition, and so falls into it. The cause that leads to evil is forbidden, just as the cause that leads to good is commanded. On this basis is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The eyes commit adultery." Since looking leads to familiarity, familiarity leads to love, and that leads to committing the act, the look became the beginning of adultery. On this basis is His saying: ﴿And do not approach adultery﴾ [al-Isra: 32] and ﴿do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra: 34].

Ibn al-Arabi said: I heard al-Shashi in a session of disputation say: When it is said *lā taqrab* with a fatha on the *rāʾ*, its meaning is "do not engage in the act." When it has a damma on the *rāʾ* (*lā taqrub*), its meaning is "do not come near." Ibn Muflih transmitted this in the *Kitab al-Istiʿadha*. Al-Sayyid Murtada also transmitted the said distinction between them in his commentary on the *Qamus*, from his teacher, the scholar al-Fasi. He said: The masters of verbal forms have stated it explicitly, while the apparent meaning of the *Qamus* is that the two are synonyms, for it says: "He came near to it" (*qaraba minhu*), like *karuma*; and "he came near to it" (*qaribahu*), like *samiʿa*, *qurban* and *qurbanan*; and *qirbanan*: he drew near, so he is *qarib*, for the singular and plural. End.

[p. 107] **A subtle point:**

In the verse of al-Araf it is "*fa-kulā*" (then eat), but here it is with *wāw* (*wa-kulā*). This is because whenever a verb has something coordinated after it, and that verb functions like a condition while mention of the thing functions like a consequence, it is conjoined with *fāʾ* rather than *wāw*, as in His saying: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, freely"﴾ [al-Baqara: 58]. Since the existence of eating from it was dependent on entering it, it was mentioned with *fāʾ*, as if He said: "If you enter it, you will eat from it," so the existence of eating depends on the existence of entering. As for His saying in al-Araf: ﴿Dwell in this town and eat from it﴾ [al-Araf: 161], with *wāw* rather than *fāʾ*, this is because it is from dwelling (*sukna*), which in context involves a long stay, and the existence of eating is not restricted to the existence of entering, since one who enters a garden may eat from it even if he is merely passing through. So when the second was not linked to the first in the manner of consequence to condition, it was conjoined with *wāw*. Having established this, we say: The imperative "*uskun*" may mean "remain in a place you have entered and do not move from it," and it may mean "enter it and dwell in it." In al-Baqara the command came after Adam was already in the Garden, so the intended meaning was remaining, and eating is not dependent on that, so *wāw* was used. In al-Araf it came before he entered the Garden, and the intended meaning was entering, with eating dependent on it, so it came with *fāʾ*.

[p. 108] **A note:**

Neither the Glorious Qur'an nor the authentic Sunnah specifies which tree this was, since there is no need for it. The aim is not to know the identity of that tree, and what is not intended does not need to be explained. His saying "among the wrongdoers" means: among those who wronged themselves by disobedience to God Most High.

Ibn Muflih al-Hanbali said in the *Kitab al-Istiʿadha*: Ibn Hazm said: Taking a command as recommendation (*nadb*) and a prohibition as disapproval (*karaha*) is something jurists and eminent scholars often do, and it is what occurs from the prophets, peace be upon them, and they are not held accountable for it. On this basis Adam ate from the tree. The meaning of His saying "and you will be among the wrongdoers" is: wrongdoers to yourselves. Wrongdoing (*zulm*) in the linguistic sense means placing a thing in other than its proper place, so whoever places a command or prohibition in the place of recommendation or disapproval has placed the thing in other than its proper place. End.

Then he said: Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm said in *al-Milal wa-l-Nihal*: There is no innocence from disobedience greater than the state of one who thinks that no one swears falsely by God. This is exactly what Adam, peace be upon him, did. He ate from the tree which God had forbidden him, forgetting the explicit text of the Qur'an, and interpreting it, intending good, because he estimated that he would gain greater favor with God and become an angel brought near, or remain forever in what he was in. This led him to act contrary to what God had commanded him. It was obligatory for him to take his Lord's command in its outward sense, but he interpreted it and intended good, yet did not hit the mark. Had a scholar among the scholars of the Muslims done this, he would have been rewarded. But when Adam did it and was removed from the Garden to the world, he thereby wronged himself. God Most High named the one who kills by mistake a killer, just as He named the one who kills deliberately, though the one who errs did not intend sin, and He made freeing a slave the expiation for an error, though he did not intend a sin. End.

Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya and a group of later scholars said: The correct view is that Adam, peace be upon him, when the enemy of God swore to him that he was a sincere advisor, and confirmed his speech with various kinds of emphasis, one of which was an oath. The second was the use of a nominal sentence rather than a verbal one. The third was opening it with a particle of emphasis. The fourth was using the emphatic *lam* in the predicate. The fifth was using it as an active participle rather than a verb indicating an event. The sixth was [p. 109] placing the object before the verb it governs. Adam did not think that anyone would swear falsely by God, a perjurious oath (*yamin ghamus*), so he believed him sincere, and that if he ate from it he would not leave the Garden. He judged that although eating involved harm, the benefit of immortality outweighed it, and perhaps he could make up for the harm of the oath afterwards through an apology or repentance, just as you find this interpretation in the soul of every believer who commits a sin. End.

Ibn Muflih said: Adam, peace be upon him, did not leave the Garden except through interpretation. The interpretation of God's text is what removed him, otherwise he did not intend disobedience, opposition, or to be a wrongdoer deserving misery. End.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[36] ﴿So Satan caused them to slip from it, and removed them from that in which they had been, and We said: "Go down, some of you being enemies to others. And for you on earth there is a dwelling-place and provision for a time."﴾

"فَأزَلَّهُما الشَّيْطانُ عَنْها" (So Satan caused them to slip from it): i.e., he took them away from the Garden and distanced them from it. It is said: zalla ʿan martabatihi (he slipped from his rank), and zalla ʿannī dhāka (that departed from me), when it has gone away from you; and zalla min al-shahr kadhā (a certain number of days of the month passed). Ibn Jarir said: fa-azallahumā, with the lam doubled, means istazallahumā (caused them to slip), from your saying zalla al-rajul fī dīnihi (a man slipped in his religion) when he erred in it and made a mistake, arriving at something he should not have come to; and azallahu ghayruhu means that someone else caused him to slip, by bringing about for him what made him slip, in his religion or in his worldly affairs. It has also been read fa-azālahumā with an alif, from tanḥiyah (removal): ﴿fa-akhrajahumā mimmā kānā fīhi﴾ (and removed them from that in which they had been), namely the ease, the blessings and the honour. "وقُلْنا اهْبِطُوا" (And We said: Go down): i.e., descend to the earth. It is addressed to Adam, Eve and Satan, or it is addressed to Adam and Eve specifically, based on His words in the other verse: ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 123). The pronoun is in the plural because the two of them are the origin of mankind, so it is as if they were all of mankind. "بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ" (some of you being enemies to others): mutually hostile, some of you seeking to oppress others. "ولَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ" (And for you on earth there is a dwelling-place): a residence and a place of settling. "ومَتاعٌ" (and provision): enjoyment of life. "إلى حِينٍ" (for a time): i.e., until death.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 37:

(p-110) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[37] ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

"Then Adam received from his Lord words" — he received them by taking them up and accepting them, and by acting upon them once he knew them. Ibn Jarir said: They are the words through which he related, reporting it, that he spoke them, confessing to his Lord and acknowledging his sin, and they are His words: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], and the verse continues. He supplicated with them so that they would be a sign for him and for his descendants of repentance. "And He turned to him" — He returned to him with mercy and acceptance, and overlooked his sin. His words, exalted is He: "Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful" — in the combining of the two names is a promise to the penitent of kindness together with pardon.

The discussion of the Exalted's words:

[38] ﴿We said: "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance—there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."﴾

"We said" to Adam and Eve, "Go down from it" from the Garden, "all of you." Then He mentioned the descendants of Adam and said, "fa-immā" (so when), with the nūn of "in" (the conditional particle) assimilated into the superfluous "mā," "there comes to you from Me guidance" — a Book I will send down to you, and a Messenger I will send to you. "Whoever follows My guidance" — who turns to the guidance and accepts it: ﴿there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ in the Hereafter, by entering the Garden.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[39] ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs — those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾ — with the Book and the Messenger — ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾: they will not die, nor will they leave.

(p-111) Notice: The command to descend was repeated for emphasis and to signal the inevitability of its requirement and its certain realization. Or because the intended meanings differ. The first indicates that their descent was to an abode of trial in which they would be enemies to one another and would not abide forever. The second suggests that they were sent down for obligation (taklif): whoever follows guidance is saved, and whoever strays is destroyed.

Benefits:

The First:

Many scholars held that the Garden from which Adam, peace be upon him, was made to descend was on earth. Some said: it is on the top of a mountain in the East, beneath the equator. They took "descent" to mean moving from one place to another, as in His saying: ﴿Go down to a city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. They argued for this with several points:

The first: If this garden were the abode of reward, it would be the Garden of Eternity; and if Adam had been in the Garden of Eternity, he would not have been deceived by Satan's saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], and the statement ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] would not be valid.

The second: Whoever enters this Garden does not leave it, according to His saying: ﴿and they will never be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48].

(p-112) The third: There is no dispute that God Most High created Adam, peace be upon him, on the earth, and He did not mention in this story that He transported him to the heavens. Had God Most High transported him to the heavens, that would have been more fitting to mention, since his transfer from the earth to the heavens is among the greatest blessings. This indicates that it did not occur, and that requires that the intended Garden is other than the Garden of Eternity.

The fourth: Muslim related in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Sayhan and Jayhan, al-Furat and al-Nil, are each of the rivers of Paradise."

Ibn Muflih said: Most people hold that the Garden in which Adam was made to dwell is the Garden of Eternity, the abode of reward. Then he said: Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyyah said: This is the view of the People of the Sunnah and the Community, and whoever says it is a garden on earth in India or Jeddah, or otherwise, is one of the heretical innovators. The Book and the Sunnah refute this view. The discussion of it has been fully treated in "Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah" and "Hadi al-Arwah ila Bilad al-Afrah."

The Second Benefit: People agree that Satan was the one who undertook the seduction of Adam, but they differed on the manner. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority of scholars said: he seduced them verbally (mushafahah, face to face), and the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], and His saying: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], and his swearing to them: ﴿Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors﴾ [al-A'raf: 21] (p-113). Mushafahah (direct speech) is the apparent meaning of "swearing." Others said: that occurred through whisperings (waswasah), as He said: ﴿So Satan whispered to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. Thus his seduction is his incitement by his whispering and the authority given to him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Satan runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs."

They claimed that Satan did not enter the Garden to Adam after he had been expelled from it. Waswasah linguistically means the soul's inner talk and thoughts, Satan's speech with what has no benefit or good in it, and hidden speech. The apparent meaning of the verses supports the first view.

The Third Benefit:

Satan is not named in the verse, since there is no pressing need to mention his name, as was noted regarding the tree.

When God Most High had first addressed mankind generally and mentioned their origin, He then addressed the Children of Israel specifically, who are the Jews, because they were the most deserving of people to believe in the Prophet ﷺ, since they find him written in their possession in the Torah. The discourse with them has continued (from here to verse number 142). At times He addressed them with gentleness, mentioning the favours bestowed upon them and upon their forefathers; at times with warning; at times by establishing proof and rebuking them for their evil deeds, and mentioning the punishments with which He punished them, as its detail will come. So God Most High said:

(p-114) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[40] ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, [and] I will fulfil your covenant, and fear none but Me.﴾

"O Children of Israel" means: the descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob). God, exalted is He, has stirred them by mentioning their father Israel, as if it were said: "O children of the righteous servant who obeyed God, be like your father, just as you say: 'O son of the noble man, do such-and-such,' and 'O son of the scholar, seek knowledge.'" ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. Ibn Jarir said: His favours which He bestowed upon the Children of Israel were: His choosing from among them the messengers, His sending down the Scriptures to them, and His rescuing them from the affliction and hardship they suffered at the hands of Pharaoh and his people, through to His establishing them in the land, the gushing forth of water from the rock for them, and the provision of manna and quails. So He, majestic is His praise, commanded their descendants that what had preceded from Him to their forefathers should remain in remembrance, and that they should not forget His kindness to their predecessors and fathers, lest there befall them of the vengeance what befell those among them who forgot His blessings and denied them, and rejected His benefactions: ﴿And fulfil My covenant, [and] I will fulfil your covenant, and fear none but Me.﴾ The covenant (al-'ahd) is the compact (al-mithaq), and it was alluded to in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God had already taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains. And God said, "Indeed, I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan God a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 12], to the end of the verse. Thus the covenant of God is His charge to them, as mentioned in the verse. Among it is belief in His messengers, which includes their final one (peace be upon him), because they find him written in their possession in the Torah. And His covenant to them is that if they do that, He will admit them to Paradise. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear none but Me.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: that is, fear Me and be wary of Me, O you who neglect My covenant among the Children of Israel and who deny My messenger, whom I took your covenant to believe in and follow in what I sent down to My prophets, lest I bring upon you of My punishment if you do not repent to Me by following him and acknowledging what I have sent down to him, the like of what I brought upon those who opposed My command and denied My messengers among your predecessors.

"The explanation of His words, exalted is He:

[41] ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it. And do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone.﴾

"And believe in what I have sent down" — i.e., of the Qur'an — "confirming what is with you" — i.e., agreeing with it in monotheism, the description and attributes of Muhammad ﷺ, and some of the laws, [in agreement with] what is with you of the Book — as in al-Tanwir. Ibn Jarir said: He commanded them to affirm the Qur'an, and informed them that in their affirmation of the Qur'an there is an affirmation by them of the Torah, because what is in the Qur'an of the command to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, to confirm him and follow him, is similar to what is in the Gospel and the Torah concerning that. Thus, in their affirmation of what was sent down to Muhammad, there is an affirmation by them of what they have of the Torah, and in their denial of it there is a denial by them of what they have of the Torah. End.

Restricting the revealed book by its being confirmatory of what is with them is to emphasise the obligation of compliance with the command, for their belief in what is with them necessarily requires belief in what confirms it.

Note:

Often the disputants among the People of the Book cite this verse and similar ones, such as the verse: ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101], and the verse: ﴿but [it is] a confirmation of that which was before it﴾ [Yunus: 37], and others, as evidence that their books have not been altered. Yet it has been established by conclusive proofs that a large part of their books has been lost, and that the truth in what remains is mixed with falsehood, and several works have been composed on this subject. Their use of this verse and the like as evidence for what they claim has been refuted: the meaning of the Qur'an's being confirmatory of what is with them is what we mentioned earlier in its explanation. Its essence is that what was sent down to him ﷺ corresponds to what they hold regarding the truth of his prophethood and the soundness of the good tidings about him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when there came to them a messenger from Allah confirming what was with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101], i.e., that he, peace be upon him, came in accordance with what they had concerning him in the Torah and the Gospel, in the sense that all his circumstances agree with the good tidings.

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ — meaning, from among your kind, the People of the Book, after hearing of his mission. The "first" is relative, for the Jews of Medina were the first of the Children of Israel to be addressed with the Qur'an. Or it is an allusion that they should have been the first to believe in it, given their knowledge of it and its description, and because they were the ones who heralded the time of the one to whom revelation was sent, and who sought victory through him over those who disbelieved, and they used to regard his followers as the first of all people. When he was sent, their situation was the reverse, as in His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾ — i.e., do not take in exchange for faith in My signs and affirmation of My messenger, worldly gain and its desires, for it is small and perishing. Thus "exchange" (ishtira') is a metaphor for substitution. ﴿And fear Me alone﴾ — by faith and following the truth, and turning away from the trash of this world."

(p-١١٧)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it].﴾ [43] ﴿And establish prayer (al-Salah), give zakah (almsgiving, al-Zakah), and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43]

﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it].﴾ ﴿And establish prayer, give zakah, and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43] Al-labs (لَبْس) means mixing, and it may entail confusion between the things mixed. The meaning is: do not mix the revealed truth with the falsehood that they invent or that they mention in its interpretation, so that one is confused with the other. His saying "wa-taktumu" (وتَكْتُمُوا, "and conceal") is in the jussive mood (مَجْزُومٌ) and falls under the ruling of the prohibition. The repetition of "al-haqq" (the truth) serves to intensify the reprehensibility of what is forbidden, since by explicitly naming "the truth" [in the second clause] there is something that is not in their hearts. The restriction by His saying "while you know" serves to intensify the reprehensibility of their condition, since the ignorant person may perhaps be excused. His saying "And establish prayer" and what follows is a command to adhere to the sacred laws (al-Shara'i', الشَّرائِع) after faith. That consists of establishing prayer by performing it with its obligatory parts and guarding it, giving the obligatory charity, and bowing (al-Ruku', الرُّكُوع) to God, that is, submitting to His commands by obeying them.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: This is a command from God, Glorified is His praise, to those of the rabbis of the Children of Israel and their hypocrites whom He mentioned, to turn back to Him in repentance, to establish prayer, to give zakah, to enter Islam alongside the Muslims, and to submit to Him through obedience. It is also a prohibition from Him to them against concealing what they knew of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), after His proofs had become manifest to them, after warning and admonition had been given to them, and after He reminded them of His favours bestowed upon them and upon their forefathers, showing them kindness through this and affording them full clarity regarding it. End of quotation.

It has been said regarding His saying "and bow with those who bow" that it is an exhortation to establish prayer in congregation, because in it there is the coming together of souls in intimate communion with God.

(p-١١٧)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it].﴾ [43] ﴿And establish prayer (al-Salah), give zakah (almsgiving, al-Zakah), and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43]

﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood or conceal the truth while you know [it].﴾ ﴿And establish prayer, give zakah, and bow with those who bow.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43] Al-labs (لَبْس) means mixing, and it may entail confusion between the things mixed. It is also a prohibition from Him to them against concealing what they knew of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), after His proofs had become manifest to them, after warning and admonition had been given to them, and after He reminded them of His favours bestowed upon them and upon their forefathers, showing them kindness through this and affording them full clarity regarding it. Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 44:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[44] ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people and forget yourselves, while you recite the Book? Will you not then use your reason?﴾

"Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people" means: that which contains the pleasure of God, whether of speech or of action. The sum of al-Birr (righteousness) is everything in which there is obedience to God, exalted is He. The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for confirmation together with rebuke and wonder at their state. "And forget yourselves" means: you leave them out of righteousness as if they were forgotten. The meaning is that you contradict in your own conduct what you command others to do, turning to something other than it. His saying "while you recite the Book" is a rebuke similar to His saying "while you know," meaning: you recite the Torah, and in it is the threat against treachery, abandoning righteousness, and speech that contradicts action. "Will you not then use your reason?" is a great rebuke, meaning: will you not perceive the ugliness of what you have undertaken, so that its being deemed ugly would restrain you from committing it? It is as if you were deprived of your intellects, because the intellects reject it and repel it.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir al-Dimashqi related in his Tafsir, from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "Indeed I dislike storytelling (al-qasas) because of three verses: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people and forget yourselves﴾; and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2] ﴿It is most hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3]; and His saying, reporting about Shu'ayb: ﴿And I do not intend to differ from you in that which I forbid you. I intend only reform as much as I am able. And my success is not but through God. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back﴾ [Hud: 88]."

And seek help through patience and prayer. [Seeking help] in fulfilling the covenant. "And prayer," the prayer whose secret is the humility of the heart before the Lord, for it is among the greatest aids to steadfastness in the matter.

Ibn Jarir said: That is, seek help in fulfilling My covenant that you pledged to Me in your Book, of obedience to Me, following My command, and abandoning what you desire of leadership and love of this world in favor of what you dislike: submission to My command and following My messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), by being patient in it, and by prayer. Thus the verse is connected to what precedes it, as if they, when commanded with what was hard for them because of its burden, and because of giving up leadership and turning away from wealth, were being treated with this remedy.

And indeed it: the pronoun refers to prayer. Singling out prayer for the pronoun's return is due to its great station and its including many kinds of patience. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to seeking help through both patience and prayer.

Is indeed hard: burdensome and heavy, like His saying: ﴿It is grievous to the polytheists what you call them to﴾ [Ash-Shura: 13], ﴿except for the humble﴾.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[46] ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him.﴾

﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ means they will be gathered to Him on the Day of Resurrection for recompense. And *ẓann* (supposition) here means *yaqīn* (certainty)(p-120), and like it is His saying: ﴿Indeed I assumed that I would encounter my reckoning﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 20].

Ibn Jarīr said: The Arabs sometimes call certainty *ẓann*, just as they call darkness *sudfah* and light *sudfah*, and the one who gives aid *ṣārikh* and the one who seeks aid *ṣārikh*, and similar names by which a thing and its opposite are both called.

The evidence for this from the poetry of the Arabs is more than can be counted.

﴿And that they will return to Him﴾ means after death, so that He will recompense them.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[47] ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾: He repeated the reminder for emphasis, and to connect what follows it of severe threat to it. "And that I preferred you" is conjoined to "My favour," being the conjunction of the specific to the general, for its completeness. That is: I preferred your forefathers "over the worlds," meaning the worlds of their time, by sending down the Book upon them, sending Messengers among them, and making them kings. They are the forefathers who were in the era of Musa, upon him be peace, and after him, before they changed. And the preference of the forefathers is an honour to the descendants.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[48] ﴿And guard against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

"And guard against a Day" means the Day of Resurrection, i.e., its reckoning or its punishment. "No soul will avail" on it "another soul in anything" means no soul will discharge for it any of the rights (owed to God or others). The accusative of "shay'an" (anything) is as a direct object; or it may be "shay'an" of recompense, in which case its accusative is as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq). Its being indefinite (munkar), together with the indefiniteness of "soul," is for generality and total despair. (p-121) ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken﴾: "no compensation" from it, i.e., no ransom (fidyah), "nor will they be helped," i.e., they will not be protected from the punishment of God. The plural is used because the indefinite "soul" denotes many souls, and the verb is given masculine form in view of the meaning of "servants" (ibad) or "humans" (anasi).

(Note) The Mu'tazilah held on to this verse to prove that intercession is not accepted for sinners, because He negated that any soul could discharge for another soul a right it had neglected, whether by an act or an omission, and then negated that an intercessor's intercession be accepted from it; so it is known that it is not accepted for sinners.

The answer: it is specific to the disbelievers. This is supported by the fact that the address is with them, as He said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 48], and as He said concerning the people of the Fire: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100] ﴿nor a close friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 101]. The meaning of the verse is that He, exalted is He, does not accept a ransom or intercession for one who disbelieved in Him, and no one rescues anyone from His punishment, and no one escapes from it.

In al-Intisaf: whoever denies intercession is deserving of not attaining it. As for whoever believes in it and affirms it, namely the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jama'ah), those hope for the mercy of God, and their belief is that it will reach the sinners among the believers, and it has been stored up for them. There is no proof in the verse for those who deny it, because His saying "a Day" (yawman) brought it indefinite, and there is no doubt that the Resurrection has stations, and its day is measured as fifty thousand years. So some of its times are not a time for intercession, and some of them are the promised time, in which is the Praiseworthy Station (al-maqam al-mahmud) of the Master of mankind, upon him be the best of prayers and peace. Many verses have come guiding to the multiplicity of its days and the variation of its times. Among them is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they question one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101], together with His saying: ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27]. (p-122) Thus it is necessary to interpret the two verses as referring to two different days and two distinct times: one of them is a place for acceptance, and the other is not a place for it. Likewise is intercession, and the evidences for its establishment are too numerous to count. May God grant us intercession, and gather us in the company of the People of the Sunnah and the Community.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:

[49] ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who subjected you to terrible torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ is a reminder of the details of what was summarized in His saying, ﴿My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 47], from among the various kinds of blessings. That is: remember the time when We delivered you, meaning your forefathers, for their deliverance is a deliverance for their descendants. By "al-Al" (the people) is meant Pharaoh and his followers, for "al" is applied to the person himself and to his family, followers and supporters (so said al-Qamus).

Then He explained what they were delivered from by His saying, "yasumunakum" (they subjected you to), meaning: they sought for you, "sU'a al-'adhab" (terrible torment), meaning its most grievous and severest form: ﴿slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive﴾, meaning they left them alive. ﴿And in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ The word "bala'" (trial) may be either an ordeal, if "that" refers to the conduct of Pharaoh, or a blessing, if "that" refers to the deliverance. Ibn Jarir said: the Arabs call good "bala'" and evil "bala'" too.

Note: Pharaoh (fir'awn) is a title for whoever ruled Egypt while being a disbeliever, like Kisra for the king of the Persians, Qaysar for the king of the Romans, Tubba' for whoever ruled Yemen while being a disbeliever, al-Najashi for whoever ruled Abyssinia, and Khaqan for the king of the Turks. From his tyranny the verb "tafara'na al-rajul" (the man acted as a Pharaoh) was derived, meaning he transgressed and rebelled.

The reason for Pharaoh's subjecting the Children of Israel to terrible torment, including the slaughter of their sons (as is related in the Tawrat, the Torah), was his fear of their growth and their great increase in number. The land of Egypt had been filled with them, for when Yusuf (peace be upon him) brought his father, his brothers and their families from the land of Canaan to Egypt, he gave them a domain in the land of Egypt, in its best part, as the king of Egypt had commanded. They had a great standing in Egypt because of Yusuf (peace be upon him), so they multiplied and reproduced. When Yusuf (peace be upon him) died, and the king who had made him his vizier was gone, that esteem for the Children of Israel came to an end. Then one of the Pharaonic kings of Egypt came to power, and he saw the multitude of the Israelites and said to his people: "The Children of Israel have become a people more numerous and greater than us. Come, let us devise a plan against them, lest they multiply, for if war breaks out they will join our enemies, fight against us and leave our land." So he appointed over them overseers of forced labour to humiliate them with their burdens. Whenever their servitude intensified, they increased in number and strength, so the Egyptians were troubled by their multitude and feared them. The Egyptians therefore enslaved them unjustly and made their lives bitter through hard labour in clay and brick, in all kinds of tilling of the land, and in every task with which they enslaved them through hardship.

Pharaoh ordered the slaughter of their sons, as Allah, exalted be He, has related. The matter remained in this severe state for them until Allah, glorified be He, delivered them by sending Musa (peace be upon him).

And this is His saying, exalted be His remembrance.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[50] ﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you, and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were watching.﴾

﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ explains the cause of the deliverance and depicts its manner, following the reminder of it and the statement of its magnitude and terror. Within this, He mentions another great blessing, which is the rescue from drowning. That is: remember when We split it (the sea) by your passage through it, or while you were in it, or because of your deliverance. We separated its parts from one another until paths were formed. The *bā'* (the particle "by") in the first sense is for instrumentality (*isti'āna*), like its use in "I wrote with the pen." In the second sense it is for accompaniment (*muṣāḥaba*), like its use in "I leaned my back against the wall." In the third sense it is for causation (*sababiyya*). The first sense (p-124) is weak, since its implication is that the parting of the sea was done by the Children of Israel, whereas what is stated in the revelation is that the sea was split only by the staff of Moses. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and every part was like a great mountain﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 63]. So the instrument of the parting was the staff, not the Children of Israel.

﴿And We saved you﴾ means from drowning, by bringing you out onto the shore. ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾: Pharaoh and his people are intended. He mentioned only "the people of Pharaoh" because it is known that they are more deserving of it than the others. ﴿And you were watching﴾ means: watching that and witnessing it, with no doubt about it, so that this would be more healing to your hearts and more effective in humiliating your enemy.

The story of the drowning of the people of Pharaoh, referred to in this verse, is, as is related, that when God, exalted is He, willed to bring the Children of Israel out of Egypt from the house of servitude, He placed in Pharaoh's mind the idea of releasing them from Egypt, after a severe refusal on his part and after seeing divine signs that nearly brought ruin upon him and his people. He summoned Moses and Aaron and said: "Go out from among my people, you and the Children of Israel, all of you. Go and serve the Lord as you have spoken." When they set out and Pharaoh was informed that the people had fled, his heart turned against them and he said: "What have we done, that we have released them from our service?" He harnessed his chariot, took his people with him, and pursued them. He caught up with them while they were encamped at the Sea of Qulzum, which is well known as the Sea of Suez. When the Children of Israel saw Pharaoh's army behind them, they said: "O Moses, where is what you promised us of victory and triumph? Had we remained in the service of the Egyptians, it would have been better for us than to perish in this wilderness." ﴿Moses said to his people: "Seek help in God and be patient. Indeed the earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance to whom He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the righteous"﴾ [al-A'rāf: 128], and he said: ﴿"It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and see how you will act"﴾ [al-A'rāf: 129]. God revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, that he should strike the sea with his staff, so he struck it and it split, and its bed dried up, and the Children of Israel entered into it. Pharaoh and his soldiers followed them. Moses and his people came out from the other side, and the sea closed over Pharaoh and those with him, and they all drowned. The reference to this story will come in other places in the revelation, and its most detailed account is in Surah al-Shu'arā'.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[51] ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And when We appointed for Moses﴾ meaning: after he had finished confronting the people of Pharaoh and destroying them. "Forty nights" meaning: so that We might give him the Torah at the end of them, that you might act upon it. It has been narrated in the translation of the Torah that God, Exalted is He, said to Moses: "Go up to the mountain and remain there, and I will give you tablets of stone, and the Law and the Commandment which I have written so that you may teach them." So Moses went up to the mountain and remained there forty days and forty nights. "Moses" is a Hebrew word whose meaning is "drawn out of the water." "Then you took the calf" meaning: as a god and an object of worship. "After him" meaning: after his departure for the appointed time. "While you were wrongdoers" meaning: by placing worship in other than its proper place. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "you took," or an parenthetical concluding remark (i'tirāḍ tadhyīlī). That is: you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[52] ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾

"Then We pardoned you" means: We erased your sins. "After that" means: after the taking (of the calf) and the grave wrongdoing. "That you might be grateful" means: so that you would give thanks for the blessing of pardon and persist in obedience after that.

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[53] ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that you might be guided.﴾

﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾ means: combining being a revealed Book and a Criterion that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. That is the Torah. It is like your saying: "I saw the rain-cloud and the lion," meaning a man who combines generosity and boldness. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48], meaning the Book combining being a Criterion, a light and a reminder; or the Torah and the proof that distinguishes between disbelief and faith, through the staff, the hand and other signs; or the Law that distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful. It has been said: the Criterion is the parting of the sea. It has been said: it is the victory that separated him from his enemy, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on the day of the Criterion﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], meaning the day of Badr. "That you might be guided" means: so that you may be guided, by acting upon it, away from error.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[54] ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship], so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you with your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship], so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you with your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ (p-127) This verse explains how the pardon mentioned in the previous verse came about. It is related that when Moses, peace be upon him, returned from the appointed time (mīqāt) and saw what his people had done after him by worshipping the calf, he became angry and threw the two tablets from his hand, and he broke them at the foot of the mountain. Then he burned the calf that they had made. Then he said: "Whoever is of the party of the Lord, let him come to me." So all the sons of Lawi (Levi) gathered to him. He said to them: "This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Let every man of you gird his sword. Pass through the camp from gate to gate and return, and let each man kill his brother, his companion, and his relative." So the sons of Lawi did as Moses commanded them, and on that day there fell from the people about twenty-three thousand men (and in another narration about three thousand men). On the day after that, Moses spoke to the people and said to them: "You have committed a great sin, and now I will go up to the Lord and entreat Him on account of your sin." So Moses went up, pleaded before the Lord, and asked forgiveness for his people. —end of quotation.

Lawi (Levi): the third son born to Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, among his twelve sons. Its meaning in Arabic is "adhering" or "connected."

The Levitical priests (al-Aḥbār al-Lāwiyyūn) are ascribed to him. God, Exalted is He, chose them from among the Children of Israel through the words of Moses, peace be upon him, for the sacred service, and made them among those brought near to Him.

From what we have presented, it is known that His words, Exalted is He, "﴿kill yourselves﴾" are a command to those who did not worship the calf, namely the Levites, that they should kill the worshippers. This is not as some of them understood it, namely that they should kill one another without restriction.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God outright," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ [56] ﴿Then We revived you after your death, that you might give thanks.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55–56]

That is, remember My blessing upon you in raising you up after your being struck senseless (al-sa'q), when you asked to see Me directly, something that cannot be endured by you or by those like you in this worldly abode. Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) have held that those who spoke to Moses this way were the seventy chosen men. This is supported by the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. Then when the quake seized them, he said, "My Lord..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], and the verse continues.

The People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) have erred in their claim that these men saw God, exalted and majestic is He, for Moses the Interlocutor (al-Kalim), upon him be peace, asked for that very thing and was denied it. How then could these seventy attain it? This is the view of Ibn Kathir. I have seen their claim mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj). This is among the places where distortion (tahrif) is definitively established. What indicates this is what is in the thirty-third chapter of the same Book, that He, exalted is He, said to Moses: "You cannot see My face, for no man can see Me and live." Ended.

Jahratan (outright), in its original sense, is the verbal noun of your saying "I recited aloud" (jahartu bi'l-qira'ah). It was borrowed for direct seeing (mu'ayanah) because of the connection between them in clarity and disclosure. However, the first (jahr) applies to things heard, and the second to things seen. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is a kind of seeing, so it is governed by its verb, just as al-qurfusa'  is governed by the verb of sitting. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring either to the subject or to the object.

Ibn Jarir said: The root of al-sa'iqah is every frightening matter that one sees, witnesses, or is struck by, until from its terror and great severity one comes to destruction and ruin, and to the loss of reason and the fading of understanding, or the loss of some bodily faculty. Whether it is a sound, or fire, or an earthquake, or a quaking. (He said:) Among what indicates that one may be struck senseless while still alive and not dead is the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "And Moses fell down unconscious (sa'iqan)," meaning, swooned. From the same root is the verse of Jarir:

*Was al-Farazdaq anything but a monkey, that the thunderbolts struck, so it spun around?*

It is known that Moses, when he was overcome and struck senseless, was not dead, because God, mighty and majestic, reported of him that when he came to, he said: "I have repented to You." Jarir did not liken al-Farazdaq, who was alive, to a dead monkey; rather, the meaning is what we have described.

His saying, exalted is He, "while you were looking on," means: at that thunderbolt. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We revived you after your death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56], al-Raghib al-Isfahani said in his tafsir: *al-ba'th* (raising up) is sending forth the one who is raised from the place where he is. However, its applications differ according to the difference in what it is connected with. It is said: "I raised the camel from its resting place," meaning I roused it; "I urged it on in travel," meaning I stirred it; "God raised the dead," meaning He gave them life; and "the army was dispatched" when they were ordered to march. All of this is one in reality, and it differs only because the forms of the things raised differ. Then he said: Death is taken in its known sense, and it is also taken to mean grievous conditions that run in the manner of death. And His saying, "the thunderbolt seized you," does not necessarily mean that they died. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And Moses fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]? However, the verse admits both meanings, and what actually occurred is to be relied upon only through transmitted report free of such possibilities. Ended.

The second of these meanings is supported by the aforementioned verse of al-A'raf: ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. Then when the quake seized them, he said, "My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me as well."﴾ [al-A'raf: 155] So the quake (al-raj fah) is what is called the thunderbolt here, and revelation explains one part of itself by another, and the basic principle is the harmony of the verses. Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi mentioned that those whom the quake seized were those who asked Moses to see God outright, and the full account of this will come in al-A'raf, God willing.

The verse indicates that asking to see Him, exalted is He, in this world is reprehensible and impermissible. For this reason, whenever God, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the request to see Him, He described it as monstrous. This occurs in several verses, of which this is one. Another is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. They had asked Moses for something greater than that, when they said, "Show us God outright," so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing﴾ [al-Nisa': 153]. Another is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say, "Why are the angels not sent down upon us, or why do we not see our Lord?" They have indeed become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression﴾ [al-Furqan: 21]. These dreadful threats directed at those who seek it in this world show that it is impossible in this world. Just as God, exalted is He, informed us that He is not seen in this world, He, mighty and majestic is He, has also promised, in His true promise, that He will be seen in the Hereafter, in many verses. The sound hadiths have also been transmitted with this meaning in mass-transmission (tawatur), and their indication is decisive (qat'iyyat al-dalalah). It is not befitting for a fair-minded person to cling, in opposition to them, to those theological principles (al-qawa'id al-kalamiyyah) brought by the early Mu'tazilah, who claimed that reason had ruled in their favor.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[55] ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God outright," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾ [56] ﴿Then We revived you after your death, that you might give thanks.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55–56]

That is, remember My blessing upon you in raising you up after your being struck senseless (al-sa'q), when you asked to see Me directly, something that cannot be endured by you or by those like you in this worldly abode. Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) have held that those who spoke to Moses this way were the seventy chosen men. This is supported by the verse of al-A'raf: ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. Then when the quake seized them, he said, "My Lord..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], and the verse continues.

The People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab) have erred in their claim that these men saw God, exalted and majestic is He, for Moses the Interlocutor (al-Kalim), upon him be peace, asked for that very thing and was denied it. How then could these seventy attain it? This is the view of Ibn Kathir. I have seen their claim mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter of the Book of Exodus (Sifr al-Khuruj). This is among the places where distortion (tahrif) is definitively established. What indicates this is what is in the thirty-third chapter of the same Book, that He, exalted is He, said to Moses: "You cannot see My face, for no man can see Me and live." Ended.

Jahratan (outright), in its original sense, is the verbal noun of your saying "I recited aloud" (jahartu bi'l-qira'ah). It was borrowed for direct seeing (mu'ayanah) because of the connection between them in clarity and disclosure. However, the first (jahr) applies to things heard, and the second to things seen. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is a kind of seeing, so it is governed by its verb, just as al-qurfusa'  is governed by the verb of sitting. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring either to the subject or to the object.

Ibn Jarir said: The root of al-sa'iqah is every frightening matter that one sees, witnesses, or is struck by, until from its terror and great severity one comes to destruction and ruin, and to the loss of reason and the fading of understanding, or the loss of some bodily faculty. Whether it is a sound, or fire, or an earthquake, or a quaking. (He said:) Among what indicates that one may be struck senseless while still alive and not dead is the saying of God, mighty and majestic is He: "And Moses fell down unconscious (sa'iqan)," meaning, swooned. From the same root is the verse of Jarir:

*Was al-Farazdaq anything but a monkey, that the thunderbolts struck, so it spun around?*

It is known that Moses, when he was overcome and struck senseless, was not dead, because God, mighty and majestic, reported of him that when he came to, he said: "I have repented to You." Jarir did not liken al-Farazdaq, who was alive, to a dead monkey; rather, the meaning is what we have described.

His saying, exalted is He, "while you were looking on," means: at that thunderbolt. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We revived you after your death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56], al-Raghib al-Isfahani said in his tafsir: *al-ba'th* (raising up) is sending forth the one who is raised from the place where he is. However, its applications differ according to the difference in what it is connected with. It is said: "I raised the camel from its resting place," meaning I roused it; "I urged it on in travel," meaning I stirred it; "God raised the dead," meaning He gave them life; and "the army was dispatched" when they were ordered to march. All of this is one in reality, and it differs only because the forms of the things raised differ. Then he said: Death is taken in its known sense, and it is also taken to mean grievous conditions that run in the manner of death. And His saying, "the thunderbolt seized you," does not necessarily mean that they died. Do you not see His saying: ﴿And Moses fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]? However, the verse admits both meanings, and what actually occurred is to be relied upon only through transmitted report free of such possibilities. Ended.

The second of these meanings is supported by the aforementioned verse of al-A'raf: ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. **The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[57] ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down to you the manna and the quail. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

When Exalted is He mentioned what He had warded off from them of the punishments, He began to remind them also of the blessings He had lavished upon them. Among these is the shading of the clouds over them, for they were shaded by a cloud whenever they journeyed, so that the heat of the sun would not harm them. The detailed account of this matter is mentioned in their Torah, in the ninth chapter of the Book of Numbers. Among the blessings is the sending down of the manna.

It is related in the Torah that when they set out from Elim and came to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai, in the middle of the second month after their departure from Egypt, they murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness and said to them: "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger." So Exalted is He revealed to Moses, peace be upon him: "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you. The people shall go out and gather a certain amount every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in My law or not. And on the sixth day they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily. For the seventh day is a day of rest, a holy assembly, on which they shall not go out to seek anything or to gather."

Then Moses said to them: "The Lord will give you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning until you are satisfied." So it was that in the evening the quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning also the dew lay around the camp. When the dew had covered the face of the earth, there was on the surface of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, as fine as frost on the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said: "What is it?" for they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: "This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat. The Lord has commanded that each one gather according to what is needed for his household, each man according to the number of persons in his tent." So the children of Israel did so, and they gathered some more and some less. Moses said to them: "Let none of you leave any of it until morning." But they did not obey Moses; some of them left part of it until the morning, and it bred worms and became foul. So Moses was angry with them. They gathered it every morning, each one according to his eating, and when the sun grew hot it melted. On the sixth day they were given a double portion of bread, two days' worth, so that every man might remain in his place on the seventh day, as rest and sanctification for Him. When some of the people went out on the seventh day to gather, they found nothing on the ground. The children of Israel named it manna; it was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like wafers made with honey. The children of Israel ate the manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land and reached the borders of the land of Canaan. It is also related in a translation of the Torah that the manna was like the color of pearls. The people would go about, gather it, grind it in mills, pound it in mortars, cook it in pots, and make from it cakes whose taste was like bread kneaded with oil. And whenever the dew descended on the camp at night, the manna descended with it. End of quotation.

This is what concerned the manna. As for the quail, it is also related that a group among those who came out with the children of Israel from Egypt longed for meat; they sat weeping, and the children of Israel agreed with them in craving it. They said: "Who will feed us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we used to eat in Egypt without cost, and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. But now our souls are dried up, and our eyes see nothing but the manna." When Moses heard the people weeping by their clans, and perceived the anger of the Lord against them, he prayed to his Lord and said: "Where am I to get meat to give to this whole people, when they weep before me and say, 'Give us meat to eat'?" Then his Lord revealed to him that he should gather seventy men from the elders and officers of his people, and bring them to the tent of meeting, that they might stand with him. Then his Lord spoke to him and promised to give them meat to eat for a month, until it came out of their nostrils and they loathed it. Moses told the people of this. Then he withdrew to the camp, he and the elders of his people. A wind arose, bringing quail from the sea, and cast them on the camp, a day's journey on every side of the camp, and they flew about at two cubits above the ground. The people rose that whole day and night. On the next day they gathered the quail, the least gathered being ten homers; they spread them out and dried them around the camp. Before the meat was finished among them, the anger of Exalted is He was kindled against the people, and He struck them with a very great plague; that place was called the Graves of Craving, because there they buried the people who had craved. Then they set out from the Graves of Craving and journeyed on to another place. End of quotation.

His saying, Exalted is He, "Eat" is by way of intending speech, meaning: saying to them, or it was said to them, "Eat." His saying "and they did not wrong Us" is a statement diverted from the course of the preceding address, to signal that the offenses of those addressed call for turning away from them and enumerating their ugly deeds in the presence of others, by way of rebuke. It is coordinated with an omitted implied clause, omitted for brevity and to convey that it is a certain matter needing no explicit statement. That is: so they wronged, by excessively complaining and grumbling against their Lord, and by lamenting their dwelling in the wilderness and their separation from Egypt. "And they did not wrong Us by that, but they were wronging themselves," by disobedience, since its harm does not pass beyond them, and by that the punishment with which they were struck became due upon them, as we have mentioned.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verses 58–59:

The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say, 'Hittah' (remission), and We will forgive you your sins and increase the reward of the doers of good."﴾

[59] ﴿But those who wronged changed the word to other than that which had been said to them, so We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the sky because they used to defy.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58–59]

This refers to what befell the Children of Israel when they shrank from jihad and refused to enter the holy land (al-ard al-muqaddasah), the land of Canaan, when they came from the lands of Egypt in the company of Musa, peace be upon him. The term "town" (qaryah) was applied to the aforementioned land because the qaryah is every place where buildings are joined together and which is settled as a dwelling. It applies to cities and other places, as stated in "Kifayat al-Mutahaffiz." Moreover, what is narrated here has been mentioned in Surah al-Ma'idah in His words: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, remember the favor of Allah upon you when He appointed among you prophets and made you kings and gave you what He had not given anyone else among the worlds."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 20] ﴿"O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you and do not turn back on your heels, for you will become losers."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21] ﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed in it are a people of great strength, and we will never enter it until they leave it. But if they leave it, then we will enter."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22] and the verses that follow.

As for His words, "enter the gate prostrating," the commentators' interpretations: the word "gate" may mean the literal gate, that is, the gate of the town into which they were commanded to enter. It may also mean the town itself and not the literal gate, as in His words, "And when We said, 'Enter this town'," where He mentions the town and does not mention the gate. This is permissible in the language. (It is said, "So-and-so entered into the gate of such-and-such," and they do not mean the literal gate, but his being in a matter in which he is involved.)

As for His words, "prostrating," the meaning of prostration may be literal prostration. This may be understood in several ways: as a salutation to that place; or as thanks for it, because it destroyed their tyrannical enemies; or it may be a metaphor for prayer, since the Arabs sometimes call prostration "prayer" (salah), as if they were commanded to pray there. It may also be that the command to prostrate is not literal prostration or prayer, but a command to humble oneself before it, to obey, and to give thanks for its favors. And Allah knows best.

As for His words, "and say, Hittah," it is a deleted predicate (khabar mahdhuf), meaning "our request is hittah." The original form would be the accusative (naṣb), with the meaning, "Remit our sins for us, a remission." It was put in the nominative (raf') so as to convey the sense of permanence.

As for His words, glorified is He: ﴿But those who wronged changed the word to other than that which had been said to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], meaning: they changed His command to them, which was to enter the land as fighters, by refraining from it and discouraging people. For this reason Abu Muslim said: "His words, 'fa-baddala' (so changed), indicate that they did not do what they were commanded, not that they brought something in its place. The proof of this is that the changing of a word (tabdil al-qawl) may be used for opposition. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who were left behind will say when you set out...﴾ [al-Fath: 15] up to His words: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 15], and their changing was nothing but disagreement in action, not in speech. So it is here too. The meaning then is: when they were commanded to enter the land and what was mentioned with it, they did not comply with Allah's command and did not heed it."

The repetition of "those who wronged" serves to heighten the condemnation of their conduct and to indicate that the sending down of the punishment upon them was because of their wrongdoing. The rijz (punishment) is sudden death, as has already been explained.

Al-Raghib said: The specification of His words, "a punishment from the sky," is that punishment is of two kinds. One kind may, in some respects, be warded off, or it is thought that it can be warded off, and this is every punishment at the hand of a human being or from the created things, such as collapse or drowning. The other kind cannot be warded off, nor is it thought that it can be warded off by human strength, such as plague, thunderbolt, and death. This is what is meant by His words, "a punishment from the sky." End of quotation.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[60] "And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. Eat and drink of God's provision, and do not go about in the land causing corruption."

This is a reminder of another blessing which they disbelieved. It is narrated in their Torah that all the community of the Children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sinai by God's command, and they camped at Ruqadin, and there was no water there for them to drink. So they disputed with Moses and said to him: "Give us water to drink. Did you bring us out of Egypt to kill us, our children, and our animals with thirst?" Moses then entreated his Lord for water, and He revealed to him: "Go on ahead of the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel. And take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river. Go to the rock of Horeb and strike it, and water will come out of it for the people to drink." So Moses did this before the elders of Israel. End of quotation.

His words, Exalted Is He, "twelve springs," mean the number of the twelve tribes of Jacob, with a spring for each tribe, which they recognised. Al-Raghib said: Some natural philosophers denied this and considered it unlikely. This denial, although it did not conceive of God's power to change natures and of extraordinary events outside of customary patterns, has abandoned reasoning by its own method. For it is established among them that the magnet attracts iron, that a certain stone repels bees, and that a stone shaves hair, and all of this is among them one of the secrets of nature. If such things are not considered strange by them, it is not impossible that God should create a stone which He makes subservient to drawing water from beneath the earth. End of quotation.

His words, "and do not go about in the land causing corruption" mean: do not walk in the land with corruption and in opposition to Moses' command. Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, what is the benefit of His words "causing corruption," since ʿuluw (transgression, ʿathw) is a kind of corruption? It is answered: Some grammarians have said that this is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl muʾakkida), and they mentioned similar expressions. Some verifiers said: Although ʿuluw (ʿathw) implies corruption, it is not formally coined for it; rather, it is like iʿtidāʾ (aggression), and aggression may occur without being corruption, namely the response to an aggressor with his own act, as in: "So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you" [al-Baqarah: 194]. This aggression is not corruption, but rather, in relation to what it responds to, it is justice. Were it not a recompense, it would be corruption. So God clarified that the forbidden ʿuluw is that intended to be corruption. Corruption is therefore disliked absolutely, and for this reason He said: "And do not cause corruption in the land after its reform" [al-Aʿraf: 56]. And ʿuluw and transgression may take the form of what is righteousness and justice, as has preceded. This is evident. End of quotation.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked for." And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That was because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾

﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food"﴾ Qatadah said: When they tired of their food and remembered the life they had before that, they said this. Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, how did He say, "we will not endure one kind of food," when they had the manna and the quail? It is said that this refers to the sameness of it across different times, as when you say, "So-and-so does one action every day," even if his actions are many, when he follows one method and persists in it. This meaning is more emphatic in denouncing the food, because in their denunciation they did not suffice with saying "we will not endure food," but emphasized it further with "one kind." Or they meant by "one" that which does not vary and does not change. (p-138)

﴿So call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic﴾ The "garlic" (fum) is thūm, according to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "wa-thumiha," and because it is stated explicitly in the Torah in this story. Ibn Jarir mentioned examples of the substitution of the letter thā' with fā' because their articulation points are close, such as their saying for the "athāfī" (the three stones of a cooking pot) "athāthī," and their saying, "they fell into ʿāthūr of evil" and "ʿāfūr of evil," and for "al-maghāfīr" (gum resin) "maghāthīr." "...and its lentils and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange what is lower (adnā)" meaning: lower in rank. The root of dunuww is nearness in place, and it is used metaphorically for baseness, just as distance is used metaphorically for nobility and elevation, so one says "distant in aspiration" (baʿīd al-himma). "For what is better" meaning: in exchange for what is better, that is, higher and more majestic, which is the manna, in which there is the sweetness to which the majority of human natures are attached, and the quail is among the most delicious meats of birds, and in both together there is nourishment by which the body is sustained. There is nothing in what they requested that equals them in pleasure or nourishment. "Go down to a city (miṣran)": thus it is written with tanwīn and with diacritical alif in the 'Uthmanic Mushafs, and it is the recitation (qirāʾa) of the majority, with the ṣarf (declension).

Ibn Jarir said: I do not permit a recitation other than this, because of the consensus of the Mushafs upon it; that is, [the word means] from the cities. That is, descend to it. "For indeed you will have" therein "what you asked for," meaning: indeed what you asked for will be in the cities, not in the deserts. The meaning is that this which you asked for is not a rare matter, rather it is abundant; in whatever land you enter, you will find it. So it is not worth, with its lowliness and its abundance in the cities, that I ask Allah concerning it. When Allah, exalted is He, related Moses's denunciation, peace be upon him, of the Jews for their exchanging what is lower for what is better, after enumerating the blessings, He came with a narration of the evil of their conduct toward the prophets, their disbelief, their transgression, and the stamping of humiliation upon them for this, by way of digression (istiṭrād). So He said: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾. From here until His saying, ﴿Nor shall they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] is an interjection (muʿtarid) within the stories related to the narration of the conditions of the Children of Israel who were in the time of Moses. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿That was because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets﴾, for the killing of the prophets was done by their descendants and offspring.

Al-dhilla, with a kasra, is lowliness, disgrace, and contemptibility; al-dhull, with a ḍamma, is the opposite of might. Al-maskana is a form (maf'ala) from sukūn (stillness), because the miskīn (poor man) is little in movement and rising, due to the poverty he has. Al-miskīn is a form (mif'īl) derived from it, as stated in al-Samīn. (p-139) In "al-dhilla" there is a metaphor by implication (istiʿāra bi'l-kināya), in that it is likened to a dome in comprehensiveness and encompassing, or the humiliation is likened to them by the clinging of mud to a wall in not being separated. This report which Allah, exalted is He, gave is known in all times, for the Jews are the most humiliated of the sects, the most abject in poverty, and the most inclined to make themselves small. No community was ever organized for them, no banner ever fluttered over their heads, and no authority was ever established for them; rather they have always remained subjects under the rod and mounted by every stallion in every age.
