Whoever among them holds a share of wealth, however great its abundance, is clothed in the garments of poverty.

﴿And they returned with anger from Allah﴾: that is, they returned bearing it, meaning it became upon them, or they became deserving of it. From the saying: "Fulān bā'a bi-fulān," meaning he became deserving to be killed in exchange for him. So the bāʾ, under both interpretations, is connected to bāʾū, not for accompaniment (mulābasa), for otherwise it would require considering the thing returned to, and there would be no indication of it in the speech.

﴿That﴾ refers to what preceded of the stamping of humiliation and poverty and returning with a great anger. ﴿Because they﴾ — because ﴿they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾, the dazzling signs that appeared through the hands of Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾, such as Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them both. The killing of prophets among the Children of Israel was apparent, and the killing of no messenger among the messengers is mentioned. This is, and Allah knows best, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed We will surely support Our messengers﴾ [Ghafir: 51] and His saying: ﴿Indeed they would be the supported﴾ [al-Saffat: 172]. Some people said: No one among the messengers was killed; only prophets were killed, or the messengers of messengers. Allah knows best. Thus in al-Ta'wilat.

His saying "without right" (bi-ghayr al-ḥaqq) did not come as a restriction, so that it might be said that the killing of prophets is never with right in any state, because of their infallibility ('iṣma). Rather the intent is to censure this matter upon them and to magnify it, and that it is pure injustice in reality, which their following of desire and love of the world and their excess in disobedience and transgression impelled them to, (p-140) as His saying, exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. That is: disobedience and persistence in aggression drew them to what was mentioned of disbelief and the killing of the prophets, peace be upon them.

It is said: the indication was repeated to show that what befell them is, just as it was due to disbelief and killing, also due to their committing sins and their transgression of the limits of Allah, exalted is He. In accordance with this, the mention of the causes of the descent of punishment upon them is in the utmost fine ordering, for it began first with what they did regarding the right of Allah, exalted is He, which is their disbelief in His signs. Then it was followed by what comes after it in gravity, which is the killing of the prophets. Then by what is among their sins specific to themselves. Then by what is among their sins that transgress upon others, such as aggression. And this is among the subtleties of the style of the revelation.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that the door of repentance is open in general to the Jews and others, and that whoever commits the major sins that necessitate the divine wrath and the stamping of humiliation and poverty, as befell the Jews, if he believes and repents, then he has what the believers have, in this world and the Hereafter. It is the custom of the revelation that whenever a promise or a threat is mentioned, it is followed by its opposite, so that the speech may be complete. Thus it is said:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[62] ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—those will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

That is: indeed, those who believed in what Muhammad (ﷺ) called to, and became among his followers. Al-Alusi said in Fath al-Bayan: "It is as if He, glory be to Him, intended to show that the condition of this Islamic religion, and the condition of those religions before it, all return to one thing: whoever among them believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds deserves the reward that God mentioned. Whoever misses that has missed all good, both the small and the great of the reward." The meaning of faith (iman) here is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained in his words, when Jibril (peace be upon him) asked him about faith: "That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Decree, its good and its evil."

This faith is attributed only to one who has entered the Islamic religion. Whoever does not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) or in the Qur'an is not a believer. Whoever believes in both becomes a Muslim and a believer, and no longer remains a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian. End of quotation.

Al-Raghib said in his tafsir: It has been previously established that faith (iman) is used in two ways. The first is the affirmation of the two testimonies, which secures a person's life and property, rendering them inviolable except by right; after this religion became established, this belongs exclusively to it, as in Islam. The second is the pursuit of certainty regarding what a person undertakes in matters of his religion. So His words, "Indeed, those who believed," refer to those who adhere to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), and His words, "whoever believes in God," refer to the one who seeks certain conviction in belief; the latter is other than the former. Since the most prominent religions are these four, God, exalted is He, made clear that everyone who adhered to one of these religions in its time of legislation, and before it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation), and who sought certain belief in it, and followed his belief with righteous deeds, then "no fear will there be for them, nor will they grieve."

Then he said: As for the statement of Ibn Abbas, that this verse is abrogated by His words, "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him" (Al 'Imran: 85), they mean that all these religions were abrogated by the religion of Islam, and that God, mighty and majestic, had granted them the reward before the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him). But in his time, all religions were abrogated by his religion. End of quotation. That is, the intention of Ibn Abbas, and of whoever agrees with him, is not that God had promised the Jews, and those mentioned with them, who did righteous deeds, Paradise in the Hereafter for their deeds, and then abrogated that with the verse, "And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him" (Al 'Imran: 85). Rather, their meaning is what al-Raghib mentioned, and there is no doubt about this. For this reason Ibn Jarir said: The apparent meaning of the revelation indicates that God did not single out some of His creatures over others for the reward for righteous deeds together with faith, and the predicate of His words, "whoever believes in God and the Last Day," applies to all that was mentioned at the beginning of the verse.

Note:
The apparent meaning of this verse, together with al-Raghib's interpretation of "whoever believes" as one who seeks certain conviction, is something by which al-Anbari may argue for his school of thought. The jurists (usuliyyun) mentioned in the chapter on ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) and taqlid (following authority) that al-Anbari held that every mujtahid is correct, even in the fundamentals of belief, and al-Jahiz agreed with him. Al-Ghazali said in al-Mustasfa: Al-Jahiz held that one who opposes the religion of Islam, among the Jews, Christians, and the materialists (al-dahriyya), if he is obstinate in opposition to his conviction, then he is sinful; but if he examines and is unable to reach the truth, then he is excused and not sinful; and if he does not examine, because he does not know the obligation to examine, then he is also excused. Only the sinful one who is punished is the obstinate one, because God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Such people have been unable to reach the truth and have held to their beliefs out of fear of God, since the path of knowledge was closed to them. Al-Ghazali then refuted him with necessary textual evidence, such as our necessary knowledge that He commanded the Jews and Christians to believe in him and rebuked them for persisting in their beliefs, and that is not limited to the Book and the Sunnah.

Then al-Ghazali said: As for his statement (i.e., al-Jahiz's), "How can He burden them with what they cannot bear?" we say: we know necessarily that He did burden them. As for whether they can bear it or cannot, let us examine it. Rather, God, exalted is He, has alerted them that He has empowered them to do it by giving them intellect, establishing proofs, and sending messengers supported by miracles, who alerted their minds and stirred their motives to reflect, until no argument remained for anyone against God after the messengers. End of quotation.

And His words, "and those who were Jews" (alladhina hadu): that is, they became Jews. It is said: "hada yahudu" and "tahawwada," when one enters Judaism. He is "ha'id," and the plural is "hud." They are the nation of Musa (peace be upon him). This name became attached to them because the Israelites who returned from seventy years of exile and from the captivity of Babylon to their ancient homeland were mostly descended from Yahudha ibn Ya'qub (Judah son of Jacob), with the dhal (ذ) pronounced as a voiced consonant, which the Arabs changed to the unpointed dal (د).

And His words, "and the Christians" (al-nasara) is the plural of nasran, like nadama is the plural of nadman. It is said: a man is "nasran," and a woman is "nasraniyya," and the "ya" in "nasrani" is for emphasis, as in "ahmari." They were named so because they supported (nasaru) the Messiah (peace be upon him), as in al-Kashshaf. Or it is the plural of nasrani, altered from naseri, in reference to Nasira, the well-known village, to which the Messiah (peace be upon him) was attributed because he was raised there. In the Gospel it came, "Jesus the Nazarene" (Yasu' al-Nasiri).

And His words, "and the Sabians" (al-sabi'in) is the plural of sabi', and they are also called al-sabi'a. Ibn Jarir said: The sabi' is one who innovates a religion other than his own, like an apostate from the people of Islam from his religion. Every person who departs from a religion he was on to another is called "sabi'" by the Arabs. From this it is said: "sabá fulan yasbu sibaan" (so-and-so turned away), and it is said: "sabat al-nujum" (the stars rose) when they appeared.

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have differed about who bears this name among the religious communities. Some of them said: this name applies to every person who leaves one religion for another religion. They said: the one God meant by this name is a people with no religion. Regarding Mujahid: The Sabians are neither Jews nor Christians, and they have no religion. Regarding Ibn Zayd: The Sabians are a religion among the religions that existed in the island of Mosul; they say "there is no god but God," and they have no deed, no book, and no prophet. Regarding Qatada: They are a people who worship the angels. End of quotation.

Al-Imam al-Shahrastani said, in speaking about the Sabians, something of this sort: "Al-sabwa" is the opposite of hanifiyya. In linguistic usage, "sabá al-rajul" means a man inclined and deviated. So, because these people inclined away from the paths of truth and deviated from the way of the prophets, they were called "al-Sabi'a." They say: "al-sabwa" is the release from the bond of men. The basis of their doctrine is devotion to the spiritual beings (al-ruhaniyyin), just as the basis of the doctrine of the hanifs is devotion to corporeal humans. The Sabians claim that their doctrine is acquired (iktisab), and the hanifs claim that their doctrine is innate nature (fitra). So the call of the Sabians is to acquisition, and the call of the hanifs is to innate nature. The Sabians are a people who hold to rational limits and rulings, and they do not hold to the Law (shari'a) or Islam. Thus they stand in opposition to the adherents of the religions, as complete contraries. The first Sabians were those who spoke of Agathodaemon (Aghadhimun) and Hermes (Hirmis), who are Seth (Shith) and Idris, and they did not speak of any other prophets. They are the masters of the spiritual realities (al-ruhaniyyat). They believe that the world has a wise Maker, sanctified above the attributes of created things. What is obligatory upon us is to recognize our incapacity to reach His majesty, and one draws near to Him only through the intermediaries who are close to Him, namely the spiritual beings who are purified, sanctified in substance, action, and state. As for their substance, they are sanctified from corporeal matter, created in purity, and formed in sanctification and glorification; they do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. They said: so we draw near to them and rely upon them; among them are our lords (arbab), our gods, and our intercessors with God, and He is the Lord of lords.

As for their action, they said: the spiritual beings are the intermediary causes in originating and directing affairs from one state to another; they draw their power from the Divine Presence, and they pour out the overflow upon the lower existents. Among them are the governors of the seven wandering stars in their spheres, and these are their bodies. Every spiritual being has a body, and every body has a sphere, and the relation of the spiritual being to that body which is specific to it is the relation of the soul to the body; so it is its lord and its governor. They used to call the bodies "lords," and sometimes they called them "fathers," and the elements "mothers." So the action of the spiritual beings is to move them in a specific measure, so that from their movements affections arise in the natures and elements, and from that arise compositions and mixtures in compounds; then physical powers follow, and spiritual souls are mounted upon them, such as the varieties of plants and the varieties of animals. Then the effects may be universal, issuing from a universal spiritual being, and they may be particular, issuing from a particular spiritual being. So with the genus of rain there is an angel, and with every drop there is an angel. Among them are the governors of the upper phenomena that appear in the air, of what rises from the earth and descends, such as rains, snow, hail, and winds, and of what descends from the sky, such as thunderbolts and meteors; and of what occurs in the air of thunder, lightning, clouds, mist, the rainbow, comets, the halo, and the Milky Way; and of what occurs on the earth of earthquakes, waters, and vapours, and so on.

They said: As for the state, the states of the spiritual beings are of spirit, fragrance, blessing, delight, and joy in the presence of the Lord of lords—how could it be hidden?

This is a summary of what the scholar al-Shahrastani conveyed in his book al-Milal wa'l-Nihal. Then he related debates and dialogues between the Sabians and the hanifs, which took place concerning the preference between the purely spiritual and the prophetic human; he presented them in the form of question and answer. Let it be consulted there.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya said in his book "Against the Logicians": Harran was the abode of these Sabians, and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was born there (or he moved to it from Iraq, according to the two opinions). In it was the temple of the First Connection, the temple of the First Intellect, the temple of the Universal Soul, the temple of Saturn, the temple of Jupiter, the temple of Mars, the temple of the Sun. Likewise Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. This was their religion before Christianity appeared among them. Then Christianity appeared among them alongside the persistence of those polytheist Sabians, until Islam came; and the Sabians and philosophers remained there under the rule of Islam until the last time, and among them were the Sabians who were in Baghdad and elsewhere, physicians and scribes, and some of them did not become Muslim. Likewise was the religion of the people of Damascus and elsewhere before Christianity appeared. They used to pray toward the North Pole. Beneath the Mosque of Damascus there is a great shrine that has a qibla toward the North Pole, which belonged to these people.

The Sabians are of two kinds: Sabian hanifs who are monotheists, and Sabian polytheists. The first are those whom God praised in this verse. So He praised whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, from these four communities: the believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians. These were following the Torah before its abrogation and alteration, and likewise those who followed the Gospel before its abrogation and alteration.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (*Mahasin al-Ta'wil*) on surah 2, verse 62 (part 2 of 2):

And the Sabians (al-Sabi'un), who came before these, are like those who followed the religion (millah) of Ibrahim (Abraham), the leader of the ḥunafā' (the upright monotheists), before the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel. This is unlike the Magians (al-Majus) and the polytheists (al-mushrikun), for there is no believer among them. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associated partners with God, indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, God is over all things a witness.﴾ [al-Hajj: 17]. So He mentioned these six religions, and informed that He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. He did not mention among the six who was a believer; rather, He mentioned that only regarding the four. Then the Sabians innovated association (shirk), so they became polytheists, and the polytheist philosophers are among these polytheists.

As for the early philosophers who worshipped God alone, not associating anything with Him, who believed that God originated this world, and who affirmed the resurrection of the bodies (ma'ad al-abdan), those are among the ḥunafā' Sabians whom God praised. Then the polytheist Sabians used to affirm the origination of this world, just as the polytheist Arabs used to affirm its origination. Likewise the polytheists of India. The heresiographers (ahl al-maqalat) have mentioned that the first to articulate the belief in its eternity (qidam) among these polytheist philosophers was Aristotle (Aristu). End.

What Imam Ibn Taymiyya established supports what many exegetes (mufassirun) held: that the meaning of His words, exalted is He, "whoever believed" refers to whoever among them was upon his religion before it was abrogated (nash), truly believing in his heart in the Origin and the Return, acting according to the requirements of his law (shar'), such as the People of the Two Books, or whoever was among the monotheistic Sabians. Others held that the meaning of "whoever believed" is whoever, from these groups, newly adopted sincere faith in what was mentioned. They said: because the context (maqam) calls for encouragement toward the religion of Islam. As for explaining the condition of those who followed another religion before its abrogation, it has no connection to the context, and the Sabians have no religion that may be observed at any time. So let this be considered.

His words, exalted is He, "then they will have their reward" means: that which He promised them for those deeds conditioned upon faith. It is, originally, the wage of a worker for his work. His words "with their Lord" add further kindness toward them and an indication that their reward is certain to be established and safe from being lost. His words, exalted is He, "and no fear will be upon them" means: at the time when the disbelievers fear punishment and grieve over losing reward.

(Note) The scholar al-Biqa'i said in his tafsir: What made the placement of this verse among their stories good is that they were commanded to kill every male among others than them, and perhaps they were commanded to kill women as well. So it may have been thought that whoever believed from others would not be accepted. It was also mentioned in surah al-Ma'idah, and its placement here, also among their stories, is an indication of their lying in their saying: ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered (ummiyyin)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75], and that the basis for the protection of blood and property is only faith and steadfastness. This exists in the text of the Torah in more than one place. In it there is also a threat to them, for opposing this, with humiliation and wretchedness. Some of that will come at His words ﴿You shall not worship except God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83], the verse. Indeed, in it is also what requires prohibiting the property of one who opposes the religion, for he said in the middle of the second book: "And if you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him. And if you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, and you would refrain from helping him, you shall surely help him and assist him." Then he returned to their stories in the best manner, saying:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[63] ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain (al-Tur) over you: "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾

"And when We took your covenant": a reminder of another transgression of your forefathers. That is, remember the time when We took your covenant to observe what is in the Torah (al-Tawrah). "And We raised the mountain over you": to frighten you so that you would accept the covenant. This is because the mountain (al-Tur) was uprooted from its base, lifted up, and held over them like a canopy. Al-Tur means the mountain. It was said to them while it hovered above them: "Take what We have given you" of the Book "with strength," meaning with earnestness and diligence, "and remember what is in it": keep in mind what is in the Book, study it, do not forget it, and do not neglect it, "that you may be mindful of God," so that you may refrain from disobedience, or as a hope from you that you may be counted among the God-fearing, or as a request for that.

This verse is similar to His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ [al-A'raf: 171]

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: If it is said that this would be compulsion, and that for it one would not deserve reward, it is answered: they did not deserve reward by the commitment itself, but they deserved it by acting upon it afterwards. As for their commitment to it, they were compelled. Some people (p-149) said: by the mountain is meant the intensification of the matter upon them, and this was made an example. But that is far-fetched. Similarly al-Qashani said: it refers to shaping the brain so as to be able to understand the meanings and accept them. But this is far-fetched, and the apparent meaning of the other verse rejects it, although the usage in the language is not restricted to the literal sense.

**The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

﴿Then you turned away after that. Had it not been for the grace of God upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾ [2:64]

"Then you turned away" means you turned aside from fulfilling the covenant. "After that" means after the taking of that solemn covenant. ﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you and His mercy﴾ means for you, by enabling you to repent (tawbah), or by delaying the punishment. ﴿You would have been among the losers﴾ means among those destroyed by the punishment.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: "The absolute loser (al-khasir al-mutlaq) in the Qur'an is the one who has lost the greatest thing that can be acquired, which is the bliss of eternity. This is what is mentioned in His words: ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Zumar: 15]."

Al-Qaffal said: "It is known in general that after accepting the Torah and the lifting of the Mount over them, they turned away from the Torah in many ways. They distorted its words from their places, abandoned acting upon it, killed the prophets, disbelieved in them, and disobeyed their commands. Some of these acts were committed by their earlier generations, and some by their later ones. They remained in the wandering (al-tih) while witnessing wonders night and day, opposing Moses and objecting to him, meeting him with every kind of harm, and openly committing sins in that very camp of theirs. To the point that some of them were swallowed up by the earth, some were burned by fire, and they were punished with the plague. All of this is mentioned in the translations of the Torah which they acknowledge. Then their later generations committed what is not hidden. Until they were punished with the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis, they disbelieved in the Messiah, and they plotted to kill him."

The Qur'an, although it does not explain what they turned away from in the Torah, the matter is well known. This is a report from God, exalted is He, about the obstinacy of their predecessors. So it is no wonder that they denied what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought of the Book, and rejected his truth. Their condition regarding their Book and their Prophet is as has been mentioned. And God knows best.

Then God, exalted is He, reminded them of the punishment inflicted upon those who broke His covenant and of what He had taken from them regarding the honoring of the Sabbath, with His words:

(p-150)

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[65] ﴿And you had already known those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath, so We said to them: "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾

﴿And you had already known those who transgressed﴾, meaning: they deliberately committed transgression "among you concerning the Sabbath", by deeming it permissible and devising stratagems to hunt fish on it. The reason is that God tested them: no fish remained in the sea without thrusting its snout out on Saturday, but when the day passed, they scattered, as He said: ﴿Their fish come to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they do not keep the Sabbath they do not come to them. Thus We test them﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. So they dug pools beside the sea and ran channels to them, and the fish would enter them, and they would catch them on Sunday. That confinement in the pools was their transgression. Consequent upon their aforementioned transgression was what God mentioned in His words: ﴿So We said to them: "Be apes, despised"﴾, meaning: abased, expelled, removed far from good, humiliated. It has been related from al-Dahhak and Qatadah that they were transformed into apes with tails that howl, after having been men and women. As for Mujahid, he said: their hearts were transformed, and they were not turned into apes; rather, it is a parable God struck for them, like the parable of the donkey that carries books. This was related by Ibn Jarir. Likewise al-Qashani said: "Be apes" means resembling people in form but not being them. Then he said: transformation in reality is true and not to be denied, in this world and the Hereafter; the verses and hadiths have affirmed it. And in a report it is stated that the transformations (al-musukh) are counted as thirteen, along with an explanation of their deeds, their sins, and the causes that necessitate their transformation. (p-151) The upshot is that whoever is overcome by one of the attributes of animals, and it takes root in him to the point that his capacity (for the human state) disappears, and it becomes firmly established in his nature and becomes his essential form, his nature becomes the nature of that animal and his soul becomes its soul, so his attribute becomes his form.

This story is set out at length in Surat al-A'raf, where the Exalted says: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed on the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not keep the Sabbath they did not come to them. Thus We tested them for what they used to defiantly disobey﴾ [al-A'raf: 163].

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[66] ﴿So We made it an example for those before it and those after it, and an admonition to the God-conscious.﴾

"So We made it" — that is, the transformation and the punishment — "an example" (nakal), a lesson that restrains the one who takes heed from it, i.e., prevents him and deters him. From this comes nikl, meaning the shackle for the fetter. "For those before it" — of the sins committed by the people of its own time who witnessed it. "And those after it" — of those who came after them. Or [it means] for the people of that town and those around it, or for the villages near it and those farther away from it. "And an admonition to the God-conscious" — among their own people, or to every God-conscious person who hears of it. This indicates that God-consciousness is a safeguard from every feared outcome, and that vengeance falls upon others as an admonition to them.

(Note): This verse points to the sanctity of the Sabbath day among the Israelites, for those who violated it among them were transformed into apes. In the translation of the Torah, the following text appears: "And the LORD spoke unto Moses, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, saying: Ye shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you; whoever defiles it shall surely be put to death, and whoever does any work therein, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days work may be done, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of rest, holy to the LORD; and the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to observe the Sabbath throughout their generations, for a perpetual covenant. For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day He rested." End of quotation.

And also in it, the following text: "Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest, that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the son of your female servant and the stranger may be refreshed." End of quotation.

It was forbidden for the Jews to prepare their food on it; rather, it was forbidden for them to kindle a fire. In the Book of Nehemiah, in chapter thirteen, the following text appears: "In those days I saw in Judah some treading winepresses on the Sabbath, and bringing in heaps of grain and loading them on donkeys, and also wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of burdens, which they brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. So I warned them on the day they sold food. Men of Tyre also lived there, who brought in fish and all kinds of merchandise, and sold them on the Sabbath to the children of Judah and in Jerusalem. Then I contended with the nobles of Judah and said to them, 'What evil thing is this that you are doing, by which you profane the Sabbath day? Did not your fathers do thus, and did not our God bring all this disaster upon us and upon this city? Yet you bring more wrath upon Israel by profaning the Sabbath.'" And so on to its end.

When He, exalted is He, had explained their hardness toward His exalted rights, He followed it with an explanation of their hardness regarding their own interests, as a rebuke of their characters — along with an indication of His favor upon them in the breaking of custom concerning the cow, and an explanation of who was the killer by its means, and God's raising of the slain, and His specifying of the one among them who had killed him. So He said:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[67] ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾

﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾, the Children of Israel, ﴿"Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾. This was because a slain man was found among them, and they were demanding retribution for his blood. So Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow and to strike the dead man with part of it, so that he would come back to life and name his killer. "They said" is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), which came as an answer to what the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "What did they do? Did they hasten to obey or not?" So it was said: ﴿"Do you take us in mockery?"﴾ The word "huzuwan" is read with a ḍamma on the zāy and the hamza converted into a wāw, and it was also read with the hamza with ḍamma and with sukūn. That is: "Do you make us a place of mockery, or people of mockery, or ones who are mocked, or the very essence of mockery," for emphasis. Their answer indicated the coarseness that was established in them, since in it there is bad manners toward one whose messengership was established and whom they knew it to be.

"He said" is a resumptive sentence as before: ﴿"I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because mockery in the course of conveying the command of Allah, glory be to Him, is ignorance and foolishness. He negated from himself, peace be upon him, what they had imagined from his side in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, by expressing it in the form of something beyond which there is no abhorrence, through seeking refuge from it, as a way of declaring it monstrous and magnifying what they had undertaken of the grave matter, which they had voiced to him, peace be upon him. "Al-'awdh" means taking refuge from something feared, with one who suffices for protection. "Al-jahl" (ignorance) means proceeding in matters without knowledge.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 68:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[68] ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is." He said, "Indeed, He says she is a cow neither old (fari) nor virgin (bikr), but between that, so do what you are commanded."﴾

"They said" persisting in harshness. "Call upon for us" meaning: on our behalf, "your Lord to make clear to us what she is" what her state is and her description?! For they were amazed at a dead cow, by part of which a dead man is struck so that he comes to life. So they asked about the description of that cow of wondrous affair, which departs from what cows are normally like. And "ma" (what), although it is commonly used to seek the concept of the reality (essence), may also be used to seek the attribute and state. You say, "What is Zayd?" and it is answered, "A physician or a scholar."

"He said," i.e., Musa, peace be upon him, after he had called upon his Lord, exalted and mighty is He, for clarification, and revelation came to him: "Indeed He" exalted is He: "says she is" i.e., the cow commanded to be slaughtered, "a cow neither old (fari)" i.e., not advanced in age. She has been "faradat furud" (grown old), so she is "fari," i.e., she has become aged, from "al-fard" meaning cutting, as if she has cut her age and reached its end. "Nor virgin (bikr)" i.e., not a young, small heifer whom the stallion has not impregnated. "Awan" i.e., middle-aged, "between that" i.e., between the age of the old and the virgin. "So do what you are commanded" This is a command from Musa, peace be upon him, branching from what precedes it of the explanation of the attribute of what is commanded. In it is an urging to obedience and a deterrence from returning to questioning. Despite that, they did not comply, but instead asked for clarification of the color after the clarification of the age, saying:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[69] ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its color, pleasing to the observers."﴾

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its color"﴾

[It is] intensely yellow. It is said, for emphasis: aṣfar fāqiʿ (bright yellow) and wāris (deep yellow), just as one says: aswad ḥālik (intensely black), abyaḍ yaqiq (intensely white), aḥmar qāniʾ (deep red), and akhḍar nāḍir and muddahāmm (deep green). In attributing fuqūʿ (brightness) to the color, even though it is one of the attributes of that which is colored because of its association with it, there is an emphasis that is not hidden, as if it were said: "yellow, intensely yellow in its yellowness," like in "jiddu jiddihi" (its truest essence). "Pleasing to the observers" means: it delights their souls.

Ibn Jarir narrated with a sound chain from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Had they taken any cow at all, it would have sufficed them, but they made it strict, so it was made strict upon them." Others besides him also narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn Jurayj traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah knows best.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is. Indeed, the cattle have become confused to us. And indeed, if Allah wills, we will be guided."﴾

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is"﴾ is a request for further clarification of its condition, so that it may be distinguished from what shares with it in its color and yellowness. For this reason they gave as the reason for repeating their question, with their saying, "Indeed, the cattle," which is described by what preceded, "have become confused to us," because of their multitude; that is, it became unclear to us which of them we should slaughter. Al-Biqa'i said: He used the masculine verb form, because every plural's letters are fewer than the letters of its singular, and the Arabs treat it as masculine. It is transmitted from Sibawayh: ﴿And indeed, if Allah wills, we will be guided﴾ to the cow whose slaughter is intended.

(p-155) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[71] ﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow neither trained to plough the earth nor to water the tilth, sound, with no blemish in it.﴾ They said: ﴿Now you have brought the truth.﴾ So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done it.

﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow neither trained to plough the earth nor to water the tilth﴾ That is, it has not been made submissive for ploughing the earth or watering the tilth. "Dhalul" (trained, submissive) is an attribute of "baqarah" (cow), in the sense of "ghayr dhalul" (not trained). The first "la" is for negation, and the second is redundant, for emphasis of the first, because the meaning is: "not trained, ploughing and watering," with the two verbs being attributes of "dhalul," as if it were said: "not a trained one, ploughing and watering." The intended meaning is: it is honoured, not made submissive by tilling, nor prepared for drawing water with the water-wheel. "Musallamah" (sound): God has freed it from defects, or it is free from work (its people have freed it from it), or its colour is unmixed, none of the colours mixing with its yellowness. It derives from "salima lahu kadha" (it became his purely), when it became pure for him. "La shiyata fiha" (with no blemish in it): that is, there is no colour in it differing from the colour of its skin, whether white, black or red; so it is wholly yellow. Originally it is a verbal noun: "washa, washa'an, wishyah," when one mixes another colour with its colour. In al-Sihah: "al-shiyah is every colour that differs from the majority of the colour of a horse or other animal." The "ha'" is a substitute for the omitted "waw" at its beginning. Its plural is "shiyat." It is said: "thawr ashyah," just as it is said: "faras ablaq."

﴿They said: Now you have brought the truth﴾ That is, with the reality of the description of the cow, in such a way that you have distinguished it from all others, and no doubt remains for us concerning it at all. This is unlike the first two times, for what you brought then did not reach this degree of specification. "So they slaughtered it" — the "fa" is an eloquent connective, as in "fa-infajarat" (then it burst forth), meaning: they obtained the cow and slaughtered it. "And they had almost not done it": "kada" is among the verbs of approximation, set for the nearness of the predicate to occurrence, and the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "dhabahu" (they slaughtered), meaning: they slaughtered it while they had been, before that, far from doing it. It is a parenthetical concluding remark (i'tiradh tadhyili). Its implication is a rebuke for their excessive questioning and a reproach to them: because of their great prolixity and their frequent returns to questioning, the thread of their verbosity nearly failed to end concerning it.

(Note) Al-Raghib said: Some people said: this verse indicates the abrogation of a thing before it is carried out. In the first instance they were commanded to slaughter an unspecified cow, and they could slaughter any cow they wished. In the second and third instances they were commanded to slaughter a specific cow, so it is as if they were forbidden what they had been commanded before. This is not so; the first is an absolute command, and the second and third are like its clarification, when they returned to ask, and the obligation of slaughtering a cow did not lapse from them. Rather, its attributes were added to, and the intended meaning of the first command was uncovered. The verse also indicates the permissibility of delaying clarification until the time of need.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[72] ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, but Allah would bring forth what you were concealing.﴾

﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾: that is, you differed and contended concerning its matter, since each of the disputants pushed the blame away from himself. ﴿But Allah would bring forth what you were concealing﴾: He would make manifest, without doubt, what you had hidden of the matter of the slain man, and He would not leave it concealed.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[73] ﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it." Thus Allah brings the dead to life and shows you His signs, that you may reason.﴾

"So We said, 'Strike him'" — i.e., the slain man — "with part of it" — i.e., the cow. That is, they struck him, and he came to life and informed them of his killer, as His words "Thus" indicate: like this great giving of life in this strange manner, "Allah brings the dead to life" on the Day of Resurrection, "and shows you His signs" — i.e., His proofs indicating that He, Exalted is He, is capable of everything.

It is also permissible that by the signs is meant this giving of life. Its being expressed in the plural is because it comprises wondrous matters: the life being brought about through a dead limb, the informing of them of the killer, and the other matters outside the ordinary custom that accompany it. "That you may reason" — so that, by seeing those signs, you may hope to acquire reason, which will guide you to believe in the resurrection and other matters that the messengers report from Allah, Exalted is He.

(p-157) Al-Raghib said: As for His words, ﴿Thus Allah brings the dead to life﴾, it is said that it is a report of the words of Musa, peace be upon him, to his people. It is also said that rather it is an address from Allah, Exalted is He, to this community, as a reminder to take warning from His bringing the dead to life.

Remarks:

(First): Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: why was the story not related in its proper order? Its due would have been to mention the slain man and the striking with part of the cow before the command to slaughter it, so that it would be said: 'And when you killed a soul and disputed about it, so We said: slaughter a cow and strike him with part of it'?"

(Answer): All that is related of the stories of the Children of Israel is related as an enumeration of the crimes that occurred among them, a rebuke to them for them, and of the great signs renewed among them. These are two stories, each independent with a kind of rebuke, though they are connected and unified. The first is to rebuke them for mockery and for their neglect of hastening to obey and what follows from that. The second is a rebuke for the killing of a forbidden soul and what follows from it of the great sign. The story of the command to slaughter the cow was placed before the mention of the slain man because, had it been done in reverse, it would have been one single story, and the purpose of a double rebuke would have been lost. A subtle point is observed: after the second was begun as a fresh story of its own, it was joined to the first by indicating their unity through the pronoun referring to the cow rather than its explicit name in His words "strike him with part of it," so that it becomes clear that they are two stories in respect of what pertains to rebuke, while the repetition is made by bringing the second out as a new beginning despite its being placed later; and that it is one story through the pronoun referring back to the cow. End.

Al-Harali said: The account of Musa's words, peace be upon him, was placed before the mention of their call concerning the slain man, beginning with the more noble of the two aims of legislation, which stands over acts of transgression and words of enmity. And Allah knows best.

(The Second Remark) Al-Raghib said: Some people have found this and what Allah related of it improbable, and denied that the act occurred in reality, saying: That is impossible by nature, and also no divine wisdom is known in it. As for their finding it improbable by nature, this is in fact a finding improbable of the giving of life and resurrection, and that has a place not specific to exegesis; whoever holds this view, there is no engaging with him in the exegesis of the Qur'an. As for the wisdom in it, it is evident, since it is one of the sensible miracles dazzling to minds. As for the specification of the cow, much of Allah's wisdom is not something humans can comprehend. Even if there were no purpose in specifying a cow with a particular attribute except the gathering of those commanded to seek it, the earning of reward in spending its price, and the bringing of a benefit that accrues to its owner, there would be great wisdom in that.

The verse also indicates that a group whose judgment is one may have an act attributed to them, even if it was done by some of them, and that this is not a lie, as though the composite whole of one person may be credited with what occurs from one of its limbs.

Most exegetes have related the story of the cow and its owner through various narrations, none of which we have included, because it was not transmitted by a sound chain to the Prophet ﷺ, and no great benefit depends on it. Likewise, the particular identity of the cow has not come through a sound path from an infallible source who explains it. So we leave it indefinite as Allah left it indefinite, since specifying it for us brings no religious or worldly benefit, though it is specific in reality; and whatever it was, the miracle is achieved by it.

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[٧٤] ﴿ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكم مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ فَهي كالحِجارَةِ أوْ أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً وإنَّ مِنَ الحِجارَةِ لَما يَتَفَجَّرُ مِنهُ الأنْهارُ وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَشَّقَّقُ فَيَخْرُجُ مِنهُ الماءُ وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ وما اللَّهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (Then your hearts hardened after that, so that they were like stones, or even harder in hardness. Indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them are those that split open so water comes out of them, and indeed among them are those that fall down out of fear of God. And God is not unaware of what you do.)

﴿ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكم مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ﴾ The addressees are either the People of the Book who were in his time, ﷺ, meaning: your hearts became hard, stiff and unyielding after the clear signs that came to your forefathers, the events that befell them, the punishment that descended upon those among them who persisted in disobedience, the signs that their prophets brought them, and the covenants they took upon themselves, and upon everyone who professed the Torah among others. He informs, by this, of their rebellion and harshness, along with their knowledge of the signs of God by which hearts soften. This is more appropriate, because His saying, Exalted is He, "Then your hearts hardened," is a direct address (khitab mushafahah), so applying it to those present is more fitting. Or the intended ones are those Jews who were in the time of Musa, peace be upon him, specifically, or those before the addressees among their predecessors. And God knows best.

"فَهِيَ كالحِجارَةِ" in hardness, "أوْ أشَدُّ" than them "قَسْوَةً". That is: in hardness they are like stones, or exceeding them in it. "أوْ" is for choice (lil-takhyir) or for uncertainty (lil-taraddud). The meaning: whoever knows their state likens them to stones, or to something harder such as iron; or whoever knows them likens them to stones, or says they are harder than stones. The omission of the pronoun of the comparison-object (al-mufaddal 'alayhi) is because there is no risk of confusion. ﴿وإنَّ مِنَ الحِجارَةِ لَما يَتَفَجَّرُ﴾ means it bursts open (yatafattah) with abundance and plenty, "مِنهُ الأنْهارُ" is an explanation of how much harder their hearts are than stones in hardness and in being unaffected by admonitions and calamities, by which mountains melt and rocks soften. He means that stones may be affected, since among them are those from which great waters gush forth. "وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَشَّقَّقُ" means it splits (yatashaqqaq) "فَيَخْرُجُ مِنهُ الماءُ" that is, springs, which are less than rivers. ﴿وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ means it falls down from the top of a mountain out of fear of God, submitting to what He has subjected it to of inclination toward the center with ease. This is what al-Qashani said.

Some exegetes have gone to the position of deriving from the apparent sense of the verse that inanimate things have discernment (tamyiz), so that they fear and glorify. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) hold that this verse and its like are of eloquent metaphor (majaz baligh), and that the unrestricted usage is not confined to the literal meaning (haqiqah), especially since metaphor is more common in the language than it, as expounded in the extended treatises on rhetoric.

Imam Ibn Hazm, at the beginning of his book "al-Fasl," refuted at length those who claimed that animals and inanimate things have discernment, and said: "Whoever claims that, the evidence of observation refutes him." Then he excepted what was a miracle of the prophets, peace be upon them.

(He said): Perhaps an objector will object with His saying, describing stones: ﴿وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾. We know by necessity that stones were not commanded by a law, nor by reason, nor was a prophet sent to them. Since there is no doubt in this, the statement from Him, Exalted is He, goes forth in one of three ways. The first is that the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ﴾ refers to the hearts mentioned at the beginning of the verse, in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿ثُمَّ قَسَتْ قُلُوبُكم مِن بَعْدِ ذَلِكَ فَهي كالحِجارَةِ أوْ أشَدُّ قَسْوَةً﴾. So He mentioned that among those hard hearts are some that accept faith at some point, so they descend from hardness to softness out of fear of God, Exalted is He. This is a matter witnessed by observation, for hard hearts may soften by God's gentleness, and the disobedient may fear. God, Glorified and Exalted, has informed: ﴿وإنَّ مِن أهْلِ الكِتابِ لَمَن يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وما أُنْـزِلَ إلَيْكم وما أُنْـزِلَ إلَيْهِمْ﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 199] ("And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God and in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down to them"). And as He, Exalted, informed that among the Bedouins are those who believe in God, after He had informed that ﴿الأعْرابُ أشَدُّ كُفْرًا ونِفاقًا﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97] ("The Bedouins are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy"). (He said:) This is a clear way, certain in its soundness.

The second way: the fear mentioned in the verse is only the stones' submission to the judgment of God, Exalted is He, and the course of His decrees, as we said regarding His saying, Exalted is He, quoting the heavens and the earth: ﴿قالَتا أتَيْنا طائِعِينَ﴾ [Fussilat: 11] ("They said: We come willingly").

The third way: God, Exalted is He, meant by His saying ﴿وإنَّ مِنها لَما يَهْبِطُ مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ the mountain that became crushed (dakk), when God, Exalted is He, manifested Himself to it on the day His interlocutor, peace be upon him, asked Him for the vision. That mountain is without doubt among the stones, and it descended from its place out of fear of God, Exalted is He. This is a miracle and a sign, and a suspension of nature in that mountain specifically. "يَهْبِطُ" would then mean "هَبَطَ," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وإذْ يَمْكُرُ بِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [al-Anfal: 30] ("And when those who disbelieved plotted against you"), meaning: "And when they plotted." His saying, Exalted is He, clarifies, confirming Abraham His friend, peace be upon him, in his denunciation of his father's worship of stones: ﴿لِمَ تَعْبُدُ ما لا يَسْمَعُ ولا يُبْصِرُ﴾ [Maryam: 42] ("Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees?"), and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿أمِ اتَّخَذُوا مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ شُفَعاءَ قُلْ أوَلَوْ كانُوا لا يَمْلِكُونَ شَيْئًا ولا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ [al-Zumar: 43] ("Or have they taken intercessors besides God? Say: Even though they possess nothing and do not reason?"). By this it is established, with a soundness in which there is no room for doubt, that stones do not reason. And since this is certain by text, by necessity, and by observation, speech, discernment, and fear, as commonly understood by us, are negated from them.

As for the traditions transmitted that a stone has a tongue and two lips, and the Ka'bah is likewise, and that mountains stretched out, and that such-and-such a mountain humbled itself, these are fabricated myths transmitted by every liar and weak narrator, none of which is sound at all from the perspective of the chain of transmission. It suffices, to avoid lengthy discussion on this, that none of the imams who undertook to compile the sound hadith included any of them, nor anything whose narration is permissible that approaches soundness. (End of Ibn Hazm's words.)

Ibn Jarir said: The people of grammar differed about the meaning of descending (al-hubut), i.e., what descended of the stones out of fear of God. Some of them said: the descending of what descended from them out of fear of God is the shadows of it inclining (tafayyu' zilalihi). Others said: it is that mountain which became crushed when its Lord manifested Himself to it. Others said: His saying, "yahbitu min khashyati Allah" (descends out of fear of God) is like His saying: ﴿جِدارًا يُرِيدُ أنْ يَنْقَضَّ﴾ [al-Kahf: 77] ("a wall that wanted to collapse"), though it has no will. They said: what is meant by this is that, from the magnitude of God's matter, it is seen as if it were descending, humbled out of the humiliation of fear of God. Zayd al-Khayl said:

With a host among which the spotted horses get lost in its dust; you see the hills from it prostrating to the hooves.

And as Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said, describing an enemy of his:

Prostrate of nose, not raising it, humble of gaze, deaf to what he hears.

He means that he is humiliated.

And as Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:

When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina and the humbled mountains humbled themselves.

Others said: the meaning of His saying "yahbitu min khashyati Allah" is that it causes fear in others by its indication of its Maker, as it is said: "a she-camel that trades" (naqah tajirah) when she is, by her excellence and beauty, calling people to desire her. As Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:

And one-eyed of Nabhan: as for his day, he is blind; and as for his night, he is sighted.

He attributed the description to the night and the day, while he means by it his companion, the Nabhani whom he satirizes, because in both of them he had what he described him with. Then Ibn Jarir chose what the apparent sense of the verse requires, and Ibn Hazm's refutation of it, proving it, has preceded.

(p-164) Then I saw that Imam al-Raghib attempted here to bring close what was transmitted about holding to its apparent sense, through his interpretation. His words are: Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: every stone that falls from the top of a mountain, the fear of God has descended upon it. Al-Zajjaj said: the one that descends from them has been given a form of knowledge. He said: the proof of that is His saying: ﴿لَوْ أنْـزَلْنا هَذا القُرْآنَ عَلى جَبَلٍ لَرَأيْتَهُ خاشِعًا مُتَصَدِّعًا مِن خَشْيَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Hashr: 21] ("Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of God") and His saying: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ أنَّ اللَّهَ يَسْجُدُ لَهُ مَن في السَّماواتِ ومَن في الأرْضِ﴾ [al-Hajj: 18] ("Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth") up to His saying ﴿والنُّجُومُ والجِبالُ والشَّجَرُ والدَّوابُّ﴾ [al-Hajj: 18] ("and the stars, the mountains, the trees, and the creatures"). Similar to this has been transmitted from the predecessors (al-salaf). And in knowing this there must be an introduction that uncovers the aspect of this statement and its reality. For some people have submitted to what was related to them of this kind, and so they harbored a doubt; and some people deemed that unlikely and belittled the intellect of its transmitters and proponents. So it is said, and with God is success: some of the earlier scholars mentioned that all kinds of knowledge (ma'arif) are of several types:

The first is complete knowledge, which is perfect knowledge. That belongs to the Knower of the unseen, who encompasses everything in knowledge.

The second is a growing knowledge, which belongs to the human being, for God, Exalted is He, gave him an innate knowledge (ma'rifah gharizziyyah), and made for him by it a path to recognizing much of what he did not know. This belongs to none but the human.

The third is knowledge below that, namely the knowledge of animals, which He subjected for choosing beneficial things for themselves and striving toward them, and for disliking harmful things and avoiding them, and for repelling harms from themselves.

The fourth is the knowledge of growing things, such as trees and plants, which is below what animals have, and it is only in seeking benefits and what develops them.

The fifth is the knowledge of the elements, for each one of them is subjected to occupy the place particular to it, like the stone in seeking the lowest place, and fire in seeking the height, and that is by God's subjection, without choice on its part. They said: The evidence for that is that each of these elements, when it is forcibly removed from its center, refuses except to return to it willingly. They said: What clarifies that is that the lamp draws the oils that keep it burning, and rejects the water that extinguishes it, and that the magnet draws iron and does not draw anything else. This is what they related.

Based on this, if it is said that these things have a knowledge, it is not far-fetched, provided it is granted to them that these forces are called knowledge. But if it is said that inanimate things have human knowledge, in that they discern, choose, and desire, then this is something the intellects reject. (End of al-Raghib's words.)

And this is a good interpretation, and its basis is that the terminology of the predecessors in many usages differs from the terminology of the later scholars (khalaf). And this is accepted in many usages.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وما اللَّهُ بِغافِلٍ عَمّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ("And God is not unaware of what you do") contains threat and intensification of warning that is not hidden. For God, Glorified and Exalted, since He knows what they do, observes it, and is not unaware of it, He is on watch for their recompense. When He, Glorified and Exalted, explained the hardness of their hearts, their distance from faith resulted from that. So He turned to the believers, despairing them of their success, as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he was greatly eager for, namely seeking their faith, in the context of rebuke and reproach directed at them, denouncing hope for their faith, and so He said:

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[75] ﴿Do you hope that they will believe you, when a group of them used to hear the word of Allah and then distort it after they had understood it, while they knew?﴾

"Do you hope" — O believers, after you have come to know the details of the affairs of their forebears, who have been despaired of — "that they will believe": that is, these Jews among you, who are alike in blameworthy character, from whose character nothing comes forth except the like of what came forth from their forebears. (The lām in His words) "for you" is for the implication of the meaning of compliance, as in His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿So Lot believed in him﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 26], meaning: in their belief, complying with you; or it is for causation, meaning: in their bringing about belief for the sake of your call. ﴿And a group of them had indeed﴾ — that is, a party among those who passed before them — ﴿heard the word of Allah﴾ — which is what they recite of the Torah — "then distort it." Ibn Kathir said: that is, they interpret it other than its (true) interpretation. Ibn Jarir said: by His words "distort it" He means they alter its meaning and its interpretation and change it; its root is from the deviation of a thing from its direction, which is its inclination away from it to something else. Likewise His words "distort it" mean: they incline it away from its face and from its meaning which it has, to something else. ﴿After they had understood it﴾ — that is, they comprehended it clearly, and yet they opposed it with insight. "And they knew" that they were mistaken in what they went to of distorting and interpreting it.

Ibn Jarir said: this is an report about their boldness in slander and their hostility toward Him and toward His messenger Musa, peace be upon him, and that their remnants in the Muhammadan era are upon the like of what their earlier ones were upon in the Mosaic era, out of transgression and envy. This station is similar to His exalted words: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13]. It is apparent that by "a group of them" is meant their rabbis, and they did that for a kind of aims, as Allah the Exalted explained afterward in His words: ﴿and sold it for a small price﴾ [Al 'Imran: 187], and He said: ﴿they recognize it as they recognize their sons﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146].

(p-167) One might say: how does it follow from some of them undertaking distortion that the rest of them are despaired of believing? For the obstinacy of some does not contradict the acknowledgment of the rest. Al-Qaffal answered this, saying: it is possible that the meaning is: how will these believe, when they take their religion and learn it from people who deliberately distort it out of obstinacy? Those people teach them only what they have distorted and altered from its true face, and the blind followers accept only that and do not turn to the statements of the people of truth. This is like your saying to a man: how will you prosper, when your teacher is so-and-so? That is, you take from him, and you take from no one else.

Similar to it is the statement of al-Raghib: since belief is true knowledge together with acting upon its requirement, whoever does not seek that, though some knowledges have come to him, it is fitting that it not come to one who is ignorant of all knowledges. So He mentioned that as a means of distancing their belief, not as despair of it, for it is not the case that everything not hoped for is despaired of. (Then al-Raghib said:) In the verse there is an alert that what prevents a person from seeking belief is not only ignorance of it, but may be obstinacy and the dominance of desire.

(Note) What we have transmitted from Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir regarding the explanation of "then distort it" is the most fitting in view of the context of this noble verse, and it should not be imagined from this that their verbal distortion of the Torah is thereby denied, for it is certainly occurring without doubt; they have replaced some of it, distorted its wording, and interpreted some of it with other than what is intended by it. The same is said of the Gospel. Their own rabbis' statements bear witness to this. The eminent scholar Shaykh al-Hindi, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book (Izhar al-Haqq) transmitted that the People of the Book, earlier and later, have a custom of generally translating names in their translations and putting their meanings in place of them, and that this is a great confusion and a source of corruption; and that they sometimes add something by way of explanation into the speech which in their claim is the word of Allah, (p-168) without indicating the distinction; and these two matters are for them like ordinary customs. Whoever reflects on their translations circulating in various languages will find many witnesses to these matters. Then he cited some of them, so consult it.

In (Dhakhirat al-Albab), by one of the scholars of the Christians, there is something whose example is: some of them went to the view that the Holy Spirit did not preserve the scribes from the slip of a slight error, nor sufficed them against a slip of the foot, until he would not allow that they mixed the human with the divine. And in it also: between the Hebrew, Samaritan and Greek copies of the Five Books there is a great difference concerning the matter of history. Thus the distortion of the Five Books is a clear matter. And in it also in chapter (31): that some of their scholars claimed that in the common Latin translation of the Old and New Testaments he found more than four thousand errors, and another saw in it more than eight thousand errors. End. Thus it is established from their testimony that verbal distortion has occurred in them, and that is the intended point.

As for the claim that all or most of the books were distorted, it is excessive. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said at the end of his commentary on the Sahih, in the chapter on the word of Allah: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ [al-Buruj: 21], that the claim that they were all altered is obstinate denial. The verses and reports are numerous that many things of them remained unaltered. Among that is His exalted word: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], etc. Among that (p-169) is the story of the stoning of the two Jews, in which the existence of the verse of stoning is found, and His exalted word supports it: ﴿Say: bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93]. We have previously set out the completion of this discussion in the introduction to the tafsir in the discourse on the Isra'iliyyat, so return to it.

Then He, exalted, informed, concerning the character of those Jews despaired of their belief, that they took on the characteristics of the hypocrites and the conduct of their way, with His exalted word:

(p. 170)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." And when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you tell them what God has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Do you not use your reason?"﴾

"When they meet those who believe": that is, those among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who believe in God and His Messenger. "They say, 'We believe'": that is, that you are upon the truth and that Muhammad is the Messenger foretold. It seems they say this to please their allies from the Aws and the Khazraj, or because they are openly confronted, in front of their allies, with a truth they cannot afford to keep silent about. "And when they are alone with one another": meaning those who did not become hypocrites, "with one another": that is, those who did become hypocrites. "They say": that is, rebuking them, "Do you tell them what God has disclosed to you": that is, what He has made clear to you in the Torah of the good news about the Prophet ﷺ, and of believing in the Prophet who will come to you confirming what is with you, and of supporting him.

Ibn Ishaq said: That is, "Do you acknowledge that he is a prophet, when you know that the covenant was taken from you to follow him, and he tells them that he is the Prophet whom we find in our Book? Deny him and do not acknowledge him."

Ibn Jarir said: The root of "fath" (disclosure, opening) in the speech of the Arabs is judgment and decision. The meaning is: "Do you tell them of what God has decreed upon you and decided concerning you? Among His decree and judgment concerning them is that He took their covenant to believe in Muhammad ﷺ and in what came in the Torah." End of quotation.

"So that they may argue with you about it": this is connected to "telling," not to "disclosure"; that is, so that the believers may establish the proof against you by it. "Before your Lord": that is, so that the proof may be against you before the believers on the Day of Resurrection. They will say: "Did you not tell us, in this world, what is in your Book about the truth of our religion and the truthfulness of our Prophet?" That will add to the exposure of your disgrace and to your rebuke before all creatures at the place of standing. For one who acknowledges the truth and then conceals it is not like one who persists in denial.

Al-Raghib al-Isfahani interpreted His saying "before your Lord" as meaning "in His judgment and His Book," as is one possible reading of the verse: ﴿Then, since they did not bring witnesses, it is they who are the liars before God﴾ [al-Nur: 13], that is, "in the judgment of God and His decree." This is a good reading. His saying "Do you not use your reason?" is part of the rebuke and reproach, and so it belongs to the report of them, in the manner of some of them denouncing others. Al-Raghib said: It is also possible that it is a renewed denunciation from God, Mighty and Majestic, in the manner of what is called in rhetoric "al-iltifat" (a shift in the mode of address). It is also possible that it is an address to the believers, alerting them to what the disbelievers and hypocrites do.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[77] ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾

﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal﴾ i.e., what they hide of their speech to their companions and others, "and what they reveal" i.e., what they make manifest of that, so that He informs His friends of it. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: this is a rebuke to them and a denunciation of what they engage in, despite their knowing that nothing is hidden from Allah.

When He mentioned the scholars among the Jews who obstinately distorted [the Scripture] despite knowledge and certainty, He mentioned the common folk who followed them, and drew attention to the fact that both are equal in misguidance. For the scholar is obliged to act upon his knowledge, and the layman is obliged not to be content with blind imitation (taqlid) and conjecture (zann) while he is able to acquire knowledge. So He said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[78] ﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book except as wishful thinking, and they do not do anything but guess.﴾

"And among them are unlettered people" means: they do not have skill in writing, so they cannot read the Torah and verify what it contains of the signs of prophethood, and thus believe. "Who do not know the Book" means the Torah: they do not understand what it contains of prescribed limits, rulings, and covenants. "Except as wishful thinking" — with a shadda, the plural of umniyyah (um-niyyah, a wish or desire). Its original form is umnuwiyah (u'ful'ulah), and it was altered by the rule applied to sayyid and mayyit. It is derived from tamanna al-shay', meaning he estimated it and loved to reach it; or from tamanna, meaning he lied; or from tamanna al-kitab, meaning he recited it. In every case the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), since what is wished for, what is fabricated, and what is recited are not of the same kind as knowledge of the Book. That is, they do not know the Book, but they entertain wishful thinking (p-172) according to what their rabbis have led them to hope: that God, glory be to Him, will pardon them, that their forefathers the prophets will intercede for them, and other vain wishes drawn from the Book on the claims of their leaders. Or: they do not know the Book, but they hold falsehoods fabricated that they heard from their scholars, and they accepted them by way of imitation. Or: they do not know the Book, but they receive it only to the extent that it is recited to them, and they accept it without being able to reflect and contemplate it.

Ibn Jarir said: The most sound of what we have related in the interpretation of His words "except as wishful thinking" is that these unlettered people do not understand anything of the Book that God sent down; rather, they invent lies and fabricate falsehoods, untruthfully and deceitfully. Tamanni (wishing) in this context is the fabrication, invention, and contrivance of lies, as evidenced by His words that follow: "and they do not do anything but guess," whereby He informs that they wish for what they wish of falsehoods by way of conjecture, not certainty.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: Interpreting it as wishing of the heart is more preferable, as evidenced by His words: "And they say: None will enter Paradise unless he be a Jew or a Christian. Those are their wishful thoughts" [2:111], meaning their wishes. God the Exalted also said: "It is not by your wishful thinking, nor by the wishful thinking of the People of the Book; whoever does evil will be recompensed for it" [4:123], and He said: "Those are their wishful thoughts. Say: Produce your proof" [2:111], and "And they say: There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us but time. And they have no knowledge of that; they do not do anything but guess" [45:24], in the sense of estimating and conjecturing. Many have preferred interpreting it as recitation, as in His words: "When he wishes, Satan casts into his wish" [22:52], since in the exception then there is a kind of connection to what precedes it, and it is thus more fitting to the manner of the exception. "And they do not do anything but guess" means: they are merely people whose highest attainment is conjecture and imitation, without reaching the rank of knowledge. How then can faith founded upon the foundations of certainty be hoped for from them?

(Note) Al-Raghib said: God has informed of the ignorance and blame of the unlettered people, and has intensified the blame of their scholars and rabbis. The unlettered knew only bare recitation and relied on their leaders and rabbis, who had themselves gone astray and led others astray. God has warned us, by blaming the unlettered, to acquire knowledge so that we do not need to rely on imitation and on one whose lying is not trustworthy; and by blaming their leaders, to seek truthfulness and avoid misguidance, for it is greater than error. End.

When He had explained the condition of these people in clinging to the ropes of wishful thinking and following conjecture, He followed this with an explanation of the condition of those who led them into that predicament, who are the callers to error through falsehood and lying against God, and through consuming people's wealth in vanity; and so it was said in the form of a curse upon them.

[79] ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," to trade it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾

"فَوَيْلٌ" (fa-waylun): if it is followed by a genitive (idafa), it is put in the accusative, as in *waylaka* and *waykha* ("woe to you"). When it is not followed by an idafa, it takes the nominative, as in *waylun lahu* ("woe to him"). *Al-wayl* means destruction and severe punishment. "لِلَّذِينَ يَكْتُبُونَ الكِتابَ" (*lilladhina yaktubuna al-kitab*, "to those who write the Scripture") means the distorted Scripture, or what they wrote of false interpretations (*ta'wilat za'ifa*). "بِأيْدِيهِمْ" (*bi-aydihim*, "with their own hands") is an emphasis to rule out the possibility of metaphor, as in your saying, "I wrote it with my right hand." It has been said that the purpose of such a phrase is to depict the state in the soul as it occurred, so that the hearer almost becomes a witness to the scene. "ثُمَّ يَقُولُونَ" (*thumma yaqulun*, "then they say") refers to what they wrote, falsely and slanderously: "هَذا مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ" ("This is from Allah"). "لِيَشْتَرُوا بِهِ" (*li-yashtaru bihi*, "that they may trade it") means that they take for themselves in exchange for it. "ثَمَنًا قَلِيلًا" (*thamanan qalilan*, "a small price") means a little worldly goods.

The verse may also carry another meaning: woe to those who write the Torah with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," and so bear witness to it. Given that they wrote it with their own hands, what should have followed is that the writing would have made them stop at what they would not have stopped at had it been written by others. What should follow from their saying and acknowledging that it is from Allah is that they should keep to His covenants and pacts, out of reverence for the One who sent it down and revealed it, and call people to its outward and inner meanings. But this did not happen from them. Rather, they distorted His words from their places in order to trade them for a small price. The essence of this view is that the written book remains in its original form, and that they were truthful in saying, "This is from Allah," and then opposed that. Thus His words "لِيَشْتَرُوا بِهِ" (*li-yashtaru bihi*) are a justification for an omitted element indicated by the context: "Then after that they distort it, in order to trade it." This is a good view, agreeing with the verse "They distort the words from their places" (4:46). Perhaps this view is also indicated by the statement of Mujahid (*Mujahid*, a student of Ibn 'Abbas) in what Ibn Jarir (*Ibn Jarir*, i.e., al-Tabari) transmitted: "Those who knew that it was from Allah distort it."
