"﴿فَوَيْلٌ لَهم مِمّا كَتَبَتْ أيْدِيهِمْ﴾" means: the severe punishment for them is because of what their hands have altered. "وَوَيْلٌ لَهم مِمّا يَكْسِبُونَ" (*wa-waylun lahum mimma yaksibun*, "and woe to them for what they earn") means what they obtain of the unlawful and the illicit gain (*al-suht*).

Al-Raghib (*al-Raghib*, i.e., al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: If it is asked, "Why did He mention 'يَكْسِبُونَ' (*yaksibuna*, 'they earn') in the present/future form, and 'كَتَبَتْ' (*katabat*, 'have written') in the past form?" The answer: as an alert to what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice (*sunna sayyi'a*), upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." So by the verse He alerts that what they established and affirmed of corrupt interpretations, on which the ignorant rely, is the earning of a burden that they keep acquiring moment by moment.

If it is asked, "Why did He mention the writing and not the saying?" The answer: since writing includes saying and adds to it (for he lies with the tongue and the hand), it is more eloquent, because the record of the hand's words remains, whereas the effect of speech fades.

If it is asked, "What exactly were they writing?" The answer: it is related from some of the early generations (*al-salaf*) that the chiefs of the Jews used to alter from the Torah the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), and then they would say, "This is from Allah." This is a point that needs further explanation. It must be understood that every prophet gave a description of the prophet after him, by an allusive expression and a concealed hint which only those firmly rooted in knowledge understand. The scholars have said: No heavenly Scripture has ceased to contain mention of the Prophet (ﷺ), but by hints. Had this been clear to the common people, their scholars would not have been blamed for concealing it. Then this became more obscure through its transmission from language to language: from Hebrew to Syriac to Arabic. The one who compiled (*al-muhassila*, i.e., the compiler of a collection) mentioned words from the Torah and the Gospel which, when considered, are found to indicate the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) by allusion, which is clear to those firmly rooted in knowledge, and hidden to the common people. Thus it became clear from this that what their hands wrote were distorted interpretations. Allah, exalted is He, has alerted by the verse to the warning against changing His rulings, altering His signs, concealing the truth from its people, and abandoning the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, out of greed for the goods of this world. It has already been stated that by "the small price" He meant the goods of this world, even if they are abundant, based on His saying: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is small."﴾ [4:77]. End of al-Raghib's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

(p-176)  The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few days counted." Say, "Have you taken from Allah a covenant, so Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾

﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few days counted"﴾ This explains another of their crimes, namely what they claimed for themselves: that the Fire will touch them in the Hereafter only for a brief period. Their intention by this is that they will not remain in it forever, because everything counted is finite. Mujahid said: The Jews used to say, "This world is only seven thousand years, and we are punished only one day for every thousand years, after which the punishment ends." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. And from him (Ibn 'Abbas) that the Jews said, "We will not enter the Fire except for the days in which we worshipped the calf, forty (days), and when they have passed, the punishment will end for us." Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear their falsehood, because reason has no path to knowing this, and the only way to knowing it is information from Him, exalted is He, and that is absent. So He, glorified is He, said, "Say" (in denial of their statement and as a rebuke to them): ﴿Have you taken from Allah a covenant?﴾ That is: has He made a covenant with you that He will not punish you except for this amount? ﴿So Allah will not break His covenant﴾ — that is, so that you could say, "Allah will not break His covenant." Some scholars made the particle fa' (then) an explanatory fa' (fa' fasihah), indicating a presumed condition: that is, "If the matter is so, then He will not break it." ﴿Or do you say﴾ — that is, or if that is not the case, then you are saying, fabricating ﴿about Allah what you do not know﴾ — that is, its occurrence, out of ignorance and audacity. Their stated claim, although it is not an explicit fabrication against Him, glorified is He, nevertheless implies it, because such certainty can only be based on attributing its cause to Him, exalted is He.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[81] ﴿Nay, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin surrounds him—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

"Bala" (nay, indeed) is an affirmation of what follows the particle of negation, namely His words "The Fire will not touch us" (cf. 2:80). That is: nay, you will be touched by it forever. The evidence for this is His words "they will abide therein eternally." "Whoever earns an evil deed" means whoever does it. "Sayyi'ah" and "sayyi'" are both ugly deeds; its original form was "sayyi'ah" from "sa'ahu, yasu'uhu" (it distressed him). It was then treated by the rule of "sayyid" (i.e., the weak letter was altered by the same pattern as in "sayyid"). Then He, glorified is He, made clear that the mere earning of an evil deed does not necessitate eternal abiding in the Fire; rather, its cause must be something that encompasses him. So He said: ﴿and his sin surrounds him﴾, meaning it overwhelms him from all his sides, leaving him no good deed, and blocks off the paths of salvation for him, by his doing the same deeds as yours, O Jews, and disbelieving in what you disbelieve in, until his disbelief encompasses whatever good deeds he has: ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

(Note) The People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah) hold that eternal abiding in the Fire is only for the disbelievers and polytheists, because it has been established in the Sunnah, by mass transmission (tawatur), that sinful monotheists will come out of the Fire. Therefore, the interpretation of "sayyi'ah" and "khati'ah" in this verse must be disbelief and polytheism. This is supported by the fact that it was revealed concerning the Jews.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[82] ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, they are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ It is a habit of the Mighty Revelation (al-tanzil al-'aziz) that no verse of threat (wa'id) is mentioned in it without being followed by a verse of promise (wa'd). This is for several benefits. Among them: that His justice, glory be to Him, may become manifest. For when He decreed everlasting punishment for those who persist in disbelief, it was necessary that He decree everlasting bliss for those who persist in belief. Among them: the believer must have a balance between his fear and his hope, and this balance is attained only through this method. Among them: through His promise His perfect mercy becomes apparent, and through His threat His perfect wisdom becomes apparent, and this becomes a cause of gnosis (irfan).

We have already noted, at His saying, ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-Baqarah: 25), that the salaf (the early pious predecessors) agreed that faith (iman) is speech and action. If action is conjoined to it, then either it is the mention of the specific after the general, or it is said: it is not included within it, but with the conjunction, as in the case of the words "faqir" and "miskin." So reflect on this.

(p. 178) Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: In this verse there is evidence that His saying before it, ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾ (al-Baqarah: 81), refers to disbelief, and that being encompassed by one's sin is the evil deeds; and this is because He contrasted it with faith and righteous deeds.

Then, glory be to Him, began to establish the proof that they are among those whose sin has encompassed them, so He said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 83:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿And [recall] when We took the covenant from the Children of Israel: Worship none but Allah, be good to parents, to relatives, to orphans and to the needy, speak kindly to people, establish prayer and give zakah. Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were [habitually] refusing.﴾

﴿And [recall] when We took the covenant from the Children of Israel﴾. Then He clarified the covenant by His saying, exalted is He, "Worship none but Allah." This is a report in the sense of a prohibition, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and like your saying: "Go to so-and-so and say to him such-and-such." It is more eloquent than explicit command and prohibition. It begins with the highest and greatest of rights, which is the right of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, that He be worshipped alone and that nothing be associated with Him. With this He commanded all of His creation, and for this He created them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 25], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36].

﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾. Ihsan (goodness, excellence) is the utmost of kindness, so it includes everything that is due of care and attention. Allah has emphasized the command to honor parents, to the point that He, exalted is He, linked the command to do good to them with His worship, which is His monotheism and disavowal of association, showing concern for it and magnifying it.

The sage of Egypt said in his tafsir: The correct reason for the obligation of this goodness upon the child is the sincere care that they expended in raising him, and their attending to his affairs when he was weak, helpless and ignorant, unable to bring himself benefit or ward off harm from himself. They would surround him with care and attention, and nurture him, until he became able to be independent and to take charge of his own affairs. This is the goodness that comes from them, out of knowledge and choice, indeed with true affection and great tenderness. And the reward of goodness is nothing but goodness. If a person is obliged to thank whoever helps him with a difficult matter, granting him favor and rewarding him in a manner fitting to the helper according to his condition, and that by which the help was given, then how is it not obligatory to be thankful to one's parents after being thankful to Allah, exalted is He, they being the ones who helped him with everything when everything was beyond his reach. End of quote.

﴿and to relatives﴾, that is, kinship.

The sage Ustadh said: "Ihsan is what strengthens the instincts of nature and firmly binds the natural ties, so that the houses reach, in unity of interest, the degree of perfection. The nation is composed of houses, that is, families; so its righteousness is its righteousness. Whoever has no house has no nation. This is because the feeling of mercy and the call to cooperation are at their strongest and most complete in nature between parents and children, and then among the rest of the close relatives. So whoever's nature has been corrupted, to the point that there is no good in him for his own people, what good can be expected from him toward strangers and the more distant? And whoever has no good in him for people is not fit to be part of the structure of his nation, because the kinship bond, which is the strongest natural bond connecting people, has not benefited him; so what bond after it will connect him with non-kin, making him a part of them, so that what gladdens them gladdens him, what pains them pains him, and he sees their benefit as his own benefit and their harm as his own harm? The order of nature has decreed that the sentiment of kinship be stronger than every other sentiment, and its connection firmer than every other connection. So the religion came to give the rights of the nearest precedence over all other rights, and to make their rights proportional to their nearness to the person."

(p-180) Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the rights of the needy among the rest of the people, saying, glorified is He, "and orphans and the needy." Yatama is the plural of yatim, and it is one whose father has died while he is young. He, exalted is He, put the injunction concerning him before the injunction concerning the needy, and did not restrict it to poverty or destitution, so it is known that it is intended for its own sake. Allah, exalted is He, has emphasized in revelation the injunction concerning the orphan, and there is much of such injunctions in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. It is enough for you that the Qur'an forbade oppressing the orphan and especially intensified the threat against consuming his wealth. The secret in that is that the orphan, in most cases, does not find anyone whom the instinct of mercy moves to care for his upbringing, to undertake the protection of his rights, and to attend to his religious and worldly affairs. For the mother, if she exists, is in most cases incapable, especially if she has remarried after his father. So Allah, exalted is He, the Most Merciful of the merciful, willed, through the emphasis of the injunction concerning orphans, that they be among the people in the position of their own children, raised with a religious and worldly upbringing, lest they become corrupt and corruption spread through them to others, so that corruption spreads in the nation and it dissolves in dissolution. So care for the upbringing of orphans is the means to prevent them from becoming a bad example for the rest of the children, and upbringing is not easy in the presence of this example. Neglecting orphans is therefore neglecting the rest of the nation's children. As for the needy, what is meant is not those beggars who ask insistently, who are able to earn what meets their needs or who find what they spend even without earning. Rather, they have made begging a trade by which they seek wealth without doing any work that benefits people. The needy (miskin) is one who is unable to earn what suffices him. End of quote.

﴿And speak kindly to people﴾, that is, a good word: speak to them pleasantly and be gentle with them. In it, for emphasis and urging toward good conduct in speaking with people, He placed the verbal noun (masdar) in the position of the adjective, and this is used only for exaggeration in emphasizing a description, as in "a just man" (rajul 'adl), "a fasting man" (sawm), and "a breaking-fast man" (fitr).

﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾: an address to the Children of Israel. The intended meaning is the prayer they used to perform and the zakah they used to give out.

"Then you turned away": that is, you withdrew from continuing to abide by the requirements of the covenant, in which lay your happiness, and you rejected it.

His saying, ﴿except for a few of you﴾, is an exception for some of those who were in the time of our master Musa, peace be upon him, or in every age, for no nation is free of sincere people (p-181) who guard the truth according to their knowledge and capacity.

The wisdom in mentioning this exception is to avoid depriving the good-doers of their right, and to show that the presence of a few righteous people in a nation does not prevent divine punishment from it when wrongdoing spreads in it and goodness becomes scarce. "And you were [habitually] refusing": your custom was turning away from obedience and from observing the rights of the covenant. Then He also reproached them for their failure to fulfill the obligation of the covenant taken from them concerning the rights of the servants, with His saying:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[84] ﴿And when We took your covenant: "Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes," then you acknowledged it while you were witnesses.﴾

﴿And when We took your covenant: "Do not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes"﴾ This is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition. What is intended by it is a strong prohibition against some of the Children of Israel attacking others by killing them or expelling them. That is, let none of you kill another of you, nor drive him out of his dwelling. "Then you acknowledged it" means you showed your commitment to what is required by safeguarding the aforementioned covenant. "While you were witnesses" means while you were bearing witness to its binding force. Thus it is an emphasis on the acknowledgement, like your saying: "So-and-so acknowledged it, bearing witness against himself."

**The interpretation of His, the Exalted, words:**

﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes, supporting one another against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion was forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the worldly life? And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

"Then you are those" is a direct address to those present, containing severe reproach. ﴿You kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes﴾ without regard to this firm covenant. "Supporting one another against them" means you cooperate against them. "In sin" refers to the act that deserves its doer's blame and reproach. "And aggression" means excess in wrongdoing. "And if they come to you" refers to those whom you have cooperated with or aided against them, "as captives," with a *ḍamma* on the *hamza*, a *fatḥa* on the *sīn*, and an *alif* after it. Ḥamzah read *asrā*, with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza* and a *sukūn* on the *sīn*, like *qatlā*, as the plural of *asīr* (captive). Its root meaning is one bound with a *asr* (thong), which is a *qidd*, the strip that is cut from leather (*sayr*). "You ransom them" is read with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *fā'*. It is also read *tafdūhum*, with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'* and a *sukūn* on the *fā'*, meaning you free them with wealth through ransom (*fidā'*), which is release in exchange for a compensation. ﴿And their expulsion was forbidden to you﴾: this clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring either to the pronoun in "you expel," or to "a group," or to both. The specification of the explanation of prohibition here with expulsion, although killing is its companion in the taking of the covenant, is because expulsion is a matter in which one may be lax, given its lesser gravity relative to killing. Also, the context of speech is to blame and reproach them for their crimes and for the contradiction of their actions together. This applies specifically to the case of expulsion, since it is not reported that they made amends for the slain by blood money or retaliation. This is the secret in specifying the supporting against them in the previous clause. Then He denounced their distinguishing between the rulings, saying: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book﴾, that is, the Torah, which requires ransoming, "and disbelieve in part," which is the prohibition of killing and expulsion.

Know that what we mentioned regarding His words "you ransom them" and "you believe in part of the Book" is what the majority of the exegetes (*jumhūr al-mufassirīn*) took: that this is a description of them in terms of what is obedience, namely releasing captives from captivity by paying wealth or otherwise, and believing in that. Abu Muslim mentioned that it is the opposite of that. The meaning is that you, along with killing and expulsion, when a captive falls into your hands, you are not satisfied with him except by taking wealth, even though that is forbidden to you; then, in his case, you release him from captivity.

Abu Muslim said: The exegetes were only led astray by His words: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ This is weak, because this statement refers back to what preceded concerning the mention of the Prophet ﷺ and what was revealed to them. The meaning is that if in the Book you have there is the report of Muhammad and you denied it, you have believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part.

Both views are possible for the word *mufādāh* (ransoming), because the one who pays for the captive is described as having ransomed him, and the one who takes from him for release is also described thus. However, what the exegetes have agreed upon is closer, because the return of His words, ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾, to what was mentioned earlier in this verse is more appropriate than its return to matters mentioned after several verses. Al-Razi related this.

﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that﴾: this refers either to disbelieving in part of the Book while believing in part, or to what they did of killing and expulsion together with ransoming the captives. "Except disgrace" means humiliation and degradation together with exposure of shame. The indefiniteness is for magnification. ﴿In the worldly life﴾: and indeed He, glory be to Him, did that. Banu Qurayza were killed and Banu al-Nadir were exiled to Adhri'at and Ariha in Syria.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the severest punishment﴾, meaning the Fire. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

**Regarding the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[86] ﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter. So the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be helped.﴾

"أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا" (*ushtaraw*, "they bought"): meaning they preferred "the worldly life" (*al-hayah al-dunya*) despite its baseness. They exchanged it "for the Hereafter" despite the Hereafter's preciousness. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ in either of the two abodes. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾.

Al-Hafiz (the memorizer, a title of honour for a scholar) Ibn Kathir said in his *tafsir* (Qur'anic exegesis): God, exalted is He, rebuked the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), in Medina, for what they suffered from fighting alongside al-Aws and al-Khazraj. That is because al-Aws and al-Khazraj, who were the Ansar, were idol-worshippers in the time of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*), and there were many wars between them. The Jews of Medina were three tribes: Banu Qaynuqa', allies of al-Khazraj, and Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza, allies of al-Aws. So whenever war broke out between al-Aws and al-Khazraj, Banu Qaynuqa' went out with al-Khazraj, and Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza went out with al-Aws. Each of the two groups supported its allies against its own brothers. They destroyed each other's homes, expelled each other from them, and shed each other's blood, while the Torah was in their hands, in which they knew what was incumbent upon them and what was due to them. Al-Aws and al-Khazraj were people of polytheism who worshipped idols and did not recognise Paradise, Hell, resurrection, or the Last Day, nor a Book, nor the lawful and the unlawful. When the war laid down its burdens and a man from either of the two groups was taken captive, they gathered money for him until they ransomed him. Banu Qaynuqa' would ransom the captives who were in al-Aws' hands, and Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza would ransom those who were in al-Khazraj's hands. When the Arabs reproached them for this and said, "How can you fight them and then ransom them?", they replied, "We were commanded to ransom them, and fighting them was forbidden to us." It was then asked, "Why do you fight them?" They said, "We are ashamed that our allies should be humiliated." Therefore, when God, mighty and majestic, rebuked them, He said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85], meaning: you ransom them according to the ruling of the Torah, and yet you kill them. Among the rulings of the Torah is that no one should be killed, expelled from his home, or aided against by anyone who associates partners with God and worships idols besides Him, seeking the goods of this world. This is a summary of what Ibn Kathir related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq with his chain of narration going back to Ibn 'Abbas. He also related it from al-Suddi. So the authenticity of this story should be verified.

There is another interpretation of the verse: that is, do not kill yourselves out of the severity of a calamity that befalls you, by a knife, by strangulation, or by committing what necessitates that, such as apostasy, or adultery after being married, or killing a soul without right, and the like. And do not mistreat those who are your neighbours, so that they are compelled to leave your homes. Or: do not cause corruption, so that you become the cause of your own expulsion. And God knows best.

[p-184]

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, and We followed him up with messengers after him, and We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear signs, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Yet whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant: some of them you denied, and some of them you killed.﴾

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ begins an account of another part of their crimes. Introducing it with an oath-clause shows the great care taken with it. "The Book" here means the Torah.

﴿and We followed him up with messengers after him﴾: "qaffā-hu bihi" means he made him follow it, that is, he sent him after it. It derives from "taqfiyah," which is the successive following of one thing by another, as if one were treading on its heel (qafā). "Qafā al-ṣūrah" means the back of the image, the side opposite its face. The meaning is that We did not limit the preservation of the religion to the Book that Moses left among you. Rather, after him We sent messengers in succession, to renew the affair of the religion for you and to reinforce the covenants upon you.

"And We gave Jesus": "ʿĪsā" is an arabized name whose original form is Yasūʿ, a Greek word meaning "savior," and its counterpart in Hebrew is Yashūʿ, with a shin (sh) rather than a sin (s).

"Son of Mary, the clear signs": the manifest miracles about which no doubt remains for anyone of sound intellect, such as raising the dead and healing the blind and the leper.

"And We strengthened him": that is, We empowered him to do all of that.

"With the Holy Spirit": with the holy spirit, as you say "Ḥātim al-Jūd" (the very embodiment of generosity) and "rajul ṣidq" (a man of truth). It is the pure spirit that God breathed into him, distinguishing him thereby from others of His creation. God the Exalted said: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ (al-Nisa 4:171). For this reason he, peace be upon him, had a greater share of association with the spirit, because of the many dead he brought back to life. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that "al-Qudus" is God, and His spirit is Gabriel, and the idafah (genitive construction) is for honor. The meaning would then be: We aided him with Gabriel. Al-Razi said: What indicates that the Holy Spirit is Gabriel is His saying: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾ (al-Nahl 16:102). And God knows best.

The singling out of his mention among the messengers, peace be upon them, and the description of him with the giving of clear signs and the strengthening with the Holy Spirit, serve to cut off the root of their false belief about him, peace be upon him, by showing his truth and revealing the utmost ugliness of what they did to him, peace be upon him.

﴿Yet whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire﴾ of the truth, that is, what you do not love. From "hawiya," like "faraḥa," when one loves. "You grew arrogant" against following him and believing in what he brought from God, exalted is He. "Some of them you denied" when your hands could not reach to harm him, "and some of them you killed" without being content with merely denying them.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 88:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[88] ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are uncovered." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.﴾

"And they say" introduces another kind of their disgraceful conduct. As for those who were contemporaries of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who said, "Our hearts are uncovered" (ghulf), this is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us."﴾ [Fussilat: 5], meaning: they are veiled by coverings that prevent the effect of your call from reaching them, so they do not comprehend it. It is a metaphor drawn from the uncircumcised man (al-aghlaf alladhi lam yukhtan). ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾: Allah refuted that their hearts are like that, because they are capable of accepting the truth. Rather, He expelled them from His mercy because of their disbelief and deviation. This is like what He said in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿And for their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered." Rather, Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe except a little﴾ [al-Nisa': 155]. As for His saying, ﴿so little is it that they believe﴾, the "ma" is superfluous (zā'idah) for emphasis, meaning: their faith is little, they believe. And this is their belief in part of the Book.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 89:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying:

[89] ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah, confirming what was with them, and before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved; but when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.﴾

"And when there came to them a Book" is the Noble Qur'an, which is the purpose of this surah. He described it as guidance. Its indefiniteness (tankir) is for magnification. Describing it with "from Allah" is for honour. "Confirming what was with them" refers to the Torah. The answer (jawab) of "lamma" (when) is omitted, indicated by the answer of the second "lamma". Accordingly, His saying "and they had been" etc. is a clause coordinated with the conditional clause, a coordination of narrative upon narrative. It has been said that its answer is "they disbelieved." The second "lamma" is a repetition of the first, so it needs no answer. It has also been said that "they disbelieved" is the answer of both the first and the second, since what they require is one. On both views, the clause "and before that they had been" – that is, before its coming – "seeking victory over those who disbelieved" is a circumstantial clause (hal) conveying the completeness of their obstinacy and stubbornness. Al-istiftah (seeking opening/victory) means al-istinsar, i.e., seeking victory: they would ask Allah for victory over the polytheists, because they were humiliated in the Arabian Peninsula; for this reason they would form alliances with some tribes seeking strength through them, as has been mentioned earlier. "But when there came to them that which they recognized" – its truth and its veracity. It was their duty to hasten to faith in it, since they would thereby attain their wish at that time, which is their victory over the polytheists and the attainment of honour for them along with the believers. But "they disbelieved in it" – that is, they refrained from faith in it, fearing the loss of their leadership and their wealth, and they persisted in denial while knowing the reality of his prophethood. For this reason 'Abdullah ibn Salam said, in the account of his conversion (p-188): "O assembly of Jews, fear Allah! By Allah, other than whom there is no god, you indeed know that he is the Messenger of Allah, and that he came with truth." Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on the Hijrah.

He also related that when 'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Prophet (ﷺ), he came to him and said: "I am going to ask you about three things which none knows except a prophet." When he answered them, he said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah." We shall mention the hadith in its entirety, Allah willing, at His saying: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97] etc. As for His saying: ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾, the "al" in it is for specificity (al-'ahd), i.e., upon them; the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that the descent of the curse upon them is due to their disbelief, just as the "fa" (so) indicates its consequence upon it. Or it is for the genus, and they are included in the ruling primarily, since the discourse concerns them. Whichever it is, it confirms the content of His saying: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88].

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[90] ﴿Evil is that for which they have sold their souls: that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of resentment that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants. So they incurred wrath upon wrath. And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾

﴿Evil is that for which they have sold their souls﴾. "Mā" (what) is an indefinite noun described by what follows it, in the accusative as a specifier (*tamyīz*, a grammatical term meaning a noun that clarifies the vagueness of a preceding word), explaining the subject of *bi'sa* (evil is). The meaning is: evil is the thing for which they sold themselves and took it in exchange, being content with it and preferring it. The thing being condemned is His words: ﴿that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down﴾, meaning their disbelief in the Book that confirms what is with them, after recognising its truth. "Baghyan" (out of envy) means out of envy. "That Allah should send down" means because He sends down, or "that He should send down". That is, they envied Him for sending down ﴿of His bounty﴾, which is revelation, ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, meaning He wills and chooses him for prophethood. "So they incurred wrath" means they returned, because of this, with wrath, through their envy of this Prophet (ﷺ), to the point that they disbelieved in him. "Upon wrath" refers to the wrath they had deserved before his mission (ﷺ), because of their distorting of the words (of Scripture), their neglecting some of the rulings of the Torah, and their disbelief in Jesus, peace be upon him.

Al-Razi said: His wrath, exalted is He, increases and multiplies, and this is valid for it just as it is valid for punishment. So His wrath upon one who disbelieves in a single respect is not the same as His wrath upon one who disbelieves in many respects.

I say: In the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim), from Abu Hurayrah: "The wrath of Allah intensifies against one who claims to be the King of kings; there is no king but Allah." The reports describing His wrath, exalted is He, as severe against certain forbidden acts are abundant. See *al-Jami' al-Saghir* (a collection of hadith compiled by al-Suyuti).

The meaning may also allow another reading: they became deserving of a single, compounded wrath. The intention is then not to affirm two wraths for two distinct matters or multiple matters, but rather to emphasise and intensify the wrath, because this disbelief, though one, is grave. And Allah knows best.

We have already mentioned, in the commentary on His words ﴿not of those who have incurred wrath, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], that wrath is an attribute by which Allah described Himself. His wrath is not like our wrath, just as His essence is not like our essences. He is not similar to our bodies or our souls, and His attributes are like His essence. As for what is said, that wrath is one of the emotional states of the soul, so that it is said that we and our essences are affected by it, the fact that these are affections in us does not require that Allah be affected by them, just as His holy self is not like the essences of created beings. His attributes are likewise not like the attributes of created beings. The attribution of a created being's attribute to Him is like the attribution of the Creator's attribute to Him, yet the thing attributed is not like the thing it is attributed to, nor is the one to whom it is attributed like the one to whom it is attributed. As he (ﷺ) said: "You will see your Lord just as you see the sun and the moon." He compared the seeing with the seeing, not the seen with the seen.

This becomes clear through a principle: many people imagine that some attributes, or many of them, or most of them, or all of them, resemble the attributes of created beings. Then they wish to negate what they have understood, and they fall into four kinds of error:

First: that they make Him like what they understood from the texts concerning the attributes of created beings, and they assume that the meaning of the texts is anthropomorphism.

Second: that, having made this their understanding of the texts, they nullify them, so the texts remain void of what they indicate regarding affirming attributes fitting for Allah. This involves a wrong done to the texts and an evil assumption about Allah and His Messenger, since the meaning they assign contradicts what is understood from their words, namely the affirmation of Allah's attributes and divine meanings befitting the majesty of Allah, exalted is He.

Third: that they deny those attributes of Allah without any proof. Thus they nullify what the Lord, blessed and exalted, deserves.

Fourth: that they describe the Lord with the opposites of those attributes, drawn from the attributes of the dead, the inanimate, and the non-existent. Thus they nullify the attributes of perfection that the Lord deserves, and they liken Him to deficient and non-existent things. They nullify the texts from what they indicate of attributes, and they make their meaning the likening of Him to created things. So they combine in Allah, and in the words of Allah, both nullification (*ta'til*) and anthropomorphism (*tamthil*). Glory be to Him, exalted far above what the wrongdoers say. This is what Imam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, stated in *al-Qa'idah al-Tadmuriyyah*.

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾, meaning for them. The explicit mention (of disbelievers) in place of the pronoun indicates that their disbelief is the cause of what befell them. ﴿Is a humiliating punishment﴾, intended to humiliate them, meaning to abase them. Since their disbelief was caused by rebellion and envy, and the root of that is arrogance, they were repaid with humiliation and degradation in the Hereafter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [Ghafir: 60], meaning lowly and contemptible.

Discussion of the words of His Exalted Saying:

[91] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they reject what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were [truly] believers?"﴾

"And when it is said to them" — i.e., to the Jews — "Believe in what Allah has sent down" upon Muhammad (ﷺ), and affirm him and follow him. ﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us"⦆ — of the Torah — and they acknowledge nothing except it. "And they reject what is beyond it" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in "they say," with an implied subject (taqdīr mubtada'): i.e., they say what they say while they reject what comes after it. ﴿While it is the truth confirming what is with them﴾ — from it, not contradicting it. In this there is a refutation of their statement, for when they reject what agrees with the Torah, they have rejected the Torah itself. "Say" — as a rebuke to them, by demonstrating the contradiction between their words and their deeds. ﴿Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were [truly] believers?⦆ — i.e., if you were truthful in your claim to believe in what was sent down to you, then why did you kill the prophets who came to you confirming the Torah that is in your hands, while you knew their truthfulness? You killed them out of transgression, obstinacy, and arrogance toward the messengers of Allah. Thus you follow nothing but mere desires, opinions, and whims, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you grew arrogant, so a group you denied and a group you killed?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 87]. The address is to the Jews present and those who passed away, by way of taghlīb (attributing the act of the predecessors to the descendants), and since they shared in the covenant and the practice, objecting to their forefathers was an objection to their descendants. The verse indicates that disputation in religion is among the customs of the prophets, peace be upon them, and that presenting a contradiction to the opponent is permissible.

When He had shown their lie in claiming belief in what they did after Moses, He established another proof, stronger than what preceded it. For He did not enjoin upon them in the Torah what He enjoined upon them regarding monotheism and distance from association. This is in the copies that exist among them now. Yet they violated all of that by taking the calf in the days of Moses, in the presence of Aaron, peace be upon them both. So Allah, Exalted, said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[92] ﴿And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs. Then you took the calf [as a deity] after him, while you were wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And certainly Moses came to you with clear proofs﴾: from the signs such as the splitting of the sea, the sending down of the manna and the quails, and other decisive proofs that he was the Messenger of God and that there is no god but God. "Then you took the calf" as a deity besides God, "after him," i.e., after Moses had gone away from you to Mount Sinai to converse with God, Mighty and Majestic is He. As God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the people of Moses took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf: 148]. His words, Exalted is He, "while you were wrongdoers," i.e., by worshipping it, placing worship in other than its proper place; or by neglecting the rights of the signs of God, Exalted is He; or it is a parenthetical remark, i.e., "while you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing."

Then He mentioned another matter, which is clearer in showing their obstinacy and that they were governed by their desires, so He said:

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

(p-193) [93] ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mount, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination and listen." They said, "We hear and disobey." And they were given to drink into their hearts [the love of] the calf because of their disbelief. Say, "Wretched is that which your faith orders you to do, if you are believers."﴾

"And when We took your covenant" to belief and obedience. "And We raised above you the mount" saying "Take what We have given you" i.e., what you were commanded in the Torah, "with determination" with earnestness, "and listen" obey. "They said, 'We hear'" your words "and 'We disobey'" your command. The apparent context requires that they actually said this.

Abu Muslim said: It is possible that the meaning is: they heard it and met it with disobedience. So he expressed that by "saying," even though they did not say it, as in His saying, ﴿to it He says, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. ﴿And they were given to drink into their hearts the calf﴾, i.e., its love, by omitting the modified noun and placing the modified-to noun in its position for emphasis. Or "the calf" is a metaphor for its form, so there is no need to omit the modified noun. In either case, "ushribu" (they were given to drink) is a subsequent (tab'iyyah) metaphor, either from the dyeing of cloth with dye, i.e., it penetrates into it, or from giving water to drink, i.e., it penetrates to the depths of the body, and the common element is pervasion throughout every part. Attributing the verb to them creates an ambiguity about the place of the drinking. Then it is clarified by His saying "into their hearts" for emphasis, and thus the reason for deviating from what the apparent sense requires becomes clear, which is: "and their hearts were given to drink the calf." "Because of their disbelief" on account of their disbelief.

﴿Say, "Wretched is that which your faith orders you to do, if you are believers."﴾ i.e., as you claim, by the Torah. Attributing the command to their faith is mockery, as in the story of Shu'ayb: ﴿Does your prayer order you...?﴾ [Hud: 87] (p-194) and likewise the attribution of faith to them. His saying "if you are believers" is a challenge to the soundness of their claim, for faith only commands the worship of God alone, not associating partners with Him, since that is utmost folly. So this is the utmost mockery. The summary of the statement: if you are believers in it, acting upon what it states, in word and deed, then wretched is what your faith in it orders you to do. And since faith in it cannot permit such abominations, you are certainly not believers in it. Thus the answer to the conditional is omitted, as you see, due to what preceded indicating it.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[94] ﴿Say: "If the Last Abode with God is exclusively yours, to the exclusion of other people, then wish for death, if you are truthful."﴾

"Say" repeats the command to rebuke them, in order to expose another kind of their falsehoods. This is their claim that the Last Abode is exclusively theirs, to the exclusion of other people. But it was not related from them before the command to refute it; rather, it is alluded to within the discourse through His words: "If the Last Abode with God is exclusively yours," where "exclusively" (khalisah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "the Last Abode." What is meant is the Garden (al-Jannah), i.e., pure for you, belonging specifically to you, with no one other than you having any right in it, as you say: ﴿None will enter the Garden except those who are Jews﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. "To the exclusion of other people": the lam here is either for the genus or for a specific reference, and they are the Muslims. "Then wish for death": so ask for death. "If you are truthful": because whoever is certain that he is among the people of the Garden longs for it and wishes for the speedy arrival at bliss and deliverance from the abode of troubles, and there is no way to that except through death. Whatever the desired end depends upon must itself be desired, considering that it is a means to that desired end. What is meant by "wishing" here is the uttering of what indicates it, as we have pointed out, not merely its passing through the heart and the soul's inclination toward it, for that is not intended in a situation of argument, arenas of dispute, and positions of challenge, since it belongs to the hidden matters of the hearts. There is another explanation of "wishing" (p-195) that they be called to mutual cursing (mubahalah) and to supplication for death. Ibn Jarir went to this view. The first is closer to the wording.

And His words:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 95:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[95] ﴿And they will never wish for it, ever, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And they will never wish for it, ever﴾ is among the miracles, because it is a report of the unseen, and it occurred just as He reported it. Like His saying, ﴿And you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24]. "Because of what their hands have put forth" means because of what they have sent ahead of various kinds of disobedience. The "hand" is a metaphor for the self (nafs); He expressed by it the self, because it is among the limbs of the human being the locus of most of his works, and therefore wrongdoings committed by it are more numerous than by other limbs. The metaphor was not placed in the attribution (al-isnad), so that the meaning would be "what they sent forth with their hands," in order to include what they sent forth with the rest of the limbs. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., of them. It is a concluding addition (tadhyil) to the threat, and an alert that they are wrongdoers in claiming what is not theirs, and in denying it to others. A parallel to this verse in Surat al-Jumu'ah is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: O you who have Judaized, if you claim that you are allies of Allah to the exclusion of the rest of mankind, then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 6] ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have put forth. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 7].

Al-Ghazali has treated with subtlety the reason for using "lan" here and "la" in Surat al-Jumu'ah: the claim here is greater than the second, since the highest happiness is attaining the abode of reward, whereas the rank of wilayah (closeness/friendship with Allah), though noble, is only sought as a means to reach Paradise. Since the first claim is greater, God, exalted, refuted their statement with the word "lan," because it is the strongest of negating particles. And since the second claim is not at the utmost of greatness, He sufficed in refuting it with "la," because it is not at the extreme of strength in conveying the sense of negation. And Allah knows best.

When He, exalted, reported about them that they do not wish for death, He followed it with the statement that they are in the utmost eagerness for life, by His saying:

The discussion of His words, Exalted is He:

[96] ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life, and of those who associated others with God. One of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years, but being granted such a life will not remove him from the punishment. God is Seeing of what they do.﴾

﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾ The indefinite form *ḥayāh* (life) indicates that a particular kind of life is meant, namely a long-extended life. For this reason, the reading with it is more eloquent than the reading of Ubayy (ibn Ka'b): *ʿalā al-ḥayāh* (with the definite article). ﴿And of those who associated others with God﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to what precedes it in meaning. It is as if it were said: "more eager than people and than those who associated others with God." Singling them out for mention, although they are included among "people," serves to indicate that they are distinguished among them by the intensity of their eagerness. This is for the sake of intensifying the reproach of the Jews: since their eagerness, while they acknowledge recompense, is greater than the eagerness of the polytheists who deny it, this indicates their certainty of their destiny in the Fire. It is also permissible that the conjoined element is omitted, relying on the conjoined-to element to indicate it; that is, "and more eager than those who associated others with God."

As for permitting that the *wāw* is resumptive (*istiʾnāf*), with the speech complete at His words "for life," its estimation being "and of those who associated others with God [there are] people, one of whom wishes...", with the omission of the qualified noun, and the statement of Abu Muslim that there is inversion and reordering in the speech, its estimation being: "And you will surely find them, and a group of those who associated others with God, the most eager of people for life," and then he explained this desire with His words, "One of you wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years" — its remoteness is not hidden. For if the narrative concerns the Jews specifically, then what is most fitting to the outward meaning is that what is intended is: "And you will surely find the Jews the most eager of the rest of people for life, and of those who associated others with God," so that this is more decisive in refuting their claim and in showing the falsehood of their saying that the Last Abode belongs to us and not to others. And God knows best.

﴿One of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ This is an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, by way of resumption (*istiʾnāf*). The *law* here is verbal (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "that" (*an*), and what follows it is interpreted as a verbal noun, the object of *yawaddu* (wishes). That is: one of them wishes for the lengthening of a thousand years. ﴿And being granted such a life will not remove him from the punishment﴾ The *mā* is Hijazi (i.e., it functions like *laysa*, negating the predicate). The pronoun referring back to "one of them" is its subject, *bi-muzaḥziḥihi* is its predicate, the *bāʾ* is superfluous, and *an yuʿammara* (that he be granted a long life) is the agent of *muzaḥziḥihi*. That is: "and the one among them who wishes is not one who would remove him, i.e., push him away and save him, from the punishment by his being granted long life." The judge (al-Qadi) said: "What is intended is that it has no effect at all in removing the punishment. Had He said, 'and it is not one that would distance him or save him,' it would not indicate the slightness of the effect as this statement does." ﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾, so He will requite them for it.

What some exegetes have mentioned, that *al-baṣīr* in the language means *al-ʿalīm* (the All-Knowing), is not hidden in its corruption, for *al-ʿalīm* and *al-baṣīr* are two names differing in meaning linguistically. Indeed, if one were carried over to the other metaphorically, it would not be far-fetched, but there is no need for it here. The claim that some actions cannot be seen, and so this seeing is taken to mean knowledge, is an instance of analogizing the unseen to the seen, and it is self-evidently invalid. Shams al-Din ibn al-Qayyim al-Dimashqi said in *al-Kafiyah al-Shafiyah*:

He is the Seeing, who perceives the crawl of the black ant beneath the rock and the hard stone,
and perceives the channels of sustenance in its limbs, and sees the whiteness of its veins plainly,
and perceives the treacheries of eyes by their glance, and likewise perceives the turning of eyelids.

And His words, Exalted is He:

[p. 197]

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-198) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[97] ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ [98] ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]

Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih, in the Book of Tafsir, from Anas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in his land gathering dates. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I am going to ask you about three things, which no one knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And what causes a child to resemble its father or its mother?' He said: 'Jibril has just informed me of them.' He said: 'Jibril?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels.' Then he recited this verse: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart.﴾ [Then the Prophet said:] 'As for the first sign of the Hour, it is a fire that will gather the people from the east to the west. As for the first food of the people of Paradise, it is the extra piece of the fish's liver. And when a man's water precedes the woman's water, the child resembles the man, and when the woman's water precedes, the child resembles the woman.' He said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah. O Messenger of Allah! The Jews are a people of slander, and if they learn of my Islam before you ask them, they will slander me.' The Jews came, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'What sort of man is 'Abdullah among you?' They said: (p-199) 'He is our best and the son of our best, and our leader and the son of our leader.' He said: 'What do you think if 'Abdullah ibn Salam were to embrace Islam?' They said: 'May Allah protect him from that!' Then 'Abdullah came out and said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' They said: 'He is our worst and the son of our worst.' And they belittled him. He said: 'This is what I was afraid of, O Messenger of Allah.'"

Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, that he said: "A group of Jews came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, tell us about some matters which we will ask you about, which no one knows except a prophet.' He related something similar to what has preceded. Its completion: They said: 'You are now [the one who knows], so tell us who your guardian (wali) among the angels is, for then we will either join you or part from you.' He said: 'My guardian is Jibril, and Allah has never sent a prophet except that he was his guardian.' They said: 'Then we part from you. If your guardian were someone else among the angels, we would have followed you and believed you.' He said: 'Then what prevented you from believing him?' They said: 'He is our enemy.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ up to His words: ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. Thereupon they returned with anger upon anger."

In a narration of Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i concerning the story: "Then tell us who your companion is.' He said: 'Jibril, peace be upon him.' They said: 'Jibril! That is the one who descends with war, fighting and punishment; he is our enemy. If you had said Mika'il, who descends with mercy, rain and plants, then it would have been [acceptable].' So Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ to the end of the verse."

It is understood from other narrations that the reason for their saying this was a debate that took place between them and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi, who said: "'Umar arrived at al-Rawha, and he saw men hastening to stones and praying towards them. He said: 'What are these?' They said: 'They claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed here.' He disliked that and said: 'Which is it? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was overtaken by the prayer in a valley and prayed there, then he departed and left it.' Then he began to speak to them, and said: 'I used to attend the Jews on the day of their study (midras), and I was amazed at how the Torah confirms the Furqan (the Criterion, i.e., the Qur'an), and how the Furqan confirms (p-200) the Torah! One day while I was with them, they said: 'O Ibn al-Khattab! None of your companions is more beloved to us than you.' I said: 'Why is that?' They said: 'Because you visit us and come to us.' I said: 'I come to you, and I am amazed at how the Furqan confirms the Torah, and how the Torah confirms the Furqan.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then passed by, and they said: 'O Ibn al-Khattab! That is your companion, so go to him.' I said to them then: 'I beseech you by Allah, besides whom there is no god, and by what He has entrusted you with of His right, and by what He has deposited with you of His Book: Do you know that he is the Messenger of Allah?' He said: They fell silent. Their scholar and elder said to them: 'He has indeed insisted upon you, so answer him.' They said: 'You are our scholar and our leader, so you answer him.' He said: 'As you have adjured us by Him, we know that he is the Messenger of Allah.' I said: 'Woe to you! Then you have perished.' They said: 'We have not perished.' I said: 'How is that, when you know that he is the Messenger of Allah, and yet you do not follow him or believe him?' They said: 'We have an enemy among the angels, and a peaceful one among the angels, and our enemy has been paired with him.' I said: 'Who is your enemy, and who is your peaceful one?' They said: 'Our enemy is Jibril, and our peaceful one is Mika'il.' I said: 'And why have you taken Jibril as an enemy, and why have you made peace with Mika'il?' They said: 'Jibril is the angel of harshness, severity, hardship, stringency, punishment and the like. And Mika'il is the angel of compassion, mercy, ease and the like.' I said: 'And what is their station with their Lord?' They said: 'One of them is on His right and the other on His left.' I said: 'By Allah, besides whom there is no god, indeed they and whoever is between them are an enemy to whoever is an enemy to them, and a peace to whoever makes peace with them. It is not fitting for Jibril to make peace with the enemy of Mika'il, nor for Mika'il to make peace with the enemy of Jibril.' Then I rose and followed the Prophet ﷺ, and I caught up with him as he was leaving a date-palm garden belonging to Banu Fulan. He said to me: 'O Ibn al-Khattab, shall I not recite to you verses that have been revealed?' Then he recited to me: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾ until he recited the verses. I said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah! By the One who sent you with the truth, I came intending to inform you of the news, but the Subtle, the All-Aware, had already preceded me to you with the news.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim also related it in abridged form, and in it there is a break in the chain (inqita'), for al-Sha'bi did not live to see the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. So said the Hafiz Ibn Kathir. Al-Wahidi also related it, and added at its end: 'Umar said: "I found myself in the religion of Allah harder than a stone."

The 'Allamah al-Biqa'i said: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh also related this hadith in his Musnad, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Our shaykh al-Busayri said: It is mursal with a sound chain, ended.

There are various narrations which Ibn Kathir cited in his Tafsir, which we will not lengthen our book by listing; their source is one. If it is said: There is a contradiction between the first narration of al-Bukhari and what follows it, the answer is: There is no contradiction, because his ﷺ recitation of it during the dialogue with 'Abdullah ibn Salam, in response to the words of the Jews, does not necessitate that it was revealed at that time. The relied-upon occasion of revelation is other than the story of 'Abdullah ibn Salam among the narrations that have preceded, for their chains strengthen one another. It seems that when 'Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: "Indeed Jibril is an enemy of the Jews," the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse to him, reminding him of its occasion of revelation. So said the Hafiz Ibn Hajar in al-Fath.

Al-Suyuti also pointed to this in al-Itqan, where he said: "Note: It may be that in one of the two stories ('fa-talā', he recited) the narrator erred and said ('fa-yanzilu', so it descends)."

The 'Allamah Wali Allah al-Dahlawi, may his secret be sanctified, said in his book Usul al-Tafsir: "It has become clear to this poor servant that the Companions and the Successors often used to say: 'This verse was revealed concerning such and such,' and their purpose seems to be to depict what the verse applies to, and to mention some of the events which the verse includes by its generality, whether the story preceded or came later, whether it was Israelite, pre-Islamic or Islamic, and whether it encompassed all the conditions of the verse or some of them. And Allah knows best."

From this verification it is known that ijtihad (independent reasoning) has a place in this category, and that the multiple stories there have breadth. Whoever keeps this point in mind will be able to resolve what has been disputed about the occasions of revelation with little effort. Ended.

As for His words, Exalted is He, "li-Jibril": it is read in the seven canonical readings with a kasra on the jim and the ra without a hamza, and with a fatha on the jim without it as well, and with a fatha on the jim and ra, a kasra on a hamza, then a ya, with or without it. Ibn Jinni said: When the Arabs pronounce a foreign word, they alter it.

(p-202) As for His words, "fa-innahu nazzalahu": it is a causal explanation standing in place of the response to the condition (sharṭ). The first pronoun refers to Jibril, peace be upon him, and the second refers to the Qur'an. It has been left implicit without prior mention, to signal the magnitude of its status and its being sufficiently known, owing to its complete fame and renown, especially when some of its attributes are mentioned. As for His words, "upon your heart," it is an added confirmation of the revelation, by specifying the locus of the revelation, for the heart is the first recipient of it, if by 'heart' is meant the spirit (rūḥ). And the place of understanding and memorization if by it is meant the organ. This is like His words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193] ﴿upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 194]. The proper wording would have been "upon my heart," since that matches "Say," but it came in the form of quoting Allah's speech as He spoke it, to affirm that it is the speech of Allah, and that it is a command to convey it. As for His words, "by the permission of Allah," it means: by His command. As for His words, "confirming what came before it," it means: from the Torah and the rest of the revealed scriptures. As for His words, "and as guidance and good tidings for the believers," it means: it guides to rectitude and gives them good tidings of Paradise, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and healing﴾ [Fussilat: 44], and He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. In this there is a refutation of the Jews, who said that Jibril descends with war and severity, as has preceded. So it was said: He descends also with guidance and good tidings.

If it is said: It is a requirement of the condition and the response that they be connected by causation and sequence, so how is His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" acceptable as a response to the condition? It is answered: His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is a causal explanation of the response to the condition, as we have mentioned. The meaning: Whoever among the People of the Book is hostile to Jibril, there is no basis for his hostility; rather it is obligatory for him to love him, for he has brought down to you a Book (p-203) confirming their books. If they were fair, they would love him and thank him for his favour in bringing down what benefits them and corrects what was revealed to them. It has also been said: The response is omitted, and its estimate is "let him die of rage." In that case "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is not a substitute for it. Its aspect is that the response is estimated as delayed after His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu," and that this is an explanation of the cause of the enmity, as if it were said: Whoever is hostile to him, because he has brought it down upon your heart, let him die of rage.

Al-Radi said: The fa is often placed before a cause and carries the meaning of the lam (of causation). Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿He said: Then get out of it, for indeed you are accursed﴾ [al-Hijr: 34].
