The name appears in the Seven (canonical readings) as "Mika-il" with the pattern of "mizan," and as "Mikail" with a kasra-marked hamza after the alif without a ya', and as "Mika'il" with the hamza and the ya'.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verses 97–98 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-198) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[97] ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah, confirming what came before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers.﴾ [98] ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]

Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih, in the Book of Tafsir, from Anas, who said: "'Abdullah ibn Salam heard of the arrival of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was in his land gathering dates. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'I am going to ask you about three things, which no one knows except a prophet: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food of the people of Paradise? And what causes a child to resemble its father or its mother?' He said: 'Jibril has just informed me of them.' He said: 'Jibril?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels.' Then he recited this verse: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart.﴾ [Then the Prophet said:] 'As for the first sign of the Hour, it is a fire that will gather the people from the east to the west. As for the first food of the people of Paradise, it is the extra piece of the fish's liver. And when a man's water precedes the woman's water, the child resembles the man, and when the woman's water precedes, the child resembles the woman.' He said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah. O Messenger of Allah! The Jews are a people of slander, and if they learn of my Islam before you ask them, they will slander me.' The Jews came, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'What sort of man is 'Abdullah among you?' They said: (p-199) 'He is our best and the son of our best, and our leader and the son of our leader.' He said: 'What do you think if 'Abdullah ibn Salam were to embrace Islam?' They said: 'May Allah protect him from that!' Then 'Abdullah came out and said: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' They said: 'He is our worst and the son of our worst.' And they belittled him. He said: 'This is what I was afraid of, O Messenger of Allah.'"

Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse, that he said: "A group of Jews came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'O Abu al-Qasim, tell us about some matters which we will ask you about, which no one knows except a prophet.' He related something similar to what has preceded. Its completion: They said: 'You are now [the one who knows], so tell us who your guardian (wali) among the angels is, for then we will either join you or part from you.' He said: 'My guardian is Jibril, and Allah has never sent a prophet except that he was his guardian.' They said: 'Then we part from you. If your guardian were someone else among the angels, we would have followed you and believed you.' He said: 'Then what prevented you from believing him?' They said: 'He is our enemy.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ up to His words: ﴿if they only knew﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. Thereupon they returned with anger upon anger."

In a narration of Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i concerning the story: "Then tell us who your companion is.' He said: 'Jibril, peace be upon him.' They said: 'Jibril! That is the one who descends with war, fighting and punishment; he is our enemy. If you had said Mika'il, who descends with mercy, rain and plants, then it would have been [acceptable].' So Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril﴾ to the end of the verse."

It is understood from other narrations that the reason for their saying this was a debate that took place between them and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Jarir related from al-Sha'bi, who said: "'Umar arrived at al-Rawha, and he saw men hastening to stones and praying towards them. He said: 'What are these?' They said: 'They claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed here.' He disliked that and said: 'Which is it? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was overtaken by the prayer in a valley and prayed there, then he departed and left it.' Then he began to speak to them, and said: 'I used to attend the Jews on the day of their study (midras), and I was amazed at how the Torah confirms the Furqan (the Criterion, i.e., the Qur'an), and how the Furqan confirms (p-200) the Torah! One day while I was with them, they said: 'O Ibn al-Khattab! None of your companions is more beloved to us than you.' I said: 'Why is that?' They said: 'Because you visit us and come to us.' I said: 'I come to you, and I am amazed at how the Furqan confirms the Torah, and how the Torah confirms the Furqan.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then passed by, and they said: 'O Ibn al-Khattab! That is your companion, so go to him.' I said to them then: 'I beseech you by Allah, besides whom there is no god, and by what He has entrusted you with of His right, and by what He has deposited with you of His Book: Do you know that he is the Messenger of Allah?' He said: They fell silent. Their scholar and elder said to them: 'He has indeed insisted upon you, so answer him.' They said: 'You are our scholar and our leader, so you answer him.' He said: 'As you have adjured us by Him, we know that he is the Messenger of Allah.' I said: 'Woe to you! Then you have perished.' They said: 'We have not perished.' I said: 'How is that, when you know that he is the Messenger of Allah, and yet you do not follow him or believe him?' They said: 'We have an enemy among the angels, and a peaceful one among the angels, and our enemy has been paired with him.' I said: 'Who is your enemy, and who is your peaceful one?' They said: 'Our enemy is Jibril, and our peaceful one is Mika'il.' I said: 'And why have you taken Jibril as an enemy, and why have you made peace with Mika'il?' They said: 'Jibril is the angel of harshness, severity, hardship, stringency, punishment and the like. And Mika'il is the angel of compassion, mercy, ease and the like.' I said: 'And what is their station with their Lord?' They said: 'One of them is on His right and the other on His left.' I said: 'By Allah, besides whom there is no god, indeed they and whoever is between them are an enemy to whoever is an enemy to them, and a peace to whoever makes peace with them. It is not fitting for Jibril to make peace with the enemy of Mika'il, nor for Mika'il to make peace with the enemy of Jibril.' Then I rose and followed the Prophet ﷺ, and I caught up with him as he was leaving a date-palm garden belonging to Banu Fulan. He said to me: 'O Ibn al-Khattab, shall I not recite to you verses that have been revealed?' Then he recited to me: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Jibril, then indeed he has brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾ until he recited the verses. I said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah! By the One who sent you with the truth, I came intending to inform you of the news, but the Subtle, the All-Aware, had already preceded me to you with the news.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim also related it in abridged form, and in it there is a break in the chain (inqita'), for al-Sha'bi did not live to see the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. So said the Hafiz Ibn Kathir. Al-Wahidi also related it, and added at its end: 'Umar said: "I found myself in the religion of Allah harder than a stone."

The 'Allamah al-Biqa'i said: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh also related this hadith in his Musnad, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Our shaykh al-Busayri said: It is mursal with a sound chain, ended.

There are various narrations which Ibn Kathir cited in his Tafsir, which we will not lengthen our book by listing; their source is one. If it is said: There is a contradiction between the first narration of al-Bukhari and what follows it, the answer is: There is no contradiction, because his ﷺ recitation of it during the dialogue with 'Abdullah ibn Salam, in response to the words of the Jews, does not necessitate that it was revealed at that time. The relied-upon occasion of revelation is other than the story of 'Abdullah ibn Salam among the narrations that have preceded, for their chains strengthen one another. It seems that when 'Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: "Indeed Jibril is an enemy of the Jews," the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse to him, reminding him of its occasion of revelation. So said the Hafiz Ibn Hajar in al-Fath.

Al-Suyuti also pointed to this in al-Itqan, where he said: "Note: It may be that in one of the two stories ('fa-talā', he recited) the narrator erred and said ('fa-yanzilu', so it descends)."

The 'Allamah Wali Allah al-Dahlawi, may his secret be sanctified, said in his book Usul al-Tafsir: "It has become clear to this poor servant that the Companions and the Successors often used to say: 'This verse was revealed concerning such and such,' and their purpose seems to be to depict what the verse applies to, and to mention some of the events which the verse includes by its generality, whether the story preceded or came later, whether it was Israelite, pre-Islamic or Islamic, and whether it encompassed all the conditions of the verse or some of them. And Allah knows best."

From this verification it is known that ijtihad (independent reasoning) has a place in this category, and that the multiple stories there have breadth. Whoever keeps this point in mind will be able to resolve what has been disputed about the occasions of revelation with little effort. Ended.

As for His words, Exalted is He, "li-Jibril": it is read in the seven canonical readings with a kasra on the jim and the ra without a hamza, and with a fatha on the jim without it as well, and with a fatha on the jim and ra, a kasra on a hamza, then a ya, with or without it. Ibn Jinni said: When the Arabs pronounce a foreign word, they alter it.

(p-202) As for His words, "fa-innahu nazzalahu": it is a causal explanation standing in place of the response to the condition (sharṭ). The first pronoun refers to Jibril, peace be upon him, and the second refers to the Qur'an. It has been left implicit without prior mention, to signal the magnitude of its status and its being sufficiently known, owing to its complete fame and renown, especially when some of its attributes are mentioned. As for His words, "upon your heart," it is an added confirmation of the revelation, by specifying the locus of the revelation, for the heart is the first recipient of it, if by 'heart' is meant the spirit (rūḥ). And the place of understanding and memorization if by it is meant the organ. This is like His words: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193] ﴿upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 194]. The proper wording would have been "upon my heart," since that matches "Say," but it came in the form of quoting Allah's speech as He spoke it, to affirm that it is the speech of Allah, and that it is a command to convey it. As for His words, "by the permission of Allah," it means: by His command. As for His words, "confirming what came before it," it means: from the Torah and the rest of the revealed scriptures. As for His words, "and as guidance and good tidings for the believers," it means: it guides to rectitude and gives them good tidings of Paradise, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: It is for those who believe a guidance and healing﴾ [Fussilat: 44], and He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Isra': 82]. In this there is a refutation of the Jews, who said that Jibril descends with war and severity, as has preceded. So it was said: He descends also with guidance and good tidings.

If it is said: It is a requirement of the condition and the response that they be connected by causation and sequence, so how is His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" acceptable as a response to the condition? It is answered: His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is a causal explanation of the response to the condition, as we have mentioned. The meaning: Whoever among the People of the Book is hostile to Jibril, there is no basis for his hostility; rather it is obligatory for him to love him, for he has brought down to you a Book (p-203) confirming their books. If they were fair, they would love him and thank him for his favour in bringing down what benefits them and corrects what was revealed to them. It has also been said: The response is omitted, and its estimate is "let him die of rage." In that case "fa-innahu nazzalahu" is not a substitute for it. Its aspect is that the response is estimated as delayed after His saying "fa-innahu nazzalahu," and that this is an explanation of the cause of the enmity, as if it were said: Whoever is hostile to him, because he has brought it down upon your heart, let him die of rage.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 99:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[99] ﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ That is, We have sent down to you manifest signs (ʿalamat, plural of ʿalamah) indicating your prophethood. These signs are what the Qur'an contains of the hidden secrets of the knowledge of the Jews and the concealed contents of the inner reality of their reports, and the reports of their predecessors from the Children of Israel, and the information about what their books contained, which none knew except their rabbis (aḥbar) and scholars (ʿulamaʾ), and what their earlier and later generations distorted and altered from their rulings that were in the Torah. God thus disclosed these in His Book, which He sent down upon His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and so in that there was a clear sign from Him for whoever was fair with himself and whom envy and rebellion did not drive to destroy them. For it is in the nature of everyone with a sound disposition that he affirms one who brings the like of the clear signs that Muhammad ﷺ brought, which I have described, without having learned them from any human being or taken anything from any mortal.

Interpreting the signs as the verses of the glorious Qur'an, as we have mentioned, is preferable to interpreting them as the other transmitted miracles, because when "signs" is connected to "revelation" (tanzil), they are more specific to the Qur'an. His saying "and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient" means: the rebellious among the disbelievers. The lam is for specification (al-ʿahd), meaning the particular defiantly disobedient ones, namely the Jews. Or it is for the genus (al-jins), and they are included in it as the first and foremost of them.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 100:

(p-205) The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted, words:

[100] ﴿Is it not that every time they make a covenant, a party among them casts it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.﴾

﴿Is it not that every time they make a covenant, a party among them casts it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.﴾ The hamza is for censure (inkar), and the waw is for conjunction (ʿatf) over an omitted element required by the context, i.e., "They disbelieved in the signs, the clear proofs, and whenever they make a covenant..." etc. Or: "Do they deny their wickedness, and whenever..." etc. It has been said: the waw is extra (ziyada). It has also been said: it is the "aw" meaning "one of two things," vocalized with a fatha. It has been read irregularly (shadh) with a sukun, so that it means "bal" (rather), indicated by the context, namely His words: ﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾, as an escalation from the more severe to the most severe. Ibn Jinni said: this "aw" is the one that means the disjunctive "am" (disconnected "or"), and both are widely found in speech with the meaning of "bal." al-Farra' cited the verse of Dhu al-Rumma:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brilliance of the forenoon, and her form, or you are more beautiful in the eye."

He said the same regarding His words: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they exceed﴾ [al-Saffat: 147]. According to the first view, the purpose of this interrogation is censure and magnifying what they are undertaking, because when something like this is said in this form, it is more eloquent in rebuke and reproach.

By His words "Is it not that every time they make a covenant," it indicates a covenant after a covenant that they broke and cast aside. Rather, it indicates that this is customary among them. It is as if He, the Exalted, intended to console the Messenger over their disbelief in what was revealed to him of the signs, that this is not a novelty from them; rather it is their disposition, their custom, and the custom of their predecessors, as He explained in the preceding verses concerning their breaking of covenants and pacts, state after state. For one who is habituated to this way, it is not difficult for the soul to oppose it, unlike one whose custom has not been this.

The scholar (al-ʿAllama) said: The Jews are branded with treachery and breaking covenants. How often did God take a covenant from them and from their forefathers, and they broke it; and how often did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) make covenants with them, and they did not fulfill them: ﴿those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time﴾ [al-Anfal: 56]. Nabdh means throwing away the pledge and abandoning it. Attributing it to "a party among them" is because some of them did not cast it aside. And His words "Rather, most of them do not believe" serve to repel what might be imagined, namely that those who cast it aside are the minority. His, the Exalted, words:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[101] ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾

﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾ This is an explicit statement of what was alluded to before. Their casting aside of the covenants which Allah had taken from them, to hold fast to them and to uphold their rights, led them to deny the Messenger sent to them and to all mankind, whose description is in their Books, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and so on. The indefinite form of "a Messenger" (rasul) is for glorification (tafkhim). The prepositional phrase following it is connected either to "came" (ja'a), or to an omitted element that serves as a qualifier of "a Messenger," in order to add further magnification to him, by reinforcing the inherent grandeur conveyed by the indefinite form with the grandeur of attribution (idafa). His saying "the Book of Allah" means the Torah, because by their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah, who confirms what is with them, they are disbelievers in it and casters of it aside. It has also been said that "the Book of Allah" is the Qur'an, which they cast aside after it had become binding upon them to receive it with acceptance. His saying "behind their backs" is a metaphor for their abandonment of it and their turning away from it, rendered by the image of something thrown behind the back, indicating disregard for it and little regard for it. His saying "as if they did not know" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), meaning: they cast it behind their backs, resembling those who do not know it. If by "them" is meant their rabbis, then the meaning is: as if they did not know it with certainty, and did not recognise what it contains of the proofs of his prophethood ﷺ. In this there is an indication that their knowledge of it is firm, but they feign ignorance. Or: as if they did not know that it is the Book of Allah, or did not know at all, as is the case if the whole people is intended.

In these two interpretations there is an added intensification of their turning away from what is in the Torah of the proofs of prophethood. As for this, if by what they cast aside of the Book of Allah is meant the Qur'an, then the knowledge negated in "as if they did not know" is the knowledge that it is the Book of Allah. In this there is, as in the first interpretation, an indication that they are certain of this, and that they disbelieve in it only out of obstinacy and defiance. His, Exalted, saying:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 1 of 2)**

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[102] ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic, and [they followed] what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Yet they [the two] did not teach anyone until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." And they learned from them that by which they might cause separation between a man and his wife. But they could not harm anyone thereby except by Allah's permission. And they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. How wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they had known.﴾

﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon. Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾ is a narration of another kind of their deviation and misguidance, following their rejection of the Book of Allah and their acting upon what lay before them. It is their following what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon, namely magic and disbelief. He only attained that kingdom through his knowledge of magic. They went further and attributed to him apostasy and disbelief, for reasons they fabricated against him. Allah, exalted is He, cleared him of this slander and invention, and attached disbelief to those devils who mislead minds and understandings by teaching magic and sleight of hand, by ascribing influence to other than the Creator, glory be to Him, by barring from the path of truth, and by seeking to make it crooked.

"Tatlu" (تَتْلُو) here means "relates" and "narrates," from tilawa (التِّلاوَةُ), which is recitation. Or it means "lies" and "fabricates," which is the view of Abu Muslim, who said: it is said "talā 'alayhi" when one lies, and "talā 'anhu" when one speaks the truth. Likewise al-Raghib said in his tafsir: "talā 'alayhi" means he lied against him, like "rawā 'alayhi," and [the Qur'an says] "and they speak against Allah the lie." He also said: the verse is linked to what was mentioned earlier about the Jews, and it contains two matters: the censure of the Jews for their pursuit of magic and their preference for it, and the exoneration of Solomon, peace be upon him, from what they attributed to him and fabricated against him, end of quote.

This is because they claimed that Solomon, peace be upon him, apostatized at the end of his life, worshipped idols, and built temples for them, as you see in chapter eleven of the Third Book of Kings. Behold this great audacity and this immense impudence. When the wise among the later People of the Book became aware of such lies, they acknowledged that not every statement contained in their sacred books is inspired; rather, some of them were written in the manner of historians, meaning without inspiration, as in *Izhar al-Haqq* (Manifestation of the Truth). By "the devils" is meant the devils of mankind, namely the rebellious, sinful, wicked, powerful ones who call to falsehood.

His saying "over the kingdom of Solomon" means: during the time of his reign, [they followed] those fabricated tales told about him. His saying, exalted is He, "Solomon did not disbelieve" is a declaration of his innocence, peace be upon him, from apostasy, polytheism, and the worship of idols that they attributed to him, and a refutation of whoever invented those claims. Many [scholars] said: this is an exoneration from magic, and that Allah, exalted is He, referred to magic as disbelief to show that it is disbelief, and that whoever is a prophet is protected from it. It is disbelief because it involves turning toward the celestial spheres and the devils, worshipping them, and believing that they have influence apart from Allah, exalted is He.

(p-209) The first meaning is clearer and more evident.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾ refers by "the devils" to those we mentioned before, namely the wicked among mankind and their evil ones, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they go alone to their devils, they say: "We are with you"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], and His saying: ﴿devils of mankind and jinn, inspiring one another with ornate speech﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. What specifies this meaning is His saying "tatlu," because the recitation of the devils of the jinn is not heard by anyone, and the meaning of "tatlu" is "relates," as already explained. His saying "teaching people magic" also specifies this meaning, since no one learns magic except from the devils of mankind. By His saying "disbelieved" is meant their disbelief in the revealed signs of Allah, or their worship of other than Him, or their disbelief in using magic and trickery, to conceal the truth and cover the insight [of people]. The clause "teaching people magic" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya) relating to the pronoun in "disbelieved," or a second predicate of "but" (lakinna), or a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyya). This is on the assumption that the pronoun refers to the devils. As for the assumption that it refers back to the subject of "followed," then it is either a circumstantial clause relating to that subject or a resumptive clause.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [they followed] what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. Yet they did not teach anyone until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." And they learned from them that by which they might cause separation between a man and his wife. But they could not harm anyone thereby except by Allah's permission. And they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. How wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they had known.﴾

Know that the scholars have many opinions and numerous views on this verse. Some of them took the approach of the traditionists (akhbāriyyūn), who transmit both the worthless and the valuable. Some of them clung to its literal sense and strained to resolve what troubled them, while the correct meaning would have made them independent of that. Others claimed that there is inversion (taqdīm and ta'khīr) in it and that its last part refers back to its first part, thereby making it more like riddles and enigmas, from which the explanation of the most eloquent speech is exalted. And other than that, of what the one who investigates what has been written about it would see.

What the verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn) have held is that Harut and Marut were two men who displayed righteousness and piety in Babylon, which is a city in Iraq on the Euphrates River. They used to teach people magic. The people's good opinion of them reached the point that they thought they were two angels from heaven, and what they taught people was by revelation from Allah. The deceit of these two men, and their preserving the people's belief in their goodness, reached the point that they began to say to everyone who wished to learn from them: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve," meaning: we are only people of a trial, testing you and examining you, whether you will be grateful or ungrateful, and we advise you not to disbelieve. They said this to make people think that their knowledge was divine, their craft was spiritual, and that they intended only good. Just as the charlatans of this age do, saying to those they teach writing for love and hatred according to their claims: "We advise you not to write to bring a married woman to a man other than her husband," and other such illusions and fabrications.

The Jews have many superstitions about this. They even believe that magic was sent down to these two from Allah, and that they were two angels who came to teach it to people. So the Qur'an came refuting them in their claim that it was sent down from heaven, and condemning magic and whoever learns or teaches it. He said: ﴿They taught people magic and what was sent down to the two angels﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. Here "mā" is a negation particle, according to the most correct opinion. The term "the two angels" here is used according to the custom prevailing among people at that time, just as the names of gods of good and evil appear in the writings of authors on the history of the Greeks, the Egyptians, and others, and just as the Muslim, in refuting the Christians, mentions the incarnation of God and His crucifixion, even though he does not believe in them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they learned from them that by which they might cause separation between a man and his wife﴾ is by way of illustration and showing the matter in its most ugly form. That is, what they learned of the kinds of tricks and methods of corruption reached the point that they could, through it, cause separation between the greatest of unions: such as a man and his wife.

The summary: the meaning of the verse from its beginning to its end is as follows: the Jews denied the Qur'an (p-211) and cast it behind their backs, and substituted for it the fables and superstitions they heard from their wicked ones about Solomon and his kingdom. They claimed that he disbelieved, but he did not disbelieve. Rather, their devils were the ones who disbelieved, and they began to teach people magic, and claimed that it was sent down to Harut and Marut, whom they called angels, though nothing was sent down to them. They were only two men who claimed righteousness to such a degree that they made people think they intended only good and warned them against disbelief. The matter of what they learned from them reached the point of tricks and cunning: they cause separation by it between those who are united, and untie by it the knots of those who are bound together. Thus you see from this that the whole context is for censure, so it is not correct for praise of Harut and Marut to appear in it. What shows the soundness of what we have said about them is that the Qur'an denied that any angel descends to the earth to teach people anything from Allah other than revelation to the prophets, and it explicitly stated that Allah sends none but humans to teach their own kind. He said: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Anbiya': 7]. And He said, rebuking those who asked for an angel to be sent down: ﴿And they said, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would not be reprieved﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. And He said in Surat al-Furqan: ﴿And they said, "What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why was not an angel sent down to him to be a warner with him?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 7] down to His saying: ﴿So they went astray, and they cannot find a way﴾ [al-Furqan: 9].

The storytellers (quṣṣāṣ) have wondrous tales about Harut and Marut. They claimed that they were two of the angels, and that when they saw what the people of the earth did of sins, they denounced it, considered it great, and invoked [curses] upon the people of the earth. So Allah, exalted is He, revealed to them: "If I tested you with what I tested the children of Adam with of desires, you would disobey Me." They said: "O Lord, if You tested us we would not do it; so test us." So He sent them down to the earth, and Allah tested them with the desires of the children of Adam (p-212). They stayed in a town where there was a fornicating woman called "al-Zuhra," and they invited her to fornication and had intercourse with her after they drank wine, killed a soul, and prostrated to an idol. They taught her the Greatest Name, by which they used to ascend to heaven, so the woman spoke with that name and ascended to heaven, and Allah, exalted is He, transformed her and made her into this star called Venus. Then Allah, exalted is He, made Harut and Marut aware of the ugliness of what they had done, then gave them the choice between the punishment of the Hereafter, which is deferred, and the punishment of this world, which is immediate. They chose the punishment of this world, so He placed them upside down in a well at Babylon until the Day of Resurrection, and they teach people magic and call to it, and no one sees them except one who goes to that place specifically to learn magic.

This story is a fabrication and invention of the Jews. The Qur'an never mentioned it at all. It was mentioned in the Talmud, as is known from consulting "Midrash Yidkut" (Midrash Yedikot) in chapter thirty-three, and foolish storytellers among the Muslims followed suit and took it from there.

Al-Razi said in his tafsir: the story that they mentioned is false in several respects:

The first: they mentioned in the story that Allah, exalted is He, said to them (that is, to Harut and Marut): "If I tested you with what I tested the children of Adam with, you would disobey Me." They said: "If You did that to us, O Lord, we would not disobey You." This is from them a denial of Allah, exalted is He, and an ascription of ignorance to Him, and that is clear disbelief.

The second: they were given the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and that is corrupt. Rather, the more proper thing would be that they be given the choice between repentance and punishment, and Allah, exalted is He, gave that choice to whoever associated partners with Him throughout his life and went to great lengths in harming His prophets.

The third: among the most astonishing matters is their saying that they teach magic while they are being punished and calling to it, while they are being chastised.

Thus, Imam Abu Muslim also argued against the validity of the descent of magic upon them with several arguments.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 2 of 2):

The first: If magic had been sent down to the two angels, then its sender would be Allah, and that is impermissible, because magic is disbelief and futility, and it is not fitting for Allah the Exalted to send such a thing down.
[p-213] The second: His saying, ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾, indicates that teaching magic is disbelief. So if it were established that the angels teach magic, disbelief would be necessary for them, and that is false.
The third: Just as it is not permissible for the prophets to be sent to teach magic, the same applies to the angels, all the more so.
The fourth: Magic is attributed only to the disbelievers, the sinners and the rebellious devils. How could something be attributed to Allah that He forbids and threatens with punishment? Is magic anything other than falsehood disguised as truth? Allah's customary way is to nullify it, as He said in the story of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿What you have brought is sorcery; Allah will surely nullify it﴾ [Yunus: 81]. End of quotation.

Al-Razi has cited what Abu Muslim favoured in the interpretation of this verse, but we did not wish to transmit it, because it is far from the correct view. Likewise what Imam Ibn Hazm mentioned in his book (al-Fasl) under the topic (the infallibility of the angels) contains strained and peculiar far-fetched reasoning, as can be known by consulting the two works.

Al-Raghib al-Isfahani offers possibilities for making the story sound, and strange permissions that turn away from the clear truth which we preferred to transmit first from some of the verifying scholars. And Allah knows best.

Know that the word sihr (magic), in the usage of the Shari'ah, is specific to every matter whose cause is hidden, which is imagined to be other than its reality, and which operates as deception and trickery. Whenever it is used without qualification, it conveys blame for its practitioner. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116], meaning they deceived them until they thought that their ropes and staffs were moving. It may also be used qualified in a context of praise and commendation, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Amr ibn Ahtam: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence," because its practitioner clarifies a difficult matter and reveals its reality through fine exposition and eloquent expression. In sum, unqualified sihr is nothing but imagination through sleight of hand that diverts the sights, or a decorated murmuring that obstructs the hearing. It does not change the realities of things, nor does it transform their forms.

As for His saying, ﴿and they could not harm anyone with it except by the permission of Allah﴾, al-Raghib said: "Idhn (permission) may be used for informing about a concession, it may be used for knowledge, from which comes 'I informed him of such-and-such,' and it may be used for a binding command. It should be known that permission from Allah the Exalted regarding a thing is of two kinds:
One of them: permission for the one intending the act to carry it out directly, like your saying: 'Allah has permitted you to maintain the ties of kinship.'
The second: permission regarding the subjugation of a thing, in the manner that poison is subjugated to killing the one who consumes it, and an antidote is subjugated to rescuing him from its harm. So Allah's permission regarding the occurrence and effect of subjugation belongs to the second kind, and that is what is indicated by decree (qada'). On this basis one says: 'All things are by the permission of Allah and His decree.' But one does not say: 'All things are by His command and His pleasure.'"

His saying, ﴿and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾, is guidance that there is in learning magic only harm, because it involves deception and trickery, presenting falsehood as truth, and reaching corruption and evils through it. His glorified saying, ﴿and does not benefit them﴾, is stated to announce that it is not among the matters mixed with benefit and harm, but is pure evil and unmitigated harm. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And they certainly knew﴾, refers to the Jews whose misguidance has been related. His saying, ﴿whoever purchases it﴾, means whoever exchanges what the devils recite for the Book of Allah and the truth that He sent down. His saying, ﴿he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾, means no portion, because of his devotion to deception and falsehood and his use of that for acquiring the fleeting goods of this world and its pleasures. This contains an indication that their choice of magic was not out of ignorance of its harm; rather they did what they did with knowledge of its evil outcome.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾, means what they sold with it their otherworldly portion, as though they had destroyed themselves. He negated knowledge from them by His saying, ﴿if they had known﴾, while affirming it for them with emphatic oath by His saying, ﴿And they certainly knew﴾, because its meaning is: if they had acted upon their knowledge. Thus He made them as those who do not know, because they did not act in accordance with what their knowledge requires. When He, glorified be He, clarified what was upon them for what they committed of harms, He followed it with what is in turning away from it of benefits, and said:

The Discussion of His Words, exalted is He:

[103] ﴿And if they had believed and feared God, a reward from God would have been better, if they had known.﴾

"And if they had believed" means: in what they were called to, namely the Wise Qur'an. "And feared God" means: [avoided] what would make them sinful, and among it is sorcery and deception. His words "a reward from God would have been better" are the answer to "if" (law). Its original form is: "They would have been rewarded with a reward from God, better than what they sold their souls for." He omitted the verb and altered the composition to what the noble text stands upon, indicating the permanence of the reward for them and the certainty of its superiority. The object of comparison was omitted out of reverence for the one being preferred, lest it be attributed to it. His words, exalted is He, "if they had known" mean: that God's reward is better. They were only ascribed to ignorance because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires.

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[١٠٤] ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَقُولُوا راعِنا وقُولُوا انْظُرْنا واسْمَعُوا ولِلْكافِرِينَ عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ﴾

Commentary on the meaning of His, exalted is He, words: The Qur'an quotes: "O you who have believed, do not say" to the Prophet (ﷺ) "rā'inā" (راعِنا), by which you intend watchfulness and attentiveness toward a good purpose and the safeguarding of the other party. The Jews seized upon it, because it matched a foul word in their own language, and they began twisting their tongues with it, intending by it ruʿūnah (الرُّعُونَة), which is extreme foolishness. So He forbade them from agreeing with them in speech, to prevent the sound expression that matches the ugly one in form because of its resemblance to it, and in its place gave them something that admits no corruption, and so He said: "but say unẓurnā" (انْظُرْنا), preserving the meaning and altering the wording. That is: "look at us" (unẓur ilaynā), with the particle omitted and connected, or "wait for us" (intaẓirnā), taking it as from naẓara-hu, meaning "he awaited him" when he waited for him. It was also read as "anẓirnā" (أنْظِرْنا), from al-nazrah, meaning "grant us respite until we comprehend." It was also read as "rāʿūnā" (راعُونا) in the plural form, for reverence. And "rāʿinan" (راعِنًا) in the form of the active participle, meaning a speech that has ra'an (رَعَن, foolishness), like dāriʿ and lābin, because when it resembled their saying "rāʿīnā" and was a means of reviling with ra'an, it took on that attribute.

"And listen" (واسْمَعُوا), that is: say what I have commanded you, comply with all My commands, and do not be like the Jews, who said "We hear and we disobey" (سَمِعْنا وعَصَيْنا). "And for the disbelievers" (ولِلْكافِرِينَ), that is, the Jews, who through your saying mentioned above made a way to treat with contempt the station of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "there is a painful punishment" (عَذابٌ ألِيمٌ) for the enormity they dared to commit against him. This is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for what preceded it; in it is a severe warning for them and a kind of caution for the addressees against what they were forbidden.

This verse is a parallel to His words in Surat al-Nisa': ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places and say, "We hear and we disobey," and "Hear, without being made to hear," and "rāʿinā," twisting with their tongues and defaming the religion. And if they had said, "We hear and we obey," and "Hear," and "Look at us," it would have been better for them and more upright. But Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so they do not believe, except a few.﴾ [al-Nisa': 46]. Among their twisting is what has come in the hadith, that when they greeted, they would say "al-sāmm ʿalaykum" (السّامُّ عَلَيْكُمْ), and al-sāmm is death. For this reason we were commanded to reply to them with "wa-ʿalaykum" (وعَلَيْكم), and it is only that our prayer is answered concerning them, and their prayer is not answered concerning us.

(p. 217) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[105] ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾

﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord.﴾ This is a statement of the intensity of the enmity of the disbelievers of both groups toward the believers, out of envy and transgression, so that the believers would cut off any resemblance to them. For opposing one's enemies is among the great aims of those who are firmly established in virtuous character.

Then He explained that envy does not affect the removal of that (good) by His saying: ﴿But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ "Al-ikhtisas" (singling out) is a special care that designates the one singled out for a rank in which he is alone, without others. It also contains a reminder of what He has bestowed upon the believers, namely the complete and perfect Law that He prescribed for them.

When the Jews denied that any abrogation (naskh) could occur in the verses of Allah, thereby seeking to reach the denial of the verses of the Qur'an and the affirming of the everlasting validity of the Torah, He, glorified is He, responded to them after establishing the truth of the revelation, saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[106] ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring forth one better than it or similar to it. Do you not know that Allah is competent over all things?﴾

"Whatever sign We abrogate" means: whatever sign We replace with another (such as Our abrogating the verses of the Torah with the verses of the Qur'an). "Or cause to be forgotten" means: We remove it from the hearts, as He informed in His saying: ﴿But they forgot a portion of that by which they had been reminded﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 13]. It has also been recited as "aw nansa'ha" (or We postpone it), meaning: We defer it and leave it without abrogation, just as He retained many of the rulings of the Torah within the Qur'an. According to this recitation, His saying "We bring forth one better than it" is arranged in the order of this wrapping (laff): i.e., better than the abrogated, replaced one, as He did with the verses that legislated, in the upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyyah), what contains ease and the removal of hardship and distress, so they were better than those burdens (aṣar) and shackles (aghlal). His saying "or similar to it" means: similar to those previously revealed verses, as is seen in many verses of the Qur'an that agree with what precedes them, of what wisdom required to remain and continue.

Al-Raghib said: If it is said that what was left and not abrogated is not "like" it but is precisely it, then how does He say "similar to it"? It is said: The ruling that was revealed in the Qur'an, and which was established in the law before us, may rightly be said to be "it itself" when considered in its essence without regard to its covering, which is the wording. And it may rightly be said to be "its like" when one considers not merely its essence but also the wording. Similar to this is saying: "The water of the well is the water of the river" when the kind of water is considered, and at other times one says "like the water of the river" when the settled state of the water is considered. End of quote. Moreover, the use of "like" to mean the very same thing is common, as in their saying: "One like you does not stint."

﴿Do you not know that Allah is competent over all things?﴾ So He is able to bring what is better than it, and what is better than that, and what is similar to it in goodness. Al-Raghib said: That is, do not suppose that My changing a ruling from state to state, and that I did not bring the second at the beginning, is incapacity; for whoever knows His power over all things does not suppose that. Rather, the change of that returns to the benefit of the servants, and that what is most fitting for them at an earlier time is the earlier ruling, and at a later time is the later ruling.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[107] ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper?﴾

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ So He possesses your affairs and manages them, and He knows best what He imposes on you of worship, whether it be abrogated (naskh) or abrogating. ﴿And you have, besides Allah, no protector﴾ who looks after your affairs, ﴿nor helper﴾ who supports you and prevents you from the punishment.

The implication of knowing these three matters is the firm conviction and certainty that He, exalted is He, does not do to them, in any matter of their religion or their worldly life, except what is good for them. Acting upon this requires trust in Him, reliance upon Him, and entrusting one's affair to Him, without giving ear to the claims of the Jews and their doubts, among which is what they said regarding abrogation. They denied the abrogation of the rulings of the Torah and rejected the prophethood of Jesus and Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace, because they came with what they came with from Allah, by changing what Allah had changed of the ruling of the Torah. So Allah informed them that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and their authority, and that creation are the people of His kingdom and obedience; upon them is hearing and obeying His command and prohibition; that He commands them with what He wills, prohibits them from what He wills, abrogates what He wills, and confirms what He wills. What led the Jews to prevent abrogation was nothing but disbelief and obstinacy; otherwise, abrogation had indeed occurred abundantly in their law.

The scholar, the allamah Shaykh Rahmat Allah al-Hindi, in (Izhar al-Haqq), mentioned ample examples of what occurred of that in the Torah and the Gospel. Refer to them in the third chapter of it.

Two admonitions:

The first: Some eminent scholars said: this verse was revealed when the polytheists or the Jews said: "Muhammad commands his companions with a matter, then forbids them from it and commands the opposite." The verse contains a refutation of them, by showing that the purpose of abrogating a previous ruling is the preparation of souls for something higher than it. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We bring one better than it﴾, because the Creator, exalted is He, trained the Arab nation over twenty-three years in a gradual training which could not be completed for others, through social factors, except over many centuries. Therefore, rulings were imposed upon them according to their capacity, and whenever their capacity advanced, Allah replaced that ruling with another. This is the sunnah of the Creator regarding individuals and nations alike. For if you look at living beings, from the first plant cell to the highest form of trees, and from the first rank of animals to man, you would see (p-220) that abrogation is a natural, perceptible law in both material and moral matters. Indeed, the transition of the human cell into an embryo, then into an infant, then a youth, then a young man, then an elderly man, then an old man, and what follows each of these stages, from states that abrogate the states that preceded them, shows you with the clearest evidence that change in beings is a established natural law. And if this abrogation is not objectionable in beings, how can the abrogation of a ruling and its replacement by another ruling be objectionable in a nation which is in a state of growth and gradual progress from lower to higher? Would any person possessing a measure of intellect think it wise to impose upon the Arabs, at the beginning of their affair, what they would be required to exhibit at the height of human advancement and the peak of human perfection? And if this were valid, it would follow that the laws should impose upon children what they impose upon men, and no rational person in existence has said this. And if no rational person in existence says this, how is it permissible for Allah, who is the Most Wise of judges, to impose upon the nation, while it is in its stage of childhood, what it can only bear in its stage of youth and maturity? Which of the two is better: our law, whose limits Allah Himself laid down, and whose parts He abrogated as He willed by His knowledge, and perfected, such that neither humans nor jinn can undo a single letter of it, because it fits every time and place, and does not conflict with any state of human life? Or other religious laws, whose priests distorted them, and whose existence abrogated their rulings, such that acting upon them has become impossible, because they conflict with the requirements of human life in every respect?

The second: We have previously stated, in the introduction to the tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis), that abrogation in the terminology of the early scholars (salaf) is broader than it is in the terminology of the later scholars (khalaf), which should be reviewed.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[108] ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way.﴾

﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ The particle (أم, am) here is either (a) connective, equivalent to the hamza in (ألم تعلم, "Did you not know?"), meaning: Do you not know that He is the Owner of affairs, Capable of all things, who commands and forbids as He wills? ... Or do you know and yet propose through questioning, as the Jews proposed to Moses, peace be upon him? Or it is disconnected (منقطعة), meaning "bal" (rather), serving to turn away from urging them to act according to what they know, and to move on to warning them against that, upon the appearance among them of some signs of leniency in this matter and traces of being influenced by the statements of the disbelievers. The meaning of the interrogative hamza is a denial that such a desire occurs from them, and a consideration of it as far-fetched, since the nature of faith restrains them from it. The denial is directed at the desire itself, rather than at its object, for the sake of emphasizing the denial and its remoteness, by showing that it is something that a rational person would not have as a desire, let alone that it would proceed from him. His words "and whoever exchanges disbelief" mean: chooses it and takes it for himself, "for faith," by offering it in place of it, "then he has certainly strayed from the sound way," meaning he has deviated from the straight path. This is an independent sentence containing a universal ruling, brought forth in the manner of a proverb, and it is coordinated (معطوفة) with the preceding clause, coming to emphasize the prohibition of proposing, which is understood from His words "Or do you wish" and so on. The meaning of the verse is: Do not propose, lest you stray from the middle of the way, and straying leads you to remoteness from the goal and to the exchange of disbelief for faith. Thus the reason for mentioning His words "Or do you wish" and so on after His words "whatever We abrogate" becomes clear, for the purpose of each of them is to make them steadfast in the signs and to enjoin them to trust in them.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, what is the benefit of His words "and whoever exchanges disbelief" and so on, when it is known that without disbelief a person strays from the sound way, so what of disbelief? It has been said that the meaning is: whoever exchanges disbelief for faith will know that he had already strayed from the sound way, and in this is a warning that his straying from the sound way led him to disbelief after faith. Its meaning is: Do not question your Messenger as Moses was questioned, lest you stray from the sound way, which would lead you to the exchange of disbelief for faith. So the beginning of that is straying from the sound way. Another view: He named the opposition of the prophets, peace be upon them, after the attainment of what the soul is at rest with, as disbelief, since it leads to it, like calling pressed juice "wine." So He said "whoever exchanges" meaning seeks to exchange disbelief, that is, the opposition which is the origin of disbelief, for faith, that is, for what he has attained of the evidence that calls for the soul's tranquility; "then he has certainly strayed from the sound way."

(p-222) A third view: that this is the utmost rebuke for one to whom the truth has become manifest but who turned away from it toward falsehood, and that he is like one who was on the clear road and then wandered astray in it.

A fourth view: that "the sound way" alludes to the natural disposition (الفطرة) upon which people were created, and faith alludes to what is acquired through the revealed laws. So He said "whoever exchanges disbelief for faith," meaning for acquired faith, then he has nullified it and lost the natural disposition upon which people were created, so there is no hope of his turning back from what he is upon after that.

This. What we have established regarding the verse, that the address is to the Muslims, is what is more probable and is like His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if made apparent to you, would distress you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 101]; and His words ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ support it, for the placement of its address is clear only with the believers. Al-Razi preferred that the address is with the Jews, saying: Because this surah, from His words ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40] onward, is a narration about them and an argument with them, and because no other group has been mentioned in the context, and He, Exalted, has related of them their questioning of the Prophet ﷺ in His words ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down upon them a Book﴾ [an-Nisa': 153], and so on. In that case, the meaning of "exchanging disbelief for faith," while they are far removed from faith, is their turning away from it while being able to attain it, and their preference for disbelief over it. Likewise, the attribution of the Messenger to them is by considering that they are of the nation of the call.

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[109] ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook until Allah brings His command. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy﴾ (p-223) The cause of "wish" is ﴿from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾, i.e., from the correctness of the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), by the testimony of what agrees with it in the Torah. "So pardon and overlook" means: turn away from what proceeds from them of ignorance and enmity, and do not repay them. "Until Allah brings His command" refers to the permission to fight them and expel them. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, so He will take vengeance upon them when its time comes.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[110] ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves you will find﴾ i.e., its reward "with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do," so the deed of no doer is lost in His sight.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 111:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[111] ﴿They say: None will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian. Those are their wishful thinkings. Say: Produce your proof, if you are truthful.﴾

"And they say" means the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. "None will enter Paradise unless he is a Jew or a Christian" is an explanation (nashr) of what the waw in "and they say" encompasses. "Yahud" (Jews) is the plural of "hA'id" (one who repents), like "'uudh" is the plural of "'A'idh" (one who seeks refuge). It has been recited as "illa man kana yahudiyyan aw nasraniyyan" (unless he was a Jew or a Christian). "Those are their wishful thinkings" is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridha) that clarifies the falsehood of what they said. "Amani" (wishful thinkings) is the plural of "umniyya," which is what one wishes for, like "u'jubah" (a wonder) and "udhuka" (a laughingstock). If it is asked: their saying "None will enter Paradise" is a single wish, so why did He say "their wishful thinkings" in the plural? It is answered: the plural is in view of its being uttered by all of them. Sahib al-Intisaf (the author of al-Intisaf) answered: because of the intensity of their wishing for this wish, their repeated return to it, and its being firmly established in their souls, it was made plural, so that the plural would convey that it is firmly rooted in their hearts and that they have reached every extent in it. The plural conveys this, even though its import is singular. A parallel is their saying: "mi'an jiya'" (a flock of hungry ones). They made the attribute plural, while its meaning is singular, because its described subject is singular, to emphasize the establishment and firmness of the attribute.

This meaning is one of what has been related regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 54], for He made "qalil" (few) plural, although the original form would be singular, so that it would be said "lasharthimatun qalilatun" (a small band, few), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 249], were it not for what He intended by emphasizing the meaning of fewness through pluralizing it. The way the plural conveys emphasis in such cases is that the plural, by its form, conveys an increase in the units, so it is transferred to emphasize the singular and to show its excess over its counterparts, as a wondrous figurative transfer (naql majazi). So reflect upon this section, for it is among the choicest of the craft of eloquence (sina'at al-bayan). And Allah is the Granter of success.

﴿Say: Produce your proof﴾ means your argument for your exclusive entry into Paradise, "if you are truthful" in your claim. Al-Razi said: The verse indicates that the one who makes a claim, whether he asserts a negation or an affirmation, must have evidence and proof, and that is among the clearest indications of the falsehood of the view of blind following (taqlid). The poet said:

Whoever claims something without a witness,
his claim is bound to be refuted.

The words of al-Razi end. Al-Zamakhshari preceded him to this, when he said: This is the most destructive thing to the doctrine of the blind followers, and every saying for which there is no evidence is false and unestablished. The words end.

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[112] ﴿Yes! Whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord, and there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

"Yes" (bala) is an affirmation of what they (the Jews and Christians) denied, namely that others besides them would enter Paradise. "Whoever submits his face to Allah": whoever sincerely devotes himself to Him, associating no other with Him. The expression "face" is used for the self (nafs) because the face is the noblest of the limbs, the gathering place of the senses, the place of prostration, and the manifest locus of the signs of humility. Or the meaning is: whoever sincerely directs his orientation and intention, such that he does not turn his resolve toward anything other than Him. "And he is a doer of good" in his deed, conforming to his guidance (ﷺ); otherwise it would not be accepted. Hence the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected," related by Muslim. "His reward is with his Lord" is an expression for entering Paradise, and presenting it in the form of a reward indicates the strength of its connection to the deed. "Nor is there fear for them" of encountering something disliked; "nor will they grieve" over the loss of something sought. The plural in the three pronouns is according to the meaning of "man" (whoever), just as the singular in the first pronouns is according to its wording.

The commentary on the words of God Most High:

[113] ﴿The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing to stand on," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing to stand on," though they both recite the Book. Likewise, those who have no knowledge say the same as what they say. So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾

﴿The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing to stand on," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing to stand on"﴾ This explains how each party misguides the other specifically, following the explanation of how each misguides everyone else in general. The meaning of "to stand on" (ʿalā shayʾ) is: any matter of religion that is considered valid. "Though they both recite the Book": the "wa" is for the circumstantial clause (al-ḥāl). "The Book" is generic: that is, they say this while they are people of knowledge who recite the books. Whoever carries the Torah or the Gospel, or other books of God, and believes in it, should not disbelieve in the rest, because each of the two Books confirms the other and testifies to its authenticity. Likewise, all of God's books converge on confirming one another. "Likewise" means: like that which you have heard, along that same path. "Those who have no knowledge" means the ignorant, who have neither knowledge nor a book, such as the worshippers of idols. They say to the adherents of every religion, "the same as what they say," that is, that they have nothing to stand on. This is a severe rebuke, since they placed themselves, despite their knowledge, (p-226) in the same category as those who do not know.

﴿So God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ That is, He will separate them by His just judgment, distinguishing the one in the right from the one in the wrong regarding what they differed about. This verse is like His saying in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians, and the Magians, and those who associate others with God—indeed God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed God is Witness over all things.﴾ [al-Hajj: 17] And as He said: ﴿Say, "Our Lord will bring us together, then He will judge between us with truth, and He is the Just Judge, the All-Knowing."﴾ [Saba': 26]

Al-Razi said: "Know that this very event has occurred within the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for each sect declares the others to be unbelievers, despite their agreement on reciting the Qur'an." End of quote.

Here, tears should be shed over what fanatical partisanship in religion has produced among most Muslims: hurling accusations of disbelief at one another, with no sunnah or Qur'an to support it, no clear proof from God, and no decisive argument. Rather, when the cauldrons of partisanship in religion boiled over, Satan became able to split the word of the Muslims.

The poet says:
"The youth refuses anything but following his desires, though the path of truth is clear to him."

Yet God Most High commanded unity and harmony, and forbade division and disagreement. He said: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of God, and do not separate﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 103]. He said: ﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion and became sects—you have nothing to do with them﴾ [al-Anʿām: 159]. He said: ﴿And do not be like those who separated and differed after clear proofs had come to them﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 105]. He said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they scatter you from His way﴾ [al-Anʿām: 153]. The People of Truth from this community have been distinguished by the Sunnah (the Prophetic way) and the Jamaʿah (the united body of the Muslims), from the People of Falsehood, who claim that they follow the Book while turning away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and from what the community of Muslims has adhered to.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives for their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them and strives for their ruin﴾: This is a denunciation and a declaration that it is unlikely anyone could be more unjust than one who does this. When Allah directed reproach at the Jews and Christians in what preceded, He appended to it a reproach of the polytheists in His saying, ﴿Thus say those who do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113]. Then He directed this verse also at the polytheists who expelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions from Makkah, prevented them from praying in the Sacred Mosque, and also barred them from it, when the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions came to it from Madinah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. All of this is a ruin of the Sacred Mosque, because preventing people from establishing the rites of worship in it is a striving toward its ruin. And what ruin is greater than what they did? They expelled the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions from it, and they took possession of it with their idols, their rivals (to Allah), and their polytheism, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque, though they are not its guardians? Its guardians are none but the righteous, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while testifying against themselves to disbelief. Those, their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17]. And: ﴿The mosques of Allah are maintained only by those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, establish prayer, give zakah, and fear none but Allah. It is those who may be among the guided﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque and [prevented] the offering from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. So if one who believes in Allah and the Last Day… etc. is barred from it and driven out of it, (what ruin could be greater than that?). 

Then: what ruin could be greater than that? And ʿimārah (maintenance, upkeep) means reviving a place and occupying it with that for which it was established. The intended meaning of its ʿimārah is not merely decorating it and erecting its structure; rather its ʿimārah is by the remembrance of Allah in it, the establishment of His law in it, and its purification from filth and polytheism. The prohibition was applied to the mosques, although what was prohibited were the people, because the outcome returns to them. And one should not object: "How is it said 'mosques' when only the Sacred Mosque is meant?" Because there is no harm in a ruling coming in general terms even if its cause is specific, as you say to one who harmed a single righteous man: "Who is more unjust than one who harmed the righteous?" And as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Woe to every slanderer and mocker﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], while the one revealed concerning it was a single person.

And His saying: ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾ is a good tiding from Allah to the Muslims that He would give them victory over the Sacred Mosque and humble the polytheists before them, so that none of them would enter the Sacred Mosque except in fear, fearing that he would be seized and punished, or killed if he did not embrace Islam. Allah has indeed fulfilled the truth of this promise, for He prevented them from entering the Sacred Mosque. And Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) proclaimed among them in the year he led the pilgrimage: "Let no polytheist perform the pilgrimage after this year." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) performed the pilgrimage in the second year openly, with the Sacred Mosque under his control, and no polytheist dared to perform the pilgrimage or enter the Sacred Mosque. This is the disgrace for them in this world, referred to by His saying ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, because the recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Just as they barred the believers, they were barred from it. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire, because of their violation of the sanctity of the House and their degrading of it: setting up idols around it, calling upon other than Allah, circling it naked, and other of their acts which Allah and His Messenger detest.

There is another interpretation of the verse: that the verse is a reproach of the Jews, following what precedes and follows it, and of what they committed by their disbelief against Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) of ruining it, and of their enemy being empowered over them until he destroyed it, demolished their city, killed and took captives from among them, and they remained in the Babylonian captivity for seventy years. All of that was because of their rejection of the Book of Allah and their failure to act by His law.

In His saying: ﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear﴾ there is an allusion to their return to it after the captivity, under apprehension of the enemy and with the humiliation that clung to them. This is a sound interpretation, because the word "saʿā" (سَعى, "strove") points to that. Likewise, its implicit meaning also indicates a reproach of those who undertook the ruin, namely the Christians, when their authority became established, taking revenge on their enemies, the Jews.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid, who said concerning the verse: "They are the Christians, who used to throw filth into Bayt al-Maqdis and prevent people from praying in it." Qatadah said: "Hatred of the Jews led them to help Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) the Babylonian, the Magian, in ruining Bayt al-Maqdis."

And it indicates that places of worship are to be protected and respected, because they are the public school in which wisdom and rulings are recited and guidance to the paths of peace is given.

A hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ) has also been transmitted about seeking refuge from the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, as narrated by Imam Ahmad from Busr ibn Artah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to supplicate: 'O Allah, make the outcome of our affairs good in all matters, and protect us from the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.'"

The Hafiz (a scholar of hadith) Ibn Kathir said: "This is a hasan (sound-good) hadith, and it is not in any of the Six Books, and his Companion, Busr ibn Artah (also said to be Ibn Abi Artah), has no other hadith except this one and the hadith: 'Hands are not cut off in battle.'"

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[115] ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ This is an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His dominion over all horizons, from which the vastness of His knowledge follows. In this there is a warning against acts of disobedience and a deterrent from committing them (p-231). His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾, are similar to His words: ﴿If you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ (Ar-Rahman: 33), and like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ (Al-Hadid: 4), and His words: ﴿There is no private conversation among three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ (Al-Mujadila: 7), and His words: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ (Ghafir: 7). That is, He has encompassed all things by His knowledge, His management, His encompassing of them, and His being above them.

(p. 232)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[116] ﴿They say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾

﴿They say, "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ It refers to those who said: the Messiah is the son of God, 'Uzayr (Ezra) is the son of God, and the angels are the daughters of God. God refuted all of them in their claim and their saying that God has a son. "Glory be to Him" means: He is sanctified and exalted far above what they allege, with a thorough exaltation. The word "bal" (rather) is used to retract what their false statement implies, namely that He, glory be to Him and exalted, shares any kinship with any of the created beings. That is: the matter is not as they claim; rather, He is the Creator of all existing things, of which 'Uzayr, the Messiah and the angels are part. The tanwin in "kullun" (all) is a substitute for the omitted genitive complement. That is: all that is in them, of whatever kind, of the possessors of knowledge or others, "are devoutly obedient to Him" (qanitun), submissive, none of them resisting His creating, His decree or His will. One whose condition is this cannot be conceived of as sharing a kind with anything, and it is necessary for a child to be of the same kind as the parent.

Al-Raghib said in his tafsir: He drew attention to the strongest proof for negating that. Its explanation is this: every existing thing in the world, whether a natural creation or an artificially made object, has a purpose and a perfection for which it was brought into being.
