Even if it may serve something else incidentally, like the hand for grasping, the foot for walking, the knife for a particular kind of cutting, and the saw for sawing, and even if the hand may serve for walking in some state and the foot for grasping, it is not so perfectly.

The purpose of offspring for a human is only that his species may persist through it, and a part of him remains, since God did not make for him a way to persist in his own person; so He made for him a seed to preserve his species. This is strengthened by the fact that He did not make for the sun, the moon and the rest of the heavenly bodies a seed or succession, since He did not make for them the perishing that plants and animals have.

Since God, exalted, is the Enduring, the Everlasting, without beginning or end, taking a son for Himself has no meaning. Hence He said: ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾ [al-Nisa 171], meaning He is exempt from the cause that requires offspring. (p. 233) Then, since acquiring a son is for some want, and that is as previously stated, namely that man needs an heir to succeed him because he is not complete in himself, God explained by His saying ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ that no poverty can be imagined for Him, such that He would need to take something to fill it. Thus in "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth" there is a second proof. Then He added a further proof by His saying "qanitun" (devoutly obedient). Since a son is believed to serve his father and support him, as He said: ﴿And He made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren﴾ [al-Nahl 72], He showed that everything in the heavens and the earth, besides being His possession, is also devoutly obedient to Him, either willingly, unwillingly, or subjugated. Like His saying: ﴿And to God prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd 15], and His saying: ﴿And there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra' 44]. This is the most eloquent proof for one who is on the right path.

Then al-Raghib said: If it is asked, from where did the confusion arise for them regarding the attribution of a son to God, exalted? It is said: it has been mentioned that in earlier revealed laws they used to call the Originator, exalted, "Father," and to call the eldest among them "god." So much so that they said: the father is the lesser lord, and God is the greater father. They meant by that that He, exalted, is the first cause of a person's existence, and the father is the last cause of his existence, and that the father is in one respect the worshipped of the son, that is, his master. They used to call the angels "gods," just as the Arabs called the sun "ilaha" (goddess). They intended a correct meaning by this, just as our scholars intend by saying: God is loving and beloved, willing and willed, and similar expressions. Just as one says of a sultan, "the king," and as people say: "Lord of lords," "God of gods," "King of kings," which reveals that this usage was established long ago. This is strengthened by what is related: that Jacob was called "God's firstborn," and that Jesus used to say: "I am going to my Father," and similar expressions. Then, eventually, the ignorant among them conceived the meaning of natural begetting. Thus it became forbidden in our law to utter such words, out of exaltation of God above this belief, until using them, even if one intends by them what those people intended, became a companion of disbelief. End of al-Raghib's words, may God have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 117:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[117] ﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

"Badi' al-samawati wal-ard" means: its Originator (mubdi') and Creator, without a prior pattern. Whoever does something that no one has done before is called one who has "innovated" (abda'ta). For this reason, whoever opposes the Sunnah and the Community (al-Jama'ah) is called a "mubtadi'" (innovator), because he introduces into the religion of Islam what the Companions and the Followers (al-tabi'un), may Allah be pleased with them, did not precede him in. This statement is another proof to refute their clinging to the birth of 'Isa without a father, and to 'Uzayr's knowledge of the Torah without learning. The argument is as follows: God, glorified is He, is the Originator of all things. It is therefore not far-fetched that He should bring someone into existence without a father, or that someone should know without a human intermediary.

Al-Raghib said: In this verse He mentions a fourth proof. Its explanation: the father is the element (unsur) of the child; from him the child is formed. God is the Originator of all things, so He cannot be the element of the child, and it is impossible for the one acted upon to be the agent.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, means: when He wills a matter. Qada' (decree) is the carrying out of what has been determined (al-muqaddar), and the muqaddar is that which is delimited from the absolute known. Al-Raghib said: qada' is the completion of a thing, whether by speech or by action. From speech is the verse: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra' 23] (p-235) ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isra' 4]. From action is His saying: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat 12]. Also: "So-and-so paid his debt (qada daynahu)," "he fulfilled his vow (qada nahbahu)," and "the matter came to an end (inqada al-amr)." (Then he said:) By His saying "when He decrees a matter," He also draws attention to a fifth proof, namely that the child comes into being through growth and composition, state after state. Whereas He, when He wills a thing, it is done without delay. The "idha" (when) is not intended in its literal temporal sense, since that would refer to the time before time existed. Nor is "kun" (be) intended in its literal verbal sense, nor is the "fa" (then) intended as temporal sequence. Rather, all of that is used figuratively, because it is the closest thing by which we can picture the swiftness of an action and its completion. The word qada' is mentioned because it denotes the completion of an act; amr (matter) because it encompasses both utterance and action; qawl (saying) because it is the lightest and swiftest means of bringing something into being among us; and the word "kun" because of the generality of its meaning and the brevity of its form. Then He said "fa-yakun" (and it is) as an alert that nothing He wills to bring into being is beyond Him. Although "kun fa-yakun" comes out in the form of two things, one of which is dependent on the other, it is in reality one thing. End.

As for those who held that "kun" is intended in its literal sense, a well-known objection was raised against them: "kun" is an imperative, and an imperative is addressed only to something existing. Some answered that it is a command to the thing while it is coming into being, neither before nor after. Some said: it is a command to something known to Him, and that is in the status of the existent, even though its essence is non-existent. Some said: it is a command to the non-existent, and they said that commanding the non-existent is valid just as commanding the existent is valid.

They have other answers that are more forced and far-fetched.

(p-236) Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about this, that if the one addressed by "kun" is existent, then obtaining what is already obtained is impossible; and if he is non-existent, how can addressing the non-existent be conceived? He answered: This question is built on two principles. The first: the distinction between the address of creation (khitab al-takwin), by which God, glorified is He, does not demand an act from the one addressed, but rather He brings into being the one addressed and creates him without any act on his part, or power, or will, or existence of his own; and the address of obligation (khitab al-taklif), by which an act or abstention is demanded from the commanded, which he performs by power and will, even though all of that is by the might and power of Allah, for there is no might nor power except by Allah. This address has been disputed among people: is it valid to address the non-existent with it on condition of his existence, or is it not valid to address him with it except after his existence? There is no dispute among them that the ruling of the address does not attach to him except after his existence. Likewise they disputed about the first: is it a true address, or is it an expression for power and the swiftness of creation through capability? The first is the well-known view among those who are attributed to the Sunnah. The second principle: whether the non-existent, in its state of non-existence, is a thing or not. Some groups of the Mu'tazila and Shi'a theologians held that it is a thing in external reality, an essence and a entity, and they claimed that quiddities (mahiyyat) are not made or created, and that their existence is additional to their reality. Likewise some groups of the philosophers, the Unificationists (al-Ittihadiyya), and other heretics went this way. What the majority of people hold, and what is the view of the theologians of the Affirmers (ahl al-ithbat) and those attributed to the Sunnah and the Community, is that in external reality, outside the mind, before its existence it is not a thing at all, nor an essence nor an entity, and that in external reality there are not two things, one of which is the reality and the other its existence additional to its reality. For Allah originated the essences which are the quiddities. Thus everything other than Him, glorified is He, is created, made, originated, and brought into being by Him, glorified and exalted is He. However, among these people there are those who say: the non-existent is not a thing at all, and if it is called a thing in consideration of its being fixed in knowledge, that is metaphorical. Among them are those who say: there is no doubt that it has fixity in knowledge and existence therein, so by virtue of this fixity and existence it is a thing and an essence. These people do not distinguish between existence and fixity, as the one who said "the non-existent is a thing" made a distinction. Nor do they distinguish, regarding the non-existent not being a thing, between the possible and the impossible, as those did; for (p-237) they agreed that the impossible is not a thing, and the dispute concerns only the possible. The main reason for the one who made it a thing is that it is fixed in knowledge, and on that basis it is valid to specify it with intention, creation, reporting about it, commanding it, forbidding it, and other things. They said: these specifications cannot attach to pure non-existence. If the difference is specified between existence which is objective fixity and existence which is cognitive fixity, the doubt in this matter is dispelled.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl 40]: that thing is known before its origination and before this address is directed to it. By that it was determined and decreed. For Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says and writes of what He knows whatever He wills. As the Prophet ﷺ said in the hadith narrated by Muslim in his Sahih from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah wrote the measures of the creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth." He said: "And His Throne was upon the water." In Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Imran (p-238) ibn Husayn, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Allah was, and nothing was with Him. His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote in the Remembrance (al-dhikr) everything, then He created the heavens and the earth." In the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The first thing Allah created was the pen. He said to it: Write. It said: My Lord, what shall I write? He said: Write the measures of everything until the Hour comes." And along with similar texts which show that the created thing, before it is created, was known and spoken of, written down; so it is a thing by virtue of its cognitive, verbal, written existence, even though its reality, which is its external existence, is not established in external reality. Rather, it is pure non-existence and sheer negation.

These four well-known levels are existents. Allah, glorified is He, mentioned them in the first surah He revealed to His Prophet, in His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq 1] ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ [al-'Alaq 2] ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ [al-'Alaq 3] ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ [al-'Alaq 4] ﴿taught man that which he did not know﴾ [al-'Alaq 5]. We have expanded on this in other places. Since that is so, the address is directed to whoever the will is directed to, and whom power has reached, and He creates and brings into being, as He said: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. So the one to whom "kun" is said is the one who is willed, and he, when he is willed before he is created, has fixity and distinction in knowledge and decree. Were it not so, the willed created thing would not be distinguished from others. By this the answer to the division is obtained. The questioner's statement: "If the one addressed is existent, then obtaining what is already obtained is impossible," is answered: this applies if he is existent in external reality with his own existence. There is no doubt that the non-existent is not existent, nor is it fixed in itself. As for what is known, willed, and is a thing in knowledge, will, and decree, its existence in external reality is not impossible, but (p-239) all created things are not brought into existence except after their existence in knowledge and will.

As for the questioner's statement: "If he is non-existent, how can addressing the non-existent be conceived?" It is answered: if the intention is to address the non-existent with an address that he understands and carries out, this is impossible, since a condition of the addressee is that he be able to understand and act. The non-existent cannot be conceived as understanding and acting. Therefore the address of obligation to him during his non-existence is impossible, in the sense that he is required during his non-existence to understand and act. For the same reason, it is also impossible to address the non-existent in external reality with an address of creation, in the sense of believing that he is a fixed thing in external reality and that he is addressed to be. But as for the known, mentioned, written thing, when directing the address of creation to it is like directing the will to it, this is not impossible; rather it is a possible matter. Indeed a person finds the like of this within himself: he determines in himself a matter he wishes to do, and with the direction of his will and seeking toward that willed, sought thing which he determined in himself, and the attainment of the sought thing depends on his capability. If he is able to attain it, it is attained with will and firm seeking. If he is incapable, it is not attained. A person may say: "Let it be so," and similar forms of request, and the sought thing is then according to his capability over it. Allah, glorified is He, is powerful over all things, and whatever He wills comes to be and whatever He does not will does not come to be, for His command, when He wills a thing, is to say to it "Be," and it is. End.

"The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:"

[118] ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?" Likewise said those before them, the like of their saying. Their hearts are alike. We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain.﴾

"And those who do not know" — from among the polytheists or from among the People of the Book, and this is the more apparent, because what preceded it all concerns their disputation and the refutation of their misguided claims, and [the verse] negated knowledge from them because they did not act upon it. ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us﴾ — why does He not speak to us as He speaks to the angels and spoke to Musa? [They said this out of] arrogance and insolence on their part. "Or a sign come to us" — out of denial that what came to them of the signs of Allah are signs, and out of contempt for them: ﴿Likewise said those before them, the like of their saying﴾, i.e., this shameful falsehood, and they said: "Show us Allah openly." In this is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), that just as he was subjected to obstinacy, those before him were subjected to obstinacy too. "Their hearts are alike" — i.e., the hearts of these people and of those before them are alike in blindness, obstinacy, and presuming to dictate terms to the prophets. ﴿We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾ — i.e., of the truth, in whom no doubt or uncertainty takes hold. This is a rejection of their demand for a sign. In the definiteness of "the signs" and their pluralization, and in the use of "made clear," which expresses complete clarification, in place of the "coming" they demanded, there is an eloquence that is not hidden. The meaning is that they proposed a singular sign, whereas We have made clear the great signs for a people who seek the truth and certainty. The reason it does not address their statement "Why does Allah not speak to us" is to indicate that its falsehood is so evident that it needs no refutation or answer.

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[119] ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings﴾ with reward for the believers, "and a warner" with punishment for the disbelievers, "and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire." That is: We will not ask you about them, [namely,] "Why did they not believe?" after you had conveyed [the message] and exerted your utmost effort in calling them. This is like His saying: ﴿Your duty is only to convey, and upon Us is the reckoning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 40]. In describing them as "companions of the Blazing Fire," rather than [using terms like] disbelief, denial and the like, there is a severe threat to them and an indication that they are sealed upon their hearts, and that faith is not to be hoped for from them.

Al-Jahim (the Blazing Fire) is one of the names of the Fire. It is applied to a fire that is intensely blazing, to any fire whose parts are piled one above another, to any great fire in a deep pit, and to a place of intense heat.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 120:

(p-241) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[120] ﴿Never will the Jews or the Christians be pleased with you until you follow their religion. Say, "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [only] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after what has come to you of knowledge, you would have against Allah no protector or helper.﴾

﴿Never will the Jews or the Christians be pleased with you until you follow their religion﴾, meaning: because they want to be followed absolutely. In this there is an emphasis on despairing of their becoming Muslim, and an alert that nothing will satisfy them except what it is impermissible for him (peace be upon him) to do. ﴿Say﴾: no messenger follows anything but guidance. ﴿Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾, i.e., which is Islam, ﴿is the [only] guidance﴾, i.e., there is no guidance beyond it. What you call to is not guidance; rather, it is desire, as His saying ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ expresses, i.e., their deviant opinions issuing from them by the dictate of their souls' appetites, ﴿after what has come to you of knowledge﴾ that the religion of Allah is Islam, or of the religion whose correctness is known by clear proofs. ﴿You would have against Allah no protector﴾ who would take charge of your affair, ﴿or helper﴾ who would repel His punishment from you. The address to him (ﷺ) was chosen so that those among the hypocrites who follow their desires after Islam, clinging to their alliance and hoping for their support, would enter into it by primary inclusion.

Imam al-Razi said: In the verse there is evidence that following desire is only ever falsehood. From this aspect it indicates the invalidity of blind imitation (taqlid). End.

In Fath al-Bayan, its text reads: In this verse there is a severe threat, at which hearts tremble and hearts are split, which obliges the people of knowledge who bear the proofs of Allah, glorified is He, and who stand in explaining His laws, to abandon flattery toward those who abandon acting upon the Book and the Sunnah, preferring mere opinion over them both. End.

(p-242) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[121] ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited. Those believe in it, and whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.﴾

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited. Those believe in it, and whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.﴾ When He, exalted is He, mentioned earlier that the Jews and the Christians would not be satisfied unless the believers followed their creed, because they claimed that they were upon the truth and that they believed in what was with them, He refuted their claim to believe in it by saying that whoever is given the Book and recites it as it should be recited, that person is the one who believes in it. Those mentioned (here) are among those who did not recite it as it should be recited, because of the wrongs of the Jews that He enumerated first, and because He followed that with the claim of the Christians that God has taken a son. Whoever holds that belief, how could he believe? Is he one who recites the Book as it should be recited? Their Book commands the affirmation of the oneness of their Lord, the adherence to His law, and the confirmation of every prophet who confirms what is with them, and they have disbelieved in all of that.

The clause "yatlūnahu" (they recite it) is a *ḥāl muqaddara* (a circumstantial clause describing a future or anticipated state) either from "hum" (they) or from "al-Kitāb" (the Book). It is also permitted that the verse was brought as praise for those among the People of the Book who believed in the Qur'an. In that case the pronoun in "yatlūnahu" refers to the Qur'an, and the verse is like His saying: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52], ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say: "We believed in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were Muslims before it."﴾ [al-Qasas: 53], ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Qasas: 54], and like His saying: ﴿Say: "Believe in it or do not believe. Indeed those who were given knowledge before it, when it is recited to them, fall down on their faces in prostration"﴾ [al-Isra': 107].

Among its reciting as it should be recited is believing that it is the truth from their Lord, their patience, their repelling of evil with good, their spending, and their prostration to Him, exalted is He. So the two verses explain their reciting it as it should be recited.

(p-243) It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the recitation as it should be recited is to make lawful what it makes lawful and to make unlawful what it makes unlawful, to read it as God revealed it, not to distort words from their places, and not to interpret anything from it in other than its proper interpretation (ta'wil)." Similar to this is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, exalted is He, "Those" is a reference to those described as having been given the Book and reciting it as it is due. "They believe in it": the object of benefit is what belief in it necessarily entails of gain, by the indication of His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾, where they have exchanged error for guidance.

The discussion of the words of His saying, Exalted is He:

[122] ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ [123] ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 123]

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And fear﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 123], i.e., be wary of, "a Day when no soul will avail" i.e., will not suffice, "another soul at all" in it, "nor will compensation be accepted from it" i.e., ransom, "nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped" i.e., they will not be protected from the punishment of Allah. The like of these two verses has already passed at the beginning of the surah.

Al-Qadi said: When he opened their story with the command to remember the blessings, to uphold their rights, to beware of squandering them, and to fear the Hour and its terrors, he repeated that and concluded his address to them with it, as an exaggeration in advising them, and as a notice that it is the summary (fadhlakah) of the matter and the purpose of the story.

The discussion of the words of His saying, Exalted is He:

[122] ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ [123] ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 123]

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And fear﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 123], i.e., be wary of, "a Day when no soul will avail" i.e., will not suffice, "another soul at all" in it, "nor will compensation be accepted from it" i.e., ransom, "nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped" i.e., they will not be protected from the punishment of Allah. The like of these two verses has already passed at the beginning of the surah.

Al-Qadi said: When he opened their story with the command to remember the blessings, to uphold their rights, to beware of squandering them, and to fear the Hour and its terrors, he repeated that and concluded his address to them with it, as an exaggeration in advising them, and as a notice that it is the summary (fadhlakah) of the matter and the purpose of the story.

(p. 244)

**On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:**

[124] ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them, He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people." He said, "And from my descendants?" He said, "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers."﴾

"And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them." Since He, glory be to Him, censured the people of misguidance, most of whom were descendants of Abraham, peace be upon him, and since all the sects of the religious communities revere him, including the Arabs, and his House, which he built, is their greatest pride and their most noble distinction, He reminded them all of what He had bestowed upon him. This reminder leads to the establishment of this religion through the knowledge of this unlettered Prophet, who never mixed with any scholar, of matters known only to the elite of scholars. He mentioned the House that Abraham built and made it the pillar of their righteousness, and He commanded that a part of the place be taken as a place of prayer (muṣallā), in order to magnify His command and exalt the greatness of His station. And in the reminder of his fulfillment, after mentioning those who fulfilled the due of recitation, and after calling the Children of Israel in general to fulfill [their covenant] through gratitude, there is an exhortation to follow his example. Likewise, in the mention of Islam and monotheism, there is a stirring for all who revere him to follow him in that. This was mentioned by al-Biqa'i.

The word "idh" (إذْ) is in the accusative as the object of an implied preceding verb, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of shifting address (al-talwīn). That is: "And mention to them the time when he, peace be upon him, was tested, so that they may remember what befell him of matters calling to monotheism and restraining from polytheism, and so that they may accept the truth and abandon the falsehood they are in." It is not far-fetched that it is governed by an implied verb coordinated with "udhkurū" (remember), addressed to the Children of Israel, so that they may reflect on what is related about those who belong to his religion, from Abraham and his sons, peace be upon them, of deeds and sayings, and thus follow them and walk in their path. That is: "And remember when your father Abraham was tested, and he fulfilled what he was tested with. Then what is wrong with you that you do not follow him, and do as he did at the time of trial, in fulfilling covenants and steadfastness upon promises, so that I may reward you for that with the reward of the good-doers?"

Testing (ibtilāʾ) originally means examination: seeking knowledge of the condition of the one being examined by confronting him with a matter that is generally difficult for him, whether he does it or leaves it. Testing by us is for the manifestation of what we did not know, and testing by God is for the manifestation of what is already known to Him. The outcome of testing is the appearance of what was hidden, in both the witnessed and the unseen realms, and therefore it is permissible to attribute it to God, exalted is He. His words "with words" (bi-kalimāt) mean "with laws": commands and prohibitions. The exegetes have various statements about them, and about their enumeration (p. 245). Ibn Jarir said: "It is not permissible to assert definitively that any of what they mentioned is the specific intended meaning, except by a hadith or consensus (ijmāʿ, the agreement of qualified scholars)." He said: "No report has been authenticated on this, neither by a single transmitter nor by a group of transmitters that would necessitate acceptance." End of quotation.

In my view, the closest meaning of "the words" is his being tested with Islam, so that he submitted to the Lord of the worlds; and his being tested with migration, so that he left his land and people until he reached al-Sham as a migrant to God; and his being tested with fire, so that he endured it; then his being tested with circumcision, so that he endured it; then his being tested with the sacrifice of his son, so that he submitted and sought reward.

This is also derived from tracing his biography in the Mighty Revelation (al-tanzīl al-ʿazīz) and in the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwīn) of the Torah. In both there is an explanation of what we have mentioned concerning him, peace be upon him: his performance of those words in the fullest manner, and his fulfilling them in the best fulfillment. This is the meaning of His words "and he fulfilled them," like His words: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm: 37]. And "itmām" (completion) means fulfillment.

"He said" is a new clause that came as an answer to a question arising from the discourse. It is as if it were said: "What was he rewarded for his gratitude?" It was said: "His Lord said to him: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾," that is, an exemplar for those after you. "Imām" is a name for one who is followed, and no prophet was sent after him except that he was commanded to follow his religion, and he was from his descendants, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. "He said," that is, Abraham: "And from my descendants," that is: "And make from my descendants leaders." "He said, 'My covenant does not include...'": that is, I have indeed responded to you and made a pledge that I will do good to your descendants. However, "My covenant," that is, the covenant I made with you concerning leadership, "does not include the wrongdoers," that is, of them, because they removed themselves from you in the paternity of religion. So in His words "does not include..." etc., there is a hidden answer to his supplication, peace be upon him, and a general promise from Him, exalted is He, to honor some of his descendants with attaining the covenant of leadership, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 27]. In this there is the most complete encouragement to adopt his fulfillment (p. 246), especially for those who were called before to fulfill the covenant, and an indication that if they are grateful, He will keep their elevation lasting as He kept his elevation, and if they do wrong, his supplication will not reach them, so humiliation and what goes with it will be decreed upon them, and no one will avail them anything, nor will they be helped. And it has been read "al-ẓālimūn" (in the nominative), with "ʿahdī" (my covenant) being a fronted object, for emphasis and for the sake of the rhyme endings (al-fawāṣil).

The Muʿtazila have used this verse to argue that the wrongdoer is not fit for leadership. Al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) extended the discussion here at length and excelled in presenting evidences. Likewise, the Shiʿa used it to support their view on the obligation of infallibility (ʿiṣma) in the Imams, outwardly and inwardly, as al-Razi transmitted from them and debated with them.

I say: The argument of both groups for their claims is a stopping at the general wording of the expression. However, the noble verse has nothing to do with the intention of the caliphate of rule and sovereignty.

What is meant by the covenant is that leadership about which he was asked. Was it anything other than leadership in religion, which is prophethood, and which the wrongdoers among his descendants were denied? As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac, and among their descendants are the good-doer and the one who clearly wrongs himself﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 113]. Had the verse indicated what they claimed, reality would contradict it... Indeed many wrongdoers have attained worldly leadership. Thus it is clear that what is meant by the covenant is only leadership in religion specifically. Using it as evidence for the wrongdoer's unfitness for governance is a forced interpretation (tamaḥḥul), because it takes the general wording without regard to the cause of revelation or the context; or it goes to the view that the statement carries the meaning of a command not to appoint a wrongdoer, as some have said, and that is even more forced. It is known that the imam must be one of justice and of acting by the Sharia, as has been reported. Whenever he deviates from that, he is a wrongdoer, and discussion of that belongs to a different context. And success is from God.

**The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verse 125:**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[125] ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [said], "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer." And We charged Abraham and Ishmael: "Purify My House for those who circle it, those who stay in it for worship, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾

"And when We made the House": that is, the one Abraham built, which is Umm al-Qura. It is a term that has become the dominant name for the Ka'bah, like "the Star" for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). "A place of return for the people": a resort and a destination for the pilgrims and the visitors, who disperse from it and then return to it repeatedly. The word mathaba is of the form mafaʿa (a noun of place) from al-thawb, which means returning, turning back to something entirely and repeatedly. The secret of this distinction is evident in the attraction of hearts, the longing of souls, their inclination and their love for it. Its pull on hearts is greater than the pull of a magnet on iron. Thus it is most fitting for the words of the one who said:

*Its beauty is the substance of all beauty, and the magnet of men's hearts.*

So people return to it across the passing years from all regions, and they never have their fill of it. Rather, the more they visit it, the more they long for it.

*The eye does not turn away from it when it sees it, until it returns to it longing.*

How many slain, despoiled and wounded has it claimed for God's sake! How much wealth and how many souls have been spent in its love! The lover accepts parting from the beloved children, family, friends and homeland, putting before himself all kinds of fears, perils, ruins and hardships, and yet he finds all of that sweet and savours it!

Ibn al-Qayyim, in the opening of Zad al-Ma'ad, mentioned this gem.

"And a sanctuary": a place of security. Like His words: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary, while people are snatched away around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67], and His words: ﴿Whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97]. In the pre-Islamic era people were snatched away around them while they themselves were secure, not taken captive. A man would meet the killer of his father or his brother and would not confront him. In this is the demonstration of the nobility of the House, in that it is a place that souls yearn for and never have their fill of it, even if they return to it every year, in response from God, exalted is He, to the prayer of His friend [Abraham] in His words: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them﴾ [Ibrahim: 37], up to his words: ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾ [Ibrahim: 40]. And [it is a demonstration] of its being a refuge for whoever enters it, as we have explained.

In the two Sahihs, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "This land, Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth. It remains sacred by the sanctity of Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Fighting in it was not made lawful for anyone before me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day." The hadith continues.

As for His words: ﴿And take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾, it has been read with a kasra on the kha' (ittakhidhu), as a command interposed between the two declarative clauses, or with the implied sense "And We said: take." It has also been read with a fatha on the kha' (ittakhadhu) as a past tense verb coordinated with "We made" (ja'alna), meaning: "and they took it as a place of prayer." The station of Abraham is the entire sanctuary, according to Mujahid. And from him [also]: it refers to Jam' (Muzdalifah), Mina and Makkah. It is also said that it refers to his station which is in the Masjid al-Haram. Qatadah said: "They were only commanded to pray beside it, and they were not commanded to touch it." Nations have burdened themselves with things that earlier nations had burdened themselves with.

Al-Raghib al-Isfahani said: "The more preferable view is that it is the entire sanctuary, for there is no place they have mentioned except that it is a place of prayer, or one claimed to be, or a place where prayer is performed."

I say: The original form of the verse would have been: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people, and a sanctuary, and a place of prayer." However, it departed from this wise style to that one, and did not say, for example, "and take from it a place of prayer," for several reasons:

(First) To draw attention to the matter of prayer in it, and to honour its status, by mentioning it in a separate sentence of its own, for the sake of giving it special care.

(Second) To remind [the reader] that it is the station of the great father of all the prophets. What is the station of such a figure is worthy of being respected and revered.

(Third) To state explicitly that this taking is by a divine command, not by the legislation of a human being, as a preparation for the command to face it [in prayer], and as a means of silencing those who disputed about it, namely the Jews. Al-Shaykhan and others have related that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer!" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾.

Ibn Kathir said: The station of Abraham is the stone on which the leaders of prayer stand to pray. That stone is the one on which Abraham, peace be upon him, stood when building the House. When the wall rose, Ishmael, peace be upon him, brought it to him so that he could stand on it and hand him the stones, and he would place them with his hand to raise the wall. Whenever he completed one side, he moved to the next side, circling around the Ka'bah while standing on it. Whenever he finished one wall, he moved it to the side next to it. And so on until the walls of the Ka'bah were completed, as its account has come in the story of Abraham and Ishmael in building the House, from the narration of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Bukhari.

(p-250) Ibn Kathir said: This station used to be attached to the wall of the Ka'bah in the past. Its place is known today beside the door, on the side of the stone, to the right of one entering through the door, in the separate enclosure there. It seems that the Friend [Abraham], peace be upon him, when he finished building the House, placed it against the wall of the Ka'bah, or the building reached it and he left it there. For this reason, and Allah knows best, he was commanded to pray there at the completion of the circumambulation. It is fitting that it should be by the station of Abraham, where the building of the Ka'bah ended. As the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did: when he came to Makkah, he circumambulated the House seven times, and placed the station between himself and the House, and prayed two rak'ahs.

Ibn Kathir said: It was 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who moved it from the wall of the Ka'bah to its present place, and none of the Companions objected to that. Al-Bayhaqi related with his chain to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The station was in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in the time of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, adjoining the House. Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, moved it back."

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, who was the leading scholar of the Meccans in his time, said: "The station was in the courtyard of the House during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). 'Umar moved it to its place after the Prophet (ﷺ)." He said: "The flood carried it away after 'Umar moved it from this place, and 'Umar returned it to it." Sufyan said: "I do not know how far it was from the Ka'bah before it was moved." He also said: "I do not know whether it was adjacent to it or not."

The report from 'A'ishah mentioned above indicates that it was adjacent to it. And Allah knows best.

The hafiz Shaykh 'Umar ibn al-Hafiz al-Taqi Muhammad ibn Fahd al-Makki al-Hashimi, in his book Ithaf al-Wara bi-Akhbar Umm al-Qura, under the events of the year seventeen [AH], said: In that year a great flood came, known as the Flood of Umm Nahshal, from the upper part of Makkah by way of al-Radm. It entered the Masjid al-Haram and uprooted the station of (p-251) Abraham from its place, and carried it away until it was found at the lower part of Makkah. The place where it had been was identified after the flood had effaced it, and it was brought back and fastened against the Ka'bah on its face. The flood also carried away Umm Nahshal, daughter of 'Ubaydah ibn Sa'd ibn al-'As ibn Umayyah. She died in it, and her body was recovered at the lower part of Makkah. It was a tremendous flood. News of this was written to the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was in the noble city of Madinah. This alarmed him greatly, and he rode in haste to Makkah. He entered it on an 'umrah in the month of Ramadan. When he reached Makkah, he stood at the stone of the station, which was adjoining the noble House, and said: "I adjure Allah any servant who has knowledge concerning this station!" Al-Mutallib ibn Abi Wada'ah al-Sahmi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I, O Commander of the Faithful, have knowledge of it. I used to fear for it something like this, so I took its measure from its place to the gate of the Hujur, and from its place to Zamzam with a measuring cord, and I have those measurements in my house." 'Umar said to him: "Sit with me, and send someone to bring them." He sat with him, and sent for them, and they were brought. The measurements were taken, and the stone of the station was placed in the position where it is now. It was secured, and it has remained so until now. End of quotation.

*"And We charged Abraham and Ishmael"*: that is, We commanded them both. The verb is construed with "ila" (to) because it carries the sense of "We sent ahead and inspired." *"That purify My House"*: that is, from every impurity, both physical and spiritual, so that nothing unbecoming in the Shari'ah is done in its presence. Or [it means]: build it upon purity from associating anything with Me. As He said, exalted is He: ﴿And when We settled Abraham in the place of the House, [saying]: "Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stand, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. Or [it means]: keep it free for those who circle it and those mentioned after them, so that others do not approach it. In this reading the lam in "li-tawa'ifin" is the object complement of "purify." According to the preceding reading it is the lam of purpose, meaning: purify it for their sake. His words "for those who circle it" mean: around it. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "that is, those who come to it from abroad." *"And those who stay in it"*: that is, its residents who dwell in it, or those who seclude themselves in it for worship (i'tikaf). As Ibn Abi Hatim related with his chain to Thabit, who said: "We said to 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: 'I think we will only speak to the governor, that he should forbid those who sleep in the Masjid al-Haram, for they become junub and break their wudu there.' He said: 'Do not do that, for Ibn 'Umar was asked about them (p-252) and he said: "They are the ones who stay in it."'" 'Abd ibn Humayd also related it in his Musnad. And it is established in the Sahih that Ibn 'Umar used to sleep in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was unmarried.

In al-Kashshaf: It is permissible that by "those who stay in it" is meant "those who stand," that is, those standing in prayer.

Just as He said, of those who circle and those who stand, *"and those who bow and prostrate"*: plural of rakic and sajid. The meaning is: for those who circle and those who pray, because standing, bowing and prostrating are the postures of the one who prays. Because the last two are close in essence and in time, the conjunction is omitted between the two items they describe. He used the sound plural for two of the attributes and the broken plural for the other two for the sake of antithesis, which is a kind of eloquence. He placed the form fu'ul after fu'all because it is the closing rhyme (fasila). The purpose of the verse is a rebuttal of the polytheists who associated others with Allah at His House, which was founded on the worship of Him alone with no partner. Yet despite that, they barred the believing people of the House from it, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar [people] from the way of Allah and the Masjid al-Haram, which We made for the people, equal are its resident and the visitor, and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment.﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. In this there is a rebuke to them and a reminder of their reproach for abandoning His religion.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[126] ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, make this a secure city and provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day."  He said, "As for him who disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire; and wretched is the destination."﴾

"And when Abraham said, 'My Lord, make this'" — i.e., the place where You placed Your House and commanded me to settle my offspring in it — "a city" — i.e., one in which whoever dwells finds comfort — "secure" — i.e., safe from fear; that is, its people should not be terrified. Allah has answered his supplication, as in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever enters it is safe﴾ [Al-'Imran: 97], and His words, ﴿Do they not see that We made a sanctuary secure while people are being snatched away from around them? Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favor of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 67], and other verses to that effect. Numerous hadiths are authentic regarding the prohibition of fighting in it. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Jabir, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "It is not lawful for anyone to carry weapons in Makkah." It is thus secure from calamities; no tyrant reaches it except that Allah breaks him, as He did with the People of the Elephant.

As for His words, Exalted is He, in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿this city secure﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], with "the city" definite while making it an attribute of "this," which differs from what is here, there are two possibilities. Either it is taken to mean that the question was repeated, so that the first supplication mentioned here occurred when the place had not yet been made a city, as if he had said: "Make this valley a secure city," because He, Exalted is He, related of him that he said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. So he said here: "Make this valley a secure city." The second supplication occurred after it had been made a city, so it is as if he said: "Make this place, which You have made a city, one of security and safety." Or it is taken to mean that the question was one, and the relating was repeated, as is most apparent. The apparent meaning is that both matters were requested, and this is what is related here, while there it confined itself to relating the request for security, dispensing with relating the request for becoming a city by relating the request, "make the hearts of people incline toward it." This is the summary of what they verified.

In my view, the question and the one asked are one. However, he varied the expression in the two places, omitting from each what the other mentions, by way of ihtibak (interlocking omission). The original is: "My Lord, make this city a secure city." By this the two supplications correspond in the most wondrous and purest manner, free of artificiality, along with what it conveys of emphasis, i.e., a city complete in security, as if it were said: "Make it a city known for being secure and famous for it," like your saying: "This day was a hot day."

In the Qamus and its commentary, al-Taj: "Al-balad and al-baldah" is a proper name for Makkah, may Allah exalt it, as a glorification of it, like al-Najm for the Pleiades. And every piece of land that is contained, whether inhabited or uninhabited, cultivated or wild, is a balad. In al-Nihayah: "Al-balad of the earth is that which is the abode of living creatures, even if there is no building in it."

﴿And provide its people with fruits﴾: Abraham, peace be upon him, asked this because Makkah had no crops or fruit, so Allah, Exalted is He, answered him, and thereafter the fruits of every thing were brought to it. "Those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day" is a substitution for "its people," a partial substitution, meaning: provide the believers among its people specifically. He singled them out for the supplication to show the nobility of faith, to express concern for the affairs of its people, and to observe good manners in the request, since Allah, Exalted is He, distinguished the believers from the disbelievers in the matter of leadership, in His words, ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, after he, peace be upon him, asked that it be placed among his descendants. Therefore he rightly restricted this supplication to the believers, which also encourages his people toward faith and deters them from disbelief.

"He said" — Allah, Exalted is He, informing that the comprehensiveness of the Most Merciful extends to the security and provision of this worldly life to all the inhabitants of the earth: "And whoever disbelieves" — i.e., I will also bestow upon him what I inspired you to ask of security and provision. So it is coordinated with the object of a verb that is omitted, which the speech indicates. It may be that "man" is an inchoative, either a relative or a conditional. His words "then I will grant him enjoyment" are its predicate or its apodosis. He expressed his provision by "enjoyment," which is a small provision and sustenance, as a belittling of it, and he emphasized this with "for a little," meaning enjoyment for a little, or for a little time. "Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire" — i.e., I will force him to it, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day they will be pushed into the fire of Hell with a violent push﴾ [At-Tur: 13], and ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces﴾ [Al-Qamar: 48]. It has also been read as "fa-umatti'uhu qalilan thumma adtarruhu" with the imperative in both, as being part of Abraham's supplication, peace be upon him; and in "He said" the pronoun refers to him. "And wretched is the destination" — the Fire or its punishment.

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[١٢٧] ﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّا إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ﴾

﴿وَإِذْ يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ وَإِسْمَاعِيلُ﴾ أي: اذكُر بناءَهما البيتَ ورفعَهما القواعدَ منه. وصيغةُ المضارع للاستقبال (al-istiqbal) لحكايةِ الحالِ الماضيةِ، لاستحضارِ صورتِها العجيبةِ. و"القواعدُ" جمعُ قاعدةٍ، وهي الأساسُ والأصلُ لِما فوقَه. وقال الزَّجّاجُ: القواعدُ أساطينُ البناءِ التي تعمِّدُه. ﴿رَبَّنا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّا﴾ على إرادةِ القولِ، أي: يقولانِ. وتركُ مفعولِ "تَقَبَّلْ" ليعمَّ الدعاءَ وغيرَه من القُرَبِ والطاعاتِ، التي من جملتِها ما هما بصدَدِه من البناء. كما يُعرِبُ عنه جعلُ الجملةِ الدعائيةِ حاليةً (hal, circumstantial clause): ﴿إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ السَّمِيعُ﴾ لدعائِنا، ﴿الْعَلِيمُ﴾ بضمائرِنا ونيّاتِنا.

وفي صحيحِ البخاريِّ عن ابنِ عباسٍ، في حديثِ مجيءِ إبراهيمَ لتفقُّدِ إسماعيلَ، عليهما السلامُ: «ثُمَّ قالَ: يا إسماعيلُ! إنَّ اللهَ قدْ أمرَنِي بأمرٍ. قالَ: فاصنعْ ما أمرَكَ رَبُّكَ. قالَ: وتُعِينُنِي؟ قالَ: وأُعِينُكَ. قالَ: فإنَّ اللهَ أمرَنِي أنْ أبنيَ هَهُنا بيتًا، وأشارَ إلى أكمَةٍ مرتفعةٍ على ما حولَها. قالَ: فعندَ ذلكَ رفعَا القواعدَ مِنَ البيتِ، فجعلَ إسماعيلُ يأتي بالحجارةِ، وإبراهيمُ يبني، حتى إذا ارتفعَ البناءُ، جاءَ بهذا الحجرِ فوضعَهُ لهُ، فقامَ عليهِ وهو يبني، وإسماعيلُ يناولُهُ الحجارةَ، وهما يقولانِ: ﴿رَبَّنا تَقَبَّلْ مِنَّا إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ﴾. قالَ: فجعلا يبنيانِ حتى يدورا حولَ البيتِ، وهما يقولانِ: ربَّنا تقبَّلْ مِنَّا إنَّكَ أنتَ السميعُ العليمُ».

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[128] ﴿Our Lord, make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a submissive nation to You, and show us our rites, and turn to us in forgiveness. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

"Our Lord, make us submissive to You" — sincere to You in our faces (i.e., devoting our faces to You). From His words: "He submitted his face to God" (aslama wajhahu lillah). Or "submitting" (mustaslimayn), from the saying: aslama lahu wa sallama, and istaslama, when one humbles oneself and yields. The meaning: increase us in sincerity or in submission to You. "And of our descendants" — and make of our descendants "a submissive nation to You." The "min" (of) is for partitive or for specification, like His words: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe﴾ [al-Nur: 55]. They singled out the descendants in the supplication because they are most deserving of compassion, and because when they are righteous, the followers are made righteous through them. "And show us our rites" — that is, teach us our acts of worship. The plural of manasik (manSak), with fatha and kasra on the sin, meaning the place of worship and the law of worship. It applies to the verbal noun, the time, and the place, derived from nusk, which has three vowel forms and also with two dammas, meaning worship and obedience, and everything by which one draws near to God, exalted is He.

Among the exegetes are those who understood the rites (manasik) as the rites of the Hajj, because they are widely known in its acts and places. Then the showing is for defining those acts and sites. Reports have been transmitted from some of the Companions and the Successors which include that (p-257) Gabriel showed Abraham the rites, and that Satan confronted him, and he stoned him, peace be upon him. They said: In that is a manifestation of the nobility of the act of Hajj, since it was received directly from God without intermediary, being a sign for the coming of the Day of Religion, where there is no intermediary between the Lord and the servants. What the imams of linguistics relied upon is what we mentioned first, namely taking the rites to refer to what the root of this word returns to: worship, drawing near to God, exalted is He, and adhering to what pleases Him, and making this general to everything God prescribed for Abraham, peace be upon him. That is: teach us how to worship You, where to worship You, and with what to draw near to You, so that we may serve You as a servant serves his master? "And turn to us in forgiveness, indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." This supplication is a request for repentance for what has passed of shortcoming. For the servant, even if he strives in obedience to his Lord, does not cease to fall short in some respects, either through forgetfulness and heedlessness, or through leaving what is better. Thus the supplication from both of them, upon them be peace, is for that reason.

The discussion of His words, the Exalted:

[129] ﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ This is an account of the completion of Ibrahim's (Abraham's) supplication for the people of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), that God would raise up among them a messenger from among them, that is, from the descendants of Ibrahim, and they are the Arabs of the line of Isma'il (Ishmael). God, the Exalted, answered this supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. He raised up among his descendants a messenger from among them, namely Muhammad, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to all of mankind. He (ﷺ) himself informed that he was the fulfilment of Ibrahim's supplication, and that what was meant was this supplication. This is related in what Imam Ahmad transmitted from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I, with God, am the Seal of the Prophets, and indeed Adam was still lying in his clay [p. 258], and I will inform you of the beginning of that: I am the supplication of my father Ibrahim, the glad tidings of Isa (Jesus) concerning me, and the vision my mother saw, and likewise the mothers of the prophets see visions." He also transmitted something similar from Abu Umamah, who said: "I said: O Prophet of God! What was the beginning of your matter? He said: 'The supplication of my father Ibrahim, the good news of Isa concerning me, and my mother saw that a light came forth from her by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.'"

What is meant is that the first to mention his name and make him known among the people was Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his mention remained famous among the people until Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus son of Mary), peace be upon them both, openly named him, when he said: ﴿I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what is before me of the Torah and giving good news of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad.﴾ [al-Saff: 6]. This is the meaning of his words in the hadith: "the supplication of my father Ibrahim, and the good news of Isa son of Maryam." And his words in it: "my mother saw that a light came forth from her by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated." It was said: this was from what she saw when she was pregnant with him, and she related it to her people, so it spread among them and became known among them, and that was a preparation and an announcement (irhas). The specification of Syria (al-Sham) for the manifestation of his light is an indication of the establishment of his religion and his prophethood in the lands of Syria. For this reason, at the end of time Syria will be a stronghold for Islam and its people, and in it Isa son of Maryam will descend, if he descends in Damascus, at the white eastern minaret.

For this reason it has come in the two Sahihs: "A group of my community will continue to be victorious upon the truth; those who forsake them will not harm them until the command of God comes, and they will be so." And in Sahih al-Bukhari: "and they will be in Syria."

His words, the Exalted: ﴿who will recite to them Your verses﴾ refer either to the Furqan (Criterion, i.e., the Qur'an) that was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), which is recited to them, or to the signs that indicate the existence of the Creator and His attributes, the Exalted. The meaning of his reciting them to them is that he would remind them of them, call them to them, and lead them to belief in them. His words, the Exalted, "and teach them the Book" means the complete and comprehensive one, encompassing every book, which is the Qur'an. "And wisdom" is the Sunnah; many have explained it this way. And from Malik: it is knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, and following it. His words, the Exalted, "and purify them" mean purify them from polytheism and all other impurities, like His words: ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the wicked things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

[p. 260] When he, peace be upon him, mentioned these supplications, he concluded them with praise of God, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ Al-'Aziz is the one possessing 'izza, which is strength, power, dominance, and eminence. "Al-Hakim" means the one who judges (al-hakim), or the one who governs things and perfects them. Both are among His attributes, the Exalted.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, what is the order in the verse? It is said: As for the verses (ayat), they are the signs indicating the miraculous nature of the Prophet (ﷺ). He mentioned recitation because it was the greatest indication of his prophethood, connected to the Qur'an. As for the order: the first station of the Prophet (ﷺ) after claiming prophethood was bringing the signs that indicate his prophethood. Then after that, teaching them the Book, that is, making them understand its realities and not merely its words. Then, by teaching them the Book, he leads them to deriving wisdom, which is the most noble rank of knowledge. For this reason He said: ﴿Whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. Then, by gradually advancing in wisdom, the person becomes purified (muzakka), that is, cleansed and made fit for closeness to God, Mighty and Majestic. End.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[130] ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ This is a denunciation and an expression of astonishment that there should be among the sensible anyone who turns away from the clear truth, which is the religion (millah) of Abraham, and which is what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. In this there is an allusion to the obstinate people of the Book and the polytheists: none turns away from his clear and radiant religion except one who has made a fool of himself, that is, who has driven himself to foolishness (safah), which is ignorance.

Al-Raghib said: "Making oneself a fool (safaha nafsahu) is more emphatic than being ignorant of oneself (jahila nafsahu), because ignorance is of two kinds: simple ignorance (jahl basit), which is when a person holds no belief at all about a matter; and compound ignorance (jahl murakkab), which is when a person believes the truth to be falsehood and falsehood to be truth. Foolishness (safah) is when a person holds such a belief and, in action, deliberately follows what he believes." Thus God, may He be exalted, made clear that whoever turns away from the religion of Abraham does so because of the foolishness of his own self, and this is of greater blame, for it is the source of every failing. For whoever is ignorant of himself is ignorant that he is created; and whoever is ignorant that he is created is ignorant of his Creator; and whoever does not know that he has a Creator, how can he know His command and prohibition, or what He has made good and what He has made bad? Because knowing oneself is a means to knowing the Creator, may His praise be exalted, He said: ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21], and He said: ﴿And do not be like those who forgot God, so He made them forget themselves﴾ [al-Hashr: 19].

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We had chosen him in this world﴾, that is, We selected him from among all creation with prophethood, messengership and imamate; with the multiplication of prophets from his offspring; with the giving of khullah (intimate friendship); with the manifestation of the rites upon him; and with making his House a secure place, bearing clear signs until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, who have the highest ranks. In this there is the greatest exaltation of the rank of righteousness, in that He made him one of those characterized by it; so he is worthy of the imamate, because of the lofty standing he has with God in both abodes. In this there is the greatest encouragement to follow his religion and to be guided by his guidance, and the strongest condemnation of whoever opposes him.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, how can He describe him as chosen in this world and righteous in the Hereafter, when reasoning suggests the opposite? For righteousness is a description that relates to action, and that occurs in this world, whereas chosenness (al-istifa') is a state that the servant deserves by being righteous, so its proper place should be the Hereafter?

It is said: chosenness is of two kinds. One is as I have stated, and the other is in this world, which is God's singling out of some of His servants with His guardianship and prophethood by a particular distinction. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Grateful for His blessings; He chose him﴾ [al-Nahl: 121]. Righteousness, although it is considered by the states of this world, is also rewarded in the Hereafter. Thus God made clear that he was chosen in this world, because of what God knew of His wisdom concerning him, and that he is judged to be righteous in the Hereafter, because of his righteousness in this world, as an admonition that the reward in the Hereafter was not deserved by his being chosen in this world, but was deserved by his righteousness therein. It is also permissible that His words "in the Hereafter" mean "in the acts of the Hereafter": he is among the righteous. It is also permissible that by His words "in this world" He meant his state while living, and by "in the Hereafter" his state after death, and that the reference to his righteousness is to the good praise of him, for which he asked God by saying: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 84]. It is also permissible that since people are of three kinds, the wrongdoer, the moderate, and the foremost, he expressed the foremost by "the righteous", for every one who hastens to the obedience of God and His mercy is righteous. End of quotation.

All of this is a reminder to the People of the Book of what they possess of knowledge concerning the affair of this noble Prophet, and an establishment of the proof against them, because most of it is coordinated with "remember" in His words: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour﴾ [al-Baqarah: 122].

(p-263) When he mentioned his imamate, peace be upon him, he mentioned what is followed in him, which is the cause of his being chosen and his righteousness, and that is his religion, and what he enjoined upon his sons, and what his sons enjoined upon their sons, generation after generation, especially Jacob, peace be upon him, who is the one mentioned in the People of the Book's ascription to him, so He said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[131] ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted myself to the Lord of the worlds."﴾

"Idh" (إذ): that is, We chose him, because "his Lord said to him, 'Submit'": that is, submit to your Lord, surrender to Him and devote yourself sincerely to Him; or, remain steadfast in Islam and firm upon monotheism. "He said, 'I have submitted myself to the Lord of the worlds.'" The apparent sense of the noble wording is that the speech is literal (haqiqi), nothing prevents this, and nothing has come that requires interpreting it otherwise. As for the saying of some that it is a figurative depiction (tamthil), meaning that the proofs of monotheism occurred to his mind, leading to the knowledge that calls to Islam, this is not correct. There is no sense in taking any part of speech as metaphor (majaz) when the literal meaning (haqiqah) is possible in some respect.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[132] ﴿And Abraham charged his sons with this, and [so did] Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾

"And Abraham charged his sons with it" — this begins an explanation of his (peace be upon him) perfecting others after the explanation of his perfection in himself. Tawsiyah (charge, enjoining) is advancing to another regarding a beneficial matter whose outcome is praiseworthy. The pronoun in "with it" (bihā) may refer either to his statement "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds" (aslamtu li-Rabb al-'alamin), by interpreting it as a word and a sentence (ta'wil al-kalimah wa-al-jumlah). Similar to this is the return of the pronoun in His words: ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28], referring to His words: ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 26] (p-264) ﴿except He who created me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 27]. His words "a word" (kalimah) are evidence that the feminine gender is by interpretation of "word." Or it may refer back to the religion (millah) in His words: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. The first view is supported by the charged matter agreeing in wording with "I have submitted" (aslamtu), and by the closeness of the thing referred to. Al-Qadi preferred the second view, because the referent is explicitly mentioned, and returning a pronoun to what is explicitly mentioned, when possible, is better than returning it to what is implied and understood; and because the religion (millah) is more comprehensive than that word. Both are good.

His words, exalted is He, "his sons" (banihi): the plural form indicates that Abraham (peace be upon him) had children other than Isma'il and Ishaq. I have read in the Book of Genesis (Sifr al-Takwin) of the Torah that Abraham (peace be upon him), after the death of Sarah the mother of Ishaq, married another woman named Qatura, and she bore him: Zimran, Yoqshan, Madan, Midyan, Yishbaq and Shuah. Accordingly, his sons (peace be upon him) would be eight. "And Jacob" (wa-Ya'qub) is coordinated with Abraham, and its object is omitted; its estimated form is: "And Jacob charged his sons," because Jacob also charged his sons just as Abraham charged his sons. The evidence for this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿When he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 133], as will come. It has also been read "wa-Ya'qiba" in the accusative, coordinated with "banihi," and its meaning is: "Abraham charged his sons with it, and [charged] his grandson Jacob." Jacob was born during the lifetime of his grandfather Abraham, and he lived to see fifteen years of his life, as is deduced from the Book of Genesis of the Torah, where it is said that Abraham (peace be upon him) had Ishaq born to him when he was one hundred years old, and he died at the age of one hundred and seventy-five, and Ishaq, when Jacob and Esau were born to him, was sixty years old. From this, what we have mentioned is deduced. The secret of mentioning Jacob's existence during his grandfather's lifetime is understood in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Jacob﴾ [al-An'am: 84], and in another verse: ﴿And We gave him Ishaq and Jacob as an additional gift﴾ [al-Anbiya': 72].

"O my sons" (ya banayya): i.e., each of Abraham and Jacob said it according to the first reading. According to the second reading: Abraham said: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾, i.e., He has given you the religion that is the choice of religions, which is the religion of Islam, and there is no other religion with Allah, exalted is He. "So do not" (fa-la): i.e., as a consequence of that, I say to you: do not "die except while you are Muslims." In this sentence there is eloquent brevity. The meaning is: Hold fast to Islam, and do not part from it until you die. This exception is an exception from the most general of states (mufarragh min a'amm al-ahwal), i.e., do not die in any state except in the state of being steadfast in Islam. Thus the prohibition is in reality against being in a state contrary to Islam when they die, because that is what is within their power. It cannot be said: the form of the prohibition is established to seek abstention from what it denotes, so what is understood from it is a prohibition against dying in a state contrary to Islam, and this is not intended, because it is not within one's power. Rather, what is within one's power is being in a state contrary to Islam, so the prohibition returns to it, and the intended meaning is the prohibition against being characterized by a state contrary to Islam (p-266) at the time of death, since refraining from being characterized by that state follows from refraining from dying in that state. Then either it is said: the word originally meant for the first is used for the second, and it is then a metaphor (majaz); or it is said: the word is used in its meaning so as to pass from it to what it necessarily implies, and then it is a metonymy (kinayah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: The parallel to this is your saying: "Do not pray except while you are humble (khashi'); you are not forbidding him from prayer, but from abandoning humility during his prayer. The point of bringing the particle of prohibition onto what is not forbidden is to show that their dying not in a state of steadfastness in Islam is a death in which there is no good, that it is not the death of the fortunate, and that it is fitting that this death should not befall them. Just as you say in a command: "Die while you are a martyr," your intention is not the command to die, but to be in the attribute of martyrs when he dies. You only commanded him to die because of your regard for his death and to show its superiority over others, and because it is truly worthy to be urged toward it." This is the end.

With these verses, He, exalted is He, has established the falsity of what the obstinate among the Jews and Christians hold, and has cleared His friend and the prophets of that. When He related that Abraham (peace be upon him) strongly enjoined his sons with the religion and Islam, He mentioned after it that Jacob charged his sons with the same, as a confirmation of the proof against the Jews and Christians and as an emphasis in the exposition, with His words:

القَوْلُ في تَأْوِيلِ قَوْلِهِ تَعالى:

[١٣٣ ] ﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are Muslims."﴾

﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ That is, you were not present at that time. Here "am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'a), estimated to mean "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamza, and in the hamza there is a denial that serves reproach and rebuke. "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid" or "shahid" in the sense of "present (hadir)." The presence of death means the presence of its precursors. "When he said" — that is, Ya'qub (p-٢٦٧) "to his sons." They were Ru'ubin, Shim'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Yasakar, Zabulun, Yusuf, Binyamin, Dan, Naftali, Jad, and Asher, and they are the tribes (al-asbat) whose names are mentioned later. "What will you worship after me?" That is, what will you worship after my death? By his question he intended to affirm them in monotheism and submission, and to take their covenant to remain steadfast upon them. "They said, 'We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq'": this is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) for "your fathers," and he counted Isma'il, who was his paternal uncle, among his fathers. This is because the paternal uncle is a father and the maternal aunt is a mother, since both are joined in one line, which is kinship, with no difference between them. From this is the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, traced to the Prophet: "A man's paternal uncle is the twin of his father" (ʿamm al-rajul ṣinw abīhi), meaning there is no difference between them, just as there is no difference between the two shoots (ṣinwān) of a palm tree. In the Two Sahihs, from al-Bara', traced to the Prophet: "The maternal aunt holds the position of the mother." Ibn Sa'd related from Muhammad ibn ʿAli in a mursal report: "The maternal aunt is a mother."

(p-٢٦٨)"One God" (إلهًا واحدًا) is a substitution (badal) for "the God of your fathers," like His saying ﴿by the forelock﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 15] ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 16].
