Or it is in the sense of specification (ikhtisas), meaning we intend by "the God of your fathers" one God. In this there is an affirmation of freedom from polytheism, by explicitly stating tawhid. Then, after their declaration of tawhid, they informed of their sincerity in worship by saying "and to Him we are" — that is, to Him alone, not to a father or anyone else — "Muslims," that is, obedient and submissive, as He said: ﴿To Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Al ʿImran: 83]. Islam is the creed (millah) of all the prophets, even though their laws (shara'i') differ and their methods (manahij) vary, as He said: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 25]. The verses and hadiths on this are numerous. Among them is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We, the company of prophets, are children of different mothers (ʿallat), and our religion is one." The account of the bequest of Ibrahim and Ya'qub, peace be upon them, to their sons contains subtle points that encourage adherence to the religion. Among them: God, the Exalted, did not say, "Ibrahim commanded his sons," but said "instructed them" (waṣṣahum). The word waṣiyyah is more emphatic than amr, because a bequest occurs at the fear of death, and at that time a person's care for his religion is most intense and complete. This indicates the importance of the matter bequeathed and of holding fast to it.

Among them is the specification of their sons with this, because a man's compassion for his sons is greater than his compassion for others. When the two of them singled them out with it at the end of their lives, we know that their concern (p-٢٦٩) with it was greater than their concern with anything else.

Among them is that they, peace be upon them, did not combine with this bequest another bequest, and this also indicates intense concern. There are other subtle points which al-Fakhr, may God have mercy on him, pointed out.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[134] ﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾

"That" refers to Ibrahim, Ya'qub and their descendants who were monotheists. "A community" means a generation and a group. "Has passed away" means has gone before and departed. "For them is what they earned" means in their Islam, of beliefs, deeds and morals. "And for you is what you have earned" means that what you are upon of desire is specific to you; they will not be questioned about your deeds. "And you will not be questioned about what they used to do." The meaning is that no one benefits from the earnings of another, whether he came earlier or later. Just as those people benefit only from what they themselves earned, so too you benefit only from what you earned. Therefore, the reports about them that are recounted to you, and what they were upon of Islam and calling to it, are only so that you may do what they did and thereby benefit. And if you refuse, you will not benefit from their deeds.

Al-Razi (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: The verse indicates the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation), because His words "For them is what they earned" show that each person's earning is specific to him and no one else benefits from it. Had taqlid been permissible, the earning of the one followed would benefit the follower. It is as if He said: I did not mention the account of their conditions seeking from you that you imitate them, but so that you would take heed of what is incumbent upon you, and reason, and know that what they were upon of the faith is the truth. End.

It is well known that following the Prophets, peace be upon them, and believing in them is not called taqlid, since it falls outside its defined limit as established in the books of usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence).

Then Exalted God informed that they had exchanged guidance from the chosen ones among their forefathers for becoming callers to disbelief, together with clarifying the invalidity of what they were upon in every respect, by His words:

(p-270) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[135] ﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." Say: "Rather, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾

"And they say" — i.e., the two groups of the People of the Book: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided. Say: 'Rather,'" [we follow] "the religion (millah) of Abraham" and take as our way (nastinnu) his sunnah, not turning away from it as you have turned away, "ḥanīfan" — i.e., upright, or inclining away from falsehood toward truth. This is because al-ḥanaf (ḥanaf), with a vowel on the ḥa and the nun, is applied to uprightness, and from it comes the saying that a man whose foot inclines is called aḥnaf, as an optimistic wish for uprightness, just as they call the one stung by a scorpion "salīm" (the safe one) and a deadly desert "mafāzah" (the place of escape). It is also applied to an inclination in the front of the foot and a crookedness in the leg. So the ḥanīf is one who is upright in his submission to God, Exalted is He, and who inclines away from polytheism toward the religion of God, glorified is He.

When He had affirmed his submission through being a ḥanīf, He negated from him anything else by His words "and he was not of the polytheists." In this there is an allusion to the People of the Book, and a declaration of the falsehood of their claim to follow him, peace be upon him, together with their association of partners (with God) by their saying: "Ezra is the son of God," and "the Messiah is the son of God." This noble verse has conveyed that what both groups hold is pure misguidance and the commission of falsehood, and that the religion that is pleasing to God is Islam, which is the call of creation to His oneness, Exalted is He, and to worshipping Him alone, with no partner.

When the polytheists opposed this great principle, God sent His Prophet Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, to call all people to this principle.

(p-271) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[136] ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting.﴾

"Qūlū" (say) means: O you who believe. In this there is a demonstration of the excellence of God's favour toward them, in that He dictates to them and does not make them answer, so that they might fall short in their speech. ﴿We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾, meaning: from the Book that has preceded, which is guidance. ﴿And in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes﴾, from the rulings by which they were bound to worship, of what the scrolls of their father Abraham, peace be upon him, contained, and of what was revealed to them specifically. The "asbāt" (tribes) are the twelve sons of Jacob mentioned earlier; it is the plural of "sibt" (sibt), which means grandson (ḥāfid). They were so named because they were grandsons of Abraham and Isaac. ﴿And in what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾, of the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿And in what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾, of what has been mentioned and what is other than it. ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ in faith, so that we believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did. ﴿And to Him we are submitting﴾, meaning: obedient.

Al-Bukhari has related from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The People of the Book used to read the Torah in Hebrew and explain it in Arabic to the people of Islam. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us.'"

(p-272) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[137] ﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in, then they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, then they are only in opposition (shiqaq), and Allah will suffice you against them. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

"If they believe" — that is, the People of the Book who wished to draw you into their ways — "in the like of what you believe in" — that is, in what you believe in, in the manner that has been detailed. The word "like" (mithl) here is redundant (muqhamm). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud read: "in what you believe in" (bi-ma amantum bihi). Ubayy read: "in that which you believe in" (bi-l-ladhi amantum bihi). "Then they are rightly guided" — they reach the truth and attain it, just as you have been guided — the reverse of what they said: "Be like us and you will be guided." "But if they turn away" — that is, they turn away from believing in what you believe in. "Then they are only in opposition" — that is, they are nothing but in dissension and enmity, and they have no part in seeking the truth at all.

Al-Qadi said: One scarcely says "shiqaq" of enmity directed toward the truth, or of opposition that is not sinful. Rather, that term is used only of a grave opposition which brings its bearer into the enmity, wrath and curse of Allah, and into deserving the Fire. Thus this statement becomes a threat from Him, exalted is He, against them, and the description of them by it becomes evidence that these people are hostile to the Messenger, harbour evil toward him, and lie in wait to bring him into trials. At this point Allah, exalted is He, assured him against their plotting and assured the believers against their evil and their scheming, and so He said: "Allah will suffice you against them," strengthening his heart and the hearts of the believers, for when Allah, exalted is He, undertakes to suffice in a matter, confidence in Him is achieved. He has fulfilled His promise by the killing and enslavement of the Banu Qurayza (p-273) and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. "And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing" — He follows His promise of victory and sufficiency with this, indicating that what they conceal and what they make public of their affairs is not hidden from Him, exalted is He. So He causes every word and intention of theirs to return its harm upon them. Thus it is a threat to them, or a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): that is, He hears what you call upon Him with, and knows your intention and what you desire of manifesting the religion of truth. He responds to you and brings you to your aim.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 138:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[138] ﴿The baptism of Allah. And who is better than Allah at baptism? And we are worshippers of Him.﴾

"Ṣibghata Allāh" (the baptism of Allah) is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) in the accusative, governed by His words "Āmannā billāh" (we believe in Allah). So said Sibawayh, and it stands in the place of its verb, as if it were said: "Allah has baptized us with a baptism" (ṣabagha-nā Allāhu ṣibghatan). That is: He dyed our hearts with guidance and clarity with a complete dye that is not removed by the water of doubt, and the dye of another does not overcome it. Ṣibgha (the dye) is like ṣabgh (both with a kasra in each, according to the dialects), and it is that with which garments are dyed and colored. The faith is described with this because it is a purification for the believers from the filth of disbelief, an adornment that beautifies them with its fine effects, and something that penetrates their hearts, just as the matter of dye stands in relation to cloth. It is said: "ṣabagha yadahu bil-mā'" (he dipped his hand in the water, immersing it in it). Tha'lab recited:

"Leave evil, and descend to safety, guarding yourself, if the dyer of evil has not dyed you."

Al-Raghib said: The ṣibgha is an indication from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of what He has brought into existence in people of the beginnings of intellects (p-274) by which He distinguished us from the beasts, and endowed us with them for recognizing Him, recognizing the goodness of justice, and seeking the truth. This is what is referred to as the fitra (natural disposition) in His words: ﴿The fitra of Allah upon which He created mankind; there is no altering of the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30], and what is meant by His words, upon him be peace: "Every child is born upon the fitra..." the report. Naming this as a ṣibgha is because the faculties of man with which he has been constituted, when considered in themselves, function like the dye which is the adornment of what is dyed. And since the Jews and Christians, when they teach their children Judaism and Christianity, say: "We have dyed him," He, exalted, made clear that faith in the same manner as you have believed is the ṣibghat Allah and His fitra which He placed in creation, and there is no one better in dye than Him.

Then he said: The saying of al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid, that the ṣibgha is the religion (dīn), and the saying of others that it is the sharī'a (law), and the saying of one who said it is circumcision, all point to one meaning. ﴿And who is better than Allah at baptism?﴾ The interrogative is for denial and negation: that is, there is no dye better than His dye, exalted is He, because it is a dye of the heart that does not fade, owing to its firmness by the One who guards and knows, so that no one turns away from his religion out of anger toward Him after faith has mingled with the cheerfulness of his heart. The clause is parenthetical, confirming what is in "ṣibghat Allah" of the sense of rejoicing, "and we are worshippers of Him," thankful for that blessing and for all His other blessings. How then could His dye depart from us while we reinforce it with worship, which removes the rust from the heart so that the image of guidance is imprinted upon it? And it is a conjunction with "Āmannā," entering together with it under the command.

(p-275) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[139] ﴿Say: Do you argue with us concerning God, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him.﴾

"Say" (qul), rebuking their disputation and reproaching them for it. "Do you argue with us concerning God?" That is: do you debate with us about the Oneness of God, sincerity toward Him, following guidance, and abandoning desire? "When He is our Lord and your Lord," the One deserving that worship be made sincerely for Him alone, with no partner; we and you stand equal in being servants of Him. "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds": that is, we are free of you and of what you worship, and you are free of us. As He said in another verse: ﴿And if they deny you, say: For me is my work and for you is your work. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do﴾ [Yunus: 41]. And He, Exalted, said: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 20], and so on. "And we are sincere to Him" in worship and orientation, associating nothing with Him, whereas you associate with Him 'Uzayr, the Messiah, the rabbis and the monks. Since among their sophistries was their claim that their forefathers were upon their religion, He, glorified is He, refuted it with His words:

(p-276) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[140] ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: "Are you more knowing, or is God?" And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? God is not unaware of what you do.﴾

"Or do you say that Abraham" the Friend of God (Khalil Allah), "and Ishmael and Isaac" his two sons, "and Jacob" son of Isaac, "and the Tribes" the children of Jacob: "were Jews or Christians?" That is, upon their religion, either Judaism or Christianity. "Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?" That is, He to whom all encompassing knowledge belongs is the most knowing. They cannot say, "We are." And if they say, "God," then God has cleared Abraham and those with him of that. Their claim is thereby void, and it is established that they, peace be upon them, were upon the upright monotheistic faith (al-Hanifiyyah), submitting (Muslims), free of Judaism and Christianity. Moreover, the refutation of their claim is the most evident of the evident, in that it is inconceivable that something prior should be ascribed to something later, when the latter came into being only many long ages after the former. An explicit text refuting this will come in Al 'Imran. Since the knowledge that the Friend and those mentioned with him, peace be upon them, were upon the religion of Islam was with them from God, and they were concealing what they had of that, along with God's affirmation of this to them, His questioning them about it, and His prohibition to them of concealing it and what is close to it in His words, ﴿and do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:42) and so on, He indicated the most severe threat regarding the concealment of that by His words: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾, both existing and promised, "he has from God," which is the concealment of knowledge, which is the reporting of what God has sent down. The interrogative is a denial that anyone could be more unjust than the People of the Book, since they concealed His testimony to them, peace be upon them, regarding the upright faith and their disavowal of both groups.

(p-277) Al-Taqi Ibn Taymiyyah said: God, exalted is He, called the knowledge they had a "testimony," as in His words: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:159), and so on. It is as if He said: a report with Him, a religion with Him from God, a clarification with Him from God, and knowledge with Him from God. If His words "from God" are connected to "concealed," it encompasses all testimonies. If it is connected to "with him," which is the more apt, or to "testimony," or to both, the matter is one. That is, a testimony that became established with him from God's side. So it is the concealment of testimonies of knowledge inherited from the Prophets. Thus He called reporting it a testimony.

Then he said: Likewise, prophetic reports are only meant by "testimony" in them as reporting: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a warning and a severe threat. That is, His knowledge encompasses you, and He will recompense you for it.

Al-Razi said: This is the comprehensive statement of every threat. Whoever imagines that He, exalted is He, knows both their secret and their open conduct, that nothing is hidden from Him, and that after Him is the recompense of it, good for good and evil for evil, would not pass a moment of an eye except while cautious and fearful. Do you not see that if one of us had a watcher over him from a ruler, counting his breaths, he would be constantly wary and anxious, even though that watcher knows only the outward? How much more so with the Lord, the Watcher, who knows the secret and what is more hidden, when He threatens and warns with this kind of speech?

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[141] ﴿That was a community that has passed away. It shall have what it earned, and you shall have what you earn. You will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾

﴿That was a community that has passed away. It shall have what it earned, and you shall have what you earn﴾: so they will not be questioned about your deeds [p. 278] ﴿and you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ When Exalted is He mentioned the excellent way of the earlier prophets, and left them no ground to cling to on their own account, He followed this with an indication that the religion revolves with His command in every age, and that nothing benefits them except what they newly acquire under the ruling of the revealed scripture that has been sent down, which is miraculous to all the people of the earth, the red and the black among them. That is, leave off speaking about that community, for it has what it earned. Consider instead what the Seal of the Prophets, Muhammad (ﷺ), has called you to, for that is more beneficial to you and more returns to your good. You will not be questioned except about your own deeds.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: The repetition of this verse is because it is firmly established among people, both the righteous and the wicked, that they take pride in their fathers and follow them in their practices, especially in matters of their religion.

For this reason He related the words of the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and we are guided by their footsteps﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 22]. So Exalted is God emphasized the statement in order to turn them away from this way. And after relating the bequest of Abraham and Jacob to their sons concerning this, He mentioned it as a warning that the matter is the same whether it is as you say or not. You do not receive the reward of their deeds, nor do you bear their punishment. As for the second part, when He mentioned their claim of Judaism and Christianity for their fathers, He again repeated it as an emphasis upon them, as a warning of the sort He stated: ﴿And every human being We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13], and His saying: ﴿It has what it earned, and against it is what it has acquired﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and His saying: ﴿No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ [Fatir: 18]. And in accordance with what their custom has run and what their knowledge alone has singled out: every sheep is hanged by its own legs.

[p. 279]

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[142] ﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?" Say: "To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path."﴾

﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from the qibla they used to face?"﴾ Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him) that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) liked that his qibla be toward the House (the Ka'bah). He prayed the first prayer he prayed, the 'Asr prayer, and a people prayed with him. A man who had prayed with him went out and passed by the people of the mosque while they were bowing, and he said: 'I bear witness by Allah that I prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) facing Makkah.' So they turned around as they were, facing the House."

Muslim narrated similarly from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him), and his wording is: "We prayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, then we were turned toward the Ka'bah."

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "While the people were at Quba' in the dawn prayer, someone came to them and said: 'Indeed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has had a Qur'an revealed to him tonight, and he has been commanded to face the Ka'bah, so face it.' Their faces had been toward Syria, so they turned around toward the Ka'bah." (The wording is that of Muslim.)

The narrations concerning the change of the qibla from al-Quds (Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah are abundant, and what we have mentioned is sufficient.

[p. 280] Allah, exalted is He, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers that a group of the people would deny the change of the qibla, and He called them "foolish" (sufaha', the plural of safih), which means one who is light of forbearance, the foolish, and the ignorant. Abu al-Su'ud said: that is, those whose forbearance is light and who have debased it by blind imitation and by turning away from reflection and consideration. End of quotation.

The meaning of His words "What has turned them away" is: what turned them away from their qibla which they used to face, that is, while they were steadfast in facing it, which is Bayt al-Maqdis. The basis of the denial, if those who speak are the Jews, is their dislike of being turned away from it, because it was their qibla. If they are others, then it is simply the intention to attack the religion and to disparage its rulings. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that those who spoke were the Jews; from al-Hasan that they were the polytheists of the Arabs; and from al-Suddi that they were the hypocrites.

Al-Raghib said: There is no contradiction among their statements, for each has found fault, and each is foolish.

(Note): The apparent meaning of His words, exalted is He, "The foolish will say," etc., is that it is a report of their statement mentioned, and that the report came before its occurrence. Its benefit is to prepare the soul and to provide what will silence them, for the sudden arrival of what is disliked is harder and more severe upon the soul, and a ready answer to the clamor of the most stubborn adversary is more effective. Along with that, it contains signs of prophethood, since it is a report of the unseen, and so it is a miracle. ﴿Say: "To Allah belong the east and the west"﴾ is an answer to their doubt. Its explanation is that all directions belong to Allah in ownership, so none of them deserves, in its own essence, to be a qibla. Rather, it becomes a qibla only because Allah, exalted is He, made it a qibla, so there is no objection to Him for turning from one direction to another, and what He commands is the truth. ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ contains the exaltation of the people of Islam, the manifestation of His, exalted is He, care for them, and the magnification of the status of the Ka'bah, just as He magnified it by attributing it to Himself in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and purify My House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26].

(p-281) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[143] ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation, that you may be witnesses over the people and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know who would follow the Messenger from who would turn back on his heels. And indeed, it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided. And Allah would never let your faith go to waste. Indeed, Allah is Kind and Merciful to the people.﴾

"And thus" means: just as We guided you to a qiblah which is the most moderate (awsat) and the best of the qiblahs, "We have made you a nation (ummah) of moderation (wasatan)", that is, just (ʿudulan), choice (khiyaran). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people and that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾, gives the reason for the "making" that has been highlighted, by which the favour upon them was completed.

Know that the origin of shuhud (witnessing) and shahadah (testimony) is presence together with observation, either by sight or by insight. Al-Razi said: "Shahadah, mushahadah and shuhud are seeing. One says, 'I witnessed such a thing' when you saw it and perceived it. Since there is a strong correspondence between seeing with the eye and knowing with the heart, knowledge in the heart is indeed called mushahadah and shuhud, and one who knows a thing is called shahid and mushahid. Then the indication of a thing was called shahid over the thing, because it is by it that the witness becomes a witness. And since one who reports about a thing and clarifies its state functions as evidence for that, that reporter is also called a shahid. In sum, everyone who knows the state of a thing and reveals it is a witness concerning it." End of quotation.

The shahid is originally one who witnesses (shahid and mushahid) a thing and who reports from knowledge acquired through observation by sight or insight. In the third meaning, it is one of the sublime attributes. For this reason the prophets, leaders and imams are described with it, as you see in this verse and in the verse: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you against these as a witness?﴾ [al-Nisa': 41], and the verse ﴿and call your witnesses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], and ﴿the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

Furthermore, regarding the lam in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, there are two aspects:

(The first) It is the lam of becoming and outcome (lam al-sayrurah wa al-ʿaqibah). That is, the matter ends up, through your guidance and your being made a median nation, with you being witnesses over the people, namely the adherents of other religions; that is, you are seers over their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and what they altered, changed, associated (others with Allah) and deviated in, of what He related to you in the earlier verses, until you encompass it with knowledge. Thus you know the truth of their religion from its falsehood, and their revelation from what they invented. That is: when you witness this from them and see it, thank your Lord for what He has bestowed upon you and for sparing you what He afflicted others with, in that He granted you success in the straight path and guided you to the pleasing way. Likewise, the Messenger became a witness over you, in that you recognised the truth from falsehood, guidance from misguidance, and light from darkness, through what reached you of his revelation and what he showed you of His signs. Thus the favour of Allah upon you is magnified, since you have become guided after misguidance and scholars after ignorance. This contains an indication to warn the believers against deviating after guidance, as those whom He censured for their misguidance deviated, so that the proof is established against them as it was established against those.

(The second aspect) is that the lam is for causation (taʿlil), in its original sense. The meaning: We made you a nation of choice so that you may be witnesses over the people, that is, watchers and overseers over them through calling them to the truth, guiding them to right guidance, and warning them of the deviation and misguidance they are in, just as the Messenger was a witness over you by his standing over you, through what he conveyed to you, commanded you, forbade you, warned you and admonished you. The verse is thus similar to the verse ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. Perhaps those who said "the best explanation of the Qur'an is by the Qur'an" preferred this meaning, so that the two verses correspond from the outset, for wasat means khiyar (choice), and this is explicitly stated in His saying "best nation." To this meaning points the saying of Mujahid on the verse: "that you may be witnesses for Muhammad (peace be upon him) over the nations of the Jews, Christians and Magians," that is, witnesses to the truth of his message, through calling to it, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong, which is the pivot and spirit of the call.

After writing this, I saw that al-Samarqandi in his tafsir transmitted the essence of what we have said. His wording: "There is another interpretation for the verse: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾, that is, just, ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ etc. He says: You are a proof against all who oppose you, and the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) is a proof against you. Shahadah in language means clarification, and for this the witness is called bayyinah (evidence), because he clarifies the right of the claimant. That is, you clarify for those after you, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) clarifies for you." End of quotation.

Al-Raghib al-Isfahani clarified this in another style, saying: If it is asked, in what way is the Prophet's ﷺ witnessing over the Ummah and the Ummah's witnessing over mankind? It is said: the shahid is the one who knows a thing, reports about it, and affirms its judgment. The greatest witness is one whose testimony is established by proof. Since Allah, Exalted is He, distinguished man with reason and discernment between good and evil, perfected this by sending prophets, and distinguished this Ummah with the most complete Book, as He described it: ﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾ [al-An'am: 38], and His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. (He, peace be upon him, conveyed it to us and made it clear to us, so he became a proof and a witness, so that they cannot say: ﴿There came to us no bringer of good tidings nor warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]), and He made His Ummah, specialised in knowing Him, witnesses over all other people. (If it is asked:) Are all of his Ummah witnesses, or only some of them? (It is answered:) All of them are able to be witnesses, on condition that they purify themselves through knowledge and righteous deed. Whoever does not purify himself is not a witness and is not accepted. Therefore Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9]. On this basis He said: ﴿O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. Upholding justice is the observance of equity, and it is, in summary, threefold: justice between a person and himself, justice between him and the people, and justice between him and Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever observes this has become a just witness for Allah, Mighty and Majestic. (If it is asked:) Are they witnesses over some of the Ummah or over all people? (It is answered:) Rather, each is a witness over himself, over his Ummah and over all people, for whoever knows the wisdom, generosity and mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, knows that He is not unaware of him or of anyone among the people, nor is He stingy toward them or unjust to them. Whoever knows this is a witness for Allah over those in his time, and over those before him and after him. In this sense is what is reported in the hadith: "This Ummah bears witness for the prophets over the nations." End of al-Raghib's words. The hadith to which he alludes was narrated by al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Noah will be called on the Day of Resurrection, and he will say: 'Here I am at Your service, O Lord.' He will be asked: 'Did you convey?' He will say: 'Yes.' Then his people will be asked: 'Did he convey to you?' They will say: 'No warner came to us.' He will say: 'Who will bear witness for you?' He will say: 'Muhammad and his Ummah.' They will bear witness that he did convey, and the Messenger will be a witness over you." This is His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation that you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you.﴾ It has also been narrated as marfu' (traced to the Prophet) from Jabir, recorded by al-Tabari, and from a group of the Followers (tabi'un) as their own statements.

I say: We have explained repeatedly that such a report, and everything that is related, whether marfu' or not, in the interpretation of this verse, all of it indicates that the verse has a generality encompassing what has been mentioned, not that it is restricted to it so that nothing else can be derived from it. As we clarified in the introduction regarding their saying "the verse was revealed concerning such-and-such." Accordingly, there is no contradiction between what is understood from the context of the verse, or what its meaning linguistically requires in terms of its generality, or what is carried over to it from its counterparts in the Noble Revelation, and what is related in its explanation. The outcome of multiple occasions of revelation for a single verse, or the many reports concerning its aspects, is all within the category of explaining the general by some of what its wording encompasses. For this reason it often occurs in some chains of transmission: "then the Prophet ﷺ recited His saying, Exalted is He," or "then he recited," or "recite if you wish," which indicates that the verse was mentioned as evidence for what he reported, since it falls within it. Be careful about this.

Notes:

First: The verse has been cited as evidence that consensus (ijma') is a proof, because Allah, Exalted is He, described this Ummah with justice ('adalah), and the just person is the one deserving of testimony and of its acceptance. So when they agree upon a matter and testify to it, its acceptance is obligatory. Hence the consensus of the Ummah is true; the Ummah does not agree upon error, praise be to Allah. As Allah described them with this in the Book, saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]. This is a description of them as enjoining every good and forbidding every evil. Likewise He described their Prophet ﷺ with it in His saying: ﴿who they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel, enjoining upon them what is right and forbidding them what is wrong﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], and with it He described the believers in His saying: ﴿The believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71]. If the Ummah were to say in religion something that is misguidance, it would not have enjoined the right in that matter nor forbidden the wrong in it, whereas Allah has made them witnesses over the people and placed their testimony in the position of the Messenger's testimony. It has been established in the Sahih from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Suhayb who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "They passed by a funeral bier and praised it with good, so the Prophet ﷺ said, 'It is incumbent (wajabat).' Then they passed by another and praised it with evil, and he said, 'It is incumbent.'" 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What is incumbent?" He said: "This one you praised with good, so Paradise became incumbent for him; and this one you praised with evil, so the Fire became incumbent for him. You are the witnesses of Allah on earth."

In al-Hakim's narration he recited this verse: ﴿And thus We have made you...﴾ to its end.

Since the Lord has made them witnesses, they do not testify to falsehood. So when they testify that Allah commanded something, He indeed commanded it, and when they testify that Allah forbade something, He indeed forbade it. Had they been testifying to falsehood or error, they would not be the witnesses of Allah on earth. Rather Allah has vouched for them in their testimony, just as He vouched for the prophets in what they convey from Him, that they say nothing about Him except the truth; likewise the Ummah does not testify about Allah except to the truth.

This is a portion of the words of Imam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning consensus, from some of his treatises.

**[p. 288]** The second point related to this topic is what this same Imam said in his letter to the group of ʿAdī ibn Musāfir. Its text reads:

God protected this Community from agreeing upon misguidance, and He placed within it those through whom the proof stands until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason their consensus (*ijmāʿ*) is a proof, just as the Book and the Sunna are proofs. For this reason the People of Truth from this Community were distinguished by the Sunna and the Community (*al-sunna wa-l-jamāʿa*), in contrast to the People of Falsehood, who claim that they follow the Book while turning away from the Sunna of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and from what the Muslim community has followed. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) through many channels, transmitted by the compilers of the Sunan and the Musnads, such as Imam Aḥmad, **[p. 288]** Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and others, that he said: "This Community will split into seventy-two sects, all of them in the Fire except one, and that one is the Community (*al-jamāʿa*)." In another narration: "Whoever is upon what I am upon today and my Companions." This saved sect is the People of the Sunna. They are a middle path among the sects, just as the religion of Islam is a middle path among the religions. Muslims are moderate regarding the prophets of God, His messengers and His righteous servants: they did not exaggerate about them as the Christians exaggerated, so that **[p. 289]** "they took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God, and the Messiah son of Mary, though they were commanded only to worship one God; there is no god but He, glory be to Him above what they associate" [al-Tawba: 31]. Nor did they disparage them as the Jews did, who killed the prophets without right: "and they kill those who enjoin justice among people" [Āl ʿImrān: 21]. Whenever a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire, they denied some and killed others. Rather, the believers believed in God's messengers, supported them, honored them, loved them, obeyed them, and did not worship them or take them as lords. As God, the Exalted, said: "It is not for a human that God should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to people, 'Be servants of mine besides God.' Rather, be godly (*rabbāniyyīn*) by what you teach of the Book and by what you study" [Āl ʿImrān: 79]. "And He would not command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelief after you have submitted?" [Āl ʿImrān: 80]. Among this is that the believers took the middle course regarding the Messiah: they did not say that he is God, nor the son of God, nor the third of three, as the Christians say. Nor did they disbelieve in him and speak against Mary a tremendous slander, to the point of considering him a child of adultery, as the Jews claimed. Rather they said: "He is the servant of God and His messenger, and His word which He cast to Mary the virgin, the pure, and a spirit from Him." Likewise the believers are moderate in the laws of the religion of God: they did not forbid God to abrogate (*naskh*) what He wills, erase what He wills and confirm, as the Jews said. God, the Exalted, relayed this about them in His saying: "The foolish among the people will say: what has turned them from their qibla which they were upon?" [al-Baqara: 142], and in His saying **[p. 290]** "And when it is said to them, 'Believe in what God has sent down,' they say, 'We believe in what was sent down to us,' and they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them" [al-Baqara: 91]. They did not permit their great scholars and worshippers to change the religion of God, so that they command what they wish and forbid what they wish, as the Christians do. God mentioned this about them in His saying: "They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God" [al-Tawba: 31].

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, may God be pleased with him, said: "I said: O Messenger of God, they did not worship them? He said: 'They did not worship them, but they made lawful for them what was forbidden, so they obeyed them, and they made unlawful for them what was lawful, so they obeyed them.'" The believers say: creation and command belong to God; just as no other creates, no other commands. They say: "We hear and we obey," so they obeyed **[p. 291]** everything God commanded. They say: God decides what He wills. As for the created being, it has no right to alter the command of the Creator, however great it may be. Likewise regarding God's attributes: the Jews described God, the Exalted, with the deficient attributes of created beings, saying: "He is poor and we are rich," and "God's hand is chained," and "He grew weary of creation and rested on the Sabbath," and other such things. The Christians attributed to the created being the attributes of the Creator that are specific to Him, saying that he creates, provides, forgives, shows mercy, relents toward creation, rewards and punishes. The believers believe in God, glory be to Him and exalted. He has no equal and no rival: "and there is none comparable to Him" [al-Ikhlāṣ: 4], and "there is nothing like Him" [al-Shūrā: 11]. He is the Lord of the worlds and the Creator of everything, and everything else is His servant, poor before Him.

**[p. 292]** "There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Merciful as a servant" [Maryam: 93]. "He has counted them and numbered them precisely" [Maryam: 94]. "And each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone" [Maryam: 95]. Among this is the matter of the lawful and the unlawful. The Jews, as God the Exalted said: "For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them" [al-Nisāʾ: 160]. So they do not eat animals with claws, such as camels and ducks, nor the fat of the abdominal lining (*al-tharb*: thin fat covering the rumen and intestines, plural *thurūb*), nor the two kidneys, nor a kid in its mother's milk. And other things, of what was forbidden to them in food, clothing and other matters. It is said to the point that the forbidden things for them were three hundred and sixty kinds, and the obligatory things upon them were two hundred and forty-eight commands. Likewise they were made strict regarding impurities, to the point that they would not eat with a menstruating woman, nor have intercourse with her in the houses.

As for the Christians, they made lawful the corrupt things and all forbidden things, and they touched all impurities. The Messiah only told them: "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you" [Āl ʿImrān: 50]. For this reason God, the Exalted, said: "Fight those who do not believe in God nor in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what God and His messenger have forbidden, and who do not follow the religion of truth from among those given the Book, until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled" [al-Tawba: 29].

As for the believers, they are as God described them in His saying: "My mercy encompasses all things, so I will prescribe it for those who fear God and give zakat and those who believe in Our signs" [al-Aʿrāf: 156], and "Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, and makes lawful for them the good things **[p. 293]** and forbids them the corrupt things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honor him, support him and follow the light that was sent down with him, those are the successful" [al-Aʿrāf: 157].

This is a topic whose description is long. Likewise the People of the Sunna and the Community among the sects. In the matter of the names of God, His signs and His attributes, they are a middle course between the Negators (*ahl al-taʿṭīl*), who deviate regarding the names and signs of God and deny the realities of what God described Himself with, to the point that they liken Him to nothingness and lifelessness, and the Anthropomorphists (*ahl al-tamthīl*), who coin similitudes for Him and liken Him to created things. The People of the Sunna and the Community believe in what God described Himself with and what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) described Him with, without distortion (*taḥrīf*) or negation (*taʿṭīl*), and without modality (*takyīf*) or likening (*tamthīl*). In the matter of His creation and command they are a middle course between the deniers of God's power, who do not believe in His complete power, His all-encompassing will and His creation of everything, and the corrupters of God's religion, who make the servant to have no will, no power and no action, thereby negating command, prohibition, reward and punishment. These become like the polytheists who said: "Had God willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything" [al-Anʿām: 148]. The People of the Sunna believe that God is capable of everything: He is able to guide the servants and turn their hearts. Whatever God wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. Nothing occurs in His dominion that He does not will, and He is not incapable of carrying out His will. He is the Creator of everything, of substances, attributes and movements. They believe that the servant has power, will and action, and that he is free-choosing (*mukhtār*). They do not call him compelled (*majbūr*), since the compelled is one who is forced against his own choice. God, glory be to Him, made the servant free-choosing in what he does. So he is a free-choosing, willing agent, and God is the Creator of him and the Creator of his choice. This has no parallel **[p. 294]** for God is not like anything, neither in His essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His actions.

In the matter of names, rulings, promise and threat, they are a middle course between the Waʿīdiyya, who make the people of major sins among the Muslims eternal in the Fire and expel them entirely from faith, and who deny the intercession of the Prophet (ﷺ); and the Murjiʾa, who say: the faith of sinners is like the faith of the prophets, and good deeds are not part of religion or faith, and who entirely deny threat and punishment. The People of the Sunna and the Community believe that the sinful Muslims have with them some of faith and its root, but they do not have all of the obligatory faith by which one deserves Paradise. They do not remain eternally in the Fire; rather, whoever has in his heart an atom's weight of faith, or a mustard seed's weight of faith, will be brought out of it. The Prophet (ﷺ) reserved his intercession for the people of major sins from his Community. They are also, regarding the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), may God be pleased with them, a middle course between the Extremists (*al-ghāliya*), who exaggerate about ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, preferring him over Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, and believing that he is the infallible Imam to the exclusion of the two, and that the Companions wronged and sinned, and declared the Community after them to be unbelievers, and perhaps made him a prophet or a god; and the Rejectionists (*al-jāfiya*), who believe in his disbelief and the disbelief of ʿUthmān, may God be pleased with them both, and who deem lawful the blood of both and the blood of those who support them, and who consider it recommended to revile ʿAlī, ʿUthmān and the like, and who cast doubt on the caliphate and imamate of ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him.

Likewise in all other chapters of the Sunna they are a middle course, because they hold fast to the Book of God, the Sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ), and what the foremost early Muslims agreed upon, from the Emigrants and the Helpers and those who followed them in excellence. End of quotation.

"And We did not make the qibla which you were upon": that is, We did not legislate the qibla, as in His saying: "God did not institute any bahīra" [al-Māʾida: 103], meaning He did not legislate it. "Which you were upon" is not an attribute of the qibla; rather it is the second object of *jaʿala* ("made"). That is: "and We did not make the qibla, the direction, which you were facing," that is, in Mecca, which you faced **[p. 295]** before the Hijra, and which is the Kaaba. Meaning: "We did not turn you back toward it except as a trial for people and a test." Or "you were upon it" can mean "you have now come to face it," as in His saying: "You are the best nation" [Āl ʿImrān: 110]; or it can mean "you were seeking it," that is, eager for it and desiring it, as His saying after it clarifies: "We see the turning of your face" [al-Baqara: 144], etc.

On these interpretations, the verse explains the wisdom in making the Kaaba a qibla. Or the meaning of "which you were upon" is: before this time, and it is Jerusalem. That is: We only legislated for you to face it first, then We turned you away from it toward the Kaaba, so that the state of those who follow you, wherever you face, might become manifest, distinguished from others. Thus the verse explains the wisdom in making Jerusalem the qibla first.

Then know that the wisdom is the distinction among people by His saying: "except that We might know who follows the Messenger" in everything he is commanded, so that, when rulings change, what is in his heart of true attachment to God and turning to Him is established, wherever He directs him, "from those who turn back on their heels", that is, who revert from their religion, becoming hypocrites or disbelievers, from among those who used to display following. The root of "turning back on one's heels" is the one who returns, turning around on the road he had already traveled, departing from it. It is used metaphorically for anyone who returns from a matter in which he had religion or good.

Ibn Jarir said: "Some men who had embraced Islam apologized (*irtadda*) during God's trial of the Companions of His Messenger concerning the qiblah. Many of the hypocrites also revealed their hypocrisy because of this. They said: 'What is wrong with Muhammad that he turns us once this way and once that way?' Muslims, concerning their brothers in Islam who had died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis, said: 'Our deeds and theirs have been nullified and lost.' The polytheists said: 'Muhammad is bewildered in his religion.' So that was a trial for the believers and a purification (*tamhis*) of the believers." End of quotation.

(Subtle point) *Al-'aqibayn* is the dual of *'aqib*, meaning the back part of the foot. *Al-inqilab 'alayhima* (turning back on one's heels) is a metaphor of representation (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*, a figure in which a whole scene is depicted by analogy). This metaphor is similar to God's words: ﴿Then he turned his back and was arrogant﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:23], and like His words: ﴿He denied and turned away﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:32].

(Remark) Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), may God have mercy on him, said: What is the meaning of His words "except that We might know," since that implies acquiring knowledge, while God has always been knowing of what has occurred and what will occur? It is said that such expressions are among those words which we would not dare to apply to God were it not for revelation. Their figurative sense has several aspects:

(First) The particle *lam* in such constructions implies two things: the occurrence of the action itself and the occurrence of knowledge of it. Since God's knowledge has always existed and always will, the *lam* here implies the occurrence of the action, not the occurrence of knowledge.

(Second) Knowledge relates to a thing as it actually is. God knew them before they followed him, as not-followers, and after they followed him He knew them as followers. This answer is in reality the first one, because change belongs to the known object, not to the knowledge.

(Third) Its meaning is "that He may make others know about us," and He attributed this to Himself, as in His words: ﴿God takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [al-Zumar 39:42], and in another place: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been charged with you will take you﴾ [al-Sajdah 32:11]. And He said: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:113], though He taught him through His angels.

(Fourth) Its meaning is "that We may reward," which is a common usage, as in your saying: "I will know the goodness of your trial," meaning: "I will reward you according to what my prior knowledge requires." Thus he expressed the reward by knowledge, because knowledge was its cause.

(Fifth) The custom of the forbearing person, when he informs another of knowledge, is to say: "Come, so that we may know such-and-such," while he really intends to inform the addressee, but he places himself in the position of one who shares the learning with the learner, out of gentleness. End of quotation.

The third aspect is the one chosen by the Imam Ibn Jarir, who said: As for its meaning according to us: "We did not make the qiblah which you were facing except that We might know My Messenger, My party and My allies: who follows the Messenger from among those who turn back on their heels."

He said: It is among the customs of the Arabs to attribute what the followers of a leader do to the leader, and what is done to them to him. Like their saying: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab conquered the lands of Iraq and collected its tribute," when in fact his companions did that, on account of a cause that originated from him. Similar to this is what is related of the Prophet ﷺ in a similar matter, that he said: "God, may His praise be glorified, says: 'I was sick and My servant did not visit Me; I asked him for a loan and he did not lend Me.'" So God, may His mention be exalted, attributed the asking for a loan and the visit to Himself, though it was done by others, since it was on account of Him.

It has been related from the Arabs by oral transmission: "I am hungry for other than my stomach, and naked for other than my back," meaning the hunger of his family and dependents and the nakedness of their backs. Likewise His words "except that We might know" mean: "that My allies and party may know." End of quotation.

"And indeed it was (*la-kabirah*)," that is, the turning toward it, or the appointment, or the change, "was surely a heavy burden," meaning burdensome and difficult, because parting from what is familiar, after the soul has become at peace with it, is an extremely hard matter. ﴿Except for those whom God has guided﴾, whose hearts He has guided, so that they became certain of the truthfulness of the Messenger, and that all that he brought is the truth about which there is no doubt, and that God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. He may therefore impose upon His servants whatever He wills and abrogate what He wills. He possesses perfect wisdom and conclusive proof in all of this. This is unlike those in whose hearts is a sickness, for whenever a matter occurs, it produces doubt in them, whereas certainty and affirmation arise in the believers. As He said: ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them say: "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:124]. ﴿But as for those in whose hearts is a sickness, it adds filth to their filth, and they die while they are disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:125]. He also said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra' 17:82].

His words: ﴿And God would never make your faith go to waste; indeed God is Kind and Merciful to the people﴾ are a reassurance to those Muslims and People of the Book who prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis before the abrogation, and an explanation that they will be rewarded for that. Al-Bukhari has related, from the hadith of Abu Ishaq mentioned earlier, from al-Bara': "Among those who died facing the qiblah before it was turned toward the House were men who had been killed, and we did not know what to say about them. So God revealed: ﴿And God would never make your faith go to waste﴾," meaning your prayer. He chose the word "faith," which is general and includes prayer and other acts, in order to inform them that nothing of what they did has been lost, so that the matter asked about is included at the first level, and the ruling becomes universal. It is phrased in the second person rather than the third, so that it includes both those who passed away and those who remain, giving precedence in wording to the addressed over the absent. The conclusion of the verse contains an indication of the reason for not wasting their deeds: the compassion (*ra'fah*) with which He is characterized, which contradicts what had crept into their souls about waste. Since the heart of the Prophet ﷺ harbored a desire to face the Ka'bah, because it was the qiblah of his father Abraham, the pride of the Arabs, their place of visitation and circumambulation, and in opposition to the Jews, the Truth responded to his wish with His words:

[(p-300)] The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[144] ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven. So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. Indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.﴾

﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ means the repeated turning of your face and the shifting of your gaze toward the direction of the sky, in eager anticipation of the descent of revelation concerning the change (of direction).

They said: In this there is an indication of his good manners, for he waited and did not ask. This is more subtle than what has been said: that the turning of his face is a metaphor (kinayah) for his supplication. There is no obstacle to the turning of his face ﷺ being understood literally, as a reference to the change (of direction). In that case, it conveys the distinction that Allah, exalted is He, gave the heaven regarding the face of the one who supplicates. Although this verse comes later in the recitation, it precedes in meaning, for it is the head of the story. ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾ means: We will surely give you, or We will surely direct you to, a qiblah that you love and incline toward. The particle fa (so) of causation in His words ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ indicates that the qiblah he was pleased with is the Ka'bah. That is, turn your face toward it, in its direction. The expression of the Ka'bah as "al-Masjid al-Haram" (the Sacred Mosque) indicates that what is obligatory is observing the direction and not the exact location: ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾ means: wherever you are, on land or sea, turn your faces toward it in prayer, facing the Mosque. As for the secret of the command to turn, both specific and general, al-Raghib said: As for His specific address to him, it is an honouring of him and a making obligatory of his desire. As for His general address after it, it is because he might have thought that this was a matter specific to him, peace be upon him, just as He specified him in His words ﴿Stand (in prayer) through the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]. And because the change of qiblah was a matter of great significance to him, He addressed them with a singular address so that it would be more emphatic, and so that there would be honour for them in it. And because in the general address (p-301) there is the attaching of another ruling to it, which is that there is no difference between nearness and distance in the obligation of facing the Ka'bah.

﴿Indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. Al-Fakhr said: The pronoun in His words "that it is the truth" (innahu al-haqq) refers to an antecedent already mentioned. The Messenger has been mentioned before, as the qiblah has been mentioned. So it is permissible that what is meant is that the people know that the Messenger, together with his law and his prophethood, is the truth, and this would encompass the matter of the qiblah and other things. It may also refer to this specific obligation regarding the qiblah, meaning that they know it is the truth. This last possibility is closer, because it is more fitting to the context.

Then he mentioned, among the aspects of their knowledge of this: that they knew the Ka'bah is the Ancient House (al-Bayt al-'Atiq) which Allah, exalted is He, made a qiblah for Ibrahim (Abraham) and Isma'il (Ishmael), peace be upon them both. And that they knew the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ because of the miracles that appeared through him. And once they knew his prophethood, they inevitably knew that everything he brought is true. So this change (of qiblah) was true.

I say: There is another aspect, more precise than what al-Fakhr mentioned, in their knowledge that this change was true and that it is one of the signs of his prophethood ﷺ. Its explanation is that His command to the Prophet ﷺ, and to all who followed him, to face the Ka'bah is among the manifestations (al-isti'lan) in Faran mentioned in the Torah, as an indication of the Seal of the Prophets and as glad tidings of him. In Chapter Thirty-Three of the Book of Deuteronomy, (also called the Exception), it reads thus: "And this is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death. He said: The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir to them, and shined forth from Mount Paran."

This glad tiding alludes to Moses, Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ, because Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Torah upon Moses at Mount Sinai (Tur Sina'), and the Gospel upon Jesus at Mount Seir. For he, peace be upon him, used to dwell in the land of the Friend (al-Khalil) from Seir, in a village called Nazareth. And his shining forth from Mount Paran is an expression of the sending down of the Qur'an upon Muhammad ﷺ on Mount Paran. And Paran is Mecca. The People of the Book do not dispute us in this. In Chapter Twenty-One of the Book of Genesis, concerning Isma'il (p-302) peace be upon him, it reads thus: "And God was with the lad, and he grew up. He dwelt in the wilderness and became an archer, and he dwelt in the wilderness of Paran."

There is no doubt that Isma'il, peace be upon him, dwelt in Mecca, and died there and was buried there.

Ibn al-Athir said: In the hadith, the mention of Mount Paran: it is a name for the mountains of Mecca in Hebrew. It has a mention among the signs of prophethood, and its first alif is not a hamzah.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾ is read with the ya' and with the ta'. It contains a report of their persistence in their evil conditions.

When He, exalted is He, had clarified that they know this qiblah is the truth, He informed (us) that their attribute does not change in persistent obstinacy, in His words:

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His, the Exalted's, saying:**

[145] ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla (direction of prayer). Nor are you one who will follow their qibla, nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others. And if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Scripture﴾, i.e., from the Jews and the Christians, ﴿every sign﴾, i.e., a decisive proof that facing the Ka'bah is the truth, ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾, i.e., this one to which you were turned. This is because their refusal to follow you is not due to a doubt that you could remove by presenting the argument. Rather, it is out of arrogance and obstinacy, despite their knowledge of what is in their books concerning your description, that you are upon the truth. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿nor are you one who will follow their qibla﴾ is a cutting off of their hopes of your returning to it. Or it is a form of reciprocity: meaning, they will not abandon their falsehood, and you will not abandon your truth. ﴿Nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others﴾: there is no agreement between their two groups, even though both are from the Children of Israel.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He, the Exalted, informs us of the firmness of each party in what it is upon and its steadfastness in it. The one among them who is upon the truth does not deviate from his school, because he holds fast to the proof. The one upon falsehood does not desist from his falsehood, because of the severity of his obstinacy in his opposition. In this there is relief for the Prophet (ﷺ) from longing for the guidance of some of them.

**Benefits (fawa'id)**

The first: Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: If it is asked, how is he informed that they will not follow his qibla when a group of them has believed? It is answered: Some of them said that this is a judgment upon the whole and not upon the parts. This is correct, as evidenced by the fact that if you said, "They did not believe, but some of them believed," it would not be contradictory. It is also said that it refers to specific peoples.

The second: Al-Raghib said: His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿nor are you one who will follow their qibla﴾ indicates that whoever truly knows God, it is impossible for him to apostatize. Hence it is said: "No one who turned back turned back except from the path," i.e., none who has failed in faith is one who has not truly reached it.

If it is said: Indeed, there may be one who attains knowledge of God and then apostatizes! It is answered: What he assumes to be knowledge is a supposition formed in the image of knowledge. As for one who attains true knowledge and then apostasy follows it, that is far-fetched. And by this knowledge he did not mean what God, the Exalted, has given to man by way of intelligence, for that is like a spark that dies out if it is not kindled.

The third: Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said in Badai' al-Fawa'id: The qibla of the People of the Book is not based on revelation and divine instruction from God, but on their own counsel and ijtihad (independent reasoning). As for the Christians, there is no doubt that God did not command them in the Gospel or elsewhere to face the east. And they acknowledge that the qibla of the Messiah was the qibla of the Children of Israel, which is the Rock, and that their elders established this qibla for them. So they and the Jews agree that God never legislated for His Messenger to face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The Muslims bear witness against them on this matter. As for the Jews, there is absolutely no command in the Torah to face the Rock. Rather, they used to set up the Ark (al-tabut) and pray toward it from wherever they set out. When they arrived, they set it upon the Rock and prayed toward it. When it was lifted, they prayed toward its place, which is the Rock. As for His saying ﴿And if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, after the clarification of the reality of his state, which is known to him, in His saying ﴿nor are you one who will follow their qibla﴾, it is a statement given by way of supposition and hypothesis, meaning: "And if you were to follow them, for example, after the clarity of the proof and the comprehension of the reality of the matter, ﴿indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾", i.e., those who commit gross injustice.

In this there is gentleness toward the listeners and an increase in warning and in the portrayal as monstrous of the state of one who abandons the evidence after it has been made clear and follows desire. It also serves as an incitement and a spurring toward steadfastness upon the truth. This is what al-Zamakhshari stated.

**Remarks (tanbihat)**

The first: Al-Raghib said: God warned His Prophet against following their desires. He drew attention to the fact that following desire after certainty of knowledge places the one who seeks it among the wrongdoers. God has greatly emphasized warning him against inclining toward desire, to the point that He repeated this in a number of places. As for the statement of one who says that the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended meaning is the community, there is no point in restricting it, for God warns His Prophet against following desire more than He warns others. The one of lofty station needs the warning more urgently, to preserve his station and safeguard his rank. End of quote. And this is a very precious statement.

The second: In the verse there is an honoring of the status of knowledge, in that it called the matter of prophethood, the proofs, and the miracles by the name of knowledge. This draws attention to the fact that knowledge is the greatest of created things in nobility and rank.

The third: The verse indicates that the threat directed at the scholars is more severe than that directed at others, because His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ points to this. This was mentioned by al-Razi.

[146] The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know him as they know their own sons. And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know it.﴾

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book know him as they know their own sons.﴾ That is, they know the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a knowledge free of any doubt, just as they do not doubt the identity of their own sons among the children of people. This knowledge is derived from the Book, as He, exalted is He, informed about his description in it, saying: ﴿They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-A'raf: 157]. That is, they recognize him by the attributes mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, that he is the promised Prophet, such that he is not confused for them. ﴿As they know their own sons﴾, and their persons are not confused with others. This is a comparison of the rational knowledge obtained from studying the heavenly books with sensory knowledge, in that each of them is certain and free of any uncertainty.

It has been narrated from 'Umar that he said to 'Abd Allah ibn Salam: "Do you know Muhammad as you know your son?" He said: "Yes, and more. The Trustworthy One descended from the heaven upon the trustworthy one on earth with his description, so I recognized him. And I do not know what his mother did." So 'Umar kissed his head.

﴿And indeed, a party of them﴾, that is, of the People of the Book, despite that certainty and scholarly conviction, ﴿conceal the truth﴾, that is, they hide it and do not make it known, ﴿while they know it﴾, that is, the truth, or the punishment for concealment, or that they conceal it. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: He did not say "conceal it" (referring to the Messenger), because in concealing his matter there is the concealment of the truth as a whole. And He increased their blame by saying "while they know it," for the one who commits a sin knowingly is not like the one who commits it out of ignorance.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[147] ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾

"The truth is from your Lord": that is, the truth is from God, not from anyone else. This means that the truth is what has been established as being from God, like that which you (Muhammad) follow. And what has not been established as being from God, like that which the People of the Book follow, is falsehood. That is: (p-306) this which they conceal is the truth from your Lord. ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, read "al-ḥaqqa" in the accusative, as a substitution (badal) from the first, as in al-Kashshaf, or as an object (mafʿūliyya) of "yaʿlamūna" (they know), as Abu al-Baqa' said. "So do not be among the doubters": those who doubt their concealment of the truth while they know it, or who doubt the truth that has come to you from your Lord, which is what you follow. It is well known that doubt is not to be expected from him, so there is in this an allusion (taʿrīḍ) addressed to the Community. Al-Rāghib said: This is not a prohibition against doubt, because doubt does not occur by the intention of the doubter; rather, it is an exhortation to acquire the forms of knowledge that remove doubt and to put them to use. Upon this is His words: ﴿Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46].

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[148] ﴿For each there is a direction, He is turning towards it. So race to good deeds. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

"For each there is a direction" means: for every community, or for every prophet, there is a qibla (direction of prayer), or a shir'a (law) and minhaj (path). "He is turning towards it" means: he turns his face towards it, inclining to it and following it, because it was made beloved to him and adorned for him. Abu Mu'adh said: "muwalliha" means "mutawalliha," i.e., he took it up, was pleased with it, and followed it. "So race to good deeds" means: hasten to them by competing to reach them first. This is more eloquent than a command to hurry, because it includes urging people to seize the prize of precedence. "The good deeds" means all their kinds, by which the happiness of both abodes is attained. "Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together": al-Raghib said: whatever occupation you pursue, wherever you turn, and whatever deity you take, you will be gathered and held accountable for it. "Indeed, Allah is over all things competent" gives the reason for what precedes it: He is able to gather you from the earth, even if your bodies and limbs have been scattered.

(Note) This verse indicates that people follow many paths and diverse religions, and that the intelligent person should race towards whichever of them is best and most elevated. The sages and philosophers are unanimously agreed that the religion of Islam is the most elevated of all religions, because it encompasses the necessities of human perfection, fulfils the requirements of society, the causes of civilization, [p. 307] the means of advancement, and the paths to the two happinesses. This verse is similar to His saying: ﴿For every community We appointed a rite which they perform﴾ [22:67], and His saying: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a path. Had Allah willed, He would have made you one community, but [He instead] to test you in what He has given you. So race to good deeds. To Allah is your return, all of you, and He will inform you about that over which you used to differ.﴾ [5:48]

Then He, exalted is He, affirmed the ruling on changing the direction of prayer and clarified that the matter of facing the qibla does not differ between travel and residence, by His saying:

The exposition of His words, exalted is He:

[149] ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾

"And from wherever you set out" — i.e., from whatever land you set out on a journey, "turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque" when you pray. "And indeed, it" — i.e., this command — "is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do." It is read with the yā' (ya ta'malūn, "they do"), in which case it is a warning to the disbelievers, and with the tā' (ta'malūn, "you do"), in which case it is a promise to the believers. Since the matter of the qibla was great, and the sayings of the foolish ones spread and their clamour and disputation took many forms, the situation required further emphasis on its affair, to magnify its importance and to weaken their doubts. Therefore, He, exalted is He, said:

(p-٣٠٨) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:
