Al-Raghib said: Since there is no difference between saying ﴿the ship that runs in the sea﴾ and saying "the sea in which the ship runs", in that the primary purpose of the verse is that the benefit of the sea be known, (p-356) though it is mentioned later in the wording, He mentioned first the ship, which is of our making. And since our path to knowing it is closer than to knowing His making of it, He mentioned the ship first, so that by it one may look to the traces of God's creation. ﴿And what God sends down from the sky﴾ — i.e., the clouds: ﴿of water, giving life thereby to the earth﴾ with all kinds of plants and flowers and the trees upon it; ﴿after its death﴾ by the dominance of dryness over it; ﴿and dispersing in it﴾ — i.e., spreading and scattering: ﴿every kind of creature﴾ among the rational and others; ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾ — i.e., their changing of directions: the east wind, the west wind, the south wind and the north wind, and in their states: hot and cold, violent and gentle; so at times they bring glad tidings before the clouds, at times they drive them, at times they gather them, at times they scatter them, and at times they turn them away.

Al-Tha'alibi said: When the wind comes with a weak breath and gentle breeze, it is called al-nasim (the zephyr). When it is strong, it is al-'asif (the gale). When it shakes the branches violently and uproots trees, it is al-za'za'an and al-za'za'. When it brings pebbles, it is al-hasiba. When it rises from the earth toward the sky like a pillar, it is al-i'sar, and it is also called zawba'a. When it blows with dust, it is al-habwa. When it is cold, it is al-sarsar. When with its coldness there is dew, it is al-balil. When it is hot, it is al-harur and al-samum. When it does not fertilize trees and does not bring rain, it is al-'aqim. Among those mentioned in the plural: al-a'asir, which stir up dust; al-lawaqih, which fertilize trees; al-mu'sirat, which bring rains; and al-mubashshirat, which bring the clouds and rain.

﴿And the clouds subjected between heaven and earth﴾ — i.e., they do not fall downward despite their weight; the vapour of water carries them, unlike the rest of the lofty bodies that fall, since they have no visible support; and they do not rise or disperse. Yet nature requires one of three things: the dense requires descent, the subtle requires ascent, and the intermediate requires dispersal. Mentioned by al-Biqa'i.

Two subtle points:

The first: Al-Tha'alibi said: The cloud when it first comes into being is called al-nash'; when it drags through the air (p-357) it is al-sahab; when the sky changes because of it, it is al-ghamam; when it casts shade, it is al-'arid; when it rises, carries water, thickens and covers, it is al-'ama'; when it stretches across, it is al-'anan; when it is white, it is al-muzn.

The second: Al-Raghib said: Taskhir (subjection) is compulsion upon an act, and it is more eloquent than ikrah (coercion), for it is moving another to an act without his will in a certain manner, like the turning of a millstone to grind.

As for His words ﴿Surely there are signs﴾ — i.e., great and numerous; the indefiniteness is for magnification in quantity and quality. ﴿For a people who use their reason﴾ — i.e., who reflect upon them and look at them with the eye of intellect, and so infer His overpowering might, His dazzling wisdom, and His vast mercy, which necessitate that divinity belong to Him alone, glorified is His majesty.

Al-Biqa'i said: The reason for the multiplicity of proofs is that people's intellects differ. So He, glorified is He, made the world — that is, the possible existents, which are all that is other than Him, indicating His existence and His voluntary action — into two divisions: one division is of a kind perceptible to the outward senses, and in the usage of the people of the Law it is called the witnessed (shahadah), creation (khalq), and dominion (mulk); and another division is not perceived by the outward senses, and is called the unseen (ghayb), command (amr), and malakut. The first is perceived by common people, and the second is perceived by those of understanding whose intellects are pure of illusion and whisperings. So God, by the perfection of His care, compassion and mercy, made the world with both its divisions containing totalities and details from many aspects and diverse ways, which human faculties cannot master, by which His oneness is inferred, some of them clearer than others, so that all may share in knowledge, and each attains according to what has been prepared for him, except one whose heart has been sealed — and that, God forbid, is the wretched one. End.

Al-Mahayimi said: And how could they deny God's existence, His unity, His beneficent mercy and His compassionate mercy, when the indications of the upper and lower realms and their accidents and intermediaries point to them? Then he said:

As for the indication of the heavens and the earth to the existence of God: they are both originated, because they have parts that depend on one another; so there must be an originator who is not a part of them, since composition, which is a newly arising thing, has entered them; and the eternal cannot be a locus of originated things; and the originator must necessarily be eternal, to avoid an infinite regress. As for oneness: if the god of the heavens were other than the god of the earth, the benefits of one would not be connected to the other. As for the two mercies: He, mighty and majestic, placed in the earth materials receptive to diverse forms and bestowed them one after another by moving the heavens.

(p-358) As for the indication of the alternation of night and day to the existence of God: they arise from the motions of the heavens, and their motion needs a mover; if the mover is originated, it needs an originator. As for oneness: if the god of the night were other than the god of the day, each could bring about what is his at the time the other brings about what is his, so both would coincide, which is impossible; if this is impossible, then one or both would be incapable. As for the two mercies: the equilibrium by which the affairs of living beings are organized comes only from their succession, for the continuance of night is an extreme chilling of the world, and the continuance of day is an extreme heating of it.

As for the indication of the ship to the existence of God: it is heavier than water, so its natural tendency is to sink; its staying above water is from God; and the entry of air into it, though among the causes, does not suffice when the ship is loaded with heavy goods, since the air becomes very little and its effect in supporting such a heavy thing weakens; so it should be attributed only to God Almighty from the outset. As for oneness: if the god of the ship were other than the god of the sea, one of them might prevent the other from disposing of his dominion, which would lead to disorder in the order of the world through the conflict of the benefits tied to the ship. As for the two mercies: He had mercy on the travellers in trade, and on those to whom they travel with the goods they need.

As for the indication of the sending down of water to the existence of God: it is heavier than air, so its being in its centre can only be from God. As for oneness: if the god of water were other than the god of air, one would be prevented from disposing of his dominion. As for the two mercies: He gave life by it to the earth as a means of livelihood for living beings, and spread by it the creatures, completing the benefits of man.

As for the indication of the turning of the winds to the existence of God: they are newly arising, bringing this one time and that another, and all may cease, so there must be an originator; if he is originated, he needs an eternal one. As for oneness: if every wind had its own god, all could bring about what is theirs, and the diverse winds would then coincide, which disrupts the order. As for the two mercies: they move the ships and the clouds and make the trees and fruits grow (p-359).

As for the indication of the clouds to the existence of God: if it were heavy it would descend, and if light it would rise; but it rises at times and descends at others, so it is from God, exalted is He. As for oneness: if the god of one cloud were other than the god of another cloud, each could place his cloud in the place of the other's, so there would be interpenetration of bodies or incapacity. As for the two mercies: from them come the rains.

There are other aspects of indication and countless benefits; we are content with what we have mentioned.

Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar said: The verse indicates several matters:

One: If the truth were attained by imitation, by following the fathers, and by adherence to habit and custom, this would not be valid.

Two: If knowledge were necessary and obtained by inspiration, it would not be valid to describe these matters as signs, for what is known necessarily does not need signs to be known.

Three: Although all bodies and accidents indicate the Creator, He, exalted is He, singled out these eight for mention, because they combine being indications with being blessings upon the responsible, to the greatest share and portion; and when indications are of this kind, they are more effective in hearts and more forceful in impressions. Transmitted by al-Razi.

Then God, exalted is He, only manifested these signs that indicate His existence, His oneness and His mercy, so that creation might single Him out with love and worship.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 165:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[165] ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals (andad) whom they love as they love God. But those who believe are stronger in love for God. If only those who have done wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment.﴾

{And} rather: {Among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals (andad)}, that is, equals. Although the verses forbid Him to have even one rival, let alone a multitude of them, they equate them with God, since: (p-360) ﴿they love them as they love God﴾, that is, they venerate them and submit to them as they venerate God and submit to Him. The rivals (andad) are either: the idols, which they took as gods to bring them nearer to God in closeness, and from which they hoped for benefit and harm, and to which they directed their requests, made vows, and offered sacrifices. Or: the leaders whom they follow in what they do and abstain from, especially in commands and prohibitions. This second view is preferred, because after this verse God says: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166], and that applies only to those who took men as rivals and equals to God, binding themselves to venerate them and submit to them in the way believers bind themselves to submit to God, exalted is He. ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾ than the polytheists are for their rivals, because those (polytheists) associated others in love, whereas the believers dedicated all of it to God. Also, they know that all perfections belong to Him and come from Him, and because they do not turn away from Him to anything else, unlike the polytheists, who worshipped an idol for a time and then abandoned it for another, or ate it, as the tribe of Bahila ate their god made of dates and ghee (haysk) in the year of famine.

The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim (may God have mercy on him) said in his "Sharh al-Manazil", in the chapter on repentance:

Shirk (association of partners with God) is of two kinds: major and minor. The major kind is not forgiven by God except through repentance. It is to take, besides God, a rival (nidd) whom one loves as one loves God, exalted is He. This is the shirk that involves equating the gods of the polytheists with the Lord of the worlds. That is why they said to their gods in the Fire: ﴿By God, we were certainly in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 97-98], while acknowledging that God alone is the Creator of everything, its Lord and Sovereign, and that their gods do not create, provide, cause death, or give life. This equating was only in love, veneration, and worship, as is the state of most of the polytheists of the world! Indeed, all of them love their objects of worship, cherish them, and show affection to them besides God, exalted is He! And many of them, indeed most of them, love their gods (p-361) more than they love God, exalted is He! They rejoice at mentioning them more than they rejoice when God is mentioned, exalted is He! They become angry when their objects of worship and gods, the shaykhs, are belittled, more than they become angry when anyone disparages the Lord of the worlds! When the sanctities of their gods and objects of worship are violated, they become angry like a lion or a dog! When the sanctities of God, exalted is He, are violated, they do not become angry for them. Rather, if the violator feeds them something, they are pleased with him, and their hearts do not object to him! We and others have witnessed this from them... End of quotation.

Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Ali al-Maqrizi (may God have mercy on him) said:

Among the greatest forms of shirk, and its root, is shirk in the love of God. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God﴾, to the end of the verse. He, glory be to Him, informed that whoever loves something alongside God, other than Him, as he loves Him, has taken a rival besides Him! This is, according to the more correct of the two opinions regarding the verse, that they love them as they love God. This is the "equating" (adl) mentioned in God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve in their Lord equate (yaʿdilun)﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. The meaning, according to the more correct of the two opinions, is that they equate others with Him in worship, making a comparison between Him and others in love and worship. Likewise is the saying of the polytheists in the Fire to their idols: ﴿By God, we were certainly in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 97-98]. It is certainly known that this equating was not between them and God in being their creators, for they were, as God informed about them, acknowledging that God alone is their Lord and Creator, that the earth and whoever is in it belong to God alone, that He is the Lord of the heavens and the Lord of (p-362) the Mighty Throne, and that He is the one in whose hand is the dominion of everything, and He grants protection while no one can be protected against Him... Rather, this equating between them and God, exalted is He, was in love and worship. So whoever loves other than God, exalted is He, fears him, hopes in him, and humbles himself to him as he loves God, fears Him, and hopes in Him, this is the shirk that God, exalted is He, does not forgive! Far be it from us to seek refuge in God! From the heart being stripped of tawhid (monotheism) and Islam, as a snake is stripped of its skin, while it thinks it is a Muslim and a monotheist!

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya said in one of his legal opinions (fatawa):

Whoever takes his own desire as his god has a love like the love of the polytheists for their gods, and like the love of the worshippers of the calf for it. This is a love with God, not a love for God! This is the love of the people of shirk! Souls may claim the love of God while in reality it is a love of shirk, loving what they desire, having made it a partner with God in love! Desire may be hidden from the soul, for your love of something blinds and deafens you! Likewise are the deeds that a person thinks he does for God while there is shirk within him that is hidden from him, though he knows it: either for love of leadership, or love of wealth, or love of appearance!

For this reason, "They said: O Messenger of God! A man fights out of bravery, zeal, and to be seen; which of these is in the way of God? He said: Whoever fights so that the word of God is supreme, he is in the way of God!" So when many of the later ascetic Sufis claimed love without weighing it by the measure of knowledge, the Book, and the Sunnah, a kind of shirk and following of desires entered into it. God, exalted is He, has made His love a requirement for following His Messenger, saying: ﴿Say: If you love God, then follow me; God will love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31] (p-363). This is because the Messenger is the one who calls to what God loves, and there is nothing God loves except that the Messenger calls to it! And there is nothing the Messenger calls to except that God loves it! Thus the object of the Lord's love and the object of the Messenger's call become inseparable, indeed this is that in its essence, even if its attributes vary! End of quotation.

﴿But if only those who have done wrong⦄ — that is, by taking rivals and placing them in the position of the object of worship — ﴿could see, when they see the punishment⦄ prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that all power belongs to God⦄, that is, all might belongs to God over everything, of punishment and reward, without their rivals. ﴿And that God is severe in punishment⦄, that is, severe in retribution against the wrongdoers. The benefit of connecting this clause to what precedes it is to exaggerate the terror of the matter and the enormity of the affair, for the exclusiveness of power to Him, exalted is He, does not necessarily entail severity of punishment, since He could forgive while being able to punish. The answer to "law" (law, "if only") is omitted, to indicate that the matter goes beyond the scope of explanation, either because its reality cannot be grasped, or because the expression is too narrow for it, or because mentioning it would cause such distress and anguish that the speaker or listener could not bear it. That is, there would befall them what cannot be described, of regret, grief, and the certain knowledge of their wrongdoing and error. A parallel to this omission of the answer is God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and the saying: "If only you had seen so-and-so while the whips were seizing him." It is also read as (walaw tara), with the letter ta, addressing the Messenger or every addressee; that is, if you could see that, you would see a matter of great horror and terror.

(p-364) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[166] ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their means of connection are severed﴾

"When those who were followed disown" (إذْ تَبَرَّأ الَّذِينَ اتُّبِعُوا) is a substitute (badal) for "when they see" (إذْ يَرَوْنَ) in verse 165. That is, those who were followed disowned, namely the leaders who commanded taking rivals (andad) and everything worshipped besides Him, Exalted is He. "From those who followed" means from the followers, by their acknowledging the falsity of what they used to claim for themselves in this world, or what they called them to of various kinds of disbelief and misguidance; they withdrew from associating with them and met them with cursing. The first (tabarra'a) is read in the active voice, and the second (ittubi'a) in the passive voice, meaning: the followers disowned the leaders. "And they see the punishment": the waw here is the waw of circumstance (li'l-hal), meaning they disowned at the time of seeing the punishment. "And their means of connection are severed" means the ties (wusul) that existed between them, such as agreement upon one religion, kinship, mutual affection, and the relation of following and being followed.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[167] ﴿And those who followed will say, "If only we had another return, we would disown them as they have disowned us." Thus Allah will show them their deeds as regrets upon them, and they will not emerge from the Fire.﴾

﴿And those who followed﴾ when they witness the disavowal of the leaders by them, and regret what they did of following them in the world: ﴿If only we had another return﴾, meaning: if only we had a return to the world: ﴿we would disown them﴾ there, and their worship, and we would worship Him, exalted is He, alone: ﴿as they have disowned us﴾ today. But they are lying in this, rather, if they were returned they would return to what they were forbidden, as Allah, exalted is He, informed about them: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: like that dreadful showing: ﴿Allah will show them their deeds as regrets﴾, great remorse: ﴿upon them﴾, meaning: they will go away and vanish. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23] (p-365). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The example of those who disbelieve in their Lord is that their deeds are like ashes on which the wind blows hard on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], the verse. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert, which the thirsty one thinks is water﴾ [al-Nur: 39], the verse. ﴿And they will not emerge from the Fire﴾. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord, returning word to one another. Those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Were it not for you, we would have been believers."﴾ [Saba': 31] ﴿Those who were arrogant will say to those who were oppressed, "Did we turn you away from guidance after it came to you? Rather, you were criminals."﴾ [Saba': 32] ﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant, "Rather, it was the scheming of night and day when you commanded us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him." And they will hide their regret when they see the punishment, and We will place shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ [Saba': 33]? And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they may be a source of honour for them﴾ [Maryam: 81]. ﴿No! They will reject their worship of them and will become opponents against them﴾ [Maryam: 82].

(p-366) And al-Khalil (Abraham) said to his people: ﴿You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection among you in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another and curse one another, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will have no helpers.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25] And the angels will say: ﴿We disown You; it was not us they used to worship.﴾ [al-Qasas: 63] And they will say: ﴿Glory be to You, You are our Guardian, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn; most of them were believers in them.﴾ [Saba': 41] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and they are unaware of their calling?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 5] ﴿And when people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 6] And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: "Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it to you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieved in your associating me with Allah before. Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment."﴾ [Ibrahim: 22]

[p. 367]

**The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[168] ﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the steps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful﴾: "lawful" (ḥalālan) is either a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) or an object (maf'ūl), referring to that from which the ruling of prohibition has been removed. ﴿Good﴾ (ṭayyiban) means: agreeable in itself, not harmful to the bodies or to the minds.

Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr ibn Mardawayh narrated with his chain (isnād) from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "This verse was recited in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾. Then Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Ask Allah to make me one whose supplication is answered!' He said: 'O Saʿd! Make your food pure, and you will be one whose supplication is answered. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muḥammad! Indeed, a man who puts a morsel of unlawful food into his stomach, his deeds will not be accepted for forty days. And any servant whose flesh has grown from what is unlawful (suḥt) and usury (ribā), the Fire is more deserving of him...!'"

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾: these are his ways and paths, in what he misguided his followers about, such as the prohibition of the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah (types of animals that the pre-Islamic Arabs declared forbidden) and the like, which he adorned for them in their age of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). This is as in the hadith of ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, which is in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that he said: "Allah, exalted is He, says: Indeed, every property I have bestowed upon My servants is lawful for them." And in it: "Indeed, I created My servants as ḥunafā' (upright in faith), but the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion, and made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them."

[p. 368] Among what enters into the steps of Satan is every act of disobedience to Allah, and among them are vows made in sinful matters, as some of the early generations (salaf) said regarding the verse.

Al-Shaʿbī said: "A man vowed to slaughter his son, so Masrūq issued a fatwā to him to sacrifice a ram, and said: 'This is from the steps of Satan!'"

Abū al-Ḍuḥā narrated from Masrūq: "ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd was brought a dish of udder (ḍarʿ) with salt, and he began to eat. A man from the people withdrew, so Ibn Masʿūd said: 'Give it to your companion.' He said: 'I do not want it.' He said: 'Are you fasting?' He said: 'No!' He said: 'Then what is your situation?' He said: 'I have vowed never to eat udder!' Ibn Masʿūd said: 'This is from the steps of Satan! Feed others and expiate for your oath!'" Narrated by Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

It is also narrated from Abū Rāfiʿ, who said: "One day I became angry with my wife, and she said: 'She is a Jew one day and a Christian another day, and every slave she owns is free if you do not divorce your wife!' So I came to ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, and he said: 'This is only from the steps of Satan!' Likewise said Zaynab bint Umm Salamah, who was at that time the most learned woman in Madinah. I also came to ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿUmar, and they both said the same."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Whatever oath or vow is made in anger, it is from the steps of Satan, and its expiation is the expiation of an oath!" Quoted by the Imam Ibn Kathīr al-Dimashqī.

﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾: this is a reason given for the prohibition, to create aversion to him and to warn against him, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy. He only invites his party that they may become companions of the Blaze﴾ [Fāṭir: 6]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then do you take him and his descendants as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you? Wretched is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Kahf: 50].

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[169] ﴿Indeed, he only commands you to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah what you do not know.﴾

﴿Indeed, he only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining the manner of his enmity, and a detailing of the varieties of his evil and corruption. *Al-su'* (evil) comprises all acts of disobedience, whether they are deeds of the limbs or actions of the hearts. *Al-fahsha'* (immorality) is what exceeds the limit of ugliness among grave matters. ﴿And to say about Allah what you do not know﴾ means: by fabricating against Him, exalted is He, that He has forbidden this and that without knowledge. Thus the meaning of ﴿what you do not know﴾ is: what you do not know that Allah, exalted is He, has commanded.

Al-Biqa'i said: In this verse, He, glorified is He, has gone to the utmost in encouraging His servants towards Him, out of kindness to them and mercy for them, by reminding them, in the context of argument for His oneness, of the blessings He bestowed upon them: first, by creating them; second, by making the earth suitable for them; third, by permitting it to them; fourth, by warning them of the enemy... and beyond that of the subtle kindnesses and the great favours...!

Al-Razi said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to say about Allah what you do not know﴾ encompasses all corrupt doctrines, and even includes the one who follows the truth blindly...! For he, although he follows the truth, nevertheless says what he does not know, so he deserves blame, by being included under the blame in this verse.! End of quotation.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in *A'lam al-Muwaqqi'in*: Saying about Allah without knowledge encompasses speaking about Him, glorified is He, regarding His names, His attributes, His acts, and regarding His religion and His law. Allah, exalted is He, has made it among the greatest of prohibitions, indeed in its highest rank among them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 33]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent lies against Allah. Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed﴾ [al-Nahl: 116] ﴿A brief enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Nahl: 117]! So He, glorified is He, warned in advance against lying about Him in His rulings, and their saying of what He has not made unlawful: "This is unlawful," and of what He has not made lawful: "This is lawful." This is a clarification from Him, glorified is He, that it is not permissible for the servant to say, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," except with what he knows Allah, glorified is He, has made lawful or unlawful.

Some of the *salaf* (early pious generations) said: Let each of you beware of saying about what he does not know, and about which no clear revelation has come concerning its being lawful or unlawful: "Allah has made it lawful, or Allah has forbidden it," whether merely by blind imitation or by interpretation.

(p-٣٧١) The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade, in a sound hadith, his commander Buraydah, that he should bring his enemy down to the judgment of Allah when he besieged them, and said: "For you do not know whether you will hit upon the judgment of Allah concerning them or not....? But (p-٣٧٢) bring them down to your judgment and the judgment of your companions....." So reflect on how he distinguished between the judgment of Allah and the judgment of the commander who exercises *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning), and forbade that the judgment of the mujtahids be called the judgment of Allah. From this: when the scribe wrote before the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, a ruling that he had issued, saying: "This is what Allah has shown to the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar," he said: "Do not say it thus. Rather say: This is what the Commander of the Faithful, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, has seen." Malik said: It was not the practice of the people, nor of those who passed away from our predecessors, nor did I find anyone I would follow who would say concerning anything: "This is lawful and this is unlawful." They did not dare to do that. They would only say: "We dislike such-and-such, and we see this as good."

When He, glorified is He, forbade them from following the enemy, He blamed them for following him, although he is an enemy, without any proof, but merely by blindly imitating the ignorant. So He said:

**The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[170] ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," they say, "No, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down"﴾ upon His Messenger, and strive to compel yourselves to turn away from the desire that Satan has blown into you. ﴿They say, "No, we will follow what we found"﴾, that is, what we discovered ﴿upon it our fathers﴾, that is, of the worship of idols and rivals to God. So He said, rebuking them: ﴿Even though﴾, that is, will they follow their fathers even though ﴿their fathers did not understand anything﴾, that is, of the religion, ﴿nor were they guided﴾ to the correct path, since they were ignorant of it?

Al-Harali said: In this there is an indication that the customs of the fathers are forbidden unless a witness of paternal religious authority testifies to them. Thus there is a warning at various levels, from the state of disbelief down to the lesser trial, which is that people tend to follow the customs of their fathers.

(p-373) Al-Razi said: The meaning of the verse is that God commanded them to follow what He sent down of the clear proofs. But they said, "We will not follow that; rather, we follow our fathers and forebears." It is as if they opposed the proof with imitation (taqlid, the uncritical following of another's view). God answered them with His saying: ﴿Even though their fathers…﴾ to the end.

Then he said: The establishment of this answer is from several aspects:

The first: It may be said to the one who imitates: Do you acknowledge that the condition for the permissibility of a person's imitation is that it be known that he is right or not? If you acknowledge this, you do not know the permissibility of imitating him unless you know that he is right. How, then, did you know that he is right? If you knew it by another imitation, an infinite regress (tasalsul) follows. If you knew it by reason, then that is sufficient, and there is no need for imitation…! If you say: It is not a condition for the permissibility of imitating him that it be known that he is right… then you have permitted imitating him even if he is in error…! Then you, in your imitation, do not know whether you are right or wrong…!

The second: Suppose that this predecessor had knowledge of this matter. But if we assume that this predecessor never had knowledge of that matter at all, and never chose any position regarding it, then what would you do? Given that this predecessor and his position do not exist, one must have recourse to reflection (nazar, rational inquiry), and so it is here.

The third: When you imitate those before you, how did you come to know that predecessor? Did you know him by imitation or not by imitation? If you knew him by imitation, then either circular reasoning (dawr) or infinite regress follows. If you knew him not by imitation but by proof, then when you make the imitation of that predecessor obligatory, you must seek knowledge by proof and not by imitation. For if you sought it by imitation and not by proof, while that predecessor sought it by proof and not by imitation, you would be opposing him. Thus it is established that the doctrine of imitation, if its validity is affirmed, leads to its own negation, and so it is void.

Then al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, said: God mentioned this verse immediately after the prohibition against following the steps of Satan, to draw attention to the fact that there is no difference between following the whisperings of Satan and following imitation. In this there is (p-374) the strongest evidence for the obligation of reflection and reasoning, and for abandoning reliance upon what occurs to the mind without proof, or upon what another says without proof.

Imam al-Raghib said: God censured them because they nullified what God had specially bestowed upon man of thought and deliberation, and what He had composed within him of knowledge. God distinguished man by thought, so that he might know by it the truth from falsehood in belief, the true from the false in statements, and the good from the ugly in action, so that he might seek out the truth, the true and the good, and avoid their opposites. He also gave him, from the light of the intellect, that by which he may dispense with others, guiding him to knowledge of what he seeks. When He urged people to partake of what is lawful and good, and forbade them to follow Satan, He made clear the condition of the disbelievers in their abandonment of right guidance and their following of fathers and grandfathers, so that He might warn against imitating them, abandoning the use of thought, which is the form and reality of man. Then He said: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything?﴾, that is: Will they follow them even though they were ignorant? As an admonition that it is absurd to follow one who has no intellect and no guidance.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of combining His saying "they understand" (ya'qilun) with "they are guided" (yahtadun), when one of them would suffice without the other? It is answered: It has already been stated that the rational (ʿaqil) is used in two senses. One is for the one who possesses the faculty by which obligation is valid; the other is for the one who acquires acquired knowledge, and this is what is intended here. The guided one (muhtadi) may be said of one who follows the learned man in his actions even if he is not his equal in knowledge. So He made clear that they neither understand nor are guided. Another aspect: one may understand and be guided, though these often accompany each other, since understanding is used in relation to knowledge and being guided in relation to action. It is as if it were said: they have no sound knowledge and no upright conduct.

Then God, exalted is He, set forth for the disbelievers a dreadful parable, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness﴾ [al-Nahl: 60], and He said:

(p-375) The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[171] ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out. Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not reason.﴾

﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾ i.e., who cries out. It is said: "The shepherd called (naʿaqa) to his flock": he shouted at them and drove them on. His words, exalted is He: ﴿to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out﴾ i.e., to cattle which hear nothing but the calling and crying of the one who shouts at them, which is a vocal noise directed at them and a driving of them, and they understand nothing else and do not comprehend as rational people understand and comprehend. This eloquent brevity has conveyed two comparisons in one simile. The complete form of the wording would be: "The likeness of those who disbelieve and the likeness of their caller is like the likeness of the shepherd and the likeness of what the cattle graze." This is among the highest forms of Arabic eloquent speech, and whoever's understanding does not reach the combining of the two comparisons restricts its interpretation to a single comparison, so that the speech is taken to mean: "The likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve." Al-Harrali indicated this, as transmitted by al-Biqai from him.

Al-Farra' said: God, exalted is He, attributed the likeness to those who disbelieve, then likened them to the shepherd and did not say "like the sheep." The meaning, and God knows best, is: the likeness of those who disbelieve is like the cattle which do not understand what the shepherd says beyond the sound, so the comparison is attributed to the shepherd while the meaning lies in the grazing animals. He said: a similar usage in speech is: "So-and-so fears you like the fear of the lion," meaning "like his fear of the lion," because the lion is known to be the one feared.

It was also said: what is intended is the comparison of the state of the disbeliever in his calling upon an idol to the state of one who shouts at what does not hear him. The meaning: the likeness of these people in their calling upon their gods, which do not understand their call, is like the likeness of one who shouts at his flock, so he gains nothing from his shouting except that he is in calling and crying out. Likewise the polytheist has from his calling and worship nothing but toil.

(p-376) Ibn al-Qayyim said in "I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in": You may take this as a compound comparison (tashbih murakkab), and you may take it as a divided comparison (tashbih mufarriq). If you take it as compound, it is a comparison of the disbelievers in their lack of understanding and their failure to benefit, with the sheep at which the shepherd shouts, which understand from his speech nothing but the bare sound, which is calling and crying out. If you take it as divided: those who disbelieve are in the position of cattle, the caller who calls them to the path and guidance is in the position of the one who shouts at them, their calling to guidance is in the position of the shouting, and their perception of mere calling and crying out is like the perception of cattle of the bare voice of the shouter. And God knows best.

Al-Razi said: Know that when God, exalted is He, related of the disbelievers that when they were called to follow what God had sent down, they abandoned reflection and contemplation, inclined to blind imitation, and said: "Nay, we will follow what we found our fathers upon," He set forth this likeness as an admonition to the listeners to them, that they only fell into what they fell into because of abandoning attentive listening and little concern for religion. Thus He made them, in this respect, in the position of livestock...! A likeness of this kind increases the listener's knowledge of the states of the disbelievers, and diminishes the disbeliever in his own eyes when he hears it, so it breaks his heart and constricts his breast, since He has made him like a beast; and in this is the utmost restraint and deterrence for whoever hears it from following the path of blind imitation. Then He increased their rebuke, saying: ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not reason﴾. They are in the position of the deaf in that what they heard is as though they did not hear it; in the position of the dumb in that they did not respond to what they were called to; and in the position of the blind in that they turned away from the proofs, so they became as though they had not witnessed them. Since the way of acquiring acquired reason is seeking aid from these three faculties, when they turned away from them they lost acquired reason. For this reason it is said: Whoever loses a sense loses a branch of knowledge...!

(p-377) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[172] ﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you, and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you﴾: that is, what We have made pure for you of doubtful matters, and do not expose yourselves to what is filthy, as the polytheists made lawful what is forbidden, and do not forbid what they made lawful of them, such as the sa'ibah (a free-roaming camel released for their idols) and what accompanies it. ﴿And be grateful to Allah﴾ who has provided you with these blessings. ﴿If it is Him that you worship﴾, that is, Him alone: ﴿you worship﴾, that is, if it is true that you devote worship to Him, and acknowledge that He, glory be to Him, is the sole Bestower of blessings.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said in "Jawab Ahl al-Iman" (The Response of the People of Faith): The good things (tayyibat) which He permitted are the foods beneficial to the minds and the morals, and the wicked things (khaba'ith) are those harmful to the minds and the morals, just as wine is the mother of wickedness (umm al-khaba'ith) because it corrupts the minds and the morals. So Allah permitted the good things to the God-fearing, which they use to help them in the worship of their Lord for which they were created, and He forbade them the wicked things which harm them in the purpose for which they were created. He commanded them, along with eating them, to give thanks, and forbade them to forbid them. Whoever eats them and does not give thanks has abandoned what Allah commanded and deserves punishment; and whoever forbids them, like the monks, has transgressed the limits of Allah and deserves punishment.

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) he said: "Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it." In another hadith: "The thankful eater is like the patient faster."

(p-378) And the Exalted said: ﴿Then, on that Day, you will be questioned about the pleasure [you indulged in]﴾ [al-Takathur: 8], that is, about its thanks; for He does not permit something and then punish the one who does it, but He asks him about the obligation He imposed along with it, and about what He forbade him, whether he neglected by abandoning a command or committing a prohibited act, as the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87].

When the Exalted restricted their permission to the good of provision, the matter required an explanation of the wicked part of it so that it might be avoided. So He explicitly stated what He forbade them of what the polytheists used to deem lawful while forbidding other things, and implied the lawfulness of everything else, and that it is very abundant, so that the addressee might increase in gratitude. Then He said:

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[173] ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which has been invoked [the name of] other than Allah. But whoever is forced [to eat of them], neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you carrion﴾. In the usage of the Sharia, it (al-maytah, carrion) is what dies by itself (ḥatf anfih, of its own accord), or what is killed in a manner not prescribed by the Law, whether in regard to the agent or to the object. Included in it are: the strangled animal (al-munkhaniqah), the beaten animal (al-mawqudhah), the one that falls from a height (al-mutaraddiyah), the one gored (al-naṭīḥah), and that which a beast of prey has attacked (mā ʿadā ʿalayhā al-sabu').

Ibn Kathir said: The majority have specified from this the carrion of the sea, due to His saying: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea and its food﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 96], as will come, if Allah wills, and the hadith about al-ʿanbar (the ambergris-like creature) in the Sahih.

In the Musnad, the Muwatta' and the Sunan, there is his saying ﷺ concerning the sea: "Its water is pure, and its carrion is lawful."

(p-379) Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ibn Majah and al-Daraqutni related the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us: as for the two carrions, fish and locusts; as for the two bloods, the liver and the spleen." ﴿And blood﴾, which is the flowing (al-masfuh), i.e., that which runs, as was made explicit in the other verse; and the explained (al-mufassar) governs the ambiguous (al-mubham). Some of the Arabs used to put blood into the intestines, then roast them and eat them, and they called this al-fasd. In the Qamus and its commentary: al-fasid is blood that was placed in the Jahiliyyah in a stomach taken from the bleeding of a camel's vein, and it is roasted; the people of the Jahiliyyah would eat it and feed it to the guest in times of hardship.

It is related that two men spent the night with a Bedouin, and in the morning they met, and one asked the other about the hospitality (al-qira). He said: "I was not hospitably received, but I was bled (fuṣida lī)." Then it was said: "He who is bled for is not deprived" — with a sukun on the ṣād — and this became a proverb for one who attains some of his aim. The ṣād was given sukun for lightness, i.e., he was not deprived of hospitality when his mount was bled for him and he got its blood. It is also narrated: man fazda lahu, with a zāy instead of the ṣād; and some say: man quṣida lahu, with a qāf, i.e., one who was given a little (qaṣdan), i.e., a little. The Arabic usage is with the fā'. Yaʿqub said: The explanation of this is that a man would host another man in a time of severe hardship, and he would have nothing with which to entertain him; and he would be reluctant to slaughter his mount, so he would bleed it, and when the blood flowed he would heat it for the guest until it congealed and became firm, and then he would feed it to him. ﴿And the flesh of swine﴾; its fat and the rest of its parts enter into the ruling of its flesh, either by way of predominance, or because "flesh" (laḥm) linguistically includes these, since it is what covers between the innermost part of the animal's central bone and the outermost surface of its skin; and its use is known to be predominantly for its fresh red part, but here it is in its original linguistic sense. Or it is by way of analogy according to one opinion: for when its flesh, which is the intended object of eating and its finest part, is forbidden, its other parts are more deserving of prohibition. And when He forbade what harms the body and injures the soul, He forbade what stains the heart, so He said: ﴿and that over which has been invoked [the name of] other than Allah﴾, i.e., slaughtered for other than His name, Exalted is He, from among the idols (anṣāb) and rivals (andād) and the like, (p-380) which the Jahiliyyah used to sacrifice to. The origin of ihlal is raising the voice, i.e., one raised his voice with it for the idol and the like, as in the saying of the people of the Jahiliyyah: "In the name of al-Lat and al-ʿUzza."

Al-Qurtubi mentioned, from Ibn ʿAtiyyah, that he transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basri that he was asked about a woman who made a wedding feast for her dolls, and slaughtered a camel in it; he said: "It is not to be eaten, because it was slaughtered for an idol." He also mentioned from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about what the non-Arabs slaughter for their festivals and then send some of it as gifts to the Muslims; she said: "What was slaughtered for that day, do not eat from it, but eat from their trees." The purpose is to block what could be a pretext for shirk.

Al-Nawawi said in his Sharh Muslim: If the slaughterer, along with that, intends the glorification of the one to whom it is slaughtered, and it is other than Allah Most High, and worship of it, that is disbelief; and if the slaughterer was a Muslim before that, he becomes an apostate by the slaughter. He mentioned this in the commentary on the hadith of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "May Allah curse whoever slaughters for other than Allah."

Al-Harali said: The mention of ihlal is an announcement that what is proclaimed over with other than the name of Allah is the most severe of the forbidden things; so in its implication is a lightening of address regarding what is not known of hidden mention. Al-Bukhari related from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Some people said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Some people bring us meat, and we do not know whether the name of Allah was mentioned over it or not?' He said: 'Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat it.'" She said: "And they were recently converted from disbelief." (p-381) So the forbidden is not what is not known to have had the name of Allah mentioned over it; rather, what is known is that the name of other than Allah has been openly proclaimed over it.

It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If you hear the Jews and Christians proclaiming [the name of] other than Allah, do not eat; and if you do not hear them, eat, for Allah has made lawful their slaughtered animals, and He knows what they say."

Section

On the wisdoms and wondrous secrets behind the prohibition of these mentioned things

As for carrion: al-Harali said: It is that animal which death has overtaken from the decline of its strength and the passing of its life, and it is the most corrupting thing to the body, because its composition is corrupted by death, the loss of the pleasure of its parts, its putrefaction, and the departure of the spirit of life and purity from it.

Al-Mahayimi said in his tafsir: Then He, Exalted is He, pointed out that what severs one's love (for Allah) is only eating what He has forbidden, namely carrion and what is mentioned with it. As for carrion, it is corrupt because the spirit has been removed from it without a purifier of slaughter in the name of Allah, actually or by estimation; so your spirits become attached to the corrupt and thereby become corrupt, and the love of Allah is cut off from them. The carrion of fish is permitted because its origin is pure water; just as impurity does not affect it, the removal of its spirit does not affect what comes from it. The locust is permitted because it arises without generation and without corruption in its essence, like the rest of the insects.

As for the corruption of blood: it is because it is a substance that has reverted from the state of food and has not yet reached the state of the organs, so it is carrion.

Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said: Flowing blood is forbidden because it is the gathering place of the powers of the carnal and irascible soul, and its increase necessitates the excess of these powers; and it is the course of Satan through the body, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Satan runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs."

As for the corruption of swine flesh: it is because of its harm to the soul, just as what came before it was forbidden for its harm to the body; for among the wisdom of Allah in His creation: whoever's body is nourished by the physical substance of something, his soul is nourished by the soul-quality of that thing: "Pride and arrogance are among the fadaddin (those with loud, rough cries), the people of camel-hair tents, and tranquility is among the people of sheep." So when the swine was made to have blameworthy attributes, it was forbidden to whoever wishes to guard his soul from blameworthy character. Al-Biqa'i related it.

Modern physicians have uncovered, from sensory experiments, harms of swine flesh other than what the ancients said. Among its harms: it produces the tapeworm, whose presence in the intestines causes many symptoms: colic, diarrhea, vomiting, loss of appetite or extreme voracity, headaches, fainting, dizziness, disturbance of thought, the onset of epileptic seizures, nervous convulsions, and infection with the spiral hair-worm disease, which exceeds fever and destroys the life of the afflicted... and other fatigue, difficulty of digestion, and harms besides these.

(p-383) A wise man said: Islam came not only to reform the spirit, but to reform the spirit and the body together! So it left no harm to either of them without alerting to it, explicitly or by allusion... And the later sages have expounded at length on the harms of swine flesh in many treatises.

As for the corruption of what is invoked with other than Allah: it is because it stains the heart, since it was offered in worship as a means of drawing near to other than its Originator and Creator; and that is clear shirk and reliance on other than Him, Exalted is He. So its corruption is spiritual, for its influence on souls and character is like the influence of what harms the body. The Sharia came to preserve from whatever harms absolutely, and to safeguard the station of monotheism.

Since this religion is ease with no hardship or constriction, He lifted the ruling of this prohibition from the one compelled. He said: ﴿But whoever is forced﴾, i.e., one is compelled by a compeller, by whatever necessity, to eat something of what is forbidden, to the point of being on the verge of perishing, so he eats some of it, being ﴿neither desiring﴾, i.e., not seeking it, not inclined to it for its own sake (from baghā al-shay', he sought it, desired it and was eager for it) ﴿nor transgressing﴾, i.e., exceeding what is needed to stave off hunger and remove the necessity; ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, even if its prohibition remains, because when he takes it in the state of necessity, its corruption has no effect on him, since he is unwilling of it by nature. Al-Raghib said: It is disputed whether, if one is compelled to something for medicine which nothing else can substitute for, it is permitted. The correct view is that it is permitted for him to take it for the stated reason, that is, preserving his life by means of what he sees as closest to preserving it, which is the very thing for which taking what was mentioned is permitted to him because of hunger.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what he ate in the state of necessity; ﴿Merciful﴾, in that He granted His servants this concession for the sake of preserving them.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, repeated the warning against those who conceal His rulings, after what He had mentioned of the rulings, cautioning this Ummah not to follow the path of those to whom it refers, namely the People of the Book. So He, glorified is He, said:

(p-384) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[174] ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price — those consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire. And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book⁠﴾ — that is, of its limits, its rulings, and other things to which the first verse alluded with "the clear proofs and the guidance."

﴿and exchange it⁠﴾ — that is, take in its place

﴿a small price⁠﴾ — that is, from what they enjoy of the pleasures of this fleeting world. He called it "small" to belittle it in itself, which indicates the baseness of their souls in being content with little; or it is small in comparison with what they forfeited for themselves of the bliss of the Hereafter, which cannot be described.

﴿Those consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire⁠﴾ — that is, what entails the Fire and necessitates it, so it is as if it were the very Fire, and their eating is the eating of it. And ﴿into their bellies⁠﴾ is connected to ﴿consume⁠﴾, and its benefit is to emphasize the eating and affirm it by stating the container of what is eaten.

Al-Raghib said: "The eating of fire is taking what leads to it. The eating is mentioned because it is the primary aim in acquiring wealth, and ﴿into their bellies⁠﴾ is mentioned as a warning about their greed and a condemnation of their squandering the greatest blessings for the sake of food, which is the basest of worldly things consumed....!"

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection⁠﴾ — Al-Raghib said: "It does not mean the negation of speech altogether, for He has said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers⁠﴾ [al-A'raf: 6], and He said: ﴿And on the Day He will say, 'Call upon My partners'⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 52]. Rather, it means speech that carries benefit. Hence al-Hasan said: its meaning is that He will be angry with them, as a warning (p-385) that they are unlike those of whom He said: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, 'Peace'⁠﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]." It was also said: the literal sense of "kallamtuhu" is "I made him speak," like "harraktuhu" (I made him move), because when you speak to someone, you have invited his speech; so it is as if it were said: He will not invite their speech, like His saying: ﴿nor will they be permitted to make excuses⁠﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36].

﴿Nor will He purify them⁠﴾ — that is, He will not cleanse them from the defilement of sins, because of His anger toward them, since they concealed the truth while knowing it, and so they deserved wrath.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment⁠﴾ — that is, one that causes pain.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[175] ﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. So how patient they are toward the Fire!﴾

﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. That is: they exchanged leading themselves and others astray, through concealment and distortion, for being guided. ﴿And punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾, that is, its causes in exchange for their causes. When He, glorified is He, made the first of their food fire, the last of their affair punishment, and the summary of their condition the absence of forgiveness, the middle of their condition was likewise fire. From this there followed the expression of wonder at their state: their confining themselves to that which is in fact the meaning of patience (ṣabr), because they were engaged with the Fire in reality or with what necessitates it, without concern. So He said: ﴿So how patient they are﴾, that is, how intense is their confining of themselves, or how bold they are ﴿toward the Fire﴾, which they ate in this world, and so they feel it in the Hereafter. Related by al-Biqa'i.

Then he said: If you take it as figurative (majāz, a non-literal usage), it is like your saying to someone who opposes the ruler: "How patient you are under the long imprisonment and the heavy shackles!" as a threat to him, meaning that no one undergoes that except one who is extremely patient under punishment.

It is related from al-Kisa'i that he said: The judge of Yemen in Mecca said to me: Two men from among the Arabs came before me in dispute, and one of them swore falsely concerning his companion's right, so he said to him: "How patient you are toward Allah!" That is: how patient you are toward the punishment of Allah. Related by al-Zamakhshari.

(p-386) Al-Raghib said: The one who has no patience may be described as patient, in consideration of the viewer and what is imagined about him that he is patient. The use of the expression of wonder in this is in consideration of the creatures, not of the Creator.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned the cause that necessitates this great distancing, with His saying:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[176] ﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth; and indeed those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme opposition.﴾

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth﴾: they deserve this severe punishment only because Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Book that comprises all kinds of guidance. It is suitable to refer to both the Qur'an and the Torah, "with truth," meaning clothed in it. Therefore, whoever disputes concerning it and rejects it through distortion (tahrif) and concealment is inevitably afflicted with a punishment of this kind, with its many forms. This is because he has tried to deny what Allah has affirmed, and so he has opposed Allah in His law, seeking refuge in Him, glorified is He. ﴿And indeed those who differ concerning the Book﴾: that is, concerning the category of the divine Book, by believing in some of Allah's books and disbelieving in others; or concerning the Torah, by believing in some of its verses and disbelieving in others, or by differing over its interpretation (ta'wil), so that they became bold enough, because of it, to distort it; or concerning the Qur'an, when some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients."

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: The root of ikhtilaf (difference) is deviation from the clear path. It was also said: "They differed" means they acted contrary to what Allah had sent down. It was also said: "They differed" means "they left behind" (khallafu), like "they earned" (iktasabu) and "they earned" (kasabu), or "they did" ('amilu) and "they worked" (i'tamalu), meaning they became successors in it, as in His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾ [Maryam: 59].

﴿in extreme opposition﴾: that is, in discord and contention, ﴿far﴾ from the truth and the right course, deserving the most severe punishment. And His saying, exalted is He:

(p-387) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[177] ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing captives; and [one who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise; and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.﴾

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ is a comprehensive term for acts of obedience and good deeds that bring one closer to Allah, exalted is He. Among these is kindness to one's parents. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in pleasure﴾ [al-Infitar: 13] ﴿And indeed, the wicked will be in Hellfire﴾ [al-Infitar: 14]. So He made righteousness the opposite of wickedness (fujur). He also said: ﴿And cooperate in righteousness (al-birr) and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], so He made righteousness the opposite of sin (ithm). This shows that it is a general term for everything for which a person is rewarded. That is: the goodness, obedience, and pleasing act that purifies the soul, to which you must devote such attention that it distracts you from all other kinds of righteousness, is not the matter of the qibla. Rather, the righteousness to which attention must be given is these qualities which He, whose majesty is great, has enumerated.

It is not far-fetched that some of the believers, at the abrogation of the qibla and its change, felt elation over this qibla and became overly rigid about its matter, until they thought it was the greatest aim of the religion. So Allah, exalted is He, urged them by this address to fulfill all acts of worship and obedience. Al-Razi indicated this.

Al-Raghib said: The address in this verse is to the disbelievers and the hypocrites who denied the change of the qibla. It was also said: rather, it is addressed to them and to the believers, since the believers may think they have attained all righteousness by turning toward it.

﴿But [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾ means: the faith of one who believes in Allah, the faith to which the verse of (p-388) oneness calls, so that He is ascribed the attributes of perfection and is exalted above the marks of deficiency. ﴿and the Last Day﴾, which the polytheists denied, so their order was corrupted by the oppression of some of them against others. ﴿and the angels﴾, that is, and one believes in them and that they are honored servants, intermediaries between Him and His messengers through the delivery of revelation and the sending down of books. ﴿and the Book﴾, that is, the books that were sent down from heaven upon the prophets, among whose members the noblest is the Qur'an, which is a guardian over what came before it of the books, in which every good has culminated and which contains every felicity in this world and the Hereafter. ﴿and the prophets﴾, all of them, without distinguishing between any one of them, as the People of the Two Books did.

Al-Harali said: In it, that is, in belief in them and in what came before them, is the subjugation of the self to submit to one who is of its own kind, and belief in the unseen of one who is not of its kind, so that in this there is something that restrains the self from its desires.

﴿and gives wealth, in spite of love for it﴾, that is, he gives it while loving it and desiring it. Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others among the predecessors and successors stated this, as established in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (to the Prophet): "The best charity is that you give while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty." His words ﴿relatives﴾ are a man's kin, and they are the most deserving of those to whom charity is given. Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others related from Sulayman ibn 'Amir who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Charity given to a poor person is [one] charity, and to a relative it is two: charity and kinship maintenance." And in (p-389) the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Zaynab, the wife of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that she and another woman asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is charity given on their behalf to their husbands and to orphans in their care sufficient...?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "They have two rewards: the reward of kinship and the reward of charity." Allah, exalted is He, has commanded good treatment of relatives (p-390) in more than one place in His Mighty Book.

﴿orphans﴾, who are those with no earner, whose fathers have died, who are weak, young, and below the age of maturity. ﴿and the needy﴾, who are those who do not find what suffices them for their sustenance, clothing, and housing, so they are given what fills their need and lack. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The needy person is not the one who goes around and is turned away by a date or two dates, or a morsel or two morsels, but the needy person is the one who finds no sufficiency to suffice him, and whose condition is not noticed so that charity is given to him."

﴿and the traveler﴾, who is the passing traveler whose provisions have run out, so he is given what brings him to his homeland, since he is unable in his estrangement; likewise one who wishes to travel in obedience, so he is given what suffices him for his going and returning. This includes the guest, as 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The traveler (ibn al-sabil) is the guest who stops with the Muslims."

(p-391) Likewise said Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Zuhri, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan. "Al-sabil" is the name of the road, and the traveler was made its "son" because of his constant presence on it, just as one says of a water bird: "son of the water," and of a man whom years have reached: "son of the days," and of brave men: "sons of war," and of people: "sons of the age."

﴿and those who ask﴾, who are those who expose themselves to seeking, so they are given from the zakat and charities. As Imam Ahmad related from Husayn ibn 'Ali, peace be upon them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse." Abu Dawud also related it. ﴿and for freeing captives﴾ is conjoined to the first object, which is "relatives," meaning: and he gives wealth for the freeing of captives, that is, he pays for their release, that is, for their sake and because of them.

Al-Raghib said: "al-riqab" is the plural of "raqabah." The original meaning of "raqabah" is the neck, and it is used to express the whole person, just as it is expressed by "the head."

Al-Harali said: "al-riqab" is the plural of "raqabah," which is what slavery has affected of the children of Adam. So what is meant is the enslaved persons whose release is sought by contract (kitabah), and the redemption of prisoners from it; and He placed those first, because their need is for the establishment of the structure.

It was said: The reason for the use of "fi" is that what is given to them is spent on freeing their necks, so they do not own it as with the other categories. And Allah knows best.

A subtle point:

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, how is the order mentioned in His words ﴿and gives wealth, in spite of love for it﴾ and the verse following it to be understood? It is said: Since the one a person most takes care to benefit with his kindness is his relatives, it was fitting to mention them first. Then He followed them with orphans, since aiding them after relatives is more fitting. Then He mentioned the needy, who have no wealth, present or absent. Then He mentioned the traveler, who may have wealth but it is absent. Then He mentioned those who ask, among whom there are the truthful and the liar. Then He mentioned the captives, who have masters who support them, so each of those whose mention was delayed is less in poverty than the one whose mention was advanced...!

(p-392) ﴿and establishes prayer﴾, that is, he completes its acts in their times, with its bowing, prostration, tranquility, and humility, in the legally prescribed and pleasing manner. ﴿and gives zakah﴾, that is, the obligatory zakat on wealth. The giving of wealth mentioned earlier is taken to mean voluntary charity, goodness, and kinship maintenance, mentioned before the obligatory due for emphasis in urging it; or what is meant by both is the obligatory zakat, the first explaining the categories of recipients and the second explaining the obligation of paying. Whoever understood zakah here as purification of the soul and its cleansing from base and vile morals, like His words ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9] and His words ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18], has gone too far. The reason it is far-fetched: zakah when paired with prayer in revelation means only zakat on wealth, whereas when standing alone it depends on context.

﴿and those who fulfill their promise when they promise﴾ is conjoined to "whoever believes," since it is in effect as if it said: "and those who fulfill their promises." The choice of the active participle form indicates the obligation of continuous fulfillment.

Al-Razi said: Know that this covenant is either between the servant and Allah, or between him and the Messenger of Allah, or between him and other people. The first is what he binds himself to by vows and oaths. The second is what he pledged to the Messenger concerning the pledge of allegiance: standing in support, aiding, allying with whom he allies, and opposing whom he opposes. The third may be obligatory, like what he is bound to in exchange contracts of delivery and receipt, and the conditions he undertakes in salam (advance sale) and pledges; and it may be recommended, like fulfilling promises in spending wealth and sincerity in support. The verse encompasses all these categories.

Ibn Kathir said: The opposite of this attribute is hypocrisy, as is established in the hadith: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: (p-393) when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." In another narration: "When he speaks he lies, when he makes a covenant he betrays, and when he disputes he transgresses." ﴿and the patient﴾ is in the accusative of specification (ikhtisas). Its structure was changed from what precedes it to draw attention to the excellence and distinction of patience, though in reality it is conjoined to what precedes it. Abu 'Ali said: When you mention attributes of praise or blame and some of them are varied in grammatical case, this is done for variety in style (iftinan), and this is called "qat'" (shift), because changing the familiar indicates greater encouragement to listen to what is mentioned and greater attention to its matter! It was also read as "wa al-sabirun" (nominative), just as "wa al-mufun" was read.

Al-Raghib said: Since patience is in one respect the origin of virtues, and in another respect comprehensive of virtues, for there is no virtue in which patience does not have a profound effect, its grammar was changed to draw attention to this purpose...!: ﴿in poverty﴾, that is, in adversity, at the time it befalls them; ﴿and hardship﴾, meaning poverty, which is also adversity, as he explained both by it in the Qamus. Ibn al-Athir said: "al-darra'" is the state that harms, the opposite of "al-sarra'," and both are patterns for the feminine with no masculine form. ﴿and during battle﴾, that is, at the time of struggling against the enemy in places of war. The addition of "hin" indicates that it occurs at times and ends quickly. The meaning of "ba's" in the language is hardship; one says: "la ba'sa 'alayka fi hadha," i.e., there is no hardship upon you in this; and "'adhab ba'is" means severe punishment. War is called "ba's" because of the hardship in it, and punishment is called "ba's" because of its severity. He said: ﴿Then when they saw Our might﴾ [Ghafir: 84] ﴿Then when they perceived Our might﴾ [al-Anbiya': 12] ﴿Who will help us against the might of Allah?﴾ [Ghafir: 29]. (p-394) Ibn Sidah said: "al-ba's" is war, then it became common until it was said: "la ba'sa 'alayka," i.e., there is no fear upon you.

Al-Raghib said: This phrase encompasses the types of harm: for a person either needs patience in something that is lacking to him, or he desires something and does not obtain it, and that is "poverty"; or in what afflicts his body of pain, and that is "hardship"; or in repelling one who harms him, and that is "despair" (ya's).

﴿Those are the ones who have been true﴾ in their faith, because they realized heartfelt faith through words and deeds, so circumstances did not change them and terrors did not shake them. In this is an indication that whoever does not do their deeds has not been truthful in his claim of faith...!: ﴿and it is those who are the righteous﴾ (al-muttaqun), guarding against disbelief and all other vices. The repetition of the demonstrative is for added emphasis on their status, and the insertion of the pronoun indicates that piety is restricted to them.

Al-Wahidi said: These conjunctions (waw) among the attributes in this verse are for gathering. So among the conditions of righteousness, and the completion of the condition of the righteous person, is that these attributes be gathered in him, and whoever has only one of them does not deserve the description of righteousness.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 1 of 2):**

[p. 395] The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[178] ﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retaliation (qisas) for those murdered: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., by the heirs of the slain], then pursuit [of the blood money] should be made in a reasonable manner, and payment made to him with good conduct. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾
