Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed to their prophet: Inform them that you go out to the open ground with impure bodies, and you raise to Me hands with which you have shed blood and filled your houses with the unlawful. Now, when My anger has intensified against you?! And you will not increase in nearness to Me except in distance!

Then Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Supplication is among the most beneficial remedies. It is the enemy of calamity: it repels it, treats it, prevents its descent, lifts it, or lightens it when it has descended. It is the believer's weapon. As al-Hakim narrated in [p. 436] his Sahih from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him and honor his face, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is the weapon of the believer, the pillar of religion, and the light of the heavens and the earth." It has three stages with respect to calamity: First, that it is stronger than the calamity and so repels it. Second, that it is weaker than the calamity, so the calamity prevails over it and the servant is afflicted, but it may lighten it even if weak. Third, that they are equal, and each prevents the other.

Al-Hakim also narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Caution does not avail against destiny, and supplication benefits with regard to what has descended and what has not descended. Indeed, a calamity descends, and supplication meets it, and they struggle with each other until the Day of Resurrection!" Also in it, from the hadith of Ibn Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Supplication benefits with regard to what has descended and what has not descended. So upon you, servants of Allah, is supplication!"

Also in it, from the hadith of Thawban from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Nothing turns back destiny except supplication, nothing increases life except righteousness, and indeed a man is deprived of provision because of a sin he commits..."

Then Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Among the most beneficial remedies is persistence in supplication. Ibn Majah narrated in his Sunan from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, He becomes angry with him!" In the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Anas from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not be weak in supplication, for no one perishes while supplicating." Al-Awza'i narrated from al-Zuhri, from Urwah, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah loves those who are persistent in supplication." In the Kitab al-Zuhd of Imam Ahmad, from Qatadah who said: Muwarriq said: "I have found no parable for the believer except a man in the sea on a plank of wood, who supplicates: O Lord! Perhaps Allah, mighty and majestic, will save him!"

[p. 437] Then Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah illuminate his tomb, said: Among the afflictions that prevent the effect of supplication from following it is that the servant hastens and considers the response slow, so he becomes weary and abandons supplication. This is like one who sows a seed or plants a sapling, then keeps tending and watering it, but when he finds its completion and maturity slow, he leaves it and neglects it! In al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "One of you will be answered as long as he does not hasten, saying: I supplicated but I was not answered!" In the Sahih of Muslim from him: "The servant will continue to be answered as long as he does not supplicate for sin or for severing ties of kinship, and as long as he does not hasten." It was said: O Messenger of Allah, what is hastening? He said: "He says: I have supplicated and supplicated, and I have not seen Allah respond to me, so at that point he becomes weary and abandons supplication." In the Musnad of Ahmad from the hadith of Anas, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The servant will remain in good as long as he does not hasten." They said: O Messenger of Allah, how does he hasten? He said: "He says: I have supplicated to my Lord, but He has not answered me."

Then he said:

Section.

(p. 438) When supplication is accompanied by presence of heart and by gathering one's whole self upon the thing sought, and it coincides with one of the six times of answering, which are: the last third of the night; at the call to prayer (adhan); between the adhan and the iqamah; after the obligatory prayers; when the imam ascends the pulpit on Friday until the prayer is concluded; and the last hour after 'Asr on that day; and it coincides with humility in the heart, brokenness before the Lord (p. 438), lowliness, supplication and tenderness; and the supplicant faces the qiblah, is in a state of purity, raises his hands to Allah the Exalted, begins with praising Allah and extolling Him, then follows that with blessing upon Muhammad, His servant (ﷺ), then places repentance and seeking forgiveness before his need, then enters into Allah's presence, presses his request insistently, flatters Him, and calls upon Him with both desire and fear, and seeks means to Him through His names, His attributes and His oneness, and places charity before his supplication, then this supplication is almost never rejected.

Especially so if it coincides with the supplications which the Prophet (ﷺ) informed were most likely to be answered, or which contain the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam). Among them is what is in the Sunan and in the Sahih of Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah from his father, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard a man saying: 'O Allah, I ask You, by virtue of my testifying that You are Allah, there is no god but You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten and has not been begotten, and to whom no one is equal.' He said: 'You have asked Allah by the Name which, when He is asked by it, gives, and when He is called upon by it, answers.'" And in another wording: "You have asked Allah by His Greatest Name." (p. 439)

Also in the Sunan and the Sahih of Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, that "he was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sitting, and a man was praying, then he supplicated: 'O Allah, I ask You, by virtue of Yours being all praise, there is no god but You, the Bestower, Originator of the heavens and the earth, O Possessor of majesty and honour, O Ever-Living, O Sustainer of all!' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'He has called upon Allah by His Great Name, which when He is called upon by it, answers, and when He is asked by it, gives.'" Ahmad in his Musnad and al-Tirmidhi in his Jami' both transmitted the two hadiths, from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in these two verses: ﴿And your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 163], and the opening of Al 'Imran: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 1] ﴿Allah—there is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2]." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hadith that is hasan sahih (good and sound)."

And in the Musnad of Ahmad and the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, Anas ibn Malik and Rabi'ah ibn 'Amir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Cling to (alizzu) 'Ya Dha al-Jalali wal-Ikram' (O Possessor of Majesty and Honour)." He means: hold fast to them, keep to them, and persist in them.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that "when a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would raise his head to the sky and say: 'Subhan Allah al-'Azim (Glory be to Allah, the Mighty).' And when he exerted himself in supplication he would say: 'Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum (O Ever-Living, O Sustainer).'" And in it also, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When a matter distressed the Prophet (ﷺ), he would say: 'Ya Hayy, ya Qayyum! By Your mercy I seek relief.'"

And in the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in three suras of the Qur'an: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran and Ta-Ha."

Al-Qasimi said: "So I searched for it, and behold, it is the verse of 'the Ever-Living, the Sustainer.'"

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi and the Sahih of al-Hakim, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The supplication of Dhu al-Nun (Jonah) when he called upon Him while in the belly of the fish: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers﴾. No Muslim man has ever supplicated with it for anything except that Allah answered him." Al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a sound hadith." And in the Sahih of al-Hakim also, from the hadith of Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not inform you of something which, when a grave matter befalls one of you and he supplicates with it, Allah relieves him of it? The supplication of Dhu al-Nun."

And in his Sahih also, from him (Sa'd), that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) (p. 440) saying: "Shall I guide you to the Greatest Name of Allah? It is the supplication of Yunus." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah! Was it for Yunus alone?" He said: "Do you not hear His saying: ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress, and thus We save the believers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 88]? Any Muslim who supplicates with it during his illness forty times, and then dies in that illness, will be given the reward of a martyr; and if he recovers, he recovers forgiven."

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say at times of distress: 'There is no god but Allah, the Mighty, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne.'"

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught me that when distress befalls me I should say: 'There is no god but Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous. Glory be to Allah, and blessed is Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"

And in his Musnad also, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No worry or grief ever befalls anyone and he says: 'O Allah, I am Your servant, son of Your servant, son of Your maidservant; my forelock is in Your hand; Your judgement over me is executed; Your decree concerning me is just. I ask You, O Allah, by every name which You have named Yourself with, or taught to any of Your creation, or revealed in Your Book, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You; that You make the Great Qur'an the spring of my heart, the light of my sight, the removal of my grief and the banishing of my worry...' except that Allah removes his worry and grief and replaces them with joy." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! Should we not learn it?" He said: "Rather, whoever hears it should learn it."

Ibn Mas'ud also said: No prophet among the prophets was ever distressed except that he sought relief through glorification (tasbih).

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: We often find supplications which people made and were answered, and there had accompanied the supplication the urgent need of the one who made it and his turning to Allah, or a good deed that had preceded from him, so that Allah, glorified is He, made the answering of his supplication a thanks for his good deed; or the supplication coincided with a time of answering, and the like, so his supplication was answered. Then the one who thinks supposes that the secret lies in the wording of that supplication, and takes it in isolation from those matters which accompanied it from that supplicant. This is like when a man uses a beneficial medicine at the right time and in the right manner, and benefits from it, and another supposes that the use of this medicine by itself is enough to achieve the desired result; he would be mistaken. This is a point in which many people err.

From this: it may happen that someone's supplication, made out of dire necessity at a grave, is answered; the ignorant one then supposes that the secret lies in the grave. He does not know that the secret lies in necessity and sincere reliance upon Allah. When this occurs for you in one of the houses of Allah, it is better and more beloved to Allah...

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: Supplications and seeking refuge are like weapons. A weapon strikes by its wielder, not by its edge alone! So whenever the weapon is a complete weapon with no defect, and the arm is a strong arm, and there is no obstacle, the harm is inflicted upon the enemy! And whenever one of these three is absent, the effect is absent! So if the supplication itself is not suitable, or the supplicant has not united his heart and tongue in the supplication, or there is an obstacle to answering, the effect does not occur!

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said: Here is a well-known question: that the thing supplicated for, if it has been decreed, there is no escape from its occurrence, whether the servant supplicates for it or not; and if it has not been decreed, it will not occur, whether the servant asks for it or not. A group thought this question was valid, so they abandoned supplication and said: there is no benefit in it! These people, despite their extreme ignorance and misguidance, are self-contradictory. For the consistent application of their doctrine necessitates the nullification of all causes.

(p. 442) It is said to one of them: If satiety and quenching of thirst have been decreed for you, then they must occur, whether you eat or do not eat. And if they have not been decreed, they will not occur, whether you eat or do not eat. And if a child has been decreed for you, then it must come, whether you have intercourse with a wife or a slave-woman or not; and if it has not been decreed, it will not be. So there is no need for marriage or concubinage. And so on... Would anyone say: this is a rational being, or a human? Rather, the beast is created instinctively to engage in the causes by which its sustenance and life subsist. So animals are more intelligent and more discerning than these people, who are like cattle, nay, they are further astray in the way.

Some of them became clever and said: Occupying oneself with supplication is purely an act of worship. Allah rewards the supplicant for it without it having any effect whatsoever upon the thing sought! According to this clever one, there is no difference between supplicating and refraining from it, in heart and tongue, regarding the achievement of the desired end; and their connection of supplication to it is like the connection of silence, and there is no difference... Another group, cleverer than these, said: Rather, supplication is a bare sign which Allah, glorified is He, established as an indicator of the granting of need; so whenever the servant is enabled to supplicate, that is a sign for him and an indication that his need has been granted... This is like when you see a black, cold cloud in the winter; it is a proof and sign that it will rain... They said: and likewise the ruling regarding acts of obedience and their reward, and disbelief and sins and their punishment: they are purely indicators of the occurrence of reward and punishment, not causes of them...! And likewise, according to them, breaking with being broken, burning with being burned, and killing with death, none of these is at all a cause, and there is no connection between them and what follows from them except by mere constant concomitance, not causal influence. By this they opposed sense, reason, the Sharia and all other groups of rational people. Rather, they made rational people laugh at them...

The correct view is that there is here a third category, other than what the questioner mentioned: that this decreed matter was decreed through causes, and among its causes is supplication. It was not decreed in isolation from its cause, but it was decreed through its cause. So whenever the servant brings about the cause, the decreed matter occurs, and whenever he does not bring about the cause, the decreed matter does not occur. This is like how satiety and quenching of thirst were decreed through eating and drinking, a child was decreed through intercourse, the growth of crops was decreed through sowing (p. 443), and the departure of an animal's soul was decreed through slaughtering it. Likewise, entry into Paradise was decreed through deeds, and entry into Hellfire through deeds. This category is the truth, and it is what the questioner denied and was not granted success in. In that case, supplication is among the strongest causes. When the occurrence of the thing supplicated for has been decreed through supplication, it is not valid to say: there is no benefit in supplication, just as one does not say: there is no benefit in eating and drinking, and all movements and actions; and none of the causes is more beneficial than supplication, nor more effective in achieving the desired end! And since the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were the most knowledgeable of the Ummah about Allah and His Messenger and the most learned of them in their religion, they were more upright in this cause, its conditions and its etiquette than others. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to seek victory through it over his enemy, and he was his greatest army; and he used to say to the Companions: "You are not helped by numbers, but you are helped from the heavens!" And he used to say: "I do not bear the concern of being answered, but the concern of supplicating. If you are inspired to supplicate, then the answer is with it..."

[p. 444] Whoever is inspired to supplicate, the answer has been intended for him, for Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾ [al-Ghafir: 60]. ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾.

In *Sunan Ibn Majah*, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not ask Allah, He becomes angry with him." This indicates that His pleasure lies in being asked and in obedience to Him. When the Lord, blessed and exalted, is pleased, then all good lies in His pleasure, just as all trial and calamity lie in His anger.

Imam Ahmad has mentioned in *Kitab al-Zuhd* (the Book of Asceticism) a report: "I am Allah, there is no god but Me. When I am pleased, I bless, and there is no end to My blessing. When I am angry, I curse, and My curse reaches the seventh generation of offspring."

Reason, transmitted evidence, innate nature, and the experience of nations, across their different races, religions and sects, all indicate that drawing near to the Lord of the worlds, seeking His good pleasure, and showing righteousness and kindness to His creation, are among the greatest causes of bringing about every good. Their opposites are among the greatest causes of bringing about every evil. The blessings of Allah are not secured, nor His vengeance averted, by anything like obedience to Him, drawing near to Him, and kindness to His creation.

Allah, glorified is He, has ordained in His Book that the attainment of good in this world and the Hereafter, and the attainment of happiness in this world and the Hereafter, follow from deeds in the manner of the recompense following the condition, the effect following the cause, and the causer following its cause. This occurs in the Qur'an more than a thousand times. Sometimes a natural, factual judgment or a legislated command is linked to a fitting attribute, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ [al-A'raf: 166]; ﴿And when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55]; ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]; and ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women … and the men who remember Allah often and the women who remember Him often, Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. This is very abundant!

Sometimes it is linked to it by the form of condition and recompense, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you﴾ [al-Anfal: 29]; His saying: ﴿And if they had remained on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]; and His saying: ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 11]; and its like.

[p. 445] Sometimes it comes with the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil, the lam expressing purpose or reason), as in His saying: ﴿That they may reflect upon its verses, and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad: 29], and His saying: ﴿That you may be witnesses over the people and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

Sometimes it comes with the particle kay (ك ي), which expresses causation, as in His saying: ﴿So that it will not be a perpetual circulation among the wealthy among you﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].

Sometimes it comes with the ba' of causation (ba' al-sababiyyah, the ba' expressing cause), as in His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have put forth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182]; His saying: "for what you used to do" (bima kuntum ta'malun); [p. 446] and: ﴿for what you used to earn﴾ [al-A'raf: 39]; and His saying: ﴿That is their recompense because they disbelieved in Our signs﴾ [al-Isra': 98].

Sometimes it comes with the object of purpose (al-maf'ul li-ajlihi, the object expressing the reason for an action), whether explicit or elided, as in His saying: ﴿then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other may remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]; and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; and His saying: ﴿lest you say, "The Book was only revealed to two groups before us"﴾ [al-An'am: 156]. That is, out of dislike that you should say.

[p. 447] Sometimes it comes with the fa' of causation (fa' al-sababiyyah, the fa' expressing cause), as in His saying: ﴿But they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord destroyed them over their sin﴾ [al-Shams: 14]; His saying: ﴿They disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with an overpowering seizure﴾ [al-Haqqah: 10]; and His saying: ﴿But they denied the two, so they were among the destroyed﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 48]; and its like.

Sometimes it comes with the particle lamma (لَمّا), which indicates the apodosis (the consequent clause of a conditional), as in His saying: ﴿And when they angered Us, We took retribution from them and drowned them all﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55], and its like.

Sometimes it comes with inna and what it governs (inna wa-ma 'amilat fihi, inna with its following element), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90], and His saying concerning the opposite of these: ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77].

Sometimes it comes with the particle lawla (لَوْلا), which indicates the linking of what precedes it with what follows it, as in His saying: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify Allah, he would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Saffat: 143–144].

Sometimes it comes with law (لَوِ), which indicates condition, as in His saying: ﴿And if they had done what they were admonished, it would have been better for them﴾ [al-Nisa': 66].

[p. 448] In sum, the Qur'an, from its beginning to its end, is explicit that recompense of good and evil, and both the natural and the legislated rulings, follow from causes. Indeed, the rulings of this world and the Hereafter, and their benefits and harms, follow from causes and deeds. Whoever gains understanding of this matter and reflects upon it as it deserves will benefit from it to the utmost extent, and will not rely upon divine decree (al-qadar, God's predestination) out of ignorance, incapacity, negligence, or wastefulness. Thus his trust in God becomes incapacity, and his incapacity becomes trust! Rather, the complete jurist is the one who repels divine decree with divine decree, averts divine decree with divine decree, and opposes divine decree with divine decree. A person cannot live except by this! Hunger, thirst, cold, and kinds of fears and dangers are all part of divine decree, and all creatures strive to avert this decree. And so whoever Allah has granted success and inspired with right guidance averts the decree of punishment in the Hereafter with the decree of repentance, faith, and righteous deeds. This is the measure of the frightening decree in this world and its opposite. The Lord of the two abodes is one, and His wisdom is one; some of it does not contradict another part, nor does some of it nullify another part. This matter is among the most noble matters for whoever knows its worth and observes it as it deserves. And Allah is the One sought for help.

However, two matters remain for him, through which his happiness and success are completed:

The first: that he know the details of the causes of evil and good, and have insight into them through what he has witnessed in the world, what he has experienced himself and in others, and what he has heard of the reports of nations, past and present.

Among the most beneficial means to this is reflection upon the Qur'an, for it is sufficient for this in the most perfect way, and in it are the causes of good and evil, all explained in detail. Then the Sunnah (prophetic tradition), for it is the twin of the Qur'an and is the second revelation (wahy). Whoever devotes his attention to these two needs nothing else beside them, and they show you good and evil and their causes, until it is as if you were witnessing that directly. Then, when you reflect upon the reports of nations and the days of Allah among the people of His obedience and the people of [p. 449] His disobedience, it will accord with what you have learned from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and you will see it in the details of what Allah has informed of and promised. You will also know, from His signs on the horizons, that the Qur'an is true, the Messenger is true, and that Allah will surely fulfill His promise! History is a detailed elaboration of the particulars of the general causes of good and evil that Allah and His Messenger have made known to us... End of quotation.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fal-yastajibu li* (فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي)﴾ means: when I call them to faith and obedience, as I respond to them when they call upon Me for their needs. ﴿wal-yu'minu bi* (وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي)﴾ is a command to remain steadfast in what they are upon. ﴿la'allahum yarshudun (لَعَلَّهم يَرْشُدُونَ)﴾ means: hoping to attain right guidance, which is the truth.

Two remarks:

The first: al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: "I prefer fal-yastajibu over fal-yujibu for a subtle reason: the true meaning of istijabah (responding) is seeking a response, although it may be used in the sense of ijabah (answering). Thus He clarifies that whenever the servants strive to respond to Him according to their capacity, He is pleased with them." If it is asked: how does He combine istijabah with faith, when one of them makes the other unnecessary, since no one who is not a believer can be responsive to Allah? We reply: responding to Him is the carrying out of His commands and prohibitions by the limbs, while faith is what the hearts necessitate. Moreover, the faith intended here is the faith mentioned in His saying: ﴿The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned﴾ [al-Anfal: 2], and so on.

The second: we have previously mentioned from al-Raghib the secret of the connection of this verse with what precedes it, and the aspect of its coherence. There is another secret that the Hafiz Ibn Kathir stated, and his words are:

"In His mention of this verse, which encourages supplication, interspersed among the rulings of fasting, there is guidance to exert oneself in supplication at the completion of the count, and indeed at every breaking of the fast. As Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his *Musnad* from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The fasting person has a supplication that is answered at the time of his breaking the fast.' So when Abdullah ibn Amr broke his fast, he would call his family and children and supplicate. Ibn Majah also narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, the fasting person has a supplication at his breaking of the fast that is not rejected...' And Abdullah used to say when he broke his fast: 'O Allah, I ask You by Your mercy which encompasses all things, that You forgive me...' Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Three whose supplication is not rejected: the just ruler; the fasting person until he breaks his fast; and the supplication of the oppressed, which Allah raises above the clouds on the Day of Resurrection, and the gates of heaven are opened for it, and He says: "By My might, I will surely help you, even if after a time."'"

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[187] ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in to your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you. Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn. Then complete the fast until nightfall. And do not have relations with them while you are staying in the mosques for devotion. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus Allah makes clear His verses to the people, that they may become righteous.﴾

[p. 451] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in to your wives﴾ is guidance regarding what He prescribed for the fast, after explaining its obligation for those upon whom it is incumbent, and its rulings concerning them whether resident or traveling, and its duration. This includes the permission for a husband to have intercourse with his wife at night. It seems that the Companions were reluctant about this, thinking it was part of the fast, and they felt they had no patience to refrain from it. So He made clear to them that this is lawful and that there is no blame in it.

Al-Bukhari narrated from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When the fasting of Ramadan was prescribed, they would not approach women throughout Ramadan, and some men would deceive themselves. So Allah revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you.﴾"

This indicates that He made it lawful and did not forbid it, since He did not prescribe from His bounty anything that entails hardship and distress.

Al-rafath (ribald speech, the root meaning being foul talk) here is a euphemism for intercourse and what follows from it, just as He used euphemism for it in His saying: ﴿When he covered her﴾ [al-A'raf: 189] and His saying: ﴿So go to your tillage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223]. Allah, exalted is He, is Generous and uses euphemism. The choice of euphemism here with the word al-rafath, which indicates the sense of foulness, unlike the rest of the verses, is to express disapproval of what had occurred from them before the permission, just as He called it deception of themselves. Euphemism for what is considered repugnant to mention, using a term that is pleasant in wording, is among the customs of the Arabs. Al-Tha'alibi, at the end of his book Fiqh al-Lugha, has a remarkable section on this.

Furthermore, the common usage is "rafatha bi-al-mar'a" with the preposition bi. It is used here with ila because it contains the sense of reaching out to (ifda'), as in His saying: ﴿And you have reached one another﴾ [al-Nisa': 21].

﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them.﴾ Al-Raghib said: He made the garment an metaphor for the spouse, because each one shields oneself and one's spouse, so that no shameful thing appears from either of them, just as a garment is a covering that prevents the private parts from showing. On this basis, a woman was also referred to as an izar (wrapper), and marriage was called a fortress (hisn), because it is a fortress for its people against engaging in what is ugly.

This is more subtle than the statement of some who said: each of the spouses, by embracing and enclosing the other, is likened to a garment that wraps around its wearer. On this, al-Ja'di said:

"When the bedfellow turns her side, she turns and becomes a garment over him."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the position of His saying: ﴿They are a garment for you﴾? I say: it is a resumptive clause explaining the reason for the permission, namely that when between you and them there is such close association and intimacy, your patience with them diminishes and it becomes difficult for you to avoid them; therefore He granted you permission to have relations with them.

﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves﴾ is another resumptive clause explaining the reason mentioned, which is the deception of the self, that is, its lack of restraint in its yearning toward its desire. From it comes the expression: "his legs betrayed him" (khanathu rijlahu), when he is unable to walk. That is, Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves if this had not been made lawful for you, so He made it lawful out of mercy and kindness toward you. There is another meaning of al-ikhtiyan (deception): that it refers to violating the truth by breaking the covenant, that is, you would be wronging yourselves by exposing yourselves to punishment if this had not been made lawful for you. They said: al-ikhtiyan is more intensive than al-khiyana (betrayal), just as iktisab is more intensive than kasb; so it contains additional emphasis and severity.

[p. 453] Then He pointed to His kindness toward the believers by lightening what had burdened, weighed upon, and betrayed them had it not been for His mercy, through His saying: ﴿so He turned to you in forgiveness﴾, that is, He returned to you with His bounty and facilitation by removing the hardship concerning intercourse at night. ﴿And pardoned you﴾, that is, He overlooked for you its prohibition. So pardon here means widening and lightening.

﴿So now, have relations with them.﴾ Abu al-Baqa' said: The true meaning of al-an (now) is the present time in which you are. It may also refer to the recent past relative to you, or to the near future whose occurrence is imminent, treating the near as if it were present. This is what is intended here, because His saying: ﴿So now, have relations with them﴾ means: the time during the night in which intercourse had been forbidden to you, we have now permitted to you within it. On this view, al-an is an adverbial complement to fa-bashiruhunna (so have relations with them). It has also been said that the statement is understood in meaning, and the implied sense is: "So now, We have permitted you to have relations with them." The verbal command, which is meant to express permission, indicates the omitted element. On this view, al-an retains its literal meaning.

The original meaning of mubashara (having relations) is the joining of skin to skin. It is used as a euphemism for intercourse, which necessarily involves it.

﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾ is an emphasis on what precedes it, that is: seek this concession which He has made lawful for you. Here "kataba" (decreed) may mean "made" (ja'ala), as in His saying: ﴿He has inscribed faith in their hearts﴾ [al-Mujadila: 22], that is, He made it; and His saying: ﴿So record us among the witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 53], and ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], that is, I will make it. Or it may mean "decreed" (qada), as in His saying: ﴿Say: Nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us﴾ [al-Tawbah: 51], that is, He decreed it; and His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail. Indeed Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might﴾ [al-Mujadila: 21]; and His saying: ﴿Those upon whom death was decreed would have gone forth to their place of death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154], that is, it was decreed.

Al-Raghib said: In the verse there is an allusion, regarding seeking marriage, to a subtle point. It is that Allah, exalted is He, placed in us the desire for marriage for the preservation of the human species until an appointed end, just as He placed in us the desire for food for the preservation of our individual persons until an appointed end. So it is incumbent upon a person to seek through marriage what Allah has prescribed for him, in accordance with what reason and religion require. Whenever he seeks through it the protection of the self and its fortification in the prescribed manner, he has sought what Allah has decreed for him. To this point referred one who said: it means offspring.

[p. 455] ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn.﴾ Allah, exalted is He, permitted eating and drinking, along with the previously mentioned permission for intercourse, at whatever time of the night the fasting person wishes, until the light of morning becomes distinct from the darkness of night. The two are compared to two threads, one white and one black, because the first thing that appears of the dawn spreading across the horizon, and the dim darkness of night extending with it, are like a stretched thread. Abu Du'ad al-Iyadi said:

"When the darkness was lit up for us, and a thread of the morning appeared and shone."

His saying: ﴿of the dawn﴾ is an explanation of the white thread. He dispensed with explaining the black thread, because explaining one of them is an explanation of the other. This explanation removed the confusion that had occurred at the beginning of the fasting, as al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: "The verse was revealed: ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, and ﴿of the dawn﴾ had not yet been revealed. Some men, when they wished to fast, would tie a white thread and a black thread to their legs, and continue eating until they could see both of them. Then Allah revealed after that: ﴿of the dawn﴾, and they understood that it means the night and the day." Both of them also narrated this. The wording is Muslim's: from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾, 'Adi said to him: O Messenger of Allah, I place under my pillow two cords, one white and one black, and I know the night from the day by them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Your pillow must be wide, for it is only the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day.'"

Ibn Kathir said: The meaning of his saying: "Your pillow must be wide" is: if it is wide enough to place beneath it the two threads intended in this verse; it would necessitate that it be as wide as the east and the west..! In some wordings it occurs: "You have a wide nape," and some interpreted it as dullness. This is weak; rather it returns to the same meaning, because if his pillow is wide, then his nape is also wide. And Allah knows best. End of quote.

The use of the form tafa''ala in His saying: ﴿until it becomes distinct﴾ indicates that clear distinction is required, not merely the first glimmers of light. Muslim narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let not the call of Bilal deceive you regarding your pre-dawn meal, nor the whiteness of the horizon extended thus, until it spreads thus." He illustrated it with his hands, saying, that is, horizontally. In another wording from him: "Let not the call of Bilal deceive you, nor this whiteness, until the dawn appears," or he said: "until the dawn breaks forth." Imam Ahmad narrated from Qays ibn Talq, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The dawn is not that which extends across the horizon, but it is the reddish one which spreads across [the horizon]." [p. 457] Al-Tirmidhi narrated it with the wording: "Eat and drink, and let not the rising and ascending light deceive you; eat and drink until the reddish one spreads across for you." He said: "In this chapter there are also narrations from 'Adi ibn Hatim, Abu Dharr and Samurah." Then he said: "The hadith of Talq ibn 'Ali is a good, gharib hadith from this chain. According to the scholars, the practice is that it is not forbidden for the fasting person to eat and drink until the reddish dawn spreading across the horizon appears, and this is what the people of knowledge say." End of quote.

Some said: What is meant by the reddish is the white, as the hadith "I was sent to the red and the black" is interpreted. Shimr said: They called the white "reddish" as a euphemism, by analogy with the leper (al-abras), and he related this from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. It appears that there is no need for this, since the rising of dawn is accompanied by redness. In al-Qamus: al-fajr (dawn) is the light of morning, which is the redness of the sun within the darkness of night. So understand.

The Hafiz 'Abd al-Razzaq said in his Musannaf: Ibn Jurayj informed us from 'Ata': I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "There are two dawns. As for the one which shines in the sky, it neither permits nor forbids anything. But the dawn which illuminates the tops of the mountains is the one which forbids drinking." 'Ata' said: As for when it shines in the sky, its shining being that it extends lengthwise in the sky, it does not forbid a drink to the fasting person or prayer, and it does not cause the loss of the Hajj. But when it spreads over the tops of the mountains, it forbids drinking for the fast and causes the loss of the Hajj.

Ibn Kathir said: This is a sound chain back to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'. Similarly it has been related from more than one of the early generations, may Allah have mercy on them. End of quote.

[p. 458] ﴿Then complete the fast﴾, that is, the fast of each day: ﴿until nightfall﴾, that is, until the darkness becomes visible from the direction of the east. This is by the setting of the sun. The word "until" (ila) indicates that breaking the fast occurs at sunset, as narrated in the Two Sahihs from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the night approaches from here, and the day withdraws from here, and the sun has set, the fasting person has broken his fast."

Ibn al-Qayyim said: That is, he has broken it legally, even if he did not intend it, or he has entered the time of breaking it, as in the expressions "he became morning" and "he became evening."

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to hasten the breaking of the fast and encouraged it, as in the Two Sahihs: "The people will remain in goodness so long as they hasten the breaking of the fast." Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, exalted and majestic, says: The most beloved of My servants to Me are those who hasten the breaking of the fast." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: A good, gharib hadith. And from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to break his fast before praying, with fresh dates; if there were no fresh dates, then dates; if there were no dates, he would take a few sips of water." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it [p. 459] and said: A good, gharib hadith. Imam Ahmad narrated from Layla, the wife of Bashir ibn al-Khasasiyyah, who said: "I wished to fast two days continuously, but Bashir prevented me and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade it and said: 'The Christians do that. Rather, fast as Allah has commanded you, then complete the fast until night, and when night comes, break your fast.'"

The following is a translation of the passage from al-Qasimi's commentary (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 187 (part 2 of 2).

Therefore, the authentic hadiths report the prohibition of wisal (continuous fasting). It is that one joins one day to another without eating anything between them. In the two Sahihs, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Do not practise wisal!" They said: "But you practise it." He said: "I am not like any of you. Indeed, I am fed and given drink" – or "Indeed, I spend the night being fed and given drink." At-Tirmidhi said: "And on this topic there are reports from Ali, Abu Hurairah, Aisha, Ibn Umar, Jabir, Abu Sa'id, and Bashir ibn al-Khasasiyyah." That is to say, the prohibition of it has been established through more than one chain. Yes, whoever wishes to practise wisal until the pre-dawn meal (sahur) may do so, as in the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not practise wisal. Whoever among you wishes to practise wisal, let him practise it until the pre-dawn meal." They said: "But you practise it, O Messenger of Allah!" He said: "I am not in your condition. Indeed, I spend the night with one who feeds me and one who gives me drink." Both (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in the two Sahihs. By this food and drink is meant that with which Allah nourishes him of knowledge (ma'arif), what overflows upon his heart of the delight of intimate conversation with Him, the coolness of his eye through His nearness, his delight in His love, longing for Him, and the consequences of that from the states which are the nourishment of the heart, the bliss of the spirits, the coolness of the eye, and the joy of the souls and the heart, through that which is greater nourishment, finer, and more beneficial. It may strengthen this nourishment until it suffices in place of bodily nourishment for a period of time.

Whoever has even slight experience and longing knows the body's self-sufficiency through the nourishment of the heart and spirit over much of animal nourishment, especially the one who is joyful and elated, who has attained his desire, whose eye is refreshed by his beloved, who delights in his nearness and in His approval, and whose beloved's kindnesses, gifts and presents reach him at every time. His beloved is solicitous toward him, proud of his affair, honouring him to the utmost degree of honour, together with complete love for him. Is there not in this the greatest nourishment for this lover?! How then with the Beloved, than whom there is nothing more majestic, greater, more beautiful, more perfect, or more abundant in goodness, when the heart of the lover is filled with His love, and His love possesses all parts of his heart and limbs, and His love takes firm hold of him to the greatest degree? And this is his state with his Beloved.

Is this lover not, in the presence of his Beloved, fed and given drink by Him night and day? For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I spend the night in the presence of my Lord, who feeds me and gives me drink." And if that were food and drink for the mouth – as one would say – he would not have been fasting, let alone practising wisal. Thus in Zad al-Ma'ad.

Ibn Jarir reported from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and others of the salaf that they used to practise wisal over several days. He interpreted this as their doing it as a discipline for their souls, not as an act of worship. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir said: It is possible that they understood the prohibition to be advisory, out of compassion, as came in the hadith of Aisha: "a mercy for them." So Ibn al-Zubayr and his son Amir and whoever followed their path would undertake it and practise it, because they found strength for it.

"And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoted to worship in the mosques." Ali ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn Abbas: This concerns the man who performs i'tikaf in the mosque during Ramadan or at other times. Allah forbade him to have relations with women by night or by day until he completes his i'tikaf. Al-Dahhak said: When a man performed i'tikaf and went out of the mosque, he would have intercourse if he wished. Likewise Mujahid, Qatadah and others said: They used to do that until this verse was revealed. Ibn Abi Hatim said: It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Mujahid, Ata', al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and Muqatil that they said: he should not approach them while he is in i'tikaf.

Ibn Kathir said: What he related from these scholars is the matter agreed upon among the scholars: that the one in i'tikaf is forbidden women so long as he is in i'tikaf in the mosque, even if he goes to his house for a necessity that he cannot avoid. It is not permissible for him to remain there except for the time it takes to finish that need – such as relieving himself or eating. He may not kiss his wife, nor embrace her, nor occupy himself with anything other than his i'tikaf.

Then Ibn Kathir said: By "mubashara" is meant intercourse and its preliminaries: such as kissing, embracing, and the like. As for handing someone something and the like, there is no harm in it. It is established in the two Sahihs from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would bring his head close to me and I would comb it while I was menstruating. And he would not enter the house except for a human need." Also in the two Sahihs: "Safiyyah, the Mother of the Believers, used to visit (p-462) the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in i'tikaf in the mosque. She would talk with him for an hour, then return to her dwelling. The Prophet (ﷺ) would stand up to walk with her until he had brought her to her home, and that was at night."

Two remarks:
First: Al-Raghib said: The apparent mention of "mosques" implies the permissibility of i'tikaf in every mosque.
Second: In His mention of i'tikaf after fasting there is guidance and an indication toward performing i'tikaf during the fast, or at the end of the month of fasting. As it is established in the Sunnah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that "he used to perform i'tikaf in the last ten nights of Ramadan until Allah, mighty and majestic, took him, and then his wives performed i'tikaf after him." Then, the reality of i'tikaf is staying in the House of Allah seeking nearness to Him. It is among the earlier laws.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad, regarding the Prophet's (ﷺ) guidance in i'tikaf: Since the soundness and uprightness of the heart along the path of its journey to Allah depends on its gathering upon Allah and its complete turning to Allah, the heart's dispersion is not gathered except by turning to Allah. Excesses of food and drink, excesses of mixing with people, excesses of speech, and excesses of sleep increase its dispersion, scatter it into every valley, cut it off from its journey to Allah, weaken it, or hinder and halt it. The mercy of the Mighty, the Merciful, toward His servants required that He legislate for them fasting, which removes the excesses of food and drink and purges from the heart the humours of desires that hinder it from its journey to Allah. He legislated it in proportion to the benefit, such that the servant benefits from it in this world and the next, and it does not harm him or cut him off from his immediate or deferred interests. He legislated for them i'tikaf, whose purpose and spirit is the devotion of the heart to Allah, its gathering upon Him, solitude with Him, detachment from preoccupation with creation, and occupation with Him alone, glorified is He, such that His remembrance, His love, and turning to Him come to occupy the place of the heart's worries and thoughts, so that they are replaced by Him; the whole concern becomes with Him and all thoughts are with His remembrance, and reflection is on attaining His pleasure and what brings one close to Him. Thus his intimacy with Allah replaces his intimacy with creation, and this prepares him for intimacy with Him on the day of loneliness in the graves, when there is no companion for him and nothing that brings him joy but Him. This is the greatest purpose of i'tikaf. Since the purpose is only fully achieved with fasting, he legislated i'tikaf in the best days of fasting, which is the last ten days of Ramadan. It is not reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he ever performed i'tikaf while not fasting. Indeed Aisha said: "There is no i'tikaf except with fasting." Allah, glorified is He, mentioned i'tikaf only together with fasting, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed it only together with fasting. So the preponderant position on the evidence, which the majority of the salaf hold, is that fasting is a condition of i'tikaf. This is what Shaykh al-Islam Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah used to prefer. As for speech: He legislated for the community the restraint of the tongue from everything that is not beneficial for the Hereafter. As for excess sleep: He legislated for them from the night prayer what is better than wakefulness and more praiseworthy in its outcome: moderate wakefulness that benefits the heart and body and does not hinder the servant's welfare. The affairs of those engaged in spiritual discipline and the path depend on these four pillars, and the happiest of them with them is the one who followed the Prophetic, Muhammadan way in them, not deviating into the extremism of the exaggerators nor falling short like the negligent. Then he said:

"He (ﷺ) performed i'tikaf in the last ten nights of Ramadan until Allah, mighty and majestic, took him. He once abandoned it and made it up in Shawwal. He performed i'tikaf once in the first ten, then the middle ten, then the last ten, seeking the Night of Power, until it became clear to him that it was in the last ten, so he persisted in his i'tikaf until he joined his Lord, mighty and majestic." "He would order a tent to be pitched for him in the mosque, where he would be alone with his Lord, mighty and majestic. When he intended i'tikaf, he would pray the dawn prayer and then enter it. Once he ordered it and it was pitched; he ordered his wives to pitch their tents, and they were pitched. When he prayed the dawn prayer he looked and saw those tents, so he ordered his tent dismantled, and he abandoned i'tikaf in Ramadan until he performed it in the first ten of Shawwal. He used to perform i'tikaf every year for ten days; in the year he was taken, he performed it for twenty days. Jibril would review the Qur'an with him once every year; in that year he reviewed it with him twice. He did not come into contact with any of his wives while in i'tikaf, neither by kissing nor otherwise. When he performed i'tikaf, his bedding would be spread out for him and his bed placed in his place of i'tikaf. When he went out for a need, he would pass by the sick person on his way, and would not turn aside to visit him except to ask about him. He once performed i'tikaf in a Turkish dome and placed a mat over its opening." All of this is in pursuit of the purpose and spirit of i'tikaf.

﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them.﴾ That is: these are the rulings mentioned concerning fasting and i'tikaf, namely the prohibition of eating, drinking and intercourse. He likened these rulings to the boundaries that separate things, because they form a barrier between truth and falsehood. Whoever acts upon them is within the domain of truth, and whoever contravenes them falls into falsehood. He forbade approaching them, lest one come near to falsehood, let alone step over into it. So the prohibition of approaching the limits, which are the rulings, is a metaphor (kinayah) for the prohibition of drawing near to falsehood, since the former necessitates the latter. Through this, the combination of this verse with the verse "These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them" (al-Baqarah 2:229) is achieved, and the apparent contradiction is removed. His saying "so do not approach them" is more eloquent than "do not transgress them," because it is a prohibition of nearing falsehood by way of metaphor (kinayah), which is more eloquent than explicit statement, whereas that is a prohibition of falling into falsehood by way of explicit statement.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs to mankind﴾: That is, just as He made clear what He commanded you and forbade you in this matter, He makes clear to mankind what He has legislated for them through His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿so that they may be mindful (of Allah)﴾, avoiding the forbidden things, so that they know how to obey and be guided. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who sends down to His servant clear signs, that He may bring you out from darknesses into light. And indeed Allah is to you Kind and Merciful.﴾ (al-Hadid 57:9)

Al-Razi said: The purpose of His saying "Thus" etc. is to magnify the status of clarification and to magnify His mercy toward creation in mentioning such clarification.

It also contains an affirmation of the previously mentioned rulings, and an encouragement to comply with them by the fact that they were legislated for the sake of piety (taqwa).

**The Explanation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[188] ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor send it forth to the judges so that you may consume a portion of people's wealth sinfully, while you know.﴾

﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly.﴾ Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His mention, means by this: Let none of you consume the wealth of another unjustly. Thus, one who consumes his brother's wealth unjustly is treated as one who consumes his own wealth unjustly. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not find fault with yourselves﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 29], meaning: let none of you find fault with another, and let none of you kill another, because He, exalted is He, has made the believers brothers. The Arabs also do this: they refer to themselves by their siblings and to their siblings by themselves, since a man's brother is, in their view, like his own self. So the meaning of the statement is: let none of you consume each other's wealth among yourselves unjustly. Consuming it unjustly is consuming it by a way other than that which Allah has permitted to its consumers. End of quote.

﴿Baynakum﴾ is either an adverbial of place (ẓarf) attached to ﴿ta'kulu﴾ (consume), meaning: do not take it among yourselves by consumption, or it is a circumstantial (ḥāl) qualifier of ﴿al-amwal﴾ (wealth), meaning: do not consume it while it is existing and circulating among you. ﴿Bil-batil﴾ is in the accusative position governed by ﴿ta'kulu﴾, meaning: do not take it through an unjust cause, that is, a way which Allah, exalted is He, has not permitted. It may also be a ḥāl of ﴿al-amwal﴾, meaning: do not consume it while it is entangled in falsehood; or a ḥāl of the subject (fā'il) of ﴿ta'kulu﴾, meaning: do not consume it while you are unjust (mubtilun), that is, engaged in falsehood.

﴿Wa tudlu bihā ila al-ḥukkām﴾ means: you bring a dispute over them (that is, over their wealth) before the judges. It is in the jussive mood as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the prohibition. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: ﴿wa lā tudlū﴾, with the prohibitive particle ﴿lā﴾ repeated. The word ﴿al-idlā'﴾ (sending forth) is derived from ﴿idlā' al-dalw﴾ (lowering the bucket), which is sending it into the well to draw water. Then it was used metaphorically for any casting of a statement or action in order to reach something. From this comes the saying of one who presents an argument: "He sent forth his proof (adlā bi-ḥujjatihi)," as if he sends it forth so that he reaches his aim, like the one drawing water who lowers the bucket so that he reaches the water he seeks. And it is said of a man who "sends forth" to the deceased through kinship or blood-relation: if he is connected to him, so that he claims the inheritance through that relationship. So the ﴿bāʾ﴾ (bi-) is connected to ﴿tudlu﴾ as a figurative extension of meaning toward "casting." The meaning is: do not cast their matter, and the adjudication concerning it, before the judges. Or: do not cast some of it before corrupt judges by way of bribery, so that they will help you seize people's wealth. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed "the one who gives a bribe, the one who takes a bribe, and the broker (al-rā'ish)," who is the intermediary who goes between them. This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan. That is because when the guardian of the affair (walī al-amr) consumes this illicit gain (al-suḥt), meaning the bribe called bi'l-rishwa (bribery) and sometimes called a gift (hadiyya) and other names, he needs to hear falsehood from false testimony and other things which involve aiding sin and aggression. The guardian of the affair is appointed only to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong; this is the purpose of authority. If the ruler enables wrongdoing in return for wealth he takes, he has acted contrary to the purpose, like one whom you appointed to help you against your enemy, who instead helped your enemy against you, or like one who took money to fight in the cause of Allah but then fought the Muslims.

﴿Al-ḥukkām﴾ is the plural of ḥākim (judge), who is the executor of judgment between people, like ḥakam (arbitrator), with the same root.

﴿Li-ta'kulū﴾ means: by means of their corrupt judgment and by appealing to them, ﴿farīqan﴾, that is, a group and a portion, ﴿min amwāl al-nās bil-ithm﴾, by that which entails sin, such as false testimony and a false oath and their corrupt judgment, for it does not render lawful what is unjust. The ﴿bā'﴾ here indicates causation, and its object is ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾. It is also permitted that it denotes accompaniment (muṣāḥaba), so the prepositional phrase is a ḥāl of the subject of ﴿li-ta'kulū﴾, meaning: while engaged in sin. ﴿Wa antum ta'lamūn﴾ means: while you know that you are upon falsehood. Committing disobedience while knowing its ugliness is more reprehensible, and its perpetrator is more deserving of rebuke, so the qualification serves to emphasize the ugliness of their state.

Al-Raghib said: That is, even if your injustice is hidden from people, it is not hidden from you. This is an alert that what matters is the reality of the matter itself, and what you know of it, not what appears outwardly.

Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir: Ali ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas: this verse concerns a man who owes money but has no evidence against him, so he denies the debt and brings the dispute before the judges, while he knows that the right is upon him and that he is sinful, consuming what is unlawful. The same was narrated from Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, that they said: Do not argue while you know that you are an oppressor. It is recorded in the two Sahihs from Umm Salama that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I am only a human being, and disputants come to me, so perhaps one of you is more eloquent in presenting his argument than another, and I judge for him. So whomever I judge for by the right of a Muslim, it is only a piece of Fire. Let him take it or leave it." This noble verse and this hadith indicate that the ruling of a judge does not change the reality of the matter. Thus what is unlawful in reality does not become lawful, and what is lawful is not made unlawful. Rather, it is binding only outwardly. If it agrees with the reality, that is well; otherwise, the judge has his reward, and the one who deceives bears its burden. For this reason, He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿while you know﴾, meaning: you know the falsity of what you claim and hope for in your speech. Qatada said: Know, O son of Adam, that the judgment of a judge does not make lawful what is unlawful, nor does it establish a falsehood as right for you. The judge only rules according to what he sees and what the witnesses testify to, and the judge is human; he errs and is correct. Know that whoever is granted a judgment in falsehood, his dispute does not end until Allah gathers them both on the Day of Resurrection, and then He will judge against the wrongdoer in favour of the one who is right, with what is better than what was decided in this world in favour of the wrongdoer against the one who is right.

(p-469) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[189] ﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: "They are signs of time for people and for the Hajj. Righteousness does not lie in your entering houses from their backs; rather, righteousness is in one who fears God. So enter houses through their doors, and fear God that you may succeed."﴾

﴿They ask you about the new moons. Say: "They are signs of time for people and for the Hajj."﴾ Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah: "It reached us that they said, 'O Messenger of God! Why were the new moons created?' Then this was revealed." Abu Nu'aym and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "It was revealed concerning Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanm. They said: 'O Messenger of God! What is the matter with the crescent that it appears—or rises—thin like a thread, then increases until it grows large and becomes round, then keeps diminishing and becoming thin until it returns as it was, not remaining in one state?' Then this was revealed."

The meaning of their being ﴿signs of time for people﴾ is that they are markers for them in the determination of their religious matters: for their fasting, their breaking of the fast, the times of their Hajj, their deadlines, the periods of menstruation, the waiting periods of their women, and the conditions tied to a term. All of this is such that the determination of its times is not easy except when there is variation in the shape of the moon, by increase and decrease. For this reason He made it differ from the sun, which remains always in one state.

Some exegetes said: the fruit of the verse is that the legal rulings—such as zakah, the waiting periods of women, and pregnancy—are tied to the lunar months and not to the Persian months. As for contracts and actions connected with the deeds of the children of Adam, the custom of their reckoning is followed in them, whether by the lunar months or by the Persian months. This is one ruling, and that is another ruling.

God, the Exalted, mentioned this meaning in verses such as His words: ﴿And He determined for it stations so that you might know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5], and His words: ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight, that you might seek bounty from your Lord and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [al-Isra: 12]. (p-470) That is: without needing to consult the astrologer or the calculation of the reckoner; as a mercy and bounty from Him, the Exalted.

Singling out the Hajj for mention here is to draw attention to its importance.

Al-Qaffal said: The point of singling it out is to clarify that the Hajj is restricted to the months which God, the Exalted, has designated for its performance, and that it is not permissible to shift the Hajj from those months to other months, as the Arabs used to do through the intercalation (al-nasi'). And God knows best.

The majority read the ha' of al-Hajj with a fatha, while al-Hasan read it with a kasra throughout the Qur'an. Sibawayh said: both are verbal nouns, like al-radd and al-dhikr. It was said: with the fatha it is the verbal noun (al-masdar), and with the kasra it is the name (al-ism). Al-Ahilla is the plural of hilal, and its plural form varies according to its period. The hilal is the first appearance of the moon until three or seven nights, after which it is called a moon (qamar), and the night of the full moon (badr) is the fourteenth night.

Abu al-'Abbas said: the crescent was named hilal because people raise their voices in announcing it (ihlal). And it was named badr because it hastens to rise before the sun, as if it makes the sun its setting. It is also said it was named badr for its completeness and fullness, since everything that is complete is called badr.

Note:

The answer according to the second narration about the occasion of revelation of the verse is from the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), which is addressing the questioner with other than what he seeks—by placing his question in the position of another question, to alert the questioner that this other matter is more fitting for his situation or more important for him. When they asked about the efficient cause of the luminous forms in the crescent, they were answered with the final cause that you see, to alert them that asking about the purpose and benefit is more fitting for their condition, because the knowledge of the efficient causes of those formations rests on matters of astronomy (ilm al-hay'ah) in which the Shari'ah has no concern. Had they been answered that the variation of the crescent's forms is according to the measure of its alignment with the sun—so that when an edge of it faces the sun, that edge is illuminated; then the alignment and illumination increase until, when it is fully opposite, it becomes full; then the alignment and illumination decrease until, when conjunction occurs, it becomes completely dark—this answer would have been occupation with the science of astronomy, which does not benefit one in religion and on which the welfare of their livelihood and their afterlife does not depend. The Prophet ﷺ was sent only to explain what benefits them. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever acquires knowledge from the stars has acquired a branch of magic, the more he acquires, the more it increases." Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "Whoever seeks the knowledge of the stars has become a soothsayer." It is among the knowledge of which the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "A knowledge that does not benefit, and an ignorance that does not harm." The point is that the answer, according to the second narration, is from the wise method, signaling that the better course is to ask about its wisdom.

Al-Sakkaki said in "al-Miftah": For this type—I mean, delivering speech not according to the apparent requirement—there are varied methods, for there is no apparent requirement of speech except that this type has an entry into it through some aspect of eloquence. It guides to it sometimes explicitly and sometimes by implication. Each of these methods has a root in eloquence that imbibes from the charms of its enchantment, and none is like the wise method in it, which is addressing the addressee with other than what he awaits, as he said:

She came complaining to me about her hosting of guests, and she had seen the guests heading toward my house.
So I said, as if I had not heard her words: "They are guests—hurry and be generous with them in their hospitality."

Or the questioner with other than what he seeks, as God the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾ and the verse continues. They said in the question: "What is the matter with the crescent that it appears thin...!" etc.? So they were answered with what you see. And as He said: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever you spend of good is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveler﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215]. They asked about specifying what they spend, so they were answered by specifying the recipients. The questioner's question is placed in the position of a question other than his own, to alert him in the most subtle way that he has gone beyond the subject of a question that is more fitting for his situation to ask about, or more important for him if he reflects. This wise method may coincide with the context and stir the listener's energy in a way that removes from him the judgment of the sober and displays him in the guise of one bewitched. Did it not soften the stubbornness of al-Hajjaj toward that Kharijite, and dissolve his rancor, until he preferred to do good rather than evil—by bewitching him with this method? When al-Hajjaj threatened him with chains, saying, "I will surely make you carry the dark horse (al-adham)!" he said feigning obtuseness: "A man like the Amir is carried upon the dark horse and the grey one!" Thus he displayed his threat in the guise of a promise, arriving at showing him in the most subtle way that a man like him—in the position of obeyed command—deserves to shackle, not to be shackled, and to promise, not to threaten.

﴿And righteousness does not lie in your entering houses from their backs; rather, righteousness is in one who fears God. So enter houses through their doors, and fear God that you may succeed.﴾

Al-Raghib said in his "Tafsir": The door (al-bab) is well known, and from it is borrowed the entrance to affairs by which one reaches them. It is said of knowledge: "the door of such-and-such." He, peace be upon him, was asked about the waxing and waning of the moon, so God revealed this verse as an alert to its most apparent benefit for the senses and its clearest benefit for them. Then He said: ﴿And righteousness does not lie in your entering houses from their backs﴾ (p-473) meaning: by seeking the matter from other than its proper way. That is because it is said: "So-and-so came to the house from its door" when he sought the thing from its proper way. And the poet said:

I came to manliness from its door.

And "he came to the house from its back" means he sought the matter from other than its proper way. This was made an example of their asking the Prophet ﷺ about what is not from the knowledge specific to prophethood. Such a practice is a deviation from the method, because knowledge is of two kinds:

Worldly: which concerns matters of livelihood, such as knowing crafts, knowing the movements of the stars, knowing minerals, plants, and the natures of animals. A path to knowing it has been made available to us apart from the tongue of His Prophet, peace be upon him.

Legislative: which is righteousness, and there is no way to take it except from its source, which is the rulings of piety...

When they came asking the Prophet ﷺ about what they could know by other than its proper way, he answered them, then clarified to them that righteousness is not abandoning the method in asking the Prophet about what is not specific to the knowledge of his prophethood. Rather, righteousness is pure piety. That comes through knowledge and action specific to the religion.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: The intended meaning of this verse is what they used to do of intercalation (al-nasi'). For they used to move the Hajj away from its time which God had designated for it, thereby making lawful what is unlawful and unlawful what is lawful. So the mention of entering houses from their backs is an example of violating what is obligatory concerning the Hajj and its months.

As for what al-Bukhari and others narrated from Abu Ishaq, who said: I heard al-Bara', may God be pleased with him, say: "This verse was revealed concerning us. The Ansar, when they performed Hajj and came back, did not enter from the front of their house doors, but from their backs. Then a man from the Ansar came and entered from the front of his door, and it seems he was reproached for that, so this verse was revealed: ﴿And righteousness does not lie...﴾ etc." The meaning of its revelation concerning that is that it applies to it as he saw it, not that this was the occasion of its revelation, as we have explained repeatedly the meaning of their saying: "This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such."

(p-474) Al-Raghib alluded to this—after relating this narration and what Abu Muslim said—by saying: "All of that does not preclude that the verse encompasses it. But the more fitting is that the verse be interpreted by what was mentioned before: that the meaning of ﴿And enter houses through their doors﴾ is: in every action, seek to come to a thing from its proper way, as an alert that what is sought from other than its proper way is difficult to attain. Then he said: ﴿and fear God﴾, urging us to make the fear of God our emblem in everything we seek. And he made clear that this is a means to attaining success."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 190:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[190] ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like the transgressors.﴾

﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. Fighting in the way of Allah is jihad (striving, here meaning armed struggle in the cause of God) for the elevation of the word of Allah and the strengthening of the religion. In His words ﴿those who fight you﴾ there is an incitement and encouragement against the enemies whose aim is fighting Islam and its people. That is: just as they fight you, so fight them yourselves. As He said: ﴿And fight against the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36]. ﴿But do not transgress﴾, that is: by initiating the fighting, or by fighting those whom you have been forbidden to fight, such as women, the elderly, children, the monks of the monasteries, and those between you and whom there is a covenant; or by mutilation, or by surprise attack without a call (to Islam). ﴿Indeed, Allah does not like the transgressors﴾, that is: those who exceed His ruling in this and in other matters.

(p-475) The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[191] ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them, and expel them from where they expelled you; and fitnah is worse than killing. And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein. But if they fight you, then kill them. Such is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾

﴿And kill them﴾, i.e., those who fight you. ﴿Wherever you overtake them﴾, i.e., wherever you find them. ﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾, i.e., from Makkah, for the Quraysh had expelled the Muslims from it, and the Muslims expelled the polytheists on the Day of the Conquest (al-Fath). ﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾, i.e., the trial and affliction that befalls a person, by which he is tormented, is more severe for him than killing. That is: their fitnah against you in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) concerning your religion, through torture, expulsion from the homeland, and confiscation of wealth, is more abhorrent than killing in it. For there is no affliction upon a person greater than harming him over his belief, which has taken firm root in his intellect and soul, and which he regards as his happiness in the end of his affair. So the clause is a rebuttal of what might arise from considering their killing in a place like the Sacred Precinct as grave, and an informing that retribution against them by killing is due instead of their crime of fitnah against the believers, because fitnah is worse than killing. ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you therein﴾, because its sanctity is intrinsic, and the sanctity of the rest of the Haram derives from it.
