This is in the manner of an exception to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾. ﴿But if they fight you﴾, i.e., therein, then you do not need to flee from the Haram: ﴿then kill them﴾ therein, since they have no sanctity, having violated the sanctity of al-Masjid al-Haram. ﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾, who leave them no sanctity, just as they did not respect the sanctity of God in His signs.

Caution (Tanbih):

The verse indicates the command to fight the polytheists within the Haram when they begin fighting there, to repel their aggression (sawtahum), (p-476) just as the Prophet (ﷺ) took the pledge from his companions at al-Hudaybiyah under the tree to fight, when the clans of the Quraysh and those allied with them from the tribes of Thaqif and the al-Ahabish gathered against him on that occasion. Then God restrained the fighting between them, saying: ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the heart of Makkah, after He had given you victory over them﴾ [al-Fath: 24]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Khalid and those with him on the Day of the Conquest: "If any of the Quraysh confront you, then mow them down until you meet me at al-Safa." ... So no one confronted them except that they put him to sleep (i.e., killed him), and about twelve men from the polytheists were struck, as is recorded in the Sirah.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[192] ﴿But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿But if they cease﴾, i.e., from fighting: ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, i.e., then refrain from them and do not molest them, adorning yourselves with the two attributes of the Truth, exalted is He, mentioned here, namely forgiveness and mercy. This is the apparent sense of the context.

Some of them said: ﴿But if they cease﴾, i.e., from polytheism and fighting: ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ of what has passed of their transgression: ﴿Merciful﴾ in accepting their repentance and their faith.

(p-477) On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[193] ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And fight them﴾ means: these people whom we have attributed to you as fighting you, expelling you, and tempting you away from your religion. ﴿Until there is no fitnah﴾ — that is, until it is not found in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) — meaning a trial (fitnah) by which they tempt people away from their religion and prevent them from openly practising it and calling to it. ﴿And religion is for Allah﴾ — purely — meaning that nothing is worshipped besides Him in the Sacred Precinct, nothing other than Him is feared there, so that no one is tempted away from his religion nor harmed on account of it.

In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), on the authority of Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer, and give the zakat. When they do that, they have protected their blood and their property from me, except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with Allah."

﴿But if they cease﴾ from fighting you in the Sacred Precinct: ﴿then there is no aggression﴾ — that is, there is no way for you to kill them: ﴿except against the wrongdoers﴾ — those who initiate the killing.

Al-Bukhari related in his Sahih, on the authority of Nafi', from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: Two men came to him during the fitnah of Ibn al-Zubayr and said: "People have been ruined, and you are the son of Umar and a companion of the Prophet ﷺ. What prevents you from going out?" He said: "What prevents me is that Allah has forbidden the blood of my brother..!" They said: "Did not Allah say: (p-478) ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾?" He said: "We fought until there was no fitnah and religion was for Allah, whereas you want to fight until there is fitnah and religion is for other than Allah."

Then al-Bukhari related another narration, in which there is: Ibn Umar said: "We did so during the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a man would be tempted in his religion; either they would kill him or torture him, until Islam became widespread and there was no fitnah."

The discussion of the words of His Exalted Saying:

[194] ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and sacred things are subject to retribution. So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you. And fear God, and know that God is with those who are mindful of Him.﴾

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ is a notice that observing the sanctity of the sacred month is obligatory for whoever observes its sanctity, and that whoever violates it shall be requited for it; so their violation of its sanctity is met with their violation of its sanctity. Just as they fight at the Sacred Mosque if they fight there, so they fight in the sacred month if they fight in it.

Imam Ahmad narrated with a sound chain, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would not campaign in the sacred month unless he was attacked, or they attacked him. If that occurred, he would remain until it had passed." For this reason, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out in Dhu al-Qa'dah in the sixth year as a pilgrim (mu'tamir) and camped at al-Hudaybiyah, and it reached him that Uthman had been killed, (Uthman had been sent by him with a message to the polytheists), he pledged his companions, who were one thousand four hundred, under the tree, to fight the polytheists. When it reached him that Uthman had not been killed, he refrained from that and inclined toward peace and reconciliation, and what happened happened. Likewise, when he finished fighting Hawazin on the day of Hunayn, and their remnant took refuge in al-Ta'if, he turned toward it and besieged it, and Dhu al-Qa'dah began while he was besieging it with the catapult (manjaniq). He continued against it for a full forty days, as is established in the two Sahihs from Anas. When the killing among his companions increased, he withdrew from it, (p-479) and it was not conquered. Then he returned to Mecca, and performed the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah) from al-Ji'ranah, where he divided the spoils of Hunayn; and this ʿumrah of his was also in Dhu al-Qa'dah, in the eighth year.

﴿And sacred things are subject to retribution﴾, meaning: they are equal, so no sacred month is given preference over another, such that the violation of its sanctity is forbidden because they violated the sanctity of what is less than it. Moreover, we do not violate the sanctity of the sacred month, the Sacred Mosque, and the Sacred Precinct; rather, we violate the sanctity of whoever violates the sanctity of any of them. So said al-Mahayimi.

Al-Hurumat is the plural of hurmah, which is that which is protected, observed, and not violated. Qisas is equality. The statement involves an omitted noun: that is, "possessors of retribution," or the verbal noun is used in the sense of the passive participle, that is, "mutual retaliation," or it is taken as an intensified usage. ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same way as he transgressed against you﴾ is a command to justice, even toward the polytheists, as He said: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], and He said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40]. ﴿And fear God﴾ in violating the sanctity of the month, the Mosque, and the Precinct without their having violated it first, and in exceeding the limit of retaliation. ﴿And know that God is with those who are mindful of Him﴾, meaning: with help, victory, protection, and support.

**On the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:**

[195] ﴿And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction, and do good. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾ is a command to spend in all the forms of acts of nearness to Allah and acts of obedience. Among the most important of these is spending wealth on fighting the enemies, and giving it for that by which the Muslims become strong against their enemy.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ mean: do not do what leads to ruin. That is, do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction, by exposing yourselves to what has a dire outcome, out of ignorance of it.

Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: the verse has two interpretations, from two viewpoints:

The first: it is a prohibition against extravagance in spending and against recklessness in advancing.

The second: it is a prohibition against stinginess with wealth, and against sitting back from jihad. Both meanings are intended by it. A person is forbidden from extravagance in spending and recklessness in advancing, just as he is forbidden from stinginess and from holding back from jihad. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy﴾ [al-Furqan: 67], to the end of the verse, and He said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra: 29], to the end of the verse.

Since the matter of spending applied especially to the Ansar, who were the people of wealth, because the Muhajirun had been stripped of theirs, the hadith of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari is well known in connection with this verse. It was related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, and others... The wording of al-Tirmidhi is: From Aslam Abu Imran, who said: "We were at the city of the Romans, and they brought out to us a great line of Romans, and from the Muslims there came out to them the like of them or more. Over the people of Egypt was Uqba ibn Amir, and over the whole army was Fadala ibn Ubayd. A man from the Muslims charged at the Roman line until he penetrated into them. The people cried out and said: 'Glory be to Allah! He throws himself with his own hands into destruction!' Then Abu Ayyub al-Ansari stood up and said: 'O people, you are interpreting this verse in this way, but this verse was only revealed about us, the company of the Ansar, when Allah had strengthened Islam and its helpers had become many. Some of us said to others in secret, without the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knowing: "Our wealth has been lost, and Allah has strengthened Islam and its helpers have become many. So if we remained with our wealth and set right what had been lost of it..." Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) a reply to what we had said: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. So the destruction was remaining with our wealth and tending it, and abandoning the raid.' Abu Ayyub did not cease to be occupied in the way of Allah until he was buried in the land of the Romans." This is a hadith that is hasan, gharib, sahih.

I say: Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him, denied that interpretation either because he did not hold that the wording is general but only that the occasion is specific, or to refute the claim that it was revealed about fighting, that is, about one man charging against a body of the enemy as they had interpreted it. This is the apparent meaning. Otherwise the wording requires generality, and its coming in connection with an occasion is not a qarina (contextual indicator) restricting it to that. There is no doubt that worship is by the wording that came down, and that wording is general.

'Amr ibn al-'As also cited the generality of the verse, as related by Ibn Abi Hatim with his chain: that 'Abd al-Rahman al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth reported that they besieged Damascus. A man from the Azd Shanu'a set out, and he hastened alone to the enemy to meet them. The Muslims found fault with him for that and carried his case to 'Amr ibn al-'As. 'Amr sent for him and sent him back, and 'Amr said: "Allah said: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾."

Various weak reports have been transmitted about the occasion of its revelation, which Ibn Kathir narrated, and they are, Allah knows best, of the kind that confirms the generality of the verse as they transmitted it.

Note (tanbih):

al-Hakim said: The verse indicates the permissibility of retreat in jihad when there is fear for the self, and it indicates the permissibility of abandoning enjoining good when one fears, because all of that is casting oneself into destruction. It also indicates the permissibility of making a truce with the unbelievers and the rebels when the imam fears for himself or for the Muslims, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, and as Amir al-Mu'minin 'Ali, peace be upon him, did at Siffin, and as al-Hasan, peace be upon him, did in making peace with Mu'awiya. It also indicates the permissibility of the imam making a settlement with some of the people's property when he fears destruction. This is supported by the fact that he (ﷺ) wished to make a settlement on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) by giving a third of the produce of Madina, until he consulted Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Sa'd ibn 'Ubada, and they advised against that. He does not resolve except upon what is permissible.

Subtle point (latifa):

Linguistically, al-ilqa' is throwing a thing down. It is followed by "ila" because it includes the meaning of reaching an endpoint, and the "ba'" is added to the object to emphasize the sense of the prohibition. What is meant by "the hands" is the selves, so mention of a part is used to mean the whole, for greater emphasis on its being connected with the hand, based on the fact that most actions of the self appear through it.

Al-tahluka, al-halak and al-halk are one and the same. It is a verbal noun. That is: do not bring your selves into ruin.

Al-tahluka is with a dammah on the lam. Al-Kharazanji said: I know of no verbal noun in the speech of the Arabs on the pattern taf'ula with a damma on the 'ayn except this one.

Al-Yazidi said: It is one of the rare verbal nouns, which does not follow analogy.

al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible to say that its origin is al-tahlukah, like al-tajribah and al-tabsirah and the like, as a verbal noun of halaka, and the kasra was changed to a damma, as al-jiwar came in the form al-juwar. This is what they have mentioned.

al-Fakhr al-Razi, and to God belongs his excellence, said after quoting something similar to what preceded: I am greatly astonished at the exertions of these grammarians in such places, for if they found an unknown line of poetry supporting what they intended, they would rejoice in it and take it as a strong proof. The occurrence of this word in the speech of Allah, the Exalted, which both the agreeing and the disagreeing acknowledge for its eloquence, is more deserving of indicating the soundness and correctness of this word.

﴿And do good﴾ means: strive to perform the act of good, that is, bring about everything that is good, and foremost among it is spending. His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾: al-Raghib said: By making the love of Allah for the doers of good manifest, He draws attention to the nobility of their rank and the excellence of their deeds.

(p-483) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[196] ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah. But if you are prevented, then [send] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice. And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of his head [needing to shave] - then an expiation of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice. And when you are secure, then whoever enjoys [the benefit of] ʿUmrah [combined] with Hajj [must offer] what is easy of the sacrificial animal. And whoever cannot find [one] - then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Haram. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾: that is, perform them complete with their prescribed rites, for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He.

Al-Raghib said: It has been said that "complete" (atimmu) [al-Baqarah: 187] is addressed to whoever has set out as a pilgrim (ḥājj) or a performer of ʿUmrah, so he is commanded not to turn away from it until he completes both. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and he used it as evidence for the obligation to complete every act of worship that a person has entered into voluntarily, and that if he invalidates it, its make-up (qaḍāʾ) becomes obligatory. It has also been said that it is addressed to them and to whoever has not yet entered into the act of worship. The mention of the word "completion" is an indication of fulfilling its right and perfecting its conditions. On this basis is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187]. This is the view of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, and he used it as evidence for the obligation of ʿUmrah. He said "for Allah" regarding Hajj and ʿUmrah but did not say it regarding prayer and zakat, because they used to draw near to their idols through some acts of Hajj and ʿUmrah; so He specified these two by mentioning "for Allah," exhorting sincerity in them and avoiding that prohibited belief.

﴿But if you are prevented﴾: that is, an enemy has held you back from completing the Hajj or ʿUmrah and you wish to exit the state of ihram (taḥallul). ﴿Then [send] what is easy of the sacrificial animal﴾: that is, upon you [is], or the obligatory [is], or sacrifice what is easy. It is said: "yasura al-amr" and "istaysara" [the matter became easy], just as one says "saʿuba" and "istaṣʿaba" [it became difficult]. The word hady (sacrificial animal), with the yāʾ lightened or doubled, is the plural of hadyah and hadiyyah, and it is: what is sent as a gift to Makkah of livestock to be slaughtered as a means of drawing near to Allah. Tha'lab said: hady with the lightened form is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the doubled form on the pattern fa'il is the dialect of Banu Tamim and the lower Qays. Both readings have been recited in this verse. As evidence for the doubled hadiyy in their speech is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"I swore by the Lord of Makkah and the place of prayer, and by the necks of the sacrificial animals adorned with garlands."

As evidence for hadiyyah similarly is the verse of Saʿidah ibn Juʾayyah:

"Indeed I, and their hands, and every hadiyyah / that is gushing from what its chests pour forth, flowing."

The best sacrificial animal is a camel (badanah), and the least is a sheep. The meaning: when the muhrim is prevented and wishes to exit the state of ihram, he exits it by slaughtering a sacrificial animal that is easy for him: of camels, cows, or sheep.

Note:
Al-Raghib said: The apparent meaning of His words ﴿you are prevented﴾ is that there is no difference in it between being prevented in Makkah or elsewhere, and after ʿArafah or before it. Likewise, apparently there is no difference between an enemy of Muslims preventing him or someone else. Its apparent meaning also implies that there is no distinction between being prevented by an enemy and being prevented by illness, were it not that the verse was revealed concerning the cause of the enemy, so it may not be extended except by evidence. Also, His saying ﴿and when you are secure﴾ indicates that the intended meaning of "prevention" is prevention by an enemy.

It may be said: the consideration in such cases is their generality, as some of the early scholars held. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Masʿud, Ibn al-Zubayr, ʿAlqamah, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, al-Nakhaʿi, ʿAta, and Muqatil that they said: prevention (iḥṣār) is by an enemy, or illness, or a broken limb. al-Thawri said: prevention is from anything that harms him.

It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from ʿAʾishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon Dubaʿah bint al-Zubayr ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib and she said: "O Messenger of Allah! I wish to perform Hajj, and I am ill." He said: "Perform Hajj and stipulate that your place of release is where you are held back." Muslim related the same from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Among the implications of the verse is what al-Raghib said: its apparent meaning implies that the one prevented has no obligation of make-up (qaḍāʾ), because He said ﴿then [send] what is easy of the sacrificial animal﴾ and limited it to that.

﴿And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of sacrifice﴾: that is, the place where its slaughter becomes permissible, which is its location where it is kept. That is, the place of prevention. Its reaching that place is a metaphor for slaughtering it there, and using "reaching a thing its place" to mean its arrival at what is intended from it is common. When the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions performed ʿUmrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and the disbelievers of Quraysh held them back from entering the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), they shaved and slaughtered their sacrificial animals there, and did not send them to the Haram.

The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim, in Zad al-Maʿad, cited some of the jurisprudential principles from the story of al-Hudaybiyah in a section where he said: Among them: the one prevented slaughters his sacrifice where he was prevented, whether in the non-sacred area (al-Hill) or the Haram, and he is not obliged to arrange with someone to slaughter it in the Haram if he does not reach it; and he does not exit the state of ihram until he reaches its place, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are those who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram, and the sacrificial animals [were] detained from reaching their place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. Among them: the place where the Prophet ﷺ slaughtered the sacrifice was in the non-sacred area (al-Hill), not in the Haram, because the entire Haram is a place of sacrifice.

The Imam Malik said in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ: Whoever is held back by an enemy and is prevented from reaching the House, then he exits the state of ihram from everything and slaughters his sacrifice and shaves his head where he was held back, and there is no make-up (qaḍāʾ) for him.

He said: This is our ruling concerning one who is prevented by an enemy, just as the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions were prevented.

﴿And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of his head - then an expiation of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice﴾: that is, whoever among you, O company of muhrimun, is ill with an illness by which hair harms him and necessitates shaving, or has an ailment of his head - such as a wound or lice - then if he shaves, upon him is an expiation of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice. This verse was revealed concerning Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I was brought to the Prophet ﷺ while lice were falling on my face. He said: 'I did not think the hardship had reached you to this extent! Do you not find a sheep?' I said: No. He said: 'Fast three days, or feed six poor persons, half a ṣāʿ of food for each poor person, and shave your head.' So it was revealed concerning me specifically, and it applies to you generally." Related by the two Shaykhs and others, the wording being that of al-Bukhari. Imam Ahmad related from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at al-Hudaybiyah while we were in ihram, and the polytheists had held us back, and I had a full head of hair, and the vermin began to fall upon my face. The Prophet ﷺ passed by me and said: 'Do the vermin of your head harm you?' I said: Yes. So he ordered me to shave. He said: And this verse was revealed." Ibn ʿAbbas said: when it is "aw" [or], whichever you take suffices for you. The general view of the scholars is that one is given the choice in this situation: if he wishes he fasts, and if he wishes he gives charity of a faraq - which is three ṣāʿ, half a ṣāʿ for each poor person, and it is two mudd - and if he wishes he slaughters a sheep and gives it to the poor; whichever of these he does suffices him. When the wording of the Qur'an was about explaining the concession, it came with the easiest first, then the easier. When the Prophet ﷺ commanded Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah with that, he first directed him to the better option, saying: "Do you not find a sheep?" So each is good in its place, and to Allah belongs praise and grace. Noted by Ibn Kathir.

Note:
Several rulings are derived from the verse:
First: permissibility for the muhrim to shave and to wear sewn garments out of necessity, and the obligation of expiation upon him; this is for explaining the occasion of revelation.
Second: the prohibition of shaving and wearing sewn garments without an excuse, derived from the implication, since it is stated explicitly; and this is a consensus.
Third: that the obligatory expiation is from one of three categories: fasting, or charity, or sacrifice, and its details have come in the hadith of Kaʿb.
Fourth: that the expiation is obligatory by way of choice, as we have explained.

Al-Raghib said: The apparent meaning of the verse implies that there is no difference between a little hair and much hair, unlike what Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said, since he only held the obligation to apply when a third is shaved; others held the obligation applies only when a quarter is shaved.

A subtle point:
The root of nusuk is worship, and the slaughter of livestock was called nusuk because it is among the noblest acts of worship by which one draws near to Allah, Exalted is He.

Abu al-Baqa said: nusuk, originally, is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, since it derives from nasaka yansuku, and what is meant here is the thing slaughtered; it may also be a noun rather than a verbal noun, and the sin may be vocalized with sukun. End.

﴿And when you are secure﴾: that is, you were secure from the beginning, or after the prevention you have become secure: ﴿then whoever enjoys [the benefit of] ʿUmrah﴾: that is, by entering ihram for it in the months of Hajj, in order to gain the state of non-ihram (ḥill) upon arriving at the House and to remain in a state of non-ihram during that journey: ﴿[combined] with Hajj﴾: that is, until the time of entering ihram for Hajj: ﴿then [he must offer]﴾ (ma) — that is, upon him is what: ﴿is easy﴾, that is, what is facilitated: ﴿of the sacrificial animal﴾ of livestock. This sacrifice is for what he enjoyed between the two rites, of non-ihram.

In al-Nihayah, the form of tamattuʿ is that one enters ihram for ʿUmrah in the months of Hajj; when he enters ihram for ʿUmrah after having entered ihram in Shawwal, he has become a tamattuʿ performer of ʿUmrah combined with Hajj, and it is named after this, because when he comes to Makkah, circumambulates the House, and runs between al-Safa and al-Marwah, he exits his ʿUmrah and shaves his head, and slaughters his obligatory sacrifice for his tamattuʿ, and everything that had been forbidden to him in his ihram becomes lawful to him, such as women and perfume. Then after that he begins a new ihram for Hajj at the time he sets out for Mina, or before that, without being obliged to return to the miqat from which he began his ʿUmrah. That is his tamattuʿ combined with Hajj: that is, his benefiting and enjoying what he benefited from, of shaving, perfume, cleaning, ending his state of disheveledness, and intimacy with his wife if she is with him.

The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Maʿad: It was part of the Prophet's ﷺ practice to slaughter the sacrifice of ʿUmrah at al-Marwah, and the sacrifice of qiran at Mina. Ibn ʿUmar used to do likewise. The Prophet ﷺ never slaughtered except after exiting the state of ihram, and he did not slaughter before the day of sacrifice, nor did any of the Companions at all.

﴿And whoever cannot find﴾ the sacrifice: ﴿then fasting three days during Hajj﴾: that is, after entering ihram and before finishing its rites; the preferred time is the sixth, seventh, and eighth of Dhu al-Hijjah.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked: how does He say "during Hajj" when, if he enters ihram on the day of ʿArafah, it is not possible for him to fast three days during Hajj, because fasting is forbidden on the day of sacrifice and the days of tashriq? It is answered: the obligation upon the tamattuʿ is to enter ihram for Hajj in a manner that makes it possible for him to perform fasting for three days; and that is by advancing the ihram before the day of ʿArafah. Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAʾishah said: he fasts the days of tashriq, and they interpreted the prohibition as applying to fasting the days of Mina for other than the tamattuʿ.

﴿And seven when you return﴾: that is, to your families, or when you have set out to return after finishing the rites of Hajj.

Al-Raghib said: The unrestricted wording allows both meanings, so it is valid to take it as either.

(p-489) However, what favors the first view is what is related in the two Ṣaḥīḥs from the lengthy hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, in which: "Whoever does not find a sacrifice, let him fast three days during Hajj and seven when he returns to his family."

﴿Those are ten complete﴾: that is a computation, meaning a summary after detail. Its benefit is that it is not supposed that the particle "wa" [and] means "aw" [or], and that the speech is on the basis of choice; rather the whole is the substitute for the sacrifice! And that the number be known in total as it was known in detail, so that it is grasped from two directions and knowledge is confirmed. As the proverb goes: "Two kinds of knowledge are better than one." Most Arabs do not know arithmetic, so the fitting address is that which the common and the elite both understand, which is by repeating the speech and increasing understanding...

A third benefit: that by "seven" is meant the number, not the abundance, since it is used for both...

Fourth benefit: al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) pointed to it, and it is this: His saying, ﴿That is ten complete﴾, is a digression in the speech and an alert to the excellence of the science of number (ʿilm al-ʿadad). For this reason it was said: number is the first of the sciences and the most noble of them. As for its being first, it is because everything else is derived from it and by it things are distinguished and differentiated. As for its being most noble, it is because there is no disagreement about it and no change in it; rather it remains constant in one way. So He mentioned ten and described it as complete, since it is a number in which the special properties of numbers are perfected. The one is the origin of number; the two is the first number; the three is the first odd number; the four is the first even number that is bounded, meaning it is formed by multiplying a number by itself; the five is the first circular number; the six is the first perfect number, meaning that when all its parts are taken it neither exceeds nor falls short of it; the seven is the first prime number, meaning no number precedes it that is smaller than it; the eight is the first number of even-times-even; the nine is the first triangular number; and the ten is the first number at which counting ends, because what comes after it is a repetition of what precedes it. Thus ten is the complete number...

(p-490) ﴿Complete﴾ is a confirmatory attribute of (ten), conveying emphasis on preserving the number. In it there is an added exhortation to fast them, not to be negligent about them, and not to diminish their count, as if it were said: "These are ten complete; so observe their completeness and do not diminish them." ﴿That﴾, i.e., the obligation of the sacrifice of tamattuʿ or its substitute for one who does not find it: ﴿for him whose household are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, i.e., rather, his household are at the distance of absence from it. As for one whose household are present at it, by residing in Makkah, he is in the status of nearness to God, so God, exalted is He, compensates him by His grace.

Furthermore, some of the qualified scholars (mujtahidun) said: that refers to tamattuʿ understood from His saying: ﴿So whoever enjoys tamattuʿ﴾, and not to the offering and the fasting. Therefore there is no tamattuʿ or qiran for the people of the Sacred Mosque according to him.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that Ibn ʿAbbas used to say: "O people of Makkah! There is no tamattuʿ for you. It was made lawful for the people of the distant regions and forbidden to you. Indeed, one of you crosses a valley, or he said: a valley is placed between him and the Haram, then he assumes ihram for ʿumrah..!"

ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Tawus, who said: Tamattuʿ is for people, not for the people of Makkah. Then he said: "And it has reached me from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of Tawus's saying, and God knows best."

Al-Ahl: a man's residence, including spouse and permanent dwelling. Al-Hudur: constant presence at a dwelling.

﴿And fear God﴾, regarding violation of the state of ihram, ﴿and know that God is severe in retribution﴾ toward whoever violates his ihram more severely than the severity of kings toward one who misbehaves in their presence. The manifestation of the noble Name in the place of the pronoun is for cultivating awe and bringing in dread.

Notes:

First: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So whoever enjoys tamattuʿ with the ʿumrah...﴾ the verse, there is evidence for the legislated character of tamattuʿ, as came in the two Sahihs from ʿImran ibn Husayn, who said: "The verse of tamattuʿ was revealed in the Book of God, and we performed it with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and no Qur'an came down prohibiting it, and he did not forbid it until he died." A man said by his own opinion whatever he wished.

Malik narrated in al-Muwatta', from ʿAbd Allah, from ʿUmar, that he said: "By God! For me to perform ʿumrah before Hajj and offer a sacrifice is more beloved to me than to perform ʿumrah after Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah..!"

In the two Sahihs: "Had I known from my affair what I came to know later, I would not have brought the sacrificial animal, and I would have made it an ʿumrah." That is, as his companions (ﷺ) did by his command.

Second: Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Maʿad: It is established that tamattuʿ is better than ifrad for many reasons:
Among them: he (ﷺ) commanded them to convert Hajj into ʿumrah, and it is inconceivable that he would transfer them from the superior to the inferior that is below it.
Among them: he expressed regret at not having done it, saying: "Had I known from my affair what I came to know later, I would not have brought the sacrificial animal, and I would have made it tamattuʿ."
Among them: he commanded it for everyone who had not brought the sacrificial animal.
Among them: the Hajj in which his practice and that of his companions settled is qiran for one who brought the offering, and tamattuʿ for one who did not. And for many other reasons besides these..!

Third: al-Raghib said: The sacrifice or its substitute is not obligatory in tamattuʿ except under four conditions:
Performing the ʿumrah in the months of Hajj and exiting from it therein.
The second: that he combines the Hajj with it in the same year.
The third: that he does not return to the miqat to initiate the Hajj.
The fourth: that he is not one of the people present at the Sacred Mosque.

(p-492) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[197] ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months. Whoever undertakes the Hajj in them, there shall be no sexual relations, no wickedness, and no quarrelling during the Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, for the best provision is piety. And fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾

﴿The Hajj﴾, i.e., the times of its rites, ﴿is in months﴾, which are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and Dhu al-Hijjah; that is, their first ten days, which stand in place of the whole for the sake of their great virtue.

Al-Tha'alibi said: It has been reported in the interpretation of "the months of Hajj" and "the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah" (and in some of them, nine), that whoever expresses it as nine means the days, and whoever expresses it as ten means the nights. And because of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Hajj is Arafah." And it has been made clear that the standing (at Arafah) is missed by the break of dawn.

His words ﴿well-known﴾, i.e., known among the people before the revelation of the Shari'ah, so they are not confused for them. This indicates that the matter after the Shari'ah is as it was: ﴿Whoever undertakes﴾, i.e., makes obligatory upon himself, ﴿the Hajj in them﴾ by entering into the state of ihram; ﴿there shall be no sexual relations﴾, i.e., the requirement of his ihram is that there be no intercourse, nor its preliminaries, nor obscene speech; ﴿no wickedness﴾, i.e., departure from the bounds of the Shari'ah by committing the prohibitions of ihram and other things, such as abuse and mocking by nicknames; ﴿no quarrelling﴾, i.e., disputing with anyone of the companions, the servants, or the muleteers; ﴿during the Hajj﴾, i.e., during its days. Rather, it is fitting that every good of the goods of Hajj be present in them. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun shows full concern for its matter and indicates the reason for the ruling's prohibition: visiting the Venerable House and drawing near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is among the things that necessitate abandoning the matters mentioned. The choice of negation is for emphasis in the prohibition and to indicate that this is worthy of not occurring, for what is already reprehensible and abominable in itself is more abominable during the Hajj, like wearing silk in prayer.

A subtle point:

Some of them said: The wisdom in prohibiting these things as etiquettes of speech is to magnify the sanctity of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and to make grave the matter of sin in it, since actions differ according to the difference of time and place. For public gatherings there are etiquettes other than those of privacy with one's family. What is said in a gathering of brothers is not what is said in the assembly of the sultan. It is incumbent upon a person, during times of worship and presence with Allah, Exalted is He, to be upon the most perfect etiquette and the best states; and sufficient is presence in the House which Allah, Glorified is He, has attributed to Himself!..

As for the secret in these being prohibitions of ihram, it is that the pilgrim should picture that by visiting the House of Allah, Exalted is He, he is turning toward Allah, Exalted is He, intending Him; so he strips himself of his habits and comforts, and sheds his pride and distinctions over others, such that the wealthy is made equal to the poor, and the destitute resembles the prince. Thus people of all classes are in a garb like the garb of the dead. In that is—through the purification and refinement of the soul, and making it aware of the reality of servitude to Allah and brotherhood among people—what cannot be measured in its worth, though its matter is not hidden...

﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ is an exhortation to good following the prohibition of evil, and that they should use good speech in place of foul speech, piety and righteousness in place of wickedness, and harmony and beautiful character in place of quarrelling!.. It has been narrated concerning one who performs Hajj without committing sexual relations or wickedness that he comes out of his sins like the day his mother bore him! This is because turning to Allah, Exalted is He, in that state, and moving through those rites in the prescribed manner, wipes from souls the traces of sins and their darkness, and brings them into a new life, in which they have what they earned and against them what they have acquired!

﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, and they would say: "We are the reliant ones (al-mutawakkilun)!" Then when they arrived at Makkah they would ask people (for food), so Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety﴾

That is: take provision with which you sustain yourselves and keep your faces from the people, and beware of begging for food, of burdening people, and of being a weight upon them: ﴿for the best provision is piety﴾, i.e., refraining from burdening people and being a weight upon them!.

Ibn Umar said: Indeed, part of a man's generosity is the goodness of his provision on a journey, and it was stipulated of whoever accompanied him that he be generous. Narrated by Ibn Kathir.

It is also said concerning the meaning of the verse: Take provision of piety for the Return. For a person must make a journey in this world, and in it he needs provision, requiring food, drink and a mount; and a journey from this world to the Hereafter, in which he also needs provision, which is the piety of Allah and acting in obedience to Him, and guarding against what is forbidden!.. This provision is better than the first provision, for the provision of this world leads to the desires and appetites of the soul, while the provision of the Hereafter leads to the enduring bliss of the Hereafter!.. On this meaning al-A'sha said:

When you do not depart with provision of piety,
and you meet, after death, one who has taken provision,
you will regret that you were not like him,
and that you did not prepare for what he prepared for!..

Another view: His words ﴿And take provision﴾ are a command to take provisions, which is food for the journey, and His words ﴿for the best provision is piety﴾ are guidance toward the provision of the Hereafter, which is bringing piety along to it, after the command to take provision for the journey in this world, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And finery; but the garment of piety—that is better﴾ [al-A'raf: 26]. When He mentioned sensory clothing, He alerted, guiding to the spiritual garment, which is humility and obedience, and mentioned that it is better than this and more beneficial.

﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, i.e., fear My punishment and retribution for disobeying Me and defying Me, O possessors of intellects and comprehension! For the essence of intellect is the fear of Allah, and whoever among the intelligent does not fear Him, it is as if he has no intellect!.. As He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

It has been read with the ya' affirmed in {ittaquni} according to the original form, and with it omitted for lightness, the kasrah indicating it.

The explanation of His words, Exalted is He:

[198] ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord. And when you pour forth from ʿArafat, remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram (the sacred landmark), and remember Him as He has guided you, though before it you were certainly among those astray.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord.﴾ Al-Rāghib said: The Arabs used to avoid trade during the Hajj, to the extent that they would refrain from buying and selling once the (first) ten days (of Dhu al-Hijjah) had begun. They even named the one who went about trading during the Hajj *al-dāj* (the one who strays) rather than *al-ḥājj* (the pilgrim). So Allah permitted this, and His words, ﴿And proclaim to the people the Hajj... that they may witness benefits for themselves﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 27–28], and His words, ﴿and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], indicate the permissibility of this.

Al-Bukhārī related on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Dhū al-Majāz and ʿUkāẓ were the markets of the people in the Jāhiliyyah. When Islam came, they seemed to dislike this, until the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord,﴾ during the seasons of Hajj.

So the verse grants a concession to one who performs Hajj to engage in trade and similar activities through which some provision is obtained, and this is what is meant here by *faḍl* (bounty). Included in this is His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Then disperse through the earth and seek of Allah's bounty﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 10]. That is: there is no sin upon you in seeking, during the seasons of Hajj, provision and benefit, which is profit in trade, along with your travel to fulfil what He has made obligatory upon you of Hajj.

﴿And when you pour forth from ʿArafat﴾, i.e., when you depart from it, ﴿remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram﴾, i.e., through *talbiyah* (the response of "Labbayk"), *tahlīl* (saying "lā ilāha illā Allāh"), *takbīr* (saying "Allāhu akbar"), praise and supplications. *Al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram* is a place in Muzdalifah. Its *mīm* is open (*fatḥah*), though it may be pronounced with a *kasrah*. Whoever thought it to be a small hill there has erred. It was so named because it is a marker for worship and a place for it, as stated in *al-Qāmūs* and its commentary.

Al-Fakhr (al-Rāzī) transmitted from al-Wāḥidī in *al-Basīṭ* that al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram is Muzdalifah. Allah the Exalted named it so because prayer, standing, spending the night there, and supplication occur in it. Al-Fakhr adopted this view and said: Because the *fāʾ* in His words, ﴿then remember Allah﴾, etc., indicates that remembrance at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram takes place immediately after the departure from ʿArafat, and this is only through staying overnight in Muzdalifah. End of quote.

Al-Bayḍāwī said: What supports the first view is what Jābir related: "When he (ﷺ) had prayed the Fajr (in Muzdalifah) in the darkness of the night, he mounted his she-camel until he reached al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram." That is, it indicates that Muzdalifah and al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram are distinct, based on the place to which he (ﷺ) walked from Muzdalifah to al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram. He said "supports" because it is possible to interpret al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram in the hadith as a mountain, either by omitting a noun (*muḍāf*) or by naming a part with the name of the whole. This was stated by al-Sialkūtī.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Zād al-Maʿād*, in the context of his (ﷺ) pilgrimage: When the sun set and its setting was complete, he departed from ʿArafat with tranquility, by way of al-Maʾzimayn. Then he began to proceed at a pace called *al-ʿunuq* (a moderate gait, neither fast nor slow). When he found an open space (*fajwah*, i.e., a wide area), he increased his pace (i.e., raised it above that). He would recite the *talbiyah* during that journey without ceasing it, until he reached Muzdalifah, performed ablution, then ordered the muezzin to call the adhān, and he gave it, then the iqāmah, and he prayed Maghrib before unloading the baggage and kneeling the camels. When they had unloaded their baggage, he gave the order and the prayer was established, then he prayed ʿIshāʾ, the last prayer, with one iqāmah and no adhān, and he prayed nothing between them. When Fajr dawned, he prayed it at the beginning of its time, then mounted until he reached his station near al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram, faced the qiblah, and began supplication, humble entreaty, takbīr, tahlīl and remembrance, until the light became very bright, which was before sunrise. End of the relevant quote.

Some of the imams said: How worthy is remembrance at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram of being obligatory or a rite (*nusuk*), since, in addition to it being something he (ﷺ) did, and it falls under his words (ﷺ): "Take your rites from me," there is also in it the Qur'anic text in the form of a command: ﴿Then remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Ḥaram.﴾

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, through the proofs of the Book; that is: remember Him with a good remembrance, just as He has guided you with a good guidance. The meaning of the comparison is equality in goodness and perfection, as you would say: "Serve him as he has honoured you," meaning: do not let your service fall short of his honouring you. In this is a reminder to them of the blessings Allah bestowed upon them of guidance, clarification and direction to the sites of Hajj. ﴿And though before it you were certainly among those astray﴾, i.e., before the guidance, ﴿among those astray﴾: ignorant of faith and obedience. The *in* here is the light (*mukhaffafah*) form of *inna*, and the *lām* is the distinguishing *lām* (*al-lām al-fāriqah*), which separates it from the negative *in*.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 199:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[199] ﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and ask forgiveness of God. Indeed, God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾: that is, from ʿArafah, not from Muzdalifah. In the address there are two views:

The first: it is addressed to the Quraysh. This is because of their haughtiness over the people and their exalting themselves above them, and their pride in not standing alongside them at the place of standing, and their saying: "We are the people of God and the dwellers of His sanctuary, so we do not go out from it." Thus they stood at Jamʿ (Muzdalifah), while the rest of the people stood at ʿArafat.

Al-Bukhari related from ʿAʾishah, may God be pleased with her, who said: "The Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called the Hums (the strict ones). The rest of the Arabs stood at ʿArafat. When Islam came, God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to come to ʿArafat, stand there, and then depart from it. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾."

The second: it is a command to all people to depart from where the people depart, meaning Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Al-Raghib said: "He was called 'the people' because the word 'al-nas' (the people) is used in two ways. One is for the species without regard to praise or blame. The other is for praise, in consideration of the presence of the complete form specific to humanity; this is not the case in this word, but rather in the name of every genus and species, such as: 'This is a horse,' and 'So-and-so is a man,' while this is not a horse and so-and-so is not a man, meaning it does not have the meaning specific to its species. In this sense, hearing and sight were negated from the disbelievers!" On this basis, Ibrahim was called "the people" by way of praise, which is that a single person is named with the name of a group to indicate that he stands in for them in judgment. On this basis is the saying of the poet:

"It is not unthinkable for God to gather the whole world into one person."

On this basis He said: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a community﴾ [al-Nahl: 120]. End of quote.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of the word "thumma" (then), for it implies a delay of a thing from itself, whether it is conjoined to the whole of the conditional and its consequence or to the consequence alone?

The answer: the word "thumma" is not for delay; rather it is used figuratively for the disparity between the two departures, that is, the departure from ʿArafat and the departure from Muzdalifah, and the distance between them in that one is correct and the other is wrong.

Al-Taftazani said: since the intended meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ is the allusive meaning, its meaning is: "Then do not depart from Muzdalifah." The purpose of using the word "thumma" is the disparity between the two departures in rank, in that one is correct and the other is wrong.

Some have answered that "thumma" here means "waw" (and).

﴿And ask forgiveness of God﴾ for the sins that have passed: ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

Ibn Kathir, may God have mercy on him, said: God often commands His remembrance after the completion of acts of worship. For this reason it is established in Sahih Muslim that "the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he finished the prayer, would seek God's forgiveness three times and thirty times." In the two Sahihs it is related that he encouraged glorification, praise, and magnifying (of God) thirty-three times each. Ibn Jarir has related here the hadith of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami concerning his ﷺ seeking forgiveness for his community on the evening of ʿArafah.

(p-501)

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[200] ﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik), then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance; for among the people is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾

﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ means: when you have finished the acts of the Hajj and departed from Mina. ﴿Then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance﴾ means: remember God abundantly, exert your utmost effort in praising Him and in recounting His blessings and favours, just as you do when remembering your fathers, their glories and their days, after completing your rites. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, who said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) would stand at the season's gatherings, and one of them would say, "My father used to feed people, bear the heavy burdens of others, and pay the diyat (blood money)..!" They had no remembrance except the deeds of their fathers, so God revealed this verse. It contains an indication of turning these people away from what they were accustomed to, and an exhortation to devote the remembrance to Him, exalted is His majesty.

Then, after the abundance of remembrance, God, exalted is He, directed them to supplication, for it is the place where answers are expected, and He censured the one who asks Him only concerning the affairs of his worldly life while turning away from his afterlife. So He said: ﴿Among the people﴾, that is, those who have forgotten the worth of the Hereafter and for whom the world is their greatest concern: ﴿is he who says﴾, that is, in his remembrance: ﴿"Our Lord, give us"﴾, that is, our desires: ﴿"in this world"﴾, seeking nothing other than it: ﴿and he will have no share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no portion or lot, because he has received his portion in this world by restricting his supplication to it. Thus the clause is a report from Him, exalted is He, describing his state in the Hereafter. Alternatively, the meaning is: he has no seeking of a share in the Hereafter at all. In that case it explains his state in this world, and it makes explicit what was understood implicitly from His words ﴿"Give us in this world"﴾, or it emphasises that his concern is confined to this world. In that case His words ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ are connected to ﴿share﴾, and it is a circumstantial clause describing him. This carries a censure of him and a warning against imitating one who is like this.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said, from Ibn Abbas: Some of the Bedouin used to come to the standing place (of Arafat) and say, "O God! Make this a year of rain, a year of abundance, and a year of good births..!" They mentioned nothing of the affairs of the Hereafter. So this was revealed concerning them.

(p-502) As for those whom God has described, that they confine their supplication to seeking the world, some said: they are the polytheists of the Arabs. That they have no share in the Hereafter is evident, since they have no portion in it of honour, bliss, or reward. Others said: these may be believers, but they ask God for their worldly life and not for their afterlife, and this asking of theirs is among the sins, since they asked God, at the greatest of standing places and the most noble of sites, for the debris of the world and its fleeting goods, turning away from asking for everlasting bliss in the Hereafter..! The meaning of their having no share in the Hereafter is: unless they repent, or unless God pardons them for it; or it means that he has no share in the Hereafter like the share of one who asked the Lord for his afterlife. And God knows best. Thus al-Razi is cited.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[201] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾

﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ This supplication comprises every good in this world and the Hereafter, and averts every evil. The "good" (hasanah) in this world includes everything desired in worldly life: good health, a spacious home, a good wife, abundant provision, beneficial knowledge, righteous deeds, an easy mount, a fine reputation... and other things included in the expressions of the exegetes (mufassirun). These are not mutually contradictory, for they are all subsumed under the good in this world. As for the good in the Hereafter, the highest of it is the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted, and entry into Paradise, and its consequences, including safety from the Great Terror on the plains of judgment, the facilitation of the reckoning... and other righteous matters of the Hereafter. As for deliverance from the Fire, it requires facilitating its means in this world, namely avoiding what is forbidden and sinful, and abandoning doubtful matters and what is unlawful.

The Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) has also reported encouragement to this supplication. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say it, as narrated by al-Bukhari from Anas.

(p-503) Imam Ahmad narrated: "Qatadah asked Anas: 'Which supplication did the Prophet (ﷺ) make most often?' He said: 'The supplication he most often made was: "O Allah, our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."' And whenever Anas wished to make a supplication, he would make this one, and whenever he wished to make a supplication, he would make it within it!" Muslim also narrated it, and this is his wording.

Imam al-Shafi'i narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Sa'ib: "that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, between the Rukn of Bani Jumah and the Black Stone: '﴿Our Lord, give us in this world good﴾,' the verse."

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[202] ﴿They will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

﴿They﴾ refers to the second group, by virtue of their being described by the beautiful qualities mentioned. The demonstrative carries the sense of distance, as has been repeatedly noted, indicating the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. ﴿They will have a share of what they have earned﴾ means: of the same kind as what they earned of good deeds, which is the reward, the good benefits. Or it means: on account of what they earned, as in His words, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾ [Nuh: 25]. Or it means: they will have a share of what they asked for, which We will give them in this world and the Hereafter. The supplication was called "earning" (kasb) because it is among the deeds, and deeds are described as earned. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ may mean swift in reckoning, as one is swift in travel. In that case the sentence is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for His words ﴿They﴾ and what follows, meaning: He will recompense them according to the measure of their deeds and their earnings, and no matter does distract Him from another matter, for He is swift in reckoning. Or it means: His reckoning is swift, as in "good of face." In that case the sentence is a concluding clause for His words ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200] and what follows, meaning: the Resurrection is near to being established and He will reckon with the servants. So hasten to increase remembrance and to seek the Hereafter by acquiring acts of obedience and good deeds.

Al-Raghib said: Since reckoning reveals the totals of a thing and its details, by this He draws attention to His encompassing the actions of His servants and His knowledge of their realities. Mentioning "swift" is a reminder that this reckoning from Him is not in time and not by deliberation, and this is the most eloquent way to convey to the common people the swiftness of Allah's action.

Note:

Al-Razi said: Know that Allah, Exalted is He, first explained in detail the rites of the Hajj, then after them commanded remembrance, saying: ﴿And when you pour forth from ʿArafat, remember Allah at al-Mashʿar al-Haram﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], and so on. Then He showed that it is better to leave off the remembrance of others and to confine oneself to His remembrance, saying: ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], and so on. Then after that remembrance He explained the manner of supplication, saying: ﴿Among the people is one who says﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], and so on. How excellent is this order! For it is necessary to first put worship forward to break the self and remove its darknesses. Then after worship it is necessary to occupy oneself with the remembrance of Allah, Exalted is He, to illuminate the heart and manifest the light of His majesty. Then after that remembrance, the person occupies himself with supplication, for supplication is only perfected when it is preceded by remembrance....

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verse 203:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[203] ﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him; and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for those who fear Allah. And fear Allah, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾

﴿And remember Allah during the numbered days﴾ are the days of tashriq (the three days after the Day of Sacrifice), as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said. Imam Muslim narrated from Nubayshah al-Hudhali, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The days of tashriq are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah." 'Ikrimah said: The meaning of this verse is the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") during the days of tashriq after the obligatory prayers: Allahu akbar! Allahu akbar!

Al-Bukhari narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he would say takbir in Mina during those days, after the prayers, on his bed, in his tent, in his gathering, and while walking, during all of those days. In another narration, he would say takbir in his tent, and the people of the mosque would hear him and say takbir, and the people of the markets would say takbir, until Mina shook. Al-Bukhari reported it in suspended form (ta'liq).

Among the remembrance during these days is the takbir with every pebble of the stones of the jimar (pillars) each day of the days of tashriq, for it has been reported in the Sahih that "the Prophet ﷺ said takbir with every pebble."

And it has come in the hadith narrated by Abu Dawud and others: "The circumambulation of the House, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and the stoning of the jimar were only prescribed for the establishment of the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Malik narrated in his Muwatta' from Yahya ibn Sa'id that it reached him that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on the day after the Day of Sacrifice when the sun had risen somewhat, and he said takbir, and the people said takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a second time on that same day after the sun had risen, and he said takbir, and the people said takbir with his takbir. Then he went out a third time when the sun had passed its zenith, and he said takbir, and the people said takbir with his takbir, until the takbir connected and reached the House, so that it was known that 'Umar had gone out to throw the pebbles.

Then Malik said: The takbir during the days of tashriq is obligatory for men and women, whether one is in a congregation or alone, in Mina or in all the regions.

(p-506) Then he said: The numbered days are the days of tashriq.

In al-Qamus and its commentary: tashriq means drying meat in the sun. From this the days of tashriq were named, and they are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice, because the meat of the sacrificed animals is dried in them, i.e., it is spread out in the sun. This was related by Ya'qub. It was also said: they were named so because of their saying: "Rise up, Thabir, so that we may raid," or because the offering is not slaughtered until the sun rises; this was said by Ibn al-A'rabi. Abu 'Ubayd said: Abu Hanifah used to interpret tashriq as takbir, and no one other than him held this view.

﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾: that is, whoever hastens the first departure (nafr) from these three days, and does not remain until he throws on the third day. He suffices with stoning the jimar on two of these three days, and so he does not sin by this hastening. Its explanation is that it is obligatory for the pilgrim to spend the nights of the first and second nights of the days of tashriq in Mina, so that he may throw, each day after the decline of the sun, twenty-one pebbles, seven at each jamrah. Then whoever throws on the second day and wishes to depart and forgo spending the third night, and throws on its day, that is allowed for him. ﴿And whoever delays﴾: that is, until he throws on the third day, which is the second departure, ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾ for his delay. And know that the sunnah is the delay, for the Prophet ﷺ did not hasten in two days, but delayed until he completed the stoning on all three days of tashriq. It may be objected that this phrase, namely ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾, is only used regarding one who falls short, and not regarding one who completes the act. We say: it was used to match the first phrase, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. We know that the recompense for an evil and for transgression is not itself an evil or a transgression (p-507) . So if something that is not valid in meaning is given to match the wording, then it is more fitting that something valid in meaning be given to match the wording, because the one whose pilgrimage is accepted and rewarded is correctly described as free of sin. This was said by al-Wahidi.

Al-Raghib said: The lifting of sin from the one who hastens and the one who delays is in the manner of permission, i.e., as an expression of it. It was also said: The lifting of sin means that their sins are removed by their performance of the Hajj, whether they hasten or delay, on the condition that their measure of judgment is taqwa (piety). This is indicated by the hadith: "Whoever performs Hajj and does not commit obscenity or sin returns as on the day his mother bore him."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: what has been mentioned, namely the option and the removal of sin from the one who hastens and the one who delays, or the rulings, is for those who fear Allah, because they are the true pilgrims and the ones who benefit from it, in the same manner as: ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 38], and His saying: ﴿a guidance for those who fear Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in all the matters of your lives. ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾: that is, for recompense for your deeds. This is an emphasis on the command to taqwa and an incitement to be strict in it, for whoever imagines that there must be a gathering, a reckoning, and an questioning, and that after death there is no abode except Paradise or Hellfire, this becomes one of the strongest motives for him toward taqwa. Al-hashr (gathering) is a term that applies from the beginning of their coming out of the graves until the end of the place of standing.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And among the people is one whose speech may impress you in the life of this world, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most stubborn of opponents.﴾

﴿And among the people is one whose speech may impress you in the life of this world﴾: that is, the sweetness of his speech and its eloquence in matters of the worldly life, which is the extent of his knowledge, become great in your estimation. ﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾: that is, he swears by Allah to his faith in you and his love for you, and that what is in his heart agrees with his tongue, lest disbelief and enmity be detected in him. Or its meaning: he shows you Islam and openly defies Allah with what is in his heart of disbelief and hypocrisy, in the manner in which the people of hypocrisy were described when they said: ﴿We testify that you are the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1]. And like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They conceal themselves from people, but they cannot conceal themselves from Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 108], and so on. ﴿And he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾: extremely contentious, arguing with falsehood.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[205] ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock. And Allah does not like corruption.﴾

﴿And when he turns away﴾: he departs from the one he deceived with his speech. ﴿He strives﴾: he walks about, ﴿throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾ by introducing doubts into the hearts of the Muslims, and by devising stratagems to strengthen disbelief. This meaning is called corruption (fasad), as in His saying, may He be exalted, relating the words of Pharaoh's people: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ [al-A'raf: 127], meaning: they would turn your people away from their religion and corrupt their law (shari'ah) for them. This meaning is called corruption because it causes discord among people, divides their word, and leads some of them to disown others, so that ties of kinship are severed and blood is shed. This is frequent in the Glorious Qur'an. ﴿And to destroy the crops﴾, that is, the produce of the fields, ﴿and the livestock﴾, that is, the animals that breed.

Some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: The destruction of the crops and livestock is a metaphor (kinayah) for severe harm, and using it to express this has become a proverbial idiom (mathal). The meaning is: he harms persistently in his corruption, even if it leads to the destruction of crops and livestock.

﴿And Allah does not like corruption﴾, that is, He does not approve of its doing.

Al-Raghib said: If it is asked, how does He judge that He does not like corruption when He is the one who corrupts things? It is answered: corruption in reality is removing a thing from a praiseworthy state without a sound purpose, and this does not exist in the act of Allah, the Exalted; nor does He command it, nor does He love it. What is seen of His action and appears outwardly as corruption is so only in relation to us and in our estimation of it. As for the divine perspective, all of it is good. For this reason some of the wise said: "O you whose corruption is reform!" That is, what we suppose to be corruption, owing to the shortness of our view and knowledge, is in reality reform. The sum of the matter is that man is the cream (zubdah) of this world, and everything else was created for his sake. For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. The purpose of man is to lead him to the perfection that has been established for him. Therefore, the destruction of what He has commanded to be destroyed serves the reform of man and of that which is the means of his eternal life. The explanation of this statement has another place....

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[206] ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him. So Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting place!﴾

﴿And when it is said to him﴾ in the manner of admonition: ﴿"Fear Allah"﴾ regarding hypocrisy, and beware the evil of its consequence. Or regarding corruption and destruction, and in contentious obstinacy for falsehood: ﴿pride in sin seizes him﴾, i.e., arrogance and the zeal of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah) carry him to act sinfully, which is haughtiness. Or the meaning is: the zeal for the sin that is in his heart seizes him, and it prevents him from accepting the words of the sincere advisor. ﴿So Hell is sufficient for him﴾, i.e., it suffices as his requital: ﴿Hell﴾ when he arrives at it and settles in it, as recompense and punishment. ﴿And what an evil resting place!﴾, i.e., the bed upon which he settles in place of the bedding of his pride.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: The mahd (cradle, bed) is well known, and from it is conceived the sense of preparing a place, so every trodden place is called mahd. And al-mihad is sometimes used as the plural of mahd, and sometimes as the name of an instrument, like firash (bedding). He made Hell a mihad for them just as He made punishment something they are given good news of in His words: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24].

(p-511) Al-Hakim said: This verse indicates that among the greatest sins before Allah is that it is said to a servant, "Fear Allah!" and he replies, "Take care of yourself...."

Al-Zamakhshari said: From this is the rejection of the words of the preacher.

This verse resembles His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, you recognize denial in the faces of those who disbelieve. They nearly assault those who recite Our verses to them. Say, "Shall I inform you of something worse than that? The Fire, which Allah has promised those who disbelieve. And wretched is the destination."﴾ [al-Hajj: 72]

When Exalted is He had completed the report about this misguided group of people, He followed it with its counterpart, the guided one, in order to incite the servants to avoid the attributes of the first group and to adorn themselves with the qualities of the second, so He said:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[207] ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is Kind to His servants.﴾

﴿And among the people is he who sells himself﴾ means: he sells it by expending it in obedience to Allah. ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ means: seeking His good pleasure. ﴿And Allah is Kind to His servants﴾, in that He guided them to what contains His pleasure, and bestowed upon them blessings, outward and inward, despite their disbelief in Him and their shortcoming in His command.

A subtle point:

Some have said: the contrast with the first group required that this group be described with righteous action together with not boasting in speech, or with his words matching his deeds and his tongue agreeing with what is in his heart! The verse includes this description even though it does not state it explicitly. For whoever sells himself to Allah seeks no price for it other than His pleasure; he pursues only righteous action, the speaking of truth, and sincerity in the heart. So he does not speak with two tongues (p-512), nor does he face people with two faces, nor does the fleeting worldly goods take precedence over what is with Allah... This is the believer whose faith the Qur'an counts as true...

Al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah related in his Musnad, and Ibn Abi Hatim and Razin, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "Suhayb came as an emigrant to the Prophet ﷺ, and a group of the Quraysh followed him. He dismounted from his mount, emptied what was in his quiver, and said: 'O assembly of Quraysh! You know that I am among the most skilled archers of you. By Allah! You will not reach me until I shoot every arrow I have in my quiver, then strike with my sword as long as anything remains in my hand. Then do what you wish. Or, if you wish, I will show you my wealth in Makkah and you will let my way be.' They said: 'Yes!' When he arrived before the Prophet ﷺ at Madinah, he said: 'The sale has profited, Abu Yahya! It has profited, Abu Yahya...!' And there was revealed: ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself﴾, the verse."

Al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak related something similar through the chain of Ibn al-Musayyib from Suhayb, connected. He also related it through the chain of Hammad ibn Salamah, from Thabit, from Anas, and in it is the explicit statement of the revelation of the verse, and he said: "Sahih according to the condition of Muslim." It is also narrated that it was revealed concerning Suhayb and others, as narrations regarding the revelation of the first verse were related by some exegetes.

There is no contradiction in this, because the saying "it was revealed concerning such-and-such" is sometimes meant as: a certain circumstance was the cause of its revelation, in the sense that it was not revealed except because of it. This is known either from an indication in the verse itself, or from a narration whose chain is sound beyond any criticism. And sometimes it is meant that it was revealed after an event occurred which its general wording covers. So the narrator, right after that event occurs, says: "It was revealed concerning such-and-such," and what is meant is that it applies to it, not that that event was the cause of the revelation... and what is related concerning this verse is of this kind.

Al-Zarkashi, in al-Burhan, indicated this type with his words: "It is known from the custom of the Companions and the Successors that when one of them says, 'This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such,' he means by it that it includes this ruling, not that this was the cause of its revelation. So it is of the kind of deriving a ruling from the verse, not of the kind of reporting what occurred..."

(p-513) We have already mentioned that the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is among the matters open to ijtihad, and that one should rely upon it only where its chain is sound, and that whatever falls below that and rises above the level of weakness through scholarly understanding... So be diligent in this verification. We have already presented the discussion of it in full in the introduction. And success is from Allah.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 208:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[208] ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace (al-silm) completely and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace⦅al-silm⦆﴾ — with the sin vowelled with kasra and with fatha, with the lam sukun; both are among the seven canonical readings — meaning: into Islam. Imru' al-Qays ibn Abis said:

"So I will not substitute for Allah a lord other than Him, nor will I take in place of al-silm a religion."

A similar line is the saying of the brother of Kinda:

"I called my clan to al-silm when I saw them turning their backs in flight."

Al-Razi said: The root of this word is from submission (al-inqiyad).
