It is established in the two Sahihs from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that: "The wife of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah! Rifa'ah divorced me and made my divorce final. Then I married after him 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr al-Qurazi, and what is with him is like the hem (of a garment)! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Perhaps you want to return to Rifa'ah? No, not until you taste his 'usaylah and he tastes yours.'" (p-590) In the "Sunan al-Nasa'i", from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The 'usaylah is the intercourse, even if he does not ejaculate." And in it, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a man who divorces his wife three times, then another man marries her, closes the door and lets down the curtain, then divorces her before he has consummated [the marriage] with her? He said: 'She is not lawful to the first [husband] until the other has had intercourse with her.'" This ruling therefore includes several matters:

First: The wife's claim against the husband that he is unable to have intercourse with her is not accepted.

Second: That the second husband's consummation is a condition for her lawfulness to the first, contrary to those who suffice with the contract alone; their view is rejected by the Sunnah, which cannot be rejected.

Third: That ejaculation is not required; mere intercourse, which is the tasting of the 'usaylah, is sufficient.

Fourth: That the Prophet (ﷺ) did not make the mere contract intended for its purpose - which is a marriage of desire - sufficient, nor the seclusion associated with it, the closing of doors and the lowering of curtains, until intercourse takes place... And this indicates that the mere contract of tahlil (legal marriage to restore a divorcee), in which neither husband nor wife has any purpose except the form of the contract and making her lawful to the first, is all the more insufficient.

For if the contract of desire, intended for permanence, is insufficient until intercourse occurs in it, how then can the contract of a borrowed stallion suffice to make her lawful, one who has no desire to keep her, and who is merely a loan, like a borrowed stud-donkey for mating!

He - may Allah have mercy on him - also said before this: As for the marriage of the muhallil (the one who makes lawful), in the "Tirmidhi" and the "Musnad" from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has cursed the muhallil and the muhallal lahu (the one for whom it is made lawful)." al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan sahih hadith. In the "Musnad" from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah has cursed the muhallil and the muhallal lahu," and its chain is hasan. And in it, from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it. In the "Sunan of Ibn Majah", from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not inform you of the borrowed stallion?" They said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah! He said: "He is the muhallil; Allah has cursed the muhallil and the muhallal lahu." These four are among the leading Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), and they testified concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursing those who practise tahlil, namely the muhallil and the muhallal lahu. This is either a report from Allah, and so it is a true report, or a supplication that is certainly answered. This indicates that it is among the major sins, the doer of which is cursed. There is no difference among the people of Madinah, the people of hadith and their jurists, between making this a condition explicitly or by mutual agreement and intention. For intentions in contracts are considered by them, and actions are by intentions. A condition agreed upon by the contracting parties is, to them, like what is spoken. Words are not intended for themselves but to indicate meanings; so when the meanings and purposes become manifest, words carry no weight, for they are means whose ends have been realised, so their rulings follow.

(p-592) Ibn Kathir has cited the hadiths related to this: among them what we have mentioned before, and among them what al-Hakim related in his "Mustadrak" from Nafi', who said: "A man came to Ibn 'Umar and asked him about a man who divorced his wife three times, and then his brother married her without his consent, in order to make her lawful for his brother: is she lawful to the first? He said: No. Only a marriage of desire; in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) we used to count this as fornication." Then he said: This is a hadith with a sound chain, though they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not record it. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related from 'Umar that he said: "I will not be brought a muhallil or a muhallal lahu except that I will stone them both." al-Bayhaqi related that a man was brought before 'Uthman ibn 'Affan who had married a woman in order to make her lawful for her husband, so he separated them. Similarly it is related from 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and others of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them).

In sum: tahlil is not permissible in the Shari'ah. Had it been permissible, its doer and the one who consents to it would not be cursed. And if the cursing of the doer does not indicate the prohibition of the act, there remains no expression that indicates prohibition at all. And if this act is forbidden and not permissible in the Shari'ah, then it is not the marriage which Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿until she marries another husband﴾, just as if one said: "Allah curse the seller of wine," it would not follow from the word "seller" that his sale is permitted and has become part of the sale which was allowed by His saying: ﴿And Allah has permitted trade﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275]. The matter is clear.

Section
The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in":
Obliging the one who swears by divorce or emancipation, if he breaks his oath, to divorce his wife and free his slave - this is something whose giving of fatwa began after the era of the Companions had passed. Nothing is preserved from any Companion regarding the form of oath that obliges divorce by it at all. What is preserved is the obligation of divorce by the form of conditional and consequence, in which divorce is intended upon the occurrence of the condition, as in the "Sahih of al-Bukhari" from Nafi', who said: A man divorced his wife irrevocably if she went out. Ibn 'Umar said: If she goes out (p-593) she has been separated from him, and if she does not go out, it is nothing. This is not disputed except by one who prevents the occurrence of conditional divorce absolutely. As for one who distinguishes between a pure oath and a conditional statement intended to take effect, he holds the reports narrated from all the Companions on this matter. It is established from them that they gave fatwa for taking effect in some cases, and from them there is non-effect in other cases. The correct position is what they gave fatwa on in both types, and one may not take some of their fatwas and leave others. As for taking effect: what is preserved from them is what al-Bukhari mentioned from Ibn 'Umar, and what al-Thawri related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning a man who said to his wife: If you do such and such, you are divorced; and she did it. He said: It is one (revocable divorce) and he has the right to her - though it is disconnected. Likewise what al-Bayhaqi and others related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning a man who said to his wife: You are divorced in a year. He said: He may enjoy her until a year. From this is the saying of Abu Dharr to his wife, when she pressed him about the Night of Power, he said: If you ask me again, you are divorced. These are all the reports preserved from the Companions on the taking effect of conditional divorce. As for the reports from them to the contrary: it is established from 'A'ishah, Ibn 'Abbas, Hafsah and Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with them) concerning a woman who swore that every slave of hers is free if she does not separate her slave from his wife, that she expiates for her oath and does not separate them. Al-Athram related it in his "Sunan", al-Jawzajani in "al-Mutarjim", al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi.

The principle of Imam Ahmad: what the Companions gave fatwa on does not depart from, if there is nothing in the matter that repels it. So on his own principle upon which he built his school, it is binding on him to hold this report, because of its soundness and the absence of its cause. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: It is established from Ibn 'Umar, 'A'ishah and Umm Salamah, the mothers of the believers, that they made in the statement of Layla bint al-'Ajma: "Every slave of hers is free, and every property of hers is an offering, and she is Jewish or Christian, if you do not divorce your wife" - one expiation for an oath. And since this is established from the Companions, and no opponent among them is known regarding the statement of one who swears: "My slave is free if I do such," that it suffices with an expiation for an oath, and they did not oblige him with the emancipation beloved to Allah, then not obliging him with the divorce hateful to Allah is all the more fitting and more appropriate. How, when 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (p-594) (may Allah be pleased with him) gave fatwa: the one who swears by divorce, there is nothing upon him... and no opponent is known to him among the Companions? 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Ibrahim ibn Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Taymi, known as Ibn Bariah al-Andalusi, said in his commentary on the "Ahkam" of 'Abd al-Haqq, the third chapter on the ruling of an oath by divorce or doubt about it: We have already mentioned in the Book of Oaths the scholars' disagreement about oaths by divorce, emancipation, walking and other things, whether they bind or not. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), Shurayh and Tawus said: nothing binds from that, and divorce is not ruled upon the one who swears by it and breaks it. No opponent among the Companions is known in this - this is his exact wording. This is the fatwa of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning oaths of emancipation and divorce.

We have already mentioned their fatwas on the taking effect of conditional divorce, and there is no contradiction between them, for the one swearing did not intend the divorce to take effect, but intended to restrain himself by swearing by what he does not want to happen... Until he said: If the oath by divorce enters into the statement of one who swears, "the oaths of allegiance bind me" - which are the oaths that al-Hajjaj established - then why should it not be more entitled to enter the category of oaths in the speech of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)? If the oath of divorce is a legally recognised oath - in the sense that the Shari'ah has regarded it - it must be given the ruling of oaths. And if it is not a legally recognised oath, it is void in the Shari'ah, and the one who swears by it is bound by nothing, as is established from Tawus through the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from Ibn Tawus from him: "Swearing by divorce is nothing." And it is established from 'Ikrimah, through the narration of Sunayd ibn Dawud in his "Tafsir" from him: "It is among the steps of Satan; nothing binds by it." And it is established from Shurayh, the judge of 'Ali, and Ibn Mas'ud: that divorce is not binding by it. This is the school of Dawud ibn 'Ali and all his followers. These are the positions of the leading Muslims from the Companions and the Successors and those after them. End quote.

(p-595) Section
And the Imam Ibn al-Qayyim also said in "I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in":

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verse 230 (part 2 of 3):

The one who pronounced divorce in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), in the time of Abu Bakr, and in the early part of the caliphate of Umar, if he combined the three divorces in one utterance, it was counted as one. This is established in the Sahih, as related from Ibn Abbas. Muslim related in his "Sahih," from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "Triple divorce was in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and of Abu Bakr, and for two years of Umar's caliphate, was counted as one divorce. Then Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'People have become hasty in a matter in which they had been given deliberation. So if we enforce it upon them,' and he enforced it upon them." Imam Ahmad related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Rukanah ibn Abd Yazid, brother of Banu Muttalib, divorced his wife three times in one sitting, and he grieved over her greatly. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him, 'How did you divorce her?' He said: 'Three times.' He said: 'In one sitting?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then that is only one, so take her back if you wish.' So he took her back." Ibn Abbas held that divorce is only effected at each (separate) purity. Imam Ahmad declared this chain sound and good (hasan). Then Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was not unaware that this was the Sunnah, and that it was a concession from Allah to His servants, since He made divorce occur once after another. What occurs once after another cannot be fully effected by the responsible person in a single utterance. Like li'an (the oath of mutual condemnation between spouses): if he says, "I testify by Allah four times that I am among the truthful," it counts as one testimony. And if one swears in the qasamah (the oath procedure in a homicide case) and says, "I swear by Allah fifty oaths that this man is his killer," it counts as one oath. And if one who confesses to adultery says, "I confess four times that I committed adultery," it counts as one confession. Whoever considers the four (repetitions) does not count that confession as anything but one. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, 'Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi' (Glory and praise be to Allah) one hundred times in a day, his sins will be forgiven even if they are like the foam of the sea." So if he says, "Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi" one hundred times in a single utterance, he does not obtain this reward until he says it time after time. Likewise His saying: "Whoever glorifies Allah after each prayer thirty-three times, praises Him thirty-three times, and magnifies Him thirty-three times..." (the hadith), one does not act upon it until he says that time after time; all of them cannot be combined in a single wording. Likewise His saying: "Whoever says in a day, 'La ilaha illa Allah, wahdahu la sharika lah, lahu al-mulk wa lahu al-hamd wa huwa ala kulli shay'in qadir' one hundred times, it will be a protection for him from Satan that day until evening." This is not achieved except by saying it time after time. Just as this applies to statements and words, it is likewise the same with actions. As in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will punish them twice﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101]; it means time after time. Likewise the saying of Ibn Abbas: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice," meaning time after time. And likewise the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A believer is not stung from the same hole twice." This is what is understood from the language and custom. The aforementioned hadiths, these texts, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], are all from one door and one niche. The aforementioned hadiths explain the meaning of His saying: ﴿Divorce is twice﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. This is the Book of Allah, this is the Sunnah of His Messenger, this is the language of the Arabs, this is the custom of discourse, and this is the successor of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and all the Companions with him in his era, and for three years of Umar's era (may Allah be pleased with him), upon this doctrine. If one were to count them, they would certainly exceed a thousand. Therefore some scholars claimed that this is an ancient consensus (ijma'), and the Ummah, praise be to Allah, has not agreed against it. Rather, there have always been among them those who issue fatwas according to it, century after century, down to our day. Among the Companions, Ibn Abbas, al-Zubayr, and Ibn Awf issued fatwas according to it. On Ali and Ibn Mas'ud there are two narrations. Among the Successors (tabi'un) are Ikrimah and Tawus. Among their followers are Muhammad ibn Ishaq and others. Among those after them is Dawud, the imam of the Zahiris (Ahl al-Zahir), and some companions of Malik, and some Hanafis. Some companions of Ahmad issued fatwas according to it, as related by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah from him, and he said: "The grandfather (Ibn Taymiyyah's grandfather) used to issue fatwas according to it at times."

The point is that this view is indicated by the Book, the Sunnah, analogy, and the ancient consensus. No later consensus came to invalidate it. However, the Commander of the Faithful Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) saw that people had become careless about the matter of divorce, and many of them were pronouncing it all at once, so he judged it to be in the public interest to punish them by enforcing it upon them, so that they would know that whoever pronounces it all at once, the woman becomes irrevocably separated from him and becomes forbidden to him until she marries another husband in a marriage of desire intended to last, not a marriage of tahlil (a marriage contracted to make a woman lawful again for her former husband). For they were among the most inclined to it. When they knew this, they refrained from divorce. So Umar saw this as a benefit for them in his time. He also saw that what they had been upon in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the time of the Siddiq (Abu Bakr), and the early part of his own caliphate, was the most fitting for them, because they did not follow one another in it, and they used to fear Allah regarding divorce. Allah has made a way out for everyone who fears Him. But when they abandoned the fear of Allah, trifled with the Book of Allah, and divorced in a manner other than what Allah had legislated, he obligated them to what they had committed themselves to, as a punishment for them. Indeed Allah, Glorified is He, legislated divorce time after time, and did not legislate it entirely in one go. So whoever combines the three in a single utterance has transgressed the limits of Allah, wronged himself, and trifled with the Book of Allah. He deserves to be punished and held to what he committed himself to, and not to be left in the enjoyment of the concession and latitude of Allah, which he himself has squandered. He did not fear Allah and divorce as Allah commanded and legislated for him, but hastened in what Allah had granted him deliberation regarding, out of mercy and kindness, and chose the harsher and more severe. This is what the situation changed for because of the change of time. The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) recognized the wisdom of Umar's governance and his discipline of his subjects in this matter, so they agreed with what he obligated them to. Then he said: "When the time changed, and the age of the Sunnah and the practices of the early generations became distant, and the market of tahlil was set up and flourished among people, it is obligatory that the matter be returned to what it was in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his successor, by issuing fatwas that nullify the market of tahlil, diminish it, and lessen its evil." When the matter is presented to one whom Allah has granted success, given insight into guidance, and given understanding of his religion, the question of whether three (divorces) count as one, and the question of tahlil, and he weighs one against the other, the difference becomes clear to him, and he knows which of the two questions is more fitting for the religion and more beneficial for the Muslims.

Then he (may God have mercy on him) said: "In these times it is impermissible to punish people with what Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) punished them, for two reasons:

The first: most of them do not know that combining the three is forbidden, especially since many jurists do not consider it forbidden. How then can one be punished who has not committed a prohibition in his own view?

The second: punishing them in this way opens for them the door of tahlil, which was closed in the time of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). And a punishment, if it includes a corruption greater than the act being punished, then abandoning it is more beloved to Allah and His Messenger. No one doubts that returning to what the Companions were upon in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and the early part of Umar's caliphate, is better than returning to tahlil. And Allah is the Granter of success."

(p-599) Chapter

As for the divorce of one who is angry, in "A'lam al-Muwaqqi'in" (Ibn al-Qayyim's "Informing the Signatories") the following text appears:

"Indeed the utterance only takes effect according to the meaning intended by the one who speaks it. Allah, Glorified is He, lifted accountability from one who merely thinks something to himself without uttering it or acting upon it, just as He lifted it from one who utters words without intending their meaning or willing them. For this reason, one who has a word of disbelief slip from his tongue unintentionally, out of joy, astonishment, or otherwise, is not declared a disbeliever, as in the hadith of Allah's joy at the repentance of His servant. He gave the example of a man who lost his mount, on which were his food and drink, in a desert wasteland, and despaired of it, then found it, and said: 'O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your Lord,' erring out of intense joy. He was not held accountable for that. Likewise, if one errs out of intense anger, he is not held accountable. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If Allah were to hasten for the people the evil as they seek to hasten the good, their term would already have been decreed for them﴾ [Yunus: 11]. The righteous predecessors (al-salaf) said: this is a person's supplication against himself, his child, or his family in a state of anger; if Allah, Exalted is He, were to answer it, He would destroy him and whomever he curses, but He does not answer it, because He knows that the supplicant did not intend it. From this is his (ﷺ) lifting the ruling of divorce from one who divorces under duress (ighlaq). Imam Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him) said in the narration of Hanbal: it is anger."

(p-600) This is also how Abu Dawud interpreted it. It is the view of the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq, one of the imams of the Malikis and the foremost of the jurists of Iraq among them, and for him it is also among the vain oaths (laghw al-yamin). He thus included the oath of one who is angry among the vain oath and the oath under duress. Ibn Barirah al-Andalusi, the commentator on the rulings of Abd al-Haqq, related it from him, and said: "This is also the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and others among the Companions: that all binding oaths taken in a state of anger are not binding." In the "Sunan al-Daraqutni," with a chain that contains weakness, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no oath in anger, and no emancipation regarding what one does not own." If its attribution to the Prophet (ﷺ) is not established, then it is the saying of Ibn Abbas. Al-Shafi'i interpreted "there is no divorce in ighlaq" as anger, and Masruq also interpreted it so. Thus Masruq, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and the judge Isma'il all interpreted ighlaq as anger, and it is among the best of interpretations, because the angry person has had the door of intention closed upon him by the intensity of his anger. He is like one who is coerced. Indeed the angry person is more deserving of the term ighlaq than the coerced person, because the coerced person intends to remove a greater evil by a lesser one, so he is intentional in reality. It is on this basis that whoever considers divorce to take effect from the coerced person does so. As for the angry person, the closing of the door of intention and knowledge to him is like its closing to the drunk and the insane. Wine seizes his intellect, and anger is even more severe; it is a branch of madness. No discerning jurist doubts that the divorce of such a person does not take effect. For this reason the scholar of the Ummah, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed for to have understanding of the religion, said: 'Divorce only takes effect from a purpose (watar).' Al-Bukhari recorded it in his Sahih, meaning: from a purpose on the part of the one who divorces in its occurrence. This is part of the completeness of his jurisprudence (may Allah be pleased with him), and the answer to the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) supplication for him, since the utterances only produce their effects according to the intention of the speaker. Allah did not hold us accountable for the vain (laghw) in our oaths. Among the vain oaths is what Mother of the Believers Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) and the majority of the righteous predecessors said: it is the speaker's saying, 'No, by Allah,' and 'Yes, by Allah,' in the midst of his speech without intending to form an oath. Likewise, Allah does not hold one accountable for the vain in oaths of divorce, like the speaker's saying in the midst of his speech: 'Upon me is divorce, I will not do it,' and 'Divorce is binding upon me, I will not do it' (p-601) without intending to make an oath. Indeed, if the Name of the Lord, glorified is His majesty, does not form a binding oath when used in vain oaths, then an oath of divorce is more deserving of not forming one, and it cannot be of greater sanctity than swearing by Allah. This is one of the two views in the school of Ahmad, and it is the correct one. So beware of disregarding the intention, purpose, and custom of the speaker, lest you wrong him and the Shari'ah, and attribute to it what it is free of, and oblige the swearer, the one who acknowledges, the one who vows, and the one who contracts what Allah and His Messenger did not oblige them with. The vain in utterances is like the error and forgetfulness in actions, and Allah has lifted accountability for this. This is as the believers said: ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. Their Lord, Blessed and Exalted, said: 'I have done so.'

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 230 (part 3 of 3):

Our shaykh said: The reality of *al-ighlaq* (being locked shut, i.e., duress or extreme agitation) is that a man's heart is closed off so that he does not intend speech, or does not know what he is saying, as if his intention and will have been shut in.

Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad said: *al-ghalq* is tightness of the chest and scarcity of patience, to the point that he finds no way out.

Our shaykh said: This includes the divorce of one who is coerced, of the insane, and of one whose reason has been removed by intoxication or anger, and of everyone who has no intention and no awareness of what he says.

Anger is of three kinds:

The first: that which removes reason, so that its possessor is not aware of what he says. The divorce of such a person does not take effect, without dispute.

The second: that which is at its beginning, in a state that does not prevent its possessor from conceiving what he says and intending it. The divorce of such a person takes effect.

The third: that which becomes firmly established and intense, so that it does not remove reason entirely, but comes between him and his intention, such that he regrets what he did once it has passed. This is a matter for consideration. Non-occurrence of divorce in this state is strong and well-founded.

(p-602) **Section**

As for the divorce of a menstruating woman, a woman in postnatal bleeding, or a woman who has been had sexual intercourse with during her purity, the Two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) report that Ibn Umar divorced his wife while she was menstruating, during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Umar ibn al-Khattab asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: "Tell him to take her back, then keep her until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure again. Then, if he wishes, he may keep her after that, and if he wishes, he may divorce her before he touches her. That is the waiting period by which Allah commanded that women be divorced." In Muslim's version: "Tell him to take her back, then let him divorce her when she becomes pure or while she is pregnant." In another wording: "If he wishes, he may divorce her while she is pure before he touches her; that is the divorce for the waiting period, as Allah the Exalted commanded." In a wording of al-Bukhari: "Tell him to take her back, then let him divorce her at the start of her waiting period." In a wording of Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i, from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), he said: "Abdullah ibn Umar divorced his wife while she was menstruating, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned her to him and did not count it anything, and said: 'When she becomes pure, let him either divorce or keep her.'" Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) also said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: *O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period* (65:1)," and so this ruling includes that divorce is in four ways: two are permissible and two are forbidden.

The permissible: that he divorces his wife while she is pure and he has not had intercourse with her, or that he divorces her while she is pregnant and her pregnancy is evident. The forbidden: that he divorces her while she is menstruating, or that he divorces her during a period of purity in which he had intercourse with her. This applies to a woman who has been consummated with. As for a woman who has not been consummated with, it is permissible to divorce her whether she is menstruating or pure.

Then, the disagreement over whether a forbidden divorce takes effect has remained established between the earlier and later scholars. Whoever claimed consensus on its taking effect has erred, speaking according to the limit of his own knowledge, and what others knew of the disagreement was hidden from him. Imam Ahmad said: "Whoever claims consensus is a liar. How does he know? Perhaps people have disagreed?" How could it be otherwise, when the disagreement among people on this question is well known to have been established among the earlier and later scholars...?!

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Salam al-Khushani said: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us: Abd al-Wahhab ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Thaqafi narrated to us: Ubaydullah ibn Umar narrated to us, from Nafi, the client of Ibn Umar, from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said, concerning a man who divorces his wife while she is menstruating: Ibn Umar said: "It is not counted." Ibn Hazm mentioned this in *al-Muhalla* with its chain of narration going back to him.

Abd al-Razzaq said in his *Musannaf*, from Ibn Juraij, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, that he did not consider divorce that contradicts the manner of divorce and the manner of the waiting period as valid. He used to say: The manner of divorce is that he divorces her while she is pure without having had intercourse with her, or once her pregnancy has become evident.

Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: How astonishing is the audacity of whoever claims consensus contrary to this, when he cannot find in what agrees with his position, regarding the enforcement of divorce during menstruation or during a purity in which he had intercourse with her, a single statement from any of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), except one report from Ibn Umar. And what is better than it from Ibn Umar has contradicted it.

(p-604) Abu Muhammad said: Rather, we are more fortunate in claiming consensus here, if we were to permit what they permit, and we seek refuge in Allah from that. This is because there is no disagreement among any of the people of knowledge, all of them, including all those who oppose us in this, that divorce during menstruation, or during a purity in which he had intercourse with her, is an innovation (bid'ah). So there is no doubt about this among them. How then can they permit ruling for the permissibility of an innovation which they themselves acknowledge to be an innovation and an error? Is it not evident that one who permits an innovation opposes the consensus of those who say it is an innovation...?!

Abu Muhammad said: And even if the disagreement had not reached us, one would be making a definitive judgment on all the people of Islam without certainty, and would be lying about all of them.

This is what Imam Ibn al-Qayyim conveyed in *Zad al-Ma'ad*. Then he mentioned the arguments of those who prevent its taking effect, and the arguments of those who hold that it takes effect, and the discussion of them, so refer to it if you wish.

It was also mentioned in the course of the discussion that there is no evidence in his saying "Tell him to take her back" for the taking effect of divorce, because *al-muraja'ah* (returning) has occurred in the speech of Allah and His Messenger in three meanings. Among them: the beginning of marriage, as in His saying: ﴿Then if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband. Then if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both for returning to one another if they think they can keep within the limits of Allah﴾ (2:230). There is no disagreement among any of the people of knowledge of the Qur'an that the divorcer here is the second husband, and that the returning between her and the first husband is a fresh marriage. Another meaning: the literal return to the state in which it was originally, as in his saying to Abu al-Nu'man ibn Bashir when he gave his son a slave, singling him out for it to the exclusion of his other children: "Return it." This is a return of what the reckless gift was not valid for, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called *jawr* (injustice) and informed that it is not valid, and that it is contrary to justice. From this is his saying to one who separated a slave girl from her child in a sale: he forbade him from that and annulled the sale. This return does not imply the validity of the sale, for it is an invalid sale. Rather, it is the return of two things to the state of their being together as they were. Likewise the matter of Ibn Umar returning his wife is a restoration and a return to the state of union as they were before the divorce, and there is nothing in that which requires the taking effect of divorce during menstruation at all. There are other aspects, and Allah knows best.

**Section**

As for *khul'* (divorce by consideration paid by the wife): the correct view is that it is a annulment (fasakh), not a divorce. Its waiting period is one menstrual cycle. Abu Dawud reported in his *Sunan*, from Ibn Abbas, that the wife of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas sought *khul'* from her husband, and the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered her to observe one menstrual cycle as her waiting period. In this there is evidence for two rulings. The first: that she is not obliged to observe three menstrual cycles, but one suffices her. This is the explicit Sunnah, and it is also the view of the Commander of the Faithful Uthman ibn Affan, and Abdullah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, and al-Rubayyi' bint Mu'awwidh and her paternal uncle (may Allah be pleased with them all), who are among the senior Companions. These four Companions are not known to have any dissenter among them. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Imam Ahmad, in a narration from him which Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah chose, held this view. He said: This view is what the principles of the Shari'ah require. The waiting period was only made three menstrual cycles so that the period of return would be extended, the husband would reflect, and he would have the opportunity to return within the waiting period. When there is no possibility of return for her, the purpose is merely the clearing of her womb from pregnancy, and one menstrual cycle suffices for that, like *istibra'* (establishing that the womb is clear). This is not contradicted by the divorced woman who has been divorced three times, because the law of divorce made the ruling on the waiting period one for both the irrevocable and the revocable divorce.

They said: This is evidence that *khul'* is an annulment and not a divorce. This is also the view of Ibn Abbas, Uthman, Ibn Umar, al-Rubayyi' and her uncle. It is not authentically reported from any Companion that it is a divorce at all. Imam Ahmad reported from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sufyan, from Amr, from Tawus, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them): "*Khul'* is a separation, not a divorce." Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, from Sufyan, from Amr, from Tawus, that Ibrahim ibn Sa'd asked him about a man who divorced his wife twice and then she sought *khul'* from him: may he marry her? Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Yes! Allah mentioned divorce at the beginning and end of the verse, and *khul'* is between that."

What indicates that it is not a divorce is that Allah the Glorified and Exalted attached three rulings to divorce after consummation, when the number of divorces has not been completed, all of which are absent in *khul'*:

The first: that the husband has the greater right to return in it.

The second: that it is subtracted from the three, so that after the full number is completed she is not lawful again except after another husband and consummation.

The third: that the waiting period in it is three periods (quru').

It has been established by the text and consensus that there is no return in *khul'*. It has been established by the Sunnah and the statements of the Companions that its waiting period is one menstrual cycle. And it has been established by the text that it is permissible after two divorces, and that a third divorce takes effect after it. This is very clear in showing that it is not a divorce. For He, the Glorified, said: ﴿Divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. And if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, there is no blame upon either of them concerning that by which she ransoms herself﴾ (2:229). Although this does not refer only to the woman divorced twice, it includes her and others. The pronoun cannot refer to someone not mentioned while leaving aside the one who is mentioned; rather it must either be specific to the preceding, or include it and others. Then He said: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that﴾ (2:230). This certainly includes the woman who was divorced after the ransom of two divorces, because she is the one mentioned. So she must be included under the wording. This is the understanding of the interpreter of the Qur'an, for whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed that Allah would teach him the interpretation of the Qur'an, and it is a prayer that is undoubtedly answered. And since the rulings of ransom are different from the rulings of divorce, this indicates that it is not of its kind. This is what the text, analogy and the statements of the Companions indicate. End of quote.

(p-607) This is the summary of the arguments on these important branches, which only one whose understanding is free from partisanship can appreciate. Whoever considers what has become widespread, namely separating a man from his wife merely by adopting idle talk and abandoning what the leading heroic scholars have established by evidence, will be astonished. And success is from Allah.

﴿Then if he divorces her﴾ - i.e., the second husband - ﴿there is no blame upon them both﴾ i.e., upon the woman and her first divorcer ﴿for returning to one another﴾ i.e., to the marriage they were in, by a new contract after the waiting period of the second divorce, known from what preceded in His saying: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ (2:228) and so on, ﴿if they think they can keep within the limits of Allah﴾ i.e., which He required the two spouses to observe regarding rights, ﴿And those are the limits of Allah﴾ (2:229) i.e., His rulings, protected from alteration and violation, ﴿which He makes clear to a people who know﴾ i.e., He removes the confusion from them for a people who have vigour and earnestness in *ijtihad* (independent reasoning), so they renew their consideration and reflection with the utmost effort at all times. By this Allah gives them a faculty by which they distinguish what is confusing to others: ﴿If you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion﴾ (8:29) ﴿and fear Allah, and Allah teaches you﴾ (2:282). Al-Biqa'i conveyed this.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 231:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[231] ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their prescribed term, then retain them in kindness or release them in kindness. And do not retain them, intending harm, to transgress. And whoever does that has certainly wronged himself. And do not take the verses of Allah in jest. And remember the favor of Allah upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

(p-608) ﴿And when you divorce women﴾ i.e., a revocable divorce; ﴿and they reach their term﴾ i.e., they approach the end of the waiting period ('iddah); ﴿then retain them﴾ i.e., by taking them back, if you wish; ﴿in kindness﴾ without harm; ﴿or release them in kindness﴾ i.e., by leaving them until the waiting period ends, so that they gain control over themselves. ﴿And do not retain them﴾ i.e., by returning to them; ﴿intending harm﴾ i.e., causing injury by removing affection, inflicting estrangement, and bringing about the causes of aversion; ﴿to transgress﴾. The lam here is for consequence, meaning that the outcome of your action is transgression. Or it is for causation, connected to "harm," so that it is a cause for a cause, meaning: so that you wrong them by compelling them to ransom themselves. ﴿And whoever does that has certainly wronged himself﴾ i.e., by exposing himself to the wrath of Allah and to people's aversion toward him.

﴿And do not take the verses of Allah﴾ i.e., His commands and prohibitions; ﴿in jest﴾ i.e., mocked by them, by turning away from them and being negligent in observing them. ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you﴾ i.e., in His sending the Messenger to you with guidance and clear proofs. ﴿And what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom﴾ i.e., the Sunnah. ﴿By which He instructs you﴾ i.e., by what He has sent down; that is, He commands you, forbids you, and threatens you for opposing it. ﴿And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is an emphasis and a warning.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[232] ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands if they agree among themselves in a fair manner. This is admonished to whoever among you believes in God and the Last Day. That is more pure for you and cleaner. God knows, and you do not know.﴾

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾ i.e., their 'iddah (waiting period) has ended. The context of the two statements indicates that the two uses of "reach" differ. The first indicates approaching the end, in connection with the command to retain them, while this one is literal, in connection with the prohibition on 'adl (obstructing remarriage). ﴿Do not prevent them﴾, i.e., do not hinder them, ﴿from marrying their husbands﴾ (p-609) who had divorced them, and who are now desired by them. ﴿If they agree among themselves﴾, i.e., the women and the husbands, ﴿in a fair manner﴾, i.e., in accordance with what is good in religion regarding the conditions. ﴿This﴾, i.e., the prohibition on 'adl, ﴿is admonished to whoever among you believes in God and the Last Day. That﴾, i.e., taking heed by abandoning 'adl and harm, ﴿is more pure for you﴾, i.e., more righteous for you, ﴿and cleaner﴾ for your hearts and their hearts from suspicion and enmity. ﴿God knows, and you do not know﴾, i.e., He knows what is good for your affairs in what He commands and forbids, including what He has clarified here, and you do not know it. So set aside your own opinions and obey His command and prohibition in everything you do and refrain from.

It has been narrated that this verse was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar al-Muzani and his sister.

Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar that he gave his sister in marriage to a man from the Muslims. She was with him, then he divorced her with one pronouncement and did not take her back until her 'iddah ended. Then he (the husband) desired her and she desired him. He proposed to her again along with the other suitors. Ma'qil said to him: "O wretch! I honored you by giving her to you in marriage, and you divorced her. By God, she will never return to you." God knew their need for each other, so God revealed the verse. When Ma'qil heard it, he said: "I hear and obey my Lord." Then he summoned the man and said: "I will marry her to you and honor you." Ibn Mardawayh added: "And I made expiation for my oath."

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[233] ﴿And mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. And upon the father of the child is their provision and their clothing according to what is reasonable. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you provided you hand over what you agreed upon, according to what is reasonable. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

(p-610) ﴿And mothers﴾ i.e., from among the divorced women: ﴿shall suckle their children for two complete years﴾ i.e., two full years: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ i.e., this ruling applies to whoever wishes to complete the child's nursing. This implies that weaning for a benefit is permissible before that, and that there is no nursing after completion.

Al-Harrali (ʿAlī ibn Aḥmad al-Harālī) said: That which is sufficient short of completion is what His words, Exalted is He, encompass: ﴿And his bearing and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. So if the pregnancy is nine months, the nursing is twenty-one months. And if it is two years, the total is thirty-three months, so it becomes three units and three tens, and this is the completion of pregnancy and nursing.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾ — i.e., the father — and He expressed it with this phrase to indicate the basis for the obligation of maintenance upon him, because mothers give birth for fathers, and for this reason the child is attributed to the father and not to the mother. Some of them said:

Indeed the mothers of people are only vessels, entrusted repositories, and the children belong to the fathers.

﴿their provision and their clothing﴾ i.e., upon the father of the child is the maintenance of his divorced mother for the duration of nursing, that is, their food and their clothing: ﴿according to what is reasonable﴾, which is the measure of one's means, as explained by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾ (p-611) meaning its ability. The meaning is that the child's father is not burdened in spending on him and on his mother except to the extent that his means can afford, and not to the point of exceeding his capacity. ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾ i.e., he takes her child from her after she has consented to nursing it, desires to keep it, and has strong love for it. ﴿Nor a father through his child﴾ meaning the father: ﴿through his child﴾ by casting the child upon him. That is, the woman should not hand the child over to its father after he has become attached to her, harming him thereby. This interpretation holds if "tudarra" is in the passive form. As for its being in the active form, the object is omitted and the sense is: "Let no mother harm her husband (lā tuḍārri) — with the first letter of the verb vowelled with kasra — through her child," namely by reproaching him, demanding from him what is not equitable in provision and clothing, occupying his heart with neglect regarding the child's affairs, or saying, after the boy has become attached to her: "Seek a wet-nurse for him," and similar things. And let no father harm his wife through his child, by withholding from her anything that is obligatory upon him of her provision and clothing, or by taking the child from her while she wishes to nurse him. The two meanings return to one thing: that one of them enrages the other.

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ i.e., upon the heir of the father or the heir of the child is the like of what is upon the father of maintenance and abstention from harm, if there is no father. ﴿And if they both desire﴾ meaning the husband and the wife: ﴿weaning﴾ i.e., the weaning of the child from milk before the two years — meaning, a cessation: ﴿by mutual consent between them﴾ through the agreement of the father and the mother: ﴿and consultation﴾ through their consulting each other: ﴿there is no blame upon them﴾ i.e., upon the father and the mother, if they do not nurse their child for two years. ﴿And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children﴾ meaning other than the mother, when she refuses, or is unable, or wishes to marry: ﴿there is no blame upon you provided you hand over﴾ — meaning to the wet-nurses: ﴿what you agreed upon﴾ i.e., what you intended to give them of wages: ﴿according to what is reasonable﴾, which is connected to "you hand over", i.e., you hand over the wages to the wet-nurses with good will and cheerfulness. The intent is to encourage them that, when paying the wages, they should be cheerful of countenance, speaking gracious words, and comforting the hearts of the wet-nurses, so that they are secure against negligence on their part regarding the infant's welfare. ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ — in it is a warning and caution against opposing His rulings, which is clear.

(p. 612) The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[234] ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait with themselves for four months and ten days. When they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an acceptable manner. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿Those of you who die﴾ means: those of your men who die. ﴿And leave﴾ means: leave behind. ﴿Wives﴾ means: after death. ﴿Shall wait﴾ means: shall await. ﴿With themselves﴾ means: during the 'iddah (waiting period). ﴿Four months and ten﴾ means ten days. ﴿When they have reached their term﴾ means: when their 'iddah has ended. ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ means: upon the guardians, in leaving them. ﴿For what they do with themselves﴾ means: such as exposing themselves to suitors and adorning themselves. ﴿In an acceptable manner﴾ means: in a manner that the Sharia does not disapprove of. This implies that if they do what the Sharia disapproves of, then it is incumbent upon the guardians to prevent them from that; otherwise, the blame falls upon them. ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

Know that in this verse there are several issues:

The first: From the generality of the verse is excluded the pregnant woman whose husband has died, for her 'iddah ends with giving birth, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth to their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4], and on what is in the two Sahihs (al-Sahihayn) from Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah: that she was married to Sa'd ibn Khawlah, who was from the Banu Amir ibn Lu'ayy, and was among those who witnessed Badr. He died leaving her in the Farewell Pilgrimage while she was pregnant. She did not delay before giving birth to her burden after his death. When she had become clean of her postnatal bleeding, she adorned herself for suitors. Abu al-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak, a man from the Banu Abd al-Dar, entered upon her and said: "What is this? I see you have adorned yourself for suitors. Perhaps you desire marriage? By Allah, you shall not marry until four months and ten days have passed over you." Subay'ah said: "When he said that to me, I gathered my clothes around me until evening, and I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about that. He gave me a ruling that I had become free (from the 'iddah) when I gave birth to my burden, and he commanded me to marry if I wished." And in it Ibn Shihab said: "I see no harm in her marrying once she has given birth, even if she is still in her bleeding, except that he should not approach her until she is purified."

The second: The meaning of her waiting with herself is: abstaining from marriage, abstaining from adornment, and abstaining from leaving the house in which her husband died. The first is agreed upon.

As for the second: It has been reported on this from Umm Habibah, Zaynab bint Jahsh and A'ishah, the Mothers of the Believers, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except for a husband, (for which it is) four months and ten days." Agreed upon. And from Umm Salamah: "A woman said: O Messenger of Allah! My daughter's husband has died, and her eye has become sore, so may we apply kohl to it? He said: No. He said this every time, twice or three times. Then he said: 'It is only four months and ten. And in the Jahiliyyah, one of you would remain for a year.'" Agreed upon.

And from Nafi': that Safiyyah bint Abd Allah complained of her eye, while she was in mourning for her husband Ibn Umar, and she did not apply kohl until her eyes were nearly crusted. Malik reported it in al-Muwatta.

And from Umm Salamah, she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The woman whose husband has died should not wear dyed clothes of safflower, nor clothes dyed with mashq, nor jewelry, nor dye her hands, nor apply kohl, nor perfume herself." Abu Dawud reported it. Al-Mumashshaqah is what is dyed with mashq, which is ochre (al-maghrah).

Some scholars have deduced the obligation of mourning (al-ihdad) from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves﴾, that is, of adornment and perfume, as we have mentioned. Thus it indicates the prohibition of that during the 'iddah, which is mourning.

As for abstaining from leaving the house in which her husband died: Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan reported on this the hadith of Furay'ah bint Malik, who said: "My husband went out in pursuit of some slaves of his, and he caught up with them at the Road of al-Qudum, and they killed him. The news of his death came to me while I was in a house far from my family's house. So I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. I said: The news of my husband's death came to me while I was in a house far from my family, and he left no provision nor property which I could inherit, and the dwelling is not his. Would it be more convenient for me to move to my family and my brothers, for some of my affairs?" He said: "Move." When I went out toward the mosque or toward the chamber, he called me, or he commanded that I be called, and he said: "Remain in your house in which the news of your husband's death came to you until the Book reaches its term." She said: So I observed the 'iddah there for four months and ten days. In some of its wordings: he sent to her Uthman after that, and she informed him, and he acted upon it. This hadith has been criticized with what does not detract from using it as evidence.

The third: Most jurists hold that this verse abrogates (naskh) what follows it concerning the waiting period of a year, even though it comes earlier in the recitation, for the arrangement of the Mushaf is not according to the order of revelation, but is divinely fixed (tawqifi). Mujahid held that both verses are definitive (muhkamatan), as will be explained.

The fourth: Al-Mahayimi explained the wisdom in fixing the 'iddah of the widow at this measure, saying: So that there does not arise in her heart a conflict between love for the deceased and love for the new suitor. Thus the period of her patience, which is four months, is taken, and ten days are added to it, for with that her patience ends, and she inclines entirely toward the new suitor, so that love for the deceased is severed from her heart. Moreover, the movement of the fetus becomes apparent in the case of the one who has been consummated with, since it occurs after four months, but it begins weakly and grows stronger with the passing of ten more. Then he said: The menstrual cycles, which indicate its absence here, were not relied upon alone, unlike separation during life, because voluntary separation has as its witness its absence along with the witness of the menstrual cycles, so there are two witnesses; here there is only one, and the absence of movement after this period strengthens the testimony of the first, so it is like a witness together with an oath.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 235:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[235] ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at in proposing to women, or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them, but do not promise them in secret, except to say an honorable word. And do not determine upon the marriage contract until the decreed term has reached its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at in proposing to women﴾, meaning: there is no sin upon you, O suitors, in alluding to your proposal to women whose husbands have died, before the end of their waiting period (iddah), so that you may marry them after it has ended. Ta'ridh (allusion) is conveying what is meant by words that were not coined for that meaning, either literally or figuratively. For example, one may say to her: "You are beautiful" or "virtuous," or "there is a man who desires you," or "whoever finds someone like you." Khitbah (proposal), with a kasra on the kha', is the seeking of a woman in marriage. As for "or what you conceal" (aw akננتم): ﴿what you conceal﴾ means what you hold in your hearts of desire to marry them, ﴿within yourselves﴾, meaning in your hearts. Although its ruling is prohibition, let alone allusion by the tongue, Allah has permitted it for you, since ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾, meaning you cannot restrain yourselves from voicing your desire for them. So He granted you leave for allusion rather than explicit statement. There is in this a measure of reproach for lack of self-restraint, like His words: ﴿Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

﴿But do not promise them in secret﴾. This exception follows from His words ﴿for what you hint at﴾. "Sirran" (in secret) is the object of the verb, since the verb carries the meaning of "marriage" (nikah). That is: do not promise them marriage. Or it may mean the opposite of open declaration and public announcement, in which case it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), its implied sense being: "treating that lightly." The object is then omitted, the sense being: "do not promise them marriage in secret." Or it may be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: "a promise made in secret," or the sense may be "in secret," in which case it is an adverbial of place or time (zarf). He forbade this because a promise that involves mention of intercourse and lewd speech between an unrelated man and an unrelated woman is not permitted by consensus (ijma'), just as a promise between them made in secret is not permitted, for such a promise is virtually bound to be a promise of some reprehensible thing.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The community (ummah) has agreed that speaking to a woman in her waiting period with anything that is lewd, such as mention of intercourse or urging toward it, is impermissible. He also said: The community has agreed that promising in the waiting period is disliked for the woman concerning herself, for the father concerning his virgin daughter, and for the master concerning his slave-woman.

As for His words ﴿except to say an honorable word﴾, meaning: a word that one is not ashamed to say in front of anyone among people. The matter thus comes to mean: "Do not promise them anything except what one is not ashamed to mention openly," and that is allusion. This verse therefore explicitly prohibits explicit statement, after the first verse had already implied this, out of concern for it, because of the strong pull of the soul toward it. This is the view of al-Biqa'i.

Al-Razi said: When, at the beginning of the verse, God permitted allusion, and then forbade secret conversation with her in order to prevent suspicion and backbiting, He made an exception for speaking privately in an honorable manner. That is, he may promise her in secret kindness, concern for her affairs, and taking care of her interests, so that the mention of these fine things reinforces that allusion. And God knows best.

(p-617) Note:

What we have mentioned, that His words ﴿but﴾ and what follows are a continuation (istidrak) from His words ﴿for what you hint at﴾, was said by Abu al-Baqa'.

Al-Zamakhshari, however, took the omitted continuation to be implied by ﴿you will remember them﴾, meaning: "So remember them, but do not promise them in secret."

Al-Nasir said: The implication of this stated part for what has been omitted is strengthened, because what is customary in this kind of construction is that permission follows immediately after it. A parallel to this arrangement is His words: ﴿Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187], and so on. There is a secret in this omission, and God knows best: it was avoided because the permission did not extend to mentioning it in general, but was restricted to one aspect of it, and that permitted aspect is hard to distinguish from what is not permitted. So it was mentioned as an exception with His words ﴿except to say an honorable word﴾, to indicate that the domain is narrow, the matter is difficult in it, and the original ruling concerning it is prohibition. This is not the case with intercourse during the nights of fasting, for that was permitted absolutely without restriction. Therefore the discourse began with permission and leniency. The prohibition on intimacy with a woman in seclusion (i'tikaf) in the mosque came after the permission and was mentioned as a consequence of it, because it is a unique state. The prohibition in it was not because of the fast, but the ruling is linked to it in terms of its accompaniment, namely seclusion. So reflect on this secret, for it is one of the wonderful subtleties.

﴿And do not determine upon the marriage contract until the decreed term has reached its end.﴾ ʿUqdah, with a damma on the 'ayn, refers to the marriage contract and to every contract such as sale and the like, namely its binding. Al-Farisi said: it comes from tightening and binding. Al-Razi said: the root meaning of 'aqd is tightening. Covenants and marriages are called ʿuqūd (contracts) because they are tied as a rope is tied. The word "determine" (ta'zimu) is mentioned for emphasis in forbidding the conclusion of the marriage contract, because resolve to act precedes the act. So when He forbids the resolve, He forbids the act all the more. The meaning is: do not resolve upon the binding of marriage, because intending it during the waiting period produces a great stirring from both sides, to the point that patience until the end of the waiting period cannot be sustained.

His words ﴿until the decreed term has reached its end﴾ mean: the prescribed waiting period (al-'iddah al-maktubah al-mafrudah) has reached its last point. ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls﴾, of inclination toward them before the term ends. ﴿So beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving﴾, He forgives that inclination, since the resolve did not exceed the binding of the marriage contract. ﴿Forbearing﴾, He does not hasten punishment. So do not take His delay of it as evidence that what you were forbidden from, namely resolve, is not something that entails accountability...

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[236] ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not yet touched them or specified for them a dowry. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means, a provision according to what is reasonable, an obligation upon the doers of good.﴾

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not yet touched them or specified for them a dowry﴾: (*mā*) is conditional, meaning: if you have not touched them and have not specified for them a dowry. That is, you have not designated for them a *ṣadāq* (bridal gift). Here, (*aw*) is in the sense of (*wa*, "and"). In that case, there is no dowry owed to them, but there is the *mut'a* (a compensatory provision given upon divorce), according to what is reasonable, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and provide for them﴾, meaning: from your wealth, as a consolation for the loneliness of separation. ﴿The wealthy﴾, meaning: the rich one who is in ease because of his wealth. ﴿According to his means﴾ — the vowel of the *dāl* being with sukūn and with fatḥa are two canonically recognized readings (*qirā'atān sab'iyyatān*) — meaning: it is obligatory upon the affluent person to give an amount that befits his affluence. ﴿And the poor﴾, meaning: the straitened one who is in hardship because of his poverty, who is the scant and needy one; it is said *iqtarra* when he becomes poor. ﴿According to his means﴾, meaning: an amount that befits his straitened circumstances. ﴿A provision according to what is reasonable﴾ is an emphasis on {provide for them}, meaning: provide for them a provision according to what is reasonable, that is, in the manner that is commendable. It is not increased to half the customary dowry (*mahr al-mithl*), nor reduced to an amount that is not considered worthwhile. ﴿An obligation﴾, meaning: that this is established firmly. ﴿Upon the doers of good﴾, meaning: the believers, because it substitutes for the dowry. Mentioning them under this designation is an encouragement and an incitement for them to show kindness to the women through the provision. It is considered kindness because its essential purpose is that the woman's soul be content with it, and that her inner state and the inner state of her family remain a peaceful, affectionate bond, perhaps God will bring about something new after that. This was related by al-Harali.

Al-Thawri related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The best of the divorce provision is a servant, and below that is silver, and below that is clothing." And from him: "If he is wealthy, he provides for her with a servant or the like, and if he is poor, he provides for her with three garments."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related that al-Hasan ibn ʿAli, peace be upon them both, provided for a woman with ten thousand (dirhams). The woman said: "It is a little provision from a beloved who is separating."

**A caution:**

Some exegetes have attempted to argue that the expression of negating blame here indicates its affirmation in other cases, even though there is also no blame in it. He strained to answer this, may God forgive him. Yet it is not hidden from you that such an expression is often intended in the revelation to indicate permission and facilitation, just as some have strained by positing a meaning of (*illā*, "except") or (*ḥattā*, "until"), and some have made *ḥaraj* (blame) mean the dowry. The verse is clear in itself and has no need to be pulled by these lines of inquiry. Their turning away from the closer interpretation they followed, namely that (*aw*) means (*wa*), despite its frequent occurrence in many verses, is strange. Even stranger is their rebuking of one who inclines toward this closer interpretation, though what supports it is the context of the verse that follows it.

As for what has been related concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: al-Khazin said: It was revealed concerning "a man from the Ansar who married a woman from Banu Hanifa and did not specify a bridal gift for her, then he divorced her before touching her, so the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ … The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: 'Provide for her, even if it is with your cap.'" If this report is authentic, it would bear witness to what we have adopted. And God knows best.

(p-620)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[237] ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already appointed for them a dowry, then half of what you appointed (is due), unless they forgo it or the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage forgoes it. And that you forgo is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness among yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿And if you divorce them﴾ – i.e., the wives: ﴿before you have touched them﴾, i.e., before you have had intercourse with them. Abu Muslim said: Exalted is He used the expression ﴿touch them﴾ as a euphemism for intercourse, to teach the servants to choose the best words in what they address to one another. ﴿And you have appointed﴾, i.e., named: ﴿for them a dowry﴾, i.e., a specified bridal gift. ﴿Then half of what you appointed﴾, i.e., they are entitled to half of what you named for them of the bridal gift, or it is obligatory upon you to pay that. ﴿Unless they forgo it﴾, i.e., the divorced women forgo it from their husbands, so they do not demand half the bridal gift from them. A woman may say: "He has not seen me, nor have I served him, nor has he enjoyed me, so how could I take anything from him?" ﴿Or the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage forgoes it﴾, which is the husband, so that he gives her the full bridal gift; or it is the guardian, meaning: if she is a minor – or not permitted to manage her affairs – so he gives up her share to the husband.

Malik said in his *Muwatta'* regarding this verse: it is the father concerning his virgin daughter, and the master concerning his slave-woman. Both interpretations are related from a number of the Companions and the Followers.

Al-Harali said: when this statement is linked with His saying, ﴿and do not resolve upon the bond of marriage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235], addressed to the husbands, the explanation that ﴿the one in whose hand is the bond of marriage﴾ is the husband, as a counterpart to the wives, becomes strong; and whoever restricts their forgoing to those who own their affairs – i.e., the mature and competent women – restricts this to the guardians.

Ibn Jarir reported that al-Sha'bi returned to the view that it is the husband, and he used to call people to a mutual curse (mubahalah) upon it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: the view that it is the guardian is apparently correct.

Al-Nasir said in his *Hawashi*: al-Zamakhshari was right that it is an apparently correct view, bearing the radiance of truth and the sweetness of correctness, for six reasons. He set them out with the most subtle exposition, so look at them. And Allah knows best.

(p-621) ﴿And that you forgo is nearer to righteousness﴾. This is addressed to men and women alike, and the masculine form was given precedence in view of its being the more honourable. Ibn Jarir related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "The nearer of the two to righteousness is the one who forgoes," because whoever is generous in giving up his right is a doer of good, and that is the hallmark of righteousness. ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾, i.e., the act of showing favour by kindness, for it brings harmony and good feeling. Thus it is an exhortation to forgo: whoever of the two forgoes has the favour over the other. It is known that forgetting is not within one's capacity such that it could be forbidden, so what is meant is abandonment: do not abandon it in the manner of one who has forgotten. Thus the expression "forget" is more emphatic in the prohibition. The address here too is to both groups by the predominance of the masculine, as in the preceding phrase. Al-Harali restricted it to men, saying:

It is the right of the husband – who has the excellence of manhood – to be the one who forgoes, and that women should not be pressed into forgoing. For this reason no command or incitement is addressed to them. Among the most ugly things is for a man to pressure a woman into taking back what he gave her, which is clearly stated by His saying: ﴿and if you have given one of them a heap of gold, do not take from it anything﴾ [an-Nisa': 20]. So you should not forget that favour, lest you act toward it as if you were not bound by it.

Al-Zamakhshari related from Jubayr ibn Mut'im that he married a woman and divorced her before he had consummated the marriage, so he paid her the full dowry and said: "I have more right to forgo!" And from him: he entered upon Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who offered him one of his daughters, so he married her. When he went out, he divorced her and sent her the full dowry. He was asked: "Why did you marry her?" He said: "He offered her to me, and I disliked refusing him." It was said: "Then why did you send the dowry?" He said: "Where then is the favour?"

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, i.e., your favour and your kindness will not be lost. Since the rights prescribed before this may be hard for some people to uphold, they were commanded with what lightens their burden and makes its fulfilment dear to them, and that is by safeguarding the prayers, for they forbid indecency and wrongdoing. For this reason He, Exalted is He, after what preceded, commanded it with His saying, Glorified is He:

[p. 622]

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[238] ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devout obedience.﴾

﴿Guard strictly the prayers﴾ means: persist in performing them at their appointed times, observing their obligatory and recommended parts, without neglecting any of them.

﴿And the middle prayer﴾ means: "the middle" among the prayers, in the sense of the one in the middle, or the most excellent of them. This is from the usage of calling the most excellent "al-awsat" (the middlemost). On the first sense, the command concerns a prayer situated between two prayers. Which is it: Subh (dawn), Zuhr (midday), 'Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), or 'Isha' (night)? There are reports from the Companions and the Successors (al-tabi'un) on each of these views. On the second sense, it is the prayer of Fitr (the Eid al-Fitr prayer), or Adha (the Eid al-Adha prayer), or the congregational prayer, or the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf), or Friday prayer, or the prayer that is moderate between long and short. These views too are reported from many scholars. The last view is very good, just as it would be if it were said that it is the prayer of humble devotion (dhat al-khushu'), in light of the verse: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2].

As for the scholars of transmission (ʿulamaʾ al-athar), they held that the verse refers to the 'Asr prayer, on the basis of what is in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim) from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and in another narration, on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq): "May God fill their hearts and their houses with fire, as they kept us from the middle prayer until the sun set." And in another narration: "They kept us from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr." He mentioned something similar and added in another version: "Then he prayed it between Maghrib and 'Isha'." Both of them (Bukhari and Muslim) recorded it in the two Sahihs, and the compilers of the Sunan, the Masanid and the Sihah narrated it through chains too lengthy to mention...

Those who held a different view answered this argument by saying that the hadith was not presented as an explanation of the verse so as to specify it; rather, it only reports that it is "middle", and so it is, for it is intermediate and the most excellent of the prayers.

[p. 623]

And what Muslim narrated from Abu Yunus, the freedman of 'A'isha, who said: "'A'isha ordered me to write a copy of the Qur'an for her, and she said: 'When you reach this verse, inform me: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer﴾.' So when I reached it, I informed her, and she dictated to me: 'Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and the prayer of 'Asr, and stand before God in devout obedience.' 'A'isha said: 'I heard it from the Messenger of God ﷺ.'" Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) narrated something similar from Hafsa. Nafi' said: "I read that copy and found the conjunction (waw) in it." Likewise Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr that both of them recited it in this way.

This, from 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, is an indication of what she understood by "the middle" (al-wusta). She joined the interpretation (ta'wil) to the revealed text (tanzil) in order to avoid confusion about it, because the Qur'an is transmitted by mass transmission (mutawatir), and it is secure from having anything added or removed. At the beginning of the era of its abrogation (naskh), some Companions may have appended an explanation to it, or a variant reading which they recited. That is why, when 'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, feared that people would doubt whether it was part of the revelation, although it was not part of it, he ordered that the copies of the Qur'an in his time be purged of what had been added to them of interpretation and of the variant readings that some Companions had uniquely held, and that only what was transmitted by mass transmission and received from the Prophet ﷺ be kept.

Al-Qadi Abu Bakr said in al-Intisar: "'Uthman did not intend what Abu Bakr intended in collecting the whole of the Qur'an between two covers. He intended only to unite them upon the established readings known from the Prophet ﷺ, to discard what was not so, and to have them adopt a copy with no advancing or delaying, no interpolated explanation within the revelation, and no text whose recitation was abrogated, written alongside what is confirmed in its script and obligatory in its recitation and memorization, lest corruption and doubt enter upon those who came after..."

Furthermore, the scholars of transmission have supported their view that it is the prayer of 'Asr, on the grounds that it was singled out for special emphasis, an explicit command to observe it, and a severe warning against neglecting it.
