Abu al-Malih said: "We were with Buraydah on a military campaign, and on a cloudy day he said: 'Hasten the 'Asr prayer, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever abandons the 'Asr prayer, his deed has come to nothing."'" Al-Bukhari recorded it. His words "Hasten the 'Asr prayer" mean: perform it early, at the beginning of its time.

[p. 624]

Al-Shaykhan (Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The one who misses the 'Asr prayer is as if he has been bereft of his family and his wealth!" That is: he is diminished and deprived of his family and his wealth, so that he remains alone, having lost both. The meaning: let him be as watchful against missing the 'Asr prayer as he is against losing his family and his wealth.

The Hafiz 'Abd al-Mu'min al-Dimyati, in his book Kashf al-Mughatta fi Tabyin al-Salat al-Wusta, cited the distinctive features and virtues that the 'Asr prayer possesses. He said, may God have mercy on him:

Among them: the Messenger of God ﷺ made the calamity of missing it grave, by equating it with the loss of family and wealth in the hadith mentioned above.

Among them: the nullification of the deed of one who abandons it and neglects it, in the same earlier hadith.

Among them: it was dearer to them than their own selves, their fathers, their children, their families and their wealth.

Among them: the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever preserves it will have its reward twice." Narrated by Muslim.

Among them: waiting for it after Friday prayer is like an 'Umrah (lesser pilgrimage), narrated by Abu Ya'la. And al-Hakim narrated: "Like one who performs Hajj and 'Umrah."

Among them: the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Three whom God will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify, nor look upon, and theirs is a painful punishment... – and he went on to say – and a man who displays his merchandise after 'Asr and swears by God that he took it for such-and-such a price, when another man believes him and buys it." Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim). Then he said: I say: God has magnified the oaths that servants swear regarding what they dispute after it, saying: ﴿You shall detain them after the prayer, and they will swear by God﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 106].

The majority of the exegetes (ʿamm al-mufassirin) said: "After the 'Asr prayer." For this reason the scholars made the oath of li'an (mutual imprecation) and all other grave oaths to be taken at the time of 'Asr, because of its nobility and distinction.

Among them: Sulayman, peace be upon him, destroyed a great quantity of horses when their parading distracted him from the 'Asr prayer until the sun set. God praised him for that and commended him, saying: ﴿An excellent servant, indeed he was ever turning (to God)﴾ [Sad: 30]. ﴿When there were displayed before him at evening the swift steeds﴾ [Sad: 31], and the rest of the verse.

Among them: it has been said that the hour on Friday is after 'Asr.

Among them: its time is the time when deeds are raised.

[p. 626]

Among them: the raised hadith: "God, exalted is He, reveals to the two angels: Do not record a sin against My servant who is fasting after 'Asr."

Among them: what is in the words of the Exalted: ﴿By time (al-'asr)﴾ [al-'Asr: 1], ﴿indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2].

Muqatil said: "al-'Asr is the middle prayer, by which He swore." Ibn 'Atiyyah related it.

Among them: what has been reported in the hadith: "The angels line up every day after 'Asr, and they record it in the lowest heaven. Then the angel calls out: 'Cast away that page!' He says: 'By Your might, I have recorded only what he did.' God, mighty and majestic, says: 'He did not intend it for My Face.' And He calls the other angel: 'Record for so-and-so such-and-such.' The angel says: 'By Your might, he did not do that.' God, mighty and majestic, says: 'He intended it.'"

Among them: its time is generally the time when people are occupied with their trades and livelihoods.

The discussion of the interpretation of this verse has been devoted to separate works. Al-'Allamah al-Fasi, the commentator of the Qamus, mentioned, as transmitted from him by al-Zabidi, that the views on it exceeded forty. May God be pleased with the diligent scholars and content them.

After reflection, there occurred to me, at the end of Ramadan in the year 1323, and it grew stronger, the possibility that God's words ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ after ﴿Guard strictly the prayers﴾ are a guidance and command to guard the performance of the prayer in a moderate manner, neither overlong and tiresome nor so brief as to be deficient. That is: "and the prayer that is moderate between length and brevity." This is supported by the hadiths narrated from him ﷺ on this, in word and in deed.

Then there came to my attention, in the Qamus, on the 23rd of Rabi' al-Awwal in the year 1324, a report of this as an opinion. Under the root w-s-t, it cited the views on the verse, among them his words: "or the one moderate between length and brevity." Its commentator al-Zabidi said: "This view was rejected by Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr (al-Muhit)."

[p. 627]

Then there occurred to me another possibility: that God's words ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ are intended to describe the prayer that was commanded to be guarded as being excellent, that is, possessing great merit with God. Thus "al-wusta" means "al-fudla" (the most excellent), from the usage of calling the most excellent "al-awsat." Placing the conjunction (waw) between the attribute and the qualified noun is something al-Zamakhshari verified, and he supported it with many verses. In introducing the attribute in this manner there is evident emphasis on the qualified noun. The style of the Qur'an is a unique style in the domain of eloquence, of whose wonders only a drop of the sea has been opened. Perhaps this aspect is what those who said "they are the five prayers" had in mind, and that is Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may God be pleased with him. It is as if he indicated that the conjoined item is the same as the item to which it is conjoined, except that it is expressed with a phrase that conveys description.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿and stand before God﴾ in prayer: ﴿in devout obedience﴾, meaning humbly and in silence. The two Shaykhs narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam: "We used to speak during the prayer, one of us would speak to his companion about his need, until this was revealed: ﴿Guard strictly the prayers, and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devout obedience﴾, and we were commanded to be silent." This is the wording of Bukhari. The wording of Muslim, from Zayd ibn Arqam, is: "We used to speak in the prayer; a man would speak to his companion who was beside him in the prayer, until this was revealed: ﴿and stand before God in devout obedience﴾, and we were commanded to be silent and forbidden to speak."

Abu Ya'la narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "We used to greet one another in the prayer. I passed by the Messenger of God ﷺ and greeted him, but he did not return my greeting. It occurred to me that something had been revealed concerning me. When the Prophet ﷺ had finished his prayer, he said: 'And upon you be peace, O Muslim, and the mercy of God. Indeed God renews His command as He wills. When you are in prayer, be devoutly obedient (uqnutu) and do not speak.'"

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, Imam Ahmad, and Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili in their two Musnads, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, narrated from Abu Sa'id, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every instance of the word 'qunut' mentioned in the Qur'an means obedience."

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[239] ﴿And if you fear, then [pray] on foot or while riding. And when you are secure, remember Allah as He has taught you what you did not know.﴾

﴿And if you fear﴾ means: if there is a fear of an enemy or other than that for you. ﴿On foot﴾ means: pray while walking on foot, i.e., going on your feet. It is said: rajila (as in fariha) — so he is râjil (on foot); rajula (with a ḍammah on the jīm), rajila (with a kasrah), and rajala (with a fatḥah); and rajīl and rajlān, when one has no mount on a journey and so walks on his feet. The plural is rijāl, rajjālah, and rujjāl (like rummān). ﴿Or riding﴾ means: mounted. Thus, the excess of movements, completing the bowing and prostration, and facing the qiblah are excused. This is among the concessions (rukhaṣ) of Allah Exalted, which He granted to His servants, and among His lifting of the burdens and shackles from them. The prayer of fear has been related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in various detailed forms in the books of Sunnah, because he ﷺ would seek in every situation what was most cautious for the prayer and most effective for guarding.

Al-Rāzī said: The prayer of fear has two types:

The first: that it takes place during fighting — and this is what is meant by this verse.

The second: outside of the state of fighting, and this is what is mentioned in Surat al-Nisā' in His words, Exalted: ﴿And when you are among them and establish prayer for them, let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisā': 102].

Mālik related from Nāfi': that Ibn ʿUmar, when asked about the prayer of fear, would describe it, then say: "If the fear is greater than that, they pray on foot or riding, facing the qiblah or not facing it."

Nāfi' said: "I do not think Ibn ʿUmar mentioned that except from the Prophet ﷺ." It was narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhārī and Muslim).

Also in Muslim, from Ibn ʿUmar, he said: "If the fear is greater than that, then pray riding or standing, making gestures with the head."

Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd narrated, with a good chain, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Unays al-Juhanī, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent me to Khālid ibn Sufyān al-Hudhalī — who was near ʿUranah and ʿArafāt — and said: 'Go and kill him.' He said: I saw him — and the time of the ʿAṣr prayer came — and I said: 'Indeed I fear that between me and him there is what would make me delay the prayer.' So I set off walking while praying, making gestures with my head toward him. When I drew near to him, he said to me: 'Who are you?' I said: 'A man of the Arabs who has heard that you are gathering against this man, so I came to you about that.' He said: 'Indeed I am engaged in that.' So I walked with him for a while, until when I had the opportunity, I struck him with my sword until he was cooled." This is the wording of Abū Dāwūd.

Al-Ṭayālisī, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Abū Yaʿlā and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of the Trench, and we were occupied from the Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib and ʿIshā' prayers until we were relieved of that. That is His words: ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 25]. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered Bilāl, and he gave the iqāmah for each prayer, and that was before the revelation of: ﴿And if you fear, then [pray] on foot or while riding.﴾"

Note:

This verse has stated "fear" in an unrestricted way, so it includes any fear of an enemy, a beast, or a charging camel, and this is the view of the majority. The view of al-Wāfī and some of the Ẓāhirites is anomalous: that the fear is specific to being from a human being. This verse indicates that performing it with gestures is their obligation, so there is no qaḍāʾ upon them after security is restored. In al-Tahdhīb, he said, contrary to what some of them say: but this applies if they do something that is called prayer; if none of the movements is possible for them, and they only performed remembrance (dhikr) alone. Then al-Nāṣir Zayd, Ibn Abī al-Fawāris and Abū Jaʿfar said: this is not called prayer, so making up is obligatory. Al-Rāḍī bi-llāh and al-Amīr al-Ḥusayn said: it is part of the prayer, so there is no qaḍāʾ, due to His Messenger's ﷺ saying: "If I order you to do something, then do of it what you are able." And when the concession is established in this prayer — by abandoning the full obligations — the concession also extends to doing what is needed, and to wearing what contains impurity if needed. So it is in the tafsīr of some scholars of the Zaydiyyah.

﴿And when you are secure﴾ means: when your fear has gone: ﴿remember Allah﴾ means: pray the prayer of security. It is expressed by "remembrance" because it is the greatest of its pillars. His words: ﴿as He has taught you what you did not know﴾ mean: like what He taught you of the prayer of security, or for the sake of His blessing upon you, so the kāf is for causation. This verse is like His words, Exalted: ﴿So when you are secure, establish the prayer. Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ [al-Nisā': 103]. The benefit of mentioning the object here, although a person knows only what he did not know, is to make explicit the state of ignorance from which they moved, for it is clearer in expressing the favor.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[240] ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind: a bequest for their wives, provision for a year without their being turned out. But if they leave, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

﴿Those of you who die﴾, i.e., who are taken (in death) from among your men. ﴿And leave﴾, i.e., they relinquish. ﴿Wives﴾ after death. ﴿A bequest for their wives﴾: the predicate of (alladhina, "those who") is ﴿a bequest﴾, i.e., they make a bequest, or let them make a bequest, or Allah has prescribed for them a bequest. (p-632) In another reading in the nominative, the meaning is: a bequest is incumbent upon them for their wives regarding their property. ﴿Provision for a year﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿a bequest﴾ according to the reading of whoever put it in the accusative. According to the nominative reading, it is in the accusative by ﴿bequest﴾ or by its verb. ﴿Without their being turned out﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) for ﴿their wives﴾, i.e., not expelled. The meaning: it is obligatory for the one who dies to make a bequest before the approach of death for his wives, that they be provided for after him for a year, with maintenance and lodging, without leaving their husband's dwelling. ﴿But if they leave﴾ the marital home of their own accord, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, i.e., upon the guardians of the deceased, ﴿for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾, that which the Law does not reject, such as adorning themselves, using perfume, abandoning mourning, and presenting themselves to suitors. This indicates that what is forbidden is her being expelled when she wishes to remain, and her staying in the husband's dwelling and observing mourning, without its being obligatory for her; and that she has a choice between remaining while taking maintenance and leaving while forgoing it. ﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

Then it should be known that the choice of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) is that this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by the preceding one, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They shall wait, keeping themselves, for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. They said: At the beginning of Islam, the ruling was that when a man died, his wife observed a waiting period (iddah) of one year; it was forbidden for the heir to expel her from the house before the year was complete; her maintenance and lodging were obligatory from her husband's property for that year; she had no share of the inheritance; but she had a choice. If she wished, she observed the waiting period in her husband's house, with maintenance and lodging; and if she wished, she left before the year was complete, with no maintenance or lodging. It was obligatory upon the man to make a bequest concerning this. This verse therefore indicates two things together: first, that she has maintenance and lodging from her husband's property for a year; and second, that she has a waiting period of one year. Then both of these rulings were abrogated.

(p-633) As for the bequest of maintenance and lodging, it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, so a quarter or an eighth was assigned to her in place of the maintenance and lodging. The one-year waiting period was abrogated by four months and ten days.

Al-Bukhari related from Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: I said to Uthman ibn Affan: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾ has been abrogated by the other verse, so why do you write it or leave it? He said: O nephew! I will not change anything of it from its place.

Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i reported from Ibn Abbas that he said concerning this verse: It was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, by what Allah prescribed for them of the quarter and the eighth; and the term of the year was abrogated by making their term four months and ten days.

This is so. Mujahid held that this verse is established (muhkam) like the first. Al-Bukhari reported it from him. Mujahid said: The first verse, namely ﴿They shall wait, keeping themselves, for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234], indicates that this is her prescribed waiting period, which she observes in the household of her husband. This verse, by adding seven months and twenty nights to the previous waiting period to complete a year, indicates that this belongs to the category of a bequest concerning wives, that they be enabled to reside in their husbands' houses after their death for a full year, and not be prevented from this, by His saying: ﴿without their being turned out﴾. When their waiting period has ended with the four months and ten days, or with the delivery of the child, and they choose to leave and move from that dwelling, they are not prevented from this, by His saying: ﴿But if they leave﴾, etc. Imam Ibn Kathir said: This view has a sound direction, and the wording supports it. A group of scholars has chosen it, among them Imam Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah.

Among them is Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, who said: The meaning of the verse is: whoever of you dies and leaves wives behind, (p-634) and they have made a bequest for their wives of a year's maintenance and a year's lodging; then if they leave before that and oppose the husband's bequest after they have remained the period which Allah the Exalted set for them, there is no blame: ﴿for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾, i.e., a valid marriage, because their remaining under this bequest is not binding. He said: The reason is that in the time of the Jahiliyyah they made bequests of a full year's maintenance and lodging, and the woman was obliged to observe the year's waiting period. So Allah the Exalted made clear in this verse that this is not obligatory. He supported his view with arguments which al-Fakhr al-Razi related from him, up to where he said: So turning to the view of Mujahid was more preferable than adopting abrogation without evidence. Then he said: When you know this, we say: this verse, from its beginning to its end, is one single conditional sentence. The condition is His saying: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, a bequest for their wives, provision for a year without their being turned out﴾, all of this is the condition, and the consequent is His saying: ﴿But if they leave, there is no blame upon you﴾, etc. This is al-Razi's exposition of Abu Muslim's view.

Al-Razi said: It is in the utmost soundness, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 241:

The discussion of His, the Exalted's, saying:

[241] ﴿And for divorced women there is provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the God-conscious (al-muttaqun).﴾

﴿And for divorced women there is provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the God-conscious.﴾ That is: for divorced women there is a consolation (mut'ah) from the husband, to the extent possible, as a remedy for the desolation of separation. As for the dower (mahr), it is the right of the intimate relation (al-bud').

Ibn Kathir said: Scholars who held that a consolation payment (mut'ah) is obligatory for every divorced woman have taken evidence from this verse, whether she was one for whom no dower had been specified (mufawwadah), or one for whom a dower had been fixed (mafrudun laha), or one divorced before consummation (qabl al-masis), or one who had been consummated with (madkhulun biha).

This was the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others among the early generation (al-salaf), and Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) chose it.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: Every believing woman who is divorced, free or slave, has a consolation payment. And he recited the verse.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah that he said: "When Hafs ibn al-Mughirah divorced his wife Fatimah, she came (p-635) to the Prophet ﷺ. He said to her husband: 'Give her a consolation payment.' He said: 'I do not have anything to give her as a consolation payment.' He said: 'There must indeed be a provision; give her even half a sa' of dates.'"

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Qatadah that he said: A man divorced his wife in the presence of Shurayh, and Shurayh said to him: "Give her a consolation payment!" The woman said: "There is no consolation payment due to me from him. Allah, the Exalted, only said: ﴿And for divorced women there is provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the God-conscious﴾ {And for divorced women there is provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the good-doers}. He is not among those!"

Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Shurayh that he said to a man who had separated from his wife: "Do not refuse to be among the God-conscious. Do not refuse to be among the good-doers."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 242:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[242] ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may understand.﴾

﴿Thus﴾ means: like that clear explanation (al-bayan al-shafi). ﴿Allah makes clear to you﴾ in all situations ﴿His signs﴾, which indicate His rulings. ﴿That you may understand﴾ means: so that you may comprehend what they contain and act in accordance with their implications.

## On the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[243] ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, being thousands, fearing death? So Allah said to them, "Die," and then He gave them life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾

﴿Have you not considered those who left﴾ meaning: from among those nations who preceded you. ﴿from their homes﴾ meaning: the homes they were accustomed to, because of what befell them there of death, which they had no power to withstand. The phrase ﴿Have you not considered﴾ may be used for someone whose knowledge is already established, and then it serves to express wonder, affirmation and reminder, as with the rabbis and the people of history. It may also be used for someone for whom this is not the case, and then it serves to inform him and to make him marvel.

Al-Raghib said: "ra'aytu" (I saw) is transitive without a preposition, but when "a-lam tara" was used in the sense of "a-lam tanzur" (have you not looked), it was made to take the preposition "ila" (to). The purpose of this borrowing is that looking (nazar) may be an approach to seeing (ru'ya). So when one wishes to urge a look that inevitably results in seeing, the expression is borrowed for it. This usage is rarely found outside affirmation, so one does not say "ra'aytu ila kadha" (I saw to such-and-such).

﴿being thousands﴾ meaning: in number. It is the plural of "alf" (thousand). Or it means ﴿being gathered together and united﴾, the plural of "ali'" (one who is united), with the long vowel, like "shahid" and "shuhud" (witness and witnesses). That is, their departure was not the result of any division or mutual hatred among them. Rather, ﴿fearing death﴾ is a verbal object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: fleeing from it.

His words ﴿So Allah said to them, "Die"﴾ mean: so He caused them to die. This expression was used to indicate that they died as one man's death by the command and will of Allah. That will is beyond the ordinary course, as though they were commanded to do something and they obeyed without refusal or hesitation, like His saying: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82].

﴿Then He gave them life﴾ is a conjunction. It is either linked to an implied element demanded by the context, meaning: "so they died, then He gave them life." It was omitted to indicate that it needs no mention, because it is impossible for His intended purpose, exalted is He, to fail to follow His will. Or it is linked to "said", since the command to die is itself an expression of causing death. ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ in its entirety. As for those people, He gave them life so that they might take warning from what befell them and thereby attain happiness. As for those who heard their story, He guided them to the path of reflection and insight. So He has bestowed favour upon all of them, that they might give thanks to Him. ﴿But most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ meaning: they do not give thanks for His favour as it ought to be given.

**Note:**

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that this verse refers to a large multitude who left their homes fleeing from jihad in the way of Allah. Allah caused them to die, then gave them life and commanded them to fight their enemy. So the verse was mentioned as a preparation for the command to fight that follows it, in His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 244].

[p. 637] It is well known that Surat al-Baqarah was among what was revealed in Madinah after the Hijrah, before the conquest of Makkah. The enemy was in Makkah and its surroundings in great number, strength and power. So the Muslim emigrants and those who sheltered them were commanded to fight in the way of Allah. He related to them from the news of past peoples what would incite them to jihad and give them good tidings of victory and the good outcome, even if they were in few numbers and weakness, so long as they held firmly to the rope of unity, patience and perseverance.

Some narrators have held that this verse refers to what is recounted in the Torah about Hizqil (Ezekiel), one of the prophets of the Children of Israel: that he was inspired to go out to a vast wilderness filled with dry bones of the dead of the Children of Israel, and to call upon them by His name, exalted is He. They began to draw together, then were clothed with flesh. Then he called their spirits, and they returned to their bodies, and they stood up alive on their feet by His command, exalted is He. They were a very great army. It was revealed to Hizqil that they would return to their homeland after they had been expelled from it. This story is set out at length in their Torah, in the thirty-seventh chapter of the prophecy of Hizqil.

Among those from whom it is reported that this verse refers to the account of Hizqil are Wahb ibn Munabbih, Ash'ath ibn Aslam al-Basri, al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, al-Suddi, Hilal ibn Yisaf and others. Ibn Jarir transmitted it from them. If this report is authentic, then this would be one of the miracles of Hizqil, in the raising of the dead for him, just as the dead were raised for ʿIsa, peace be upon him. His people would see what would prevent them from despairing of fighting their enemy, so that they might regain their homeland from which their enemy had expelled them, since Hizqil was among those exiled to Babylon. They said: his prophecy contains the decree sent down upon the Children of Israel and the glad tidings of deliverance that follows that decree.

Ibn Kathir transmitted from ʿAta' that he said about this verse: "It is a parable." Perhaps his meaning is: it is a parable of Allah's creating a strong nation that overpowers, prevails and governs others after reaching the utmost weakness and obscurity. Its life and death would then be an illustration of its two states, before and after. This would be an indication of what the Arabs would become, in great strength and lofty civilization, and an alert that attaining this comes only through striving against wrongdoers and the unity of the righteous in crushing the domineering tyrants. And Allah knows best.

[p. 638] Furthermore, there is no doubt that the events of the Israelites which are recounted were known in general, owing to the Jews' long association with the Arabs over many centuries.

Shah Waliyullah al-Dihlawi said in *al-Fawz al-Kabir*: "In His revelation, exalted is He, He chose from the Days of Allah, meaning: the events which Allah, exalted is He, brought about, such as the bestowing of favour upon the obedient and the punishment of the disobedient, what reached their hearing, and He mentioned to them in general terms stories such as those of the people of Nuh, ʿAd and Thamud, which the Arabs received from one generation to another, and stories such as those of our master Ibrahim and the prophets of the Children of Israel, for these were familiar to their ears because of the Jews' association with the Arabs over many centuries. He drew from the well-known stories sentences that would benefit them in reminding them, and He did not narrate the stories in full with all their particulars. The wisdom in this is that when the common people hear stories that are extremely rare, or when details are excessively emphasized before them, they become inclined to the stories themselves, and the remembrance which is the principal purpose of them escapes them. A parallel to this statement is what one of the knowers said: when people memorized the rules of tajwid (the rules of correct Qur'anic recitation), they were preoccupied from humility in recitation."

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His, exalted is He, saying:**

[244] ﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

The exegetes said: The command to fight following the preceding narrative is evidence that it was brought as an incitement to jihad (striving in the way of Allah). So He urged jihad after informing them that fleeing from death does not avail, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who said of their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed." Say, "Avert from yourselves death, if you should be truthful."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 168]. The root meaning of sabil (way) is the path, and striving was called a way to Allah, exalted is He, because a person travels along it and reaches Allah through it, so that he may be enabled to manifest His worship, spread the call to His monotheism, protect its people, and defend the truth and its people. Thus fighting is a defence in the way of Allah to remove general harm, which is the prevention of the truth and the support of polytheism, through training those who seduce people away from their religion and break their covenants, not for the sake of the soul's portions and its desires, nor out of an addiction to loving bloodshed and taking lives, nor for the sake of the pursuit of gain. In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is an incitement to sincerity of intention and purity of purpose. As in the two Sahihs (Bukhari and Muslim), on the authority of Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about a man who fights out of bravery, fights out of zeal, and fights out of showing off: which of these is in the way of Allah? He said: 'Whoever fights so that the word of Allah is supreme, he is in the way of Allah.'"

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[245] ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and extends (provision), and to Him you will be returned.﴾

﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾ — This is an exhortation from Allah, exalted is He, to His servants to give charity, and He, exalted is He, has repeated this verse in His Mighty Book in more than one place.

Al-Qurtubi said: The request for a loan in this verse is a rebuke and a bringing-near to people in terms they can understand. Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy. Yet He, exalted is He, has likened His giving to the believers, and their spending in this world for which they hope for its reward in the Hereafter, to a loan. Just as He has likened the giving of souls and wealth in exchange for Paradise to buying and selling, as will be explained in Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba). Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has spoken of the poor by means of His own exalted Self, which is free from needs, to encourage charity, just as He has spoken of the sick, the hungry, and the thirsty by means of His sacred Self. In the authentic hadith, reporting from Allah, exalted is He: "O son of Adam! I was ill and you did not visit Me. I asked you for food and you did not feed Me. I asked you for drink and you did not give Me drink." He said: "O my Lord! How could I feed You when You are the Lord of the worlds?" He said: "My servant so-and-so asked you for drink and you did not give him drink. Had you given him drink, you would have found that with Me." And likewise in what precedes it. Narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). All of this comes in the form of honouring the one spoken of by means of a figure of speech, as an encouragement to the one addressed.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani and others related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When this verse was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah al-Ansari said: O Messenger of Allah! Does Allah truly want a loan from us? He said: 'Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah.' He said: Show me your hand, O Messenger of Allah! So he gave him his hand. He said: Then I have lent my orchard to my Lord (and he had an orchard in which there were six hundred palm trees, and Umm al-Dahdah and his family lived in it). Abu al-Dahdah came and called out: O Umm al-Dahdah! She said: At your service. He said: Come out, for I have lent it to my Lord, Mighty and Majestic. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He has accepted it from you.' The Prophet ﷺ then gave it to the orphans who were in his care. The Prophet ﷺ would say: 'How many a cluster of dates belonging to Abu al-Dahdah hangs down in Paradise!' And in another narration: 'How many a cluster...'" etc.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿a goodly loan﴾ means: one whose soul is content with it, without reminder or harm.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿so that He may multiply it for him many times over﴾, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqara: 261]. When He, glorified is He, encouraged lending to Him, He followed it with a sentence that instils both fear and hope, saying: ﴿And Allah withholds and extends﴾, meaning: He restricts provision for whom He wills of His servants and extends it for others. That is: do not be stingy with Him regarding what He has extended to you, lest He replace the abundance you have with constriction.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, when He will recompense you.

Al-Mahayimi said: How can the extending and withholding of Allah be denied, He who gives the poor dominion and strips it from its people, who strengthens the weak of a small group and weakens the strong of a large group? That is, as He related in His words:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[246] ﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of God." He said, "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?" They said, "And what reason do we have not to fight in the way of God, when we have been driven out of our homes and from our children?" But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿Have you not considered the eminent men﴾, that is, the people of rank and assembly. ﴿Of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs﴾. He was left indefinite (nukkira) because there was no requirement for specifying him. The People of the Book (al-Kitabiyyun) claimed that he was Samuel. ﴿"Appoint for us a king"﴾, that is, set up for us a commander. ﴿"that we may fight"﴾, that is, under his command. ﴿"in the way of God"﴾. This was when the Amalekites, the people of Goliath (Jalut), had prevailed over much of their land. ﴿He said﴾ to them, their prophet: ﴿"Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?"﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: The predicate of ʿasaitum (ʿasaytum, "perhaps you") is "alla tuqatilu" (that you not fight), and the condition separates the two. The meaning is: "Have you come close to not fighting?" That is, "Is the matter as I expect, that you will not fight?" He intended to say "ʿasaitum alla tuqatilu" in the sense of "I expect your cowardice in fighting," so he introduced hal as an interrogative about what he expects and suspects. By the interrogation he meant affirmation (taqrir), and confirming that what he expects is certain and that his expectation is correct, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there come upon man﴾ [al-Insan: 1], meaning affirmation. It is read as ʿasaitum with a kasra on the sin, but this reading is weak.

﴿They said, "And what reason do we have not to fight in the way of God"﴾, that is, what cause do we have for leaving the fight against our enemy? ﴿"when we have been driven out of our homes and from our children"﴾, that is, while the situation has already arisen which strongly requires fighting: the seizing of our lands and the capture of our children. ﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them﴾ after their insistence in requesting it, ﴿they turned away﴾, that is, they withdrew from fighting their enemy out of cowardice. ﴿except for a few of them. And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: a warning to them for their wrongdoing in turning away from fighting, abandoning jihad, and disobeying His command, exalted is He.

One of the exegetes of the Zaydiyya said: The fruit of this noble verse is that it indicates several rulings:

The first: the obligation of jihad, because God, exalted is He, mentioned this well-known story about the Children of Israel and what befell them as a warning against following their path. Also: the laws of those before us bind us.

The second: that a commander is needed in matters of jihad to manage their affairs. The Prophet (ﷺ) "used to appoint a commander over a detachment whenever he sent one out." Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf (the Qur'anic commentary by al-Zamakhshari): It is also related that he commanded people, when they travelled, to make one of them their commander.

The third: the obligation to obey the commander in matters of policy and the management of war, because the context of the verse requires this. In a hadith from him (ﷺ): "Obey the commander, even if he is an Abyssinian slave." The scholars of the science of conduct (ʿilm al-muʿamala, the science of ethical conduct) have mentioned that on journeys it is fitting for the travelling people to appoint for themselves a commander, a guide and a leader, and this is praiseworthy, since by it disputes are ended and their affairs are organized. The same applies to every matter that requires repeated consultation of opinions, such as the affairs of endowments (awqaf), mosques, the imamate for each mosque, and the like.

Al-Hakim said: In it is evidence that the prophets had the right to impose strict covenants and pledges concerning what is binding upon them. The reason for this is that he said, "Would you perhaps...", and this is a kind of emphasis upon them. Likewise, the analogy of what al-Hakim mentioned concerning the prophet applies to the imam.

**The explanation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[247] ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent Saul (Talut) to you as king." They said, "How can he have kingship over us while we are more deserving of kingship than he, and he has not been given a abundance of wealth?" He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him in knowledge and physical stature. And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing."﴾

(p. 644) ﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent Saul to you as king"﴾ This begins a detailed account of what passed between him, peace be upon him, and them of words and deeds, following the general indication of the outcome of their situation. That is: he said to them (after what had been revealed to him was revealed), "Indeed, Allah has sent Saul to you as king," meaning: He has made him king over you, so refer the management of the war to his command. Saul was from a tribe in which kingship had not existed. "Saul" (Ṭālūt) is a non-Arabic name, like Goliath (Jālūt) and David (Dāwūd), and therefore it is not declined. Some people claimed that it is Arabic, from "height" (al-ṭūl), because of his described physical stature. But it is not of the Arabic morphological patterns, so its non-declension is due to being a proper noun and resemblance to non-Arabic. The People of the Book claimed that Saul is the one known among them as Shaul. ﴿They said﴾ objecting to their Prophet, or rather to Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"How can he have kingship over us"﴾ meaning: from where, or how, can that be? ﴿"while we are more deserving of kingship than he"﴾ meaning: because among us are those who are of the royal lineage, rather than him.

Al-Harālī (al-Harali) said: They doubled their objection with something more severe, which is boasting about their claim to deserve kingship over the one whom Allah had made king over them. There was in this a share of the pride of Iblis, when he said, when he was commanded to prostrate to Adam: ﴿"I am better than him"﴾ [Ṣād: 76].

﴿"and he has not been given an abundance of wealth"﴾ meaning: so he had two obstacles:

First: that he was not from the house of kingship.

Second: that he was poor, and a king must have wealth to rely upon.

Al-Harālī said: In this third point there was the trial of idolizing wealth, and that it is something by which kingship is established, whereas kingship is only by the granting of Allah. Thus in this third trial there was ignorance and polytheism, and the forms of their trial multiplied in what they were moved to seek from themselves.

﴿He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him in knowledge and physical stature."﴾ When they considered it unlikely that he would rule because of the lowliness of his lineage and his poverty, he answered them, first: that the criterion of the matter is the choosing of Allah, the Exalted, and He has chosen him over you, and He knows the interests better than you. Second: that the essential thing in it is abundance of knowledge, so that he may be able through it to know the matters of governance, and the largeness of body so that his weight may be great in hearts and he may be able to withstand enemies and endure wars. Allah, the Exalted, has given him a full share of both. So said Abū al-Su'ūd.

﴿"And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills"﴾ in this world, without inheritance or wealth; since nothing is required of the right of Allah, the Exalted, He is the Doer of what He wills. ﴿"And Allah is all-Encompassing"﴾ He widens (provision) for the poor and makes them rich. ﴿"Knowing"﴾ of who is fit for kingship and who is not. The stating of the Glorious Name here is to cultivate awe.

Some of the exegetes of the Zaydiyya said: The fruit of the verse is that prophethood and imamate are not earned by inheritance, and that wealth and freedom from lowly crafts are not conditions for an emir, an imam, or a judge. That is, because it is related that Saul was a tanner or a water-carrier with his poverty. Al-Ḥākim said: Thus the view of the Imamiyya that it is an inheritance is refuted, whereas what is well known from them is that the imamate is established by explicit designation (naṣṣ). The verse also indicates that an emir and the like must have the strength for what he undertakes, so that he is sound of defects and knowledgeable about what he needs, because Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the abundance in knowledge and body as a refutation of what they considered.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[248] ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of His kingship is that the chest (tabut) will come to you, in which is tranquillity (sakinah) from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."﴾

﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign"﴾, i.e., the indication, ﴿"of His kingship"﴾, that it is from God, exalted is He, ﴿"is that the chest will come to you"﴾, i.e., God will return to you the chest that was taken from you, and it is the chest of the Torah, as we will mention; ﴿"in it is tranquillity from your Lord"﴾, i.e., dignity, majesty and awe; or, in it is the calm of the souls of the Children of Israel, by which they strengthen themselves for ﴿war﴾; ﴿"and a remnant"﴾, i.e., the leftover of a whole, most of which has gone; ﴿"of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind"﴾, i.e., of their excellent relics; ﴿"carried by the angels. Indeed, in that"﴾, i.e., in the returning of the chest to you, ﴿"is a sign for you"﴾ that His kingship is from God, exalted is He; ﴿"if you are believers"﴾ in the signs of God and His prophets.

Al-'Allamah al-Biqa'i, may God have mercy on him, said: The tabut, and God knows best, is the chest in which were placed the two tablets on which the Ten Commandments were written. It is called the Tabut al-Shahadah (the Chest of Testimony). Whenever they went to war, a group of them who were appointed to carry it would bear it and go before the army, and this would be the cause of their victory. When the Amalekites, the companions of Goliath (Jalut), overcame them, they took it along with the other precious things they seized from them, and their long time without it had passed. So he (the prophet) reminded them of its virtues, to encourage them toward it and to move them to submit to Talut (Saul). So he said: ﴿"in it is tranquillity"﴾, and so on.

In the fifth chapter of the twenty-fifth book of Exodus, the text reads:

1 * And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

2 * Speak to the children of Israel, that they bring Me an offering; from everyone whose heart moves him you shall take My offering.

3 * And this is the offering which you shall take from them: gold, silver and bronze;

4 * blue, purple and scarlet, fine linen and goats' hair; (5) rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins and acacia wood; * 6 * oil for the lamp, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense; * 7 * onyx stones, and setting stones for the ephod and the breastplate. * 8 * And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them. * 9 * According to all that I show you, the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings, just so you shall make it.

10 * They shall make an ark of acacia wood; its length shall be two and a half cubits, its width a cubit and a half, and its height a cubit and a half. * 11 * You shall overlay it with pure gold inside and out, and make a molding of gold all around it. * 12 * You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on one side and two rings on the other side. * 13 * You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. * 14 * And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, that the ark may be carried with them. * 15 * The poles shall be in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it. * 16 * And you shall put into the ark the Testimony which I will give you.

In the thirty-first chapter of the book of Exodus:

18 * Then He gave to Moses, when He had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, two tablets of the Testimony, tablets of stone written with the finger of God.

In the thirty-fourth chapter of the same: that when Moses broke the two tablets, God commanded him to hew two tablets of stone like the first, and commanded him to write on them the words of the covenant, the Ten Words. Its text:

1 * Then the LORD said to Moses: Hew for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write on these tablets the words that were on the first tablets which you broke.

In the margins of the Torah: the Tabut al-Shahadah is the chest in which were the two tablets of the divine law called "Testimony."

They claimed that sakinah is an arabized form of (Shekinah) in the Hebrew language. In the First Book of Samuel, in the fourth chapter and what follows, is the account of the defeat of the Israelites before the Philistines and the taking of the chest from the Israelites, and that the chest remained in the land of the Philistines for seven months, in lengthy narratives.

(p-648) On His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So when Talut set out with the troops, he said, "Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, but whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who scoops a handful with his hand." Then they drank from it, except a few of them. And when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, "We have no power today against Jalut and his troops." Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said, "How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah! And Allah is with the patient."﴾

﴿So when Talut set out with the troops﴾: that is, he went out with the army, after they returned the ark (al-tabut) to them and accepted his kingship, and they went out with him. Talut had led them into a barren land, and they were struck by intense heat and thirst. Talut said to them, "Indeed, Allah will test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me," that is, not of my partisans who fight my enemy alongside me, and does not cross it. ﴿But whoever does not taste it is of me﴾: that is, does not taste it. The verb "ta'ima" (to taste), like "'alima" (to know) with respect to a thing, means to taste it, whether it is food or drink. Choosing the phrase "does not taste it" over "does not drink it" implies that partaking of it is forbidden even with food. This was mentioned by al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani). ﴿Except one who scoops a handful with his hand﴾: one handful, for by that he does not depart from being "of me," because he is in the sense of one who has not tasted it.

Al-Harali (al-Harali) said: the reading with a fatha on the ghayn (ghayn) indicates the meaning of it being singular, taking what it takes, whether little or much; and with a damma, it indicates its being full.

﴿Then they drank from it﴾: that is, to the point of quenching their thirst. ﴿Except a few of them﴾: they did not drink except as Allah permitted. ﴿Then when he crossed it﴾: that is, the river. ﴿He﴾: that is, Talut. ﴿And those who believed with him, they said﴾: that is, those who had overindulged in drinking. ﴿We have no power today against Jalut and his troops﴾, because their courage had been drained away.

It is mentioned in the Tawrah (Torah) that his name was Jaliyat, as we will mention. ﴿Those who thought﴾: that is, those who knew ﴿that they would meet Allah﴾, returning to Him after death: ﴿How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah! And Allah is with the patient.﴾

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 250:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[250] ﴿And when they came out before Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers, they said, "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and give us victory over the disbelieving people."﴾

﴿And when they came out﴾ means they appeared. ﴿before Jalut and his soldiers﴾ when they drew near to him. ﴿They said, "Our Lord, pour upon us patience"﴾ i.e., pour it upon us and honour us with it for their fighting, so that we do not flinch from the wounds. They asked for it first because it is the essence of the matter (p-649). ﴿And make firm our feet﴾ on the battlefield, so that we do not flee from it. ﴿And give us victory﴾ because we are believers in You. ﴿Over the disbelieving people﴾ who disbelieve in You. They are Jalut and his soldiers. This verse indicates that whoever faces a matter of this kind should ask Allah for help, for success, and devote himself to Him, exalted is He.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[251] ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and Dawud slew Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom and taught him of what He willed. And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾

﴿So they routed them﴾: i.e., these few routed those many. ﴿By the permission of Allah﴾: by His help, as He emboldened the few and made the many cowardly. ﴿And Dawud slew﴾: and he was in the army of Talut. ﴿Jalut﴾: who was the chief of the strong. ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾: i.e., Allah gave Dawud the rule of the Children of Israel. ﴿And wisdom﴾: i.e., understanding and prophethood. ﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾: such as the craft of making coats of mail and other things. ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people﴾: of the people of evil ﴿by means of others﴾: of the people of good ﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾: i.e., through the dominance of the disbelievers and the prevalence of polytheism and sins, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, oratories and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], and so on.

﴿But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds﴾: i.e., He bestowed favour upon them by the repelling. For this reason He, glory be to Him, strengthened these weak ones and gave some of them the kingdom and wisdom and other sciences, so that by the sword they might repel the corruption of the strong.

(p. 650) The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[252] ﴿These are the verses of God; We recite them to you in truth, and you are indeed among the messengers.﴾

﴿These﴾ means: the matters already mentioned, namely the death and revival of the thousands, the appointment of Talut (Saul) as king, the coming of the Ark, the defeat of Jalut (Goliath), and David's killing of him and his becoming king. ﴿The verses of God﴾, since they are reports of unseen matters that point to the perfection of His power, wisdom and kindness, may He be glorified. ﴿We recite them to you﴾ means: We send down Gabriel to you with them. ﴿In truth﴾ means: with certainty, about which there is no doubt. ﴿And you are indeed among the messengers﴾ is shown by what these verses indicate: your knowledge of them without any human teacher, and then their inimitability, which remains across the ages. In these stories there is also a lesson for this community in bearing hardships in jihad, just as the believers of earlier nations bore them. There is also consolation for the Messenger ﷺ from the unbelievers and hypocrites. It is as if it were said: through these verses you have learned what befell the prophets, peace be upon them, among the Children of Israel, of opposition to them and rejection of their words. So let not the disbelief of those who disbelieve in you grieve you, nor the opposition of those who oppose you, for you are like them. Each of them was sent only to convey the message and to comply with the command by way of choice and willing obedience, not by way of compulsion. So there is no blame on you for their opposition and disbelief, and the harm of that returns upon them. His words ﴿And you are indeed among the messengers﴾ are like an admonition regarding this. This was noted by al-Razi.

Al-Biqa'i said: Perhaps the conclusion of the stories of the Children of Israel with this story is because in it there is clear evidence for the Prophet ﷺ of the truth of his prophethood, for it is something only a few of the most learned scholars among the Children of Israel know.

I say: May God have mercy on al-Biqa'i, for he did not come across this story in the Torah, although it is recorded in chapter seventeen of the First Book of Samuel, and its text is:

1 * The Philistines gathered their armies for war and assembled at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and they camped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.

2 * Saul and the men of Israel assembled and camped in the Valley of Elah and drew up in battle array to meet the Philistines. 3 * The Philistines stood on a mountain on one side, and Israel stood on a mountain on the other side, with the valley between them. 4 * A champion came out from the camp of the Philistines named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span. 5 * He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he wore a coat of mail of scale armor, and the weight of the coat of mail was five thousand shekels of bronze. 6 * He had greaves of bronze on his legs and a bronze javelin between his shoulders.

7 * The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and its iron point weighed six hundred shekels of iron, and a shield-bearer walked before him. 8 * He stood and called out to the ranks of Israel and said to them: Why do you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not the Philistine, and you servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me. 9 * If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants; but if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us.

10 * The Philistine said: I defy the ranks of Israel this day; give me a man, that we may fight together. 11 * When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.

12 * Now David was the son of that Ephrathite man of Bethlehem in Judah, whose name was Jesse, and he had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was old and advanced in years among men. 13 * The three eldest sons of Jesse went and followed Saul to the battle; the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third. 14 * David was the youngest, and the three eldest followed Saul. 15 * But David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.

16 * The Philistine came forward morning and evening for forty days and took his stand. 17 * Jesse said to his son David: Take for your brothers an ephah of this roasted grain and these ten loaves, and run to the camp to your brothers. 18 * Take also these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand, and see how your brothers are doing, and bring back some token from them.

19 * Now Saul and they and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.

20 * So David rose early in the morning, left the flock with a keeper, loaded himself, and went as Jesse had commanded him; he came to the encampment as the army was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry. 21 * Israel and the Philistines drew up in battle array, army facing army. 22 * David left his baggage in the care of the keeper of the baggage, ran to the battle line, came and asked about the welfare of his brothers. 23 * As he was speaking with them, behold, the champion named Goliath, the Philistine of Gath, came up from the ranks of the Philistines and spoke these same words, and David heard them. 24 * When all the men of Israel saw the man, they fled from him and were greatly afraid.

25 * The men of Israel said: Have you seen this man who has come up? He comes up to defy Israel. The man who kills him, the king will enrich him with great riches, will give him his daughter, and will make his father's house free in Israel.

26 * David spoke to the men who stood with him, saying: What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?

27 * The people answered him with the same words, saying: This is what will be done for the man who kills him.

28 * His eldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, and Eliab's anger burned against David, and he said: Why have you come down here? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the evil of your heart, for you came down only to see the battle.

29 * David said: What have I done now? Was it not just a word?

30 * He turned from him toward another and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him as they had answered before.

31 * When the words that David spoke were heard, they reported them before Saul, and he sent for him.

32 * David said to Saul: Let no man's heart fail because of him; your servant will go and fight this Philistine.

33 * Saul said to David: You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight him, for you are only a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth.

34 * David said to Saul: Your servant has been keeping his father's sheep, and when a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, 35 * I went out after it, struck it, and rescued the lamb from its mouth; and when it rose against me, I caught it by its beard, struck it, and killed it. 36 * Your servant has killed both lion and bear, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God.

37 * David said: The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine. Saul said to David: Go, and may the LORD be with you.

38 * Saul clothed David with his garments, put a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him with a coat of mail. 39 * David girded his sword over his garments and tried to walk, for he had not tested them. David said to Saul: I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them. So David took them off.

40 * He took his staff in his hand, chose for himself five smooth stones from the brook, and put them in his shepherd's bag, which was in his pouch; with his sling in his hand, he approached the Philistine.

41 * The Philistine came on and drew near to David, with the shield-bearer going before him.

42 * When the Philistine looked and saw David, he despised him, for he was a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance.

43 * The Philistine said to David: Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks? And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.

44 * The Philistine said to David: Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the field.

45 * David said to the Philistine: You come to me with a sword, a spear and a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. 46 * This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head; and I will give the carcasses of the army of the Philistines this day to the birds of the sky and the wild beasts of the earth, so that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. 47 * And all this assembly shall know that the LORD does not save with sword or spear, for the battle is the LORD's, and He will give you into our hands.

48 * When the Philistine rose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.

49 * David put his hand into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on his forehead; the stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground. 50 * So David prevailed over the Philistine with the sling and the stone, struck the Philistine and killed him; there was no sword in David's hand. 51 * David ran and stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it from its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

52 * The men of Israel and Judah rose, shouted, and pursued the Philistines as far as the entrance to the valley and to the gates of Ekron... etc.

(p. 654) The rest of David's story after that, until God gave him the kingdom, is recorded in the chapters after this chapter of the Torah. Consult it, if you wish.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, verse 253:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[253] ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and some of them He raised in rank. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. And had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after clear proofs had come to them, but they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. And had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He intends.﴾

﴿Those messengers﴾: a reference to those mentioned earlier in this surah, or to those known to the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾: by singling one out for a distinction not granted to another. ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾: this is a detail of the preference, meaning that among them are those whom God preferred by speaking to them without an intermediary, and this is Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿And some of them He raised in rank﴾: such as Abraham, whom God took as a friend (khalil), and David, to whom God gave prophethood, kingship and caliphate.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, among them is the one He raised above all the other prophets, so that after their differences in merit, he became superior to them by many degrees.

The apparent meaning is that He intended Muhammad ﷺ, because he is the one preferred over them, since he was given signs that no one else received, numerous and reaching a thousand signs or more. Even if he had been given only the Qur'an, it would have sufficed as an outstanding virtue above all that the prophets were given, because it is the enduring miracle for all time, unlike the other miracles. In this indefiniteness there is a clear magnification of his merit and elevation of his rank, for it testifies that he is the unique one who cannot be likened to others and the distinguished one who cannot be confused with others. One says to a man, "Who did this?" and he replies, "One of you, or some of you," meaning the one who is known and famous for such deeds. This is more majestic than stating it explicitly and more exalting of its doer.

Al-Hutay'a was asked about the best poet among people. He mentioned Zuhayr and al-Nabigha, then said: "And if I wished, I would mention the third," meaning himself. Had he said, "And if I wished, I would mention myself," he would not have magnified his status.

Then he said: It is also possible that He intended Abraham, Muhammad and others among the Ulu al-'Azm (the prophets of steadfast resolve).

﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs﴾: such as healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead. ﴿And strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾: the discussion of this has already passed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why did God single out Moses and Jesus from among the prophets to be mentioned? I answer: because of the great signs and the dazzling miracles they were given. God has shown the aspect of preference in that He made speaking (with God) a form of merit, and it is one of the signs. Since these two prophets were given great signs, they were singled out for mention in the context of preference. This is clear evidence that whoever is further preferred through signs over others is preferred above them. And since our Prophet ﷺ is the one who was given signs that no one else received, in their multitude and greatness, he is the one indisputably acknowledged as having won the highest rank of merit.

﴿And had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾: that is, after the messengers, because of their disagreement in religion, the diversity of their paths, and their declaring one another to be disbelievers. ﴿After clear proofs had come to them, but they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. And had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He intends.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: He repeated it for emphasis. Al-Nasir said in his glosses: Behind the emphasis there is a more specific secret, which is that when the Arabs establish the beginning of their speech upon one purpose, and then another purpose intervenes, and they wish to return to the first, they mention it either with the same expression or with something close to it. This is among them an accepted and well-trodden path of eloquence. In the Book of God there are instances of this meaning, among them His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾ [al-Nahl: 106], and among them His words: ﴿Were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby incur blame without knowledge...﴾ [al-Fath: 25] up to His words: ﴿Had they been separated, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. This verse is of this pattern. When the speech began by stating that their fighting was in accordance with His will, then the speech was prolonged and it was intended to clarify that God's will, just as it took effect in this specific matter, namely the fighting of these people, it also takes effect in every event that occurs. This is the meaning expressed in His words: ﴿But God does what He intends﴾. The mention of the connection of His will to the fighting arose because it follows the general connection of His will, so that the speech fits together and each part is recognised in its own form. This is a secret that opens the breast and gladdens the inner heart. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[254] ﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided for you, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers.﴾

﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided for you﴾: This is a command to spend from part of one's wealth. It has been said: it is a command of obligation, and by it He intended obligatory spending, which is the zakat, since He followed it with the threat in His saying ﴿And the disbelievers﴾ etc., where by them are meant those who withhold it, as will come. Al-Asamm and Abu 'Ali said: He intended spending in jihad. Abu Muslim and Ibn Jurayj said: He intended the obligatory and the voluntary. And this is the most apparent (al-mutajjah). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿before there comes a Day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿in which there is no trade﴾, that is, so that you may obtain what you spend (p-657) or ransom yourselves with it from the punishment; ﴿nor friendship﴾, so that friends may help you—﴿On that Day, friends will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]; ﴿nor intercession﴾, so that you may rely on intercessors—﴿except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose word He has approved﴾ [Ta-Ha: 109]. ﴿And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers﴾: He intended, "And those who abandon zakat are the wrongdoers." His choosing this wording over the other is for emphasis and warning, as in His saying at the end of the verse on the Hajj: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97] in place of "whoever does not perform Hajj," and to indicate that abandoning zakat is one of the attributes of the disbelievers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists﴾ [Fussilat: 6] ﴿who do not give zakat﴾ [Fussilat: 7]. This was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers against themselves, by placing their wealth in other than its proper places. So do not, O believers, be like them in that you do not spend and thus place your wealth in other than its proper places." In this verse is an indication of the goodness of hastening to good deeds before their loss, by the arrival of what fear of it entails, such as death or other than it.

(p-658) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[255] ﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except for what He wills. His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not tire Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living﴾: that is, the Everlasting, for whom there is no path to annihilation. ﴿The Sustainer of existence﴾: the One who constantly stands in managing and preserving creation. It has been read as al-qayyam and al-qayyim.

﴿Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep﴾: this is an emphasis on al-Qayyum. That is, He is not heedless of the management of the affairs of creation, exalted and sanctified is He. Al-sinah is like 'idah, and al-wasan with a vowel on the middle letter; and with a ha' it is al-wasnah: the intensity of sleep, or its beginning, or drowsiness. Thus in al-Qamus.

Al-Mahayimi said: al-sinah is a lethargy that precedes sleep. And sleep is a state that befalls living beings from the relaxation of the brain due to rising moist vapours which prevent the outward senses from perceiving. These two are diminishments of life and contrary to self-subsistence, since they are among the changes incompatible with the necessary existence that belongs to al-Qayyum. Sleep was negated first by implication, then explicitly, so that the completeness of its negation indicates the establishment of the completeness of what is contrary to it. And from the completeness of His self-subsistence is His exclusive ownership of the higher and lower realms, indicated by His words: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾, of angels, the sun, the moon and the stars; ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾, of the observable worlds. This is an announcement that all are within His dominion, under His power and authority, as in His words: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93] ﴿He has enumerated them and counted them precisely﴾ [Maryam: 94].

﴿Who is it﴾ among the prophets and angels, let alone those the disbelievers claimed as intercessors among the idols: ﴿that can intercede with Him﴾, let alone oppose or contend with Him: (p-659) ﴿except by His permission﴾, that is, by His enabling, realizing servitude, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And how many an angel in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾ [an-Najm: 26], and as in His words: ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. This is from His greatness, majesty and grandeur, mighty and majestic is He: that no one dares to intercede with Him for anyone except with His permission to intercede, as in the hadith of intercession: "I come beneath the Throne and fall prostrate, and He leaves me as long as Allah wills to leave me; then it is said: Raise your head, and speak, you will be heard; intercede, you will be granted intercession. He says: then He sets a limit for me and I admit them into Paradise."

Abu al-Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah said: Allah negated of other than Himself everything the polytheists attach to Him. He negated that anything else has dominion, or a share of it, or that it be a helper to Allah. Only intercession remained, and He made clear that it benefits only those whom the Lord permits. So this intercession which the polytheists imagine is negated on the Day of Resurrection, as the Qur'an negated it. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that he comes and prostrates to his Lord and praises Him, not beginning with intercession first; then it is said to him: Raise your head, speak and you will be heard, ask and you will be given, intercede and you will be granted intercession. Abu Hurayrah said to him: "Who are the people most fortunate with your intercession? He said: 'Whoever says, (p-660) there is no deity except Allah, sincerely from his heart.'" That intercession is for the people of sincerity by Allah's permission, and it is not for those who associate partners with Allah. Its reality is that Allah, glorified is He, is the One who bestows favour upon the people of sincerity and forgives them through the mediation of the supplication of one whom He has permitted to intercede, in order to honour him and to attain the praised station. So the intercession the Qur'an negated is that which contained no shirk. For this reason intercession by His permission is affirmed in several places, and the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that it is only for the people of tawhid and sincerity.

﴿He knows what is before them﴾: that is, what has reached them of His knowledge concerning their own affairs and those of others, because what is before a person is encompassed by his senses, and what he knows is also encompassed; so it is as if it is before his heart, encompassed by his knowledge. ﴿And what is behind them﴾: which is what their knowledge has not reached, because "behind" is what the senses do not attain. Thus it informs that His knowledge, from beyond their knowledge, encompasses their knowledge, in what they know and what they do not know. This was conveyed by al-Harali. So this clause is like His words: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 9].

﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except for what He wills﴾: that is, they know nothing of what is known to Him except what He wills to inform them of through the tongues of the messengers. As He said: ﴿He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to one whom He has approved of the messengers﴾ [al-Jinn: 26–27], that is, so that what He informs him of from the knowledge of the unseen would be a proof of his prophethood.

﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾: Ibn Jarir narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that what is meant by the Kursi is knowledge. This is because of His words: ﴿and their preservation does not tire Him﴾: that is, the preservation of what He knows and encompasses of what is in the heavens and the earth does not tire Him. And as He informed about His angels that they said in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7], He informed that His knowledge encompasses all things; so likewise (p-661) His words: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾. Ibn Jarir said: this saying of Ibn 'Abbas indicates the soundness of the apparent meaning of the Qur'an in what has been mentioned.
