Also, the root of kursi is knowledge, and from it a written sheet containing written knowledge is called kurrasah. And from it is the words of the rajiz describing a hunter:

"Until, when he had taken it, he came to know"

meaning: he knew. From it the scholars are called kara-si, because they are the ones relied upon, just as they say "the pegs of the earth," meaning they are those by whom the earth is set right. And from it is the poet's words:

"Surrounding them are bright faces and a band of kara-si in the face of events when they befall"

meaning by this: His knowledge of the events of affairs and their calamities. Ibn Jarir also narrated from al-Hasan that the Kursi in the verse is the Throne, and some supported this by saying that the terms "throne of the kingdom" and "its kursi" are synonyms; for this reason Allah said, on the tongue of Sulayman: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ [an-Naml: 38]. So the Throne and the Kursi are one and the same thing, and He named it here "Kursi" to inform of another name for it.

﴿And it does not weigh Him down﴾ (p-662): that is, it does not burden Him nor is it difficult for Him. It is said: "ada-hu al-amr awdan and uwudan, like qu'ud," meaning the affair reached him in hardship and difficulty. ﴿Their preservation﴾: that is, of the heavens and the earth; so He does not need a partner or a son. And how could it be difficult for Him? ﴿And He is the Most High﴾. Ibn Jarir said: some said it means His exaltedness above likeness and counterparts. Others said its meaning is He is Most High over His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation, since He, mentioned be He, is above all His creation and they are beneath Him, as He described Himself as being on the Throne; so He is High above them by that. ﴿The Most Great﴾: that is, greatest of everything in majesty, grandeur, subjugation, power and dominion.

Note:

This verse of the Kursi has a great station and a great virtue. It has been authentically reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that it is "the greatest verse in the Book of Allah, and it contains the Greatest Name of Allah." Imam Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir and Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur have gathered what has been reported about its virtue, so consult them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: why has this verse been given such excellence that such things have been reported about it? I say: it is excellent for the same reason that Surat al-Ikhlas is excellent: it includes the affirmation of Allah's oneness, glorifying Him, exalting Him and His supreme attributes, and there is no one mentioned greater than the Lord of Might; so whatever is a remembrance of Him is better than all other remembrances.

(p-663) Al-Suyuti related in al-Itqan from al-Ash'ari, al-Baqillani and Ibn Hibban the prohibition of saying in the Qur'an "fadil" and "afdal." They said: what has been reported indicating that is to be understood as greatness in reward, not that some parts of the Qur'an are superior to others. Many have refuted this, to the point that Ibn al-Hisar said: it is strange that one mentions disagreement on this in the face of the texts that report its preference. Al-Ghazali said in Jawahir al-Qur'an: Perhaps you will say: you have pointed to the preference of some verses of the Qur'an over others, yet speech is the speech of Allah, so how can some of it vary from others, and how can some of it be nobler than others? Know that if the light of insight does not guide you to distinguish between the verse of the Kursi and the verse of debts, and between Surat al-Ikhlas and Surat Tabbat, and you are startled by the frailty of your self-conviction, absorbed in imitation, then imitate the Bearer of the Message (ﷺ), to whom the Qur'an was sent down, who said: "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an, and al-Fatihah is the best of the surahs of the Qur'an."

(p-664) The verse of the Kursi is the chief of the verses of the Qur'an. "Say: He is Allah, One" equals a third of the Qur'an. The reports concerning the virtues of the Qur'an, and the singling out of some surahs and verses for excellence and abundant reward in reciting them, are countless. End.

**The discussion on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:**

[256] ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from error. So whoever disbelieves in the false deities (al-Taghut) and believes in Allah has grasped the most reliable handhold, which will never break. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right course has become clear from error﴾. Ibn Kathir said: That is, do not compel anyone to enter the religion of Islam, for its proofs and evidences are clear and manifest. No one needs to be forced to enter it. Rather, whomever Allah guides to Islam, opens his breast to, and illuminates his insight, enters it with clear evidence. But whoever's heart is blind, entering it under compulsion and coercion will not benefit him. Thus the negation carries the meaning of a prohibition.

(p-٦٦٥) Many have taken this view of the verse's interpretation. Others held that it is a purely informative statement, meaning that Allah did not base the matter of faith on compulsion and force, but based it on enablement and free choice. Al-Qaffal, explaining this, said: When Allah, the Exalted, clarified the proofs of Monotheism with a sufficient explanation that cuts off excuse, He afterwards informed that, once these proofs were made clear, the disbeliever has no excuse to persist in disbelief, except that he be forced and compelled to faith. That is not permissible in the abode of this world, which is the abode of trial, for coercion and compulsion in religion nullifies the meaning of trial and testing. A parallel to this verse is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on the earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3], ﴿If We willed, We would send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbly subjected to it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4].

Caution:

It is known from this verse that the sword of jihad, which is legislated in Islam and which neither the justice of a just ruler nor the tyranny of a tyrant nullifies, has not been employed for compelling entry into the religion. Rather, it is employed to protect the call to the religion and to secure submission to its authority and its just rule.

﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deities (al-Taghut)﴾: that is, in Satan, i.e., in what he calls to of worshipping idols. ﴿And believes in Allah, has grasped the most reliable handhold, which will never break﴾: that is, he has held fast to the strongest means within the religion. This is likened to a strong handhold that does not break; it is itself firm and well-fastened, and its binding is strong and firm (p-٦٦٦). The clause ﴿which will never break﴾ may be a resumptive statement confirming what precedes it, or it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the handhold," with its governing element being "has grasped," or relating to the concealed pronoun in "the most reliable," or it may be a relative clause for an omitted relative pronoun, meaning "which." This was transmitted from al-Razi.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) have narrated, from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "I saw a dream during the time of Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I saw myself in a green garden, in the middle of which was an iron pillar, its base in the earth and its top in the sky, and at its top was a handhold. I was told: 'Climb it.' I said: 'I cannot.' Then a servant (called Munsif, i.e., Wasif) came to me and lifted my garments from behind, and said: 'Climb,' so I climbed until I grasped the handhold. He said: 'Hold fast to the handhold.' Then I woke up, and it was in my hand. I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and related it to him. He said: 'As for the garden, it is the garden of Islam; as for the pillar, it is the pillar of Islam; as for the handhold, it is the most reliable handhold. You will remain upon Islam until you die.'"

﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾: this is a concluding parenthetical clause that urges faith and deters from disbelief and hypocrisy, with what it contains of promise and warning.

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 257:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[257] ﴿Allah is the Ally of those who believe; He brings them out from the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve, their allies are the Taghut (false deities/transgressors), who bring them out from the light into the darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

﴿Allah is the Ally of those who believe﴾ i.e., their Guardian and Helper. ﴿He brings them out﴾ is an explanation of the wilayah (guardianship), or a second predicate: ﴿from the darknesses﴾ i.e., the darknesses of disbelief and sins; ﴿into the light﴾ i.e., the light of true, clear faith. The word "light" is given in the singular because of the oneness of the Truth, just as the word "darknesses" is given in the plural because of the multiplicity of the kinds of misguidance, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow other ways, lest they separate you from His way. That is what He has instructed you with, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-An'am: 153]. ﴿And those who disbelieve, their allies are the Taghut﴾ i.e., (p-667) the devils and all the misleaders away from the path of truth. ﴿They bring them out﴾ by whisperings and other means of misguidance and seduction: ﴿from the light﴾ i.e., the natural (fitrah) faith upon which all people have been created; or from the light of the clear proofs which they witness from the side of the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿Into the darknesses﴾ i.e., the darknesses of disbelief and error. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Then He, may He be exalted, cited as evidence for what He had mentioned, that the disbelievers' allies are the Taghut, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 258:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[258] ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, "My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was stunned. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued﴾ i.e., disputed: ﴿with Abraham about his Lord﴾ i.e., how the tyrant (al-Taghut) removed him from the light of attributing giving life and causing death to his Lord into the darkness of attributing them to himself. ﴿Because Allah had given him kingship﴾ i.e., because Allah had given him kingship. That is: the granting of kingship made him arrogant and bequeathed him pride, so he argued for that reason, or argued with him on account of it, placing the argument, which is the ugliest form of disbelief, in the place of what was obligatory upon him, which is gratitude. It is like saying: "So-and-so opposed me because I did him a kindness." You mean: he reversed what he was obligated to do, which was allegiance in return for kindness. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny [it]﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82].

Al-Harali said: In its implication is that kingship is a trial and a tribulation for the one who is given it.

﴿When Abraham said﴾ when he was asked, "Who is your Lord to whom you invite us?" ﴿"My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death"﴾ i.e., by breathing the spirit into the body and withdrawing it from it. ﴿He said, "I give life and cause death"﴾ i.e., by killing and pardoning (p-668) him. When the tyrant followed the path of confusion and deception upon the common people, the falsity of his answer was so clear and evident that it was hidden from no one, and attempting to refute it was of the nature of seeking to obtain what is already obtained, Abraham, peace be upon him, moved on, loosening the reins of the debate with him, to another proof in which sophistry does not operate and in which the tyrant cannot easily escape by way of obstinacy, contentiousness, or deception of the common people. This is what He, exalted is He, related with His saying: ﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."﴾ i.e., if you are as you claim, that you give life and cause death, then the one who gives life and causes death is the one who disposes of existence, in the creation of its essences and the subjugation of its stars and their movements. Thus this sun rises every day from the east; so if you are a god as you claim, then bring it from the west. ﴿So the one who disbelieved was stunned﴾ he was bewildered, confounded, and overcome by the proof, when he knew his incapacity and inability, and that he could not persist in obstinacy in this position.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ i.e., He does not inspire them with proof or evidence; rather, their argument is refuted before their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment.

The commentary on the saying of Allah, the Exalted:

[259] ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town, while it lay fallen upon its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled, and look at your donkey. And We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." So when it became clear to him, he said, "I know that Allah is over all things competent."﴾

(p-669) ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ is an example offered in support of what Allah, the Exalted, mentioned about His guardianship of the believers, and as a confirmation of it. It is coordinated with the preceding relative pronoun (alladhi). The choice of (aw), which signifies distinction, over (waw), which signifies combination, is made to guard against the supposition that the thing being illustrated is one and the same from the outset. The kaf (like) is either a noun, brought in to draw attention to the multiplicity of examples and that they are not confined to what has been mentioned, or it is an extra particle, and the meaning is: "Or have you not seen [something] like the one who..., or [have you not seen] the one who passed by a town, how Allah guided him and brought him out of the darkness of uncertainty into the light of direct witness and observation." ﴿while it lay fallen upon its roofs﴾: empty, its walls having collapsed upon its roofs. ﴿He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"﴾: that is, how will Allah restore this town after its ruin? This was for him like falling into darkness, so Allah showed him the proof of genuine revival within himself, as an exaggeration in uprooting doubt, bringing him out of it into the light. ﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾ so that he would be wholly effaced. ﴿Then He resurrected him﴾: that is, He restored him to life by returning his soul to his body and joining some of his parts to others after they had been dispersed. ﴿He said﴾: Allah said to him, ﴿"How long have you remained?"﴾: that is, how long did you stay dead? ﴿He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day"﴾: he said this on the basis of approximation and estimation, or as an underestimate of the length of his stay. ﴿He said﴾: Allah said, ﴿"Rather, you have remained a hundred years."﴾ Allah asked him so that his inability to grasp the matters of his own state would become evident to him, and that his revival was not after a short period, which might be thought to be a relatively easy matter, but after a long period. Thereby the root of his disbelief is cut off entirely. Within this there is revealed another matter from the marvels of the signs of Allah's power, the exalted: the preservation of food, which by its nature hastens to spoil, in the state it was in for a long time, without any change whatsoever, as the Glorified said: ﴿Look﴾, so that you may witness another sign from the signs of Our power: ﴿at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled﴾: that is, it did not change over this long period despite its tendency toward spoilage. The ha' (the pronoun ending in ha') may be the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt), added in pause. The original form of the verb in this respect has two possibilities:

The first: it is from yatasannan, from His saying: ﴿of black, moulded clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 26]. When three nun letters came together, the last was changed to a ya', as in tazannaytu, then the ya' was changed to an alif, then it was deleted for the jussive.

The second: the original of the alif is a waw, from their saying: asnā yusnī, when years passed over him. The original of sanah is sanwah, from their saying: sanawat, that is, the years have not passed over it. The meaning is by way of comparison: as if the hundred years had not passed over it, because it remained in its state and did not change. The ha' may be original, and the derivation would be from sanah, on the basis that the lam of sanah is a ha', its original form being sanhah, from their saying: sanhā', and "I dealt with him in musanahah." On this basis the ha' is retained both in connection and in pause, since the verb is jussive by its quiescence. On the first view the ha' is retained only in pause and not in connection, and whoever retains it in connection treats it as in pause. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read with the deletion of the ha' in connection and its retention in pause, while the rest read it with retention both in connection and in pause. If it is asked: what is the subject of yatasannā? It is answered: it may be the pronoun referring to the food and the drink, since each of them requires the other, so they are as one thing, and therefore the pronoun in the verb is singular. It may also be that the pronoun refers to "that" (dhālika), which is used to indicate one, two, or many with a single form. It may also be that the pronoun refers to the drink alone, since it is nearer. There is another clause omitted, indicated by this one. The estimated meaning is: "And look at your food, it has not spoiled, and at your drink, it has not spoiled." It is also possible that the singular was used in place of the dual, as the poet said:

"As if in the two eyes were clove-buds, or an ear of grain with which they were painted with kohl and which then flowed with tears."

Abu al-Baqa' pointed this out. ﴿And look at your donkey﴾: how it is. He saw that it had become bones, decayed. ﴿And We will make you a sign for the people﴾: this is coordinated with an implied element connected to a verb implied before it, by way of resumption, confirming the content of what preceded. That is: We did what We did, of reviving you after what has been mentioned, so that you may witness what you had considered unlikely of revival after a long age, and We will make you a sign for the people concerning the resurrection. Or it is connected with a verb implied after it: "And We will make you a sign for the people, We did what We did." ﴿And look at the bones﴾: that is, the bones of the donkey, so that you may witness the manner of revival. ﴿How We raise them﴾ is read with the zay (nunshizuhā), that is, We lift some of them upon others and assemble them upon it, from (al-nashz), which is the raised ground. On this reading there are two possibilities: the nun with a damma and the shin with a kasra, from (anshaztuhu), and the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma, from (nashaztuhu), and both are dialectal forms. It is also read with the ra' (nunshiruhā), and on this reading there are two possibilities:

The first: the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma, and its perfect form is (nashara). It is then either the intransitive counterpart of anshara Allāh al-mayyita, "Allah revived the dead and he was revived," in which case nashara has the meaning of anshara, and the intransitive and transitive forms have the same wording; or it is from al-nashr, which is the opposite of folding, that is, He spreads them out by reviving them.

The second: the nun with a damma and the shin with a kasra, that is, We revive them, like His saying: ﴿Then when He wills, He will revive him﴾ [‘Abasa: 22]. Abu al-Baqa' said this. ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾: that is, We cover them with it. ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾: that is, what was made evident to him was the restoration of himself along with his food, his drink and his donkey after complete perishing, and the manner of revival appeared to him. ﴿He said, "I know that Allah is over all things competent."﴾ Thus he came forth from the darkness into the light.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[260] ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be at peace." He said, "Take four birds and incline them toward yourself. Then place on every mountain a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise."﴾

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ Al-Mahayimi said: Mention, as an illustration of the story of the one who passed by the town, concerning bringing forth from darknesses into light through giving life, the story of Abraham.

﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead"﴾ He only asked this so that his knowledge would become direct sight.

﴿He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but [I ask] that my heart may be at peace"﴾ That is: Yes, I have believed, but I asked in order to increase in insight and tranquility of heart by seeing the giving of life, over and above his tranquility through revelation. For the convergence of proofs is more soothing to hearts and greater in insight and certainty. The majority of scholars hold that Abraham, peace be upon him, never doubted the giving of life to the dead at all. Rather, he sought direct observation, because human souls are created to desire seeing what they have been told about. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "The report is not like direct observation." Ibn Jarir related from a group of the people of knowledge that he asked this because he doubted the power of Allah. They cited what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ (p-672) in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, his saying: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham." And what is related from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an dearer to me in hope than it, since Allah was pleased with Abraham's saying: ﴿Yes﴾." He said: "This is for what arises in souls and what Satan whispers into them." Al-Hakim transmitted it from him in al-Mustadrak and declared it sound, and Ibn Jarir preferred this view after relating it.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "And it is, in my view, rejected," meaning the view of this group. Then he said: As for the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," its meaning is: that if he had been doubting, we would have had more right to it, and we do not doubt; so Abraham is even more deserving of not doubting. The hadith is based on negating doubt from Abraham. Ibn Atiyyah extended the discussion on this and wrote well.

Al-Qurtubi said: Such doubt is not permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah, glorified is He, has informed that His chosen servants have no authority over them by Satan, saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Hijr: 42], and the accursed one said: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40]. If he has no dominion over them, how could he cause them to doubt? Rather, he asked to witness how the parts of the dead are gathered after being scattered, and how sinews and skins are joined after being torn apart; so he wished to ascend from the knowledge of certainty to the eye of certainty.

Al-Nasir said in "al-Intisaf": The better course regarding this verse is to mention in it the preferred view of its interpretation, from the tested inquiries with refined thought and the illuminating points with matured opinion. So we say: As for the Friend's (Khalil) peace be upon him question, saying: ﴿how You give life to the dead﴾, it was not out of doubt, God forbid, regarding Allah's power to give life, but it was a question about the manner of giving life. Believing does not require encompassing its form. What is sought is knowledge of what faith does not depend upon knowing. This is shown by the question coming in the form "how," whose subject is inquiry about the state. A parallel to this question is for someone to say: "How does Zayd judge among the people?" He does not doubt that he judges among them, but he asked about the manner of his judgment, not its occurrence. If imagination might play with some thought and bring a doubt about Abraham from this verse, the Prophet, peace be upon him, cut off the root of this illusion by his saying: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," meaning: and we did not doubt, so Abraham not doubting is more fitting and more deserving. If you say: if the question is directed to the manner, whose non-conception and non-observation do not harm faith nor undermine it, what is the place of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾? I say: some skilled scholars have reached a subtle point regarding this: this phrasing is apparently used for asking about the manner, as has passed, and it may also be used for expressing inability. An example: if a claimant says he can carry a certain heavy weight, while you are certain of his inability to carry it, you say to him: "Show me how you carry this?" Since this phrasing (p-674) may take on this usage, from which Allah's knowledge encompassed that Abraham is absolved, he intended by His saying: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ that Abraham would speak the words: ﴿Yes﴾, I have believed, so as to remove from him that verbal possibility in the first expression.

So that his faith would be sincere, he stated it with a phrase which everyone who hears it understands without any doubt reaching it. If you say: The connection between the speech under the stated estimation has become clear to me. Then what is the place of Abraham's saying: ﴿but that my heart may be at peace﴾? Apparently this implies that at the time of the question he lacked tranquility. I say: its meaning is: but that the thinking about the manner of life may depart from my heart, for when I witness it, my heart will rest from roaming among its imagined manners, and it will be fixed for me by the observed depiction. This is the best that comes to me in the interpretation of this verse. And your Lord is the Opener, the All-Knowing. End.

﴿He said﴾ That is: if you wish for tranquility: ﴿Take four birds and incline them toward yourself﴾ with the ṣād vowelled with ḍamma and with kasra, meaning: incline them and gather them toward yourself. It is said: ṣārahu yaṣūruhu and yaṣīruhu, when he inclined it; both are dialects.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read: faṣurrahunna, with ṣād vowelled with ḍamma and kasra, and doubling of the rā' from ṣarrahu yaṣirruhu and yaṣurruhu, when he gathered it. And from him: faṣurhunna (from al-taṣriyah), which is also gathering. And al-Lihyani said: some of them said: the meaning of ṣurhunna is: turn them toward you; and the meaning of ṣirhunna is: cut them and split them. The well-known view is that both are dialects with one meaning. All of them explained faṣurhunna as: incline them; and kasra was explained with the meaning of cut them. Al-Fayruzabadi said in "al-Basa'ir": some said: ṣurhunna with ḍamma of the ṣād and doubling of the rā' and with fatḥa, from al-ṣarr, that is: tying. He said: it was read faṣirrahunna with kasra of the ṣād and fatḥa of the doubled rā' (from al-ṣarīr), that is: the sound; that is: call to them loudly. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is read with ḍamma of the ṣād and doubling of the rā'; then some of them vowel it with ḍamma by assimilation, and some of them vowel it with fatḥa for lightness, and some of them vowel it with kasra on the basis of meeting of two sakin letters.

I say: It is established in Arabic that when a doubled verb takes the pronominal ending hā', for the feminine there is one form, namely fatḥ of the letter before it, as in radda-hā, in consideration of the alif, by consensus. For the masculine there are three forms:

The most eloquent of them is ḍamma, then kasra, which is weak, and then fatḥa, which is the weakest of them.

Among those who mentioned it is Tha'lab in "al-Faṣīḥ" (p-675), but they regarded it as an error, because it gives the impression of its eloquence without pointing out its weakness. ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾ That is: then slaughter them, divide them, and place on every mountain a part of them. ﴿Then call them﴾ That is: by their names: ﴿they will come to you in haste﴾ That is: swiftly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the meaning of His command to bring them close to himself after taking them? I say: so that he would examine them, and know their forms, shapes, and adornments, lest they be confused for him after the giving of life, and it not be imagined that they are other than those. For this reason He said: ﴿they will come to you in haste﴾, and did not say "flying," because if they are running, his gaze upon them is more secure than if they were flying. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[261] ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that sprouts seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies [the reward] for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., in obedience to Him. ﴿is like a grain﴾, i.e., the likeness of their spending is like a grain, or their likeness is like the likeness of one who sows a grain. The omission is either on the side of the *al-mushabbah* (the thing being compared, the subject) or on the side of the *al-mushabbah bihi* (the thing it is compared to, the image), to achieve *al-munasabah* (coherence) of the expression. That is, that grain was cast into the earth, and then ﴿it sprouted seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains﴾, i.e., it sent up a stalk that branched into seven branches, and from every branch came out an ear containing a hundred grains. Thus the single grain became seven hundred grains, through Allah's multiplying it for them.

Ibn Kathir said: This parable is more eloquent to the souls than mentioning the number seven hundred, for it contains an indication that Allah, mighty and majestic, causes good deeds to grow for their doers, just as He causes the crop to grow for the one who sows it in good soil. End of quotation.

I say: The confirmation of this is what is in the two *al-Sahihayn* (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever gives charity equal to a date from lawful earnings, and nothing good ascends to Allah except the good, Allah receives it with His right hand, then He nurtures it for its giver just as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain."

﴿And Allah multiplies﴾, i.e., this multiplication or more than it: ﴿for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ The Sunnah has come with the multiplication of a good deed up to seven hundredfold. In the two *al-Sahihayn* and others, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied: a good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundredfold. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: Except fasting, for it is for Me, and I will reward it." Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "A man brought a she-camel with a halter and said: 'This is in the way of Allah.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'For you, on the Day of Resurrection, for it, there will be seven hundred she-camels, all of them with halters.'" Ahmad, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Buraydah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Spending on the Hajj is like spending in the way of Allah. A dirham [spent] is [rewarded] seven hundredfold."

There are other reports in (Ibn Kathir) and (al-Durr al-Manthur) [by al-Suyuti]. Then He, may He be exalted, praised the one who preserves himself from reminding of favors and from harm regarding what he has spent, by His saying:

**The commentary on His words, exalted is He:**

[262] ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah, and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, will have their reward with their Lord. No fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the cause of Allah, and then do not follow﴾, i.e., do not come after, ﴿what they have spent with reminders of their generosity (mann)﴾, which is mentioning to the one they spent upon what they did, so as to show him that by it they have made a right incumbent upon him; ﴿or with injury (adha)﴾, which is mentioning it to others so that it hurts him by that, or boasting over him because of it. ﴿Their reward is with their Lord﴾, the promise mentioned earlier. ﴿No fear will be upon them﴾, i.e., regarding what they will face of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62] over what has escaped them of the splendor of this world, because they will arrive at what is better than that.

**Subtle points (lata'if):**

**The first:** Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of *thumma* (then) is to show the difference between spending and abandoning reminders of generosity and injury.

In the marginal notes of al-Nasir on it, the text reads: *Thumma*, in its original usage, implies that the clause it conjoins is delayed relative to the preceding clause in time, and that there is a gap between them. Al-Zamakhshari interprets it as indicating a difference in rank and a distance between the two, since it is not possible for him to interpret it as a delay in time, given a context that rejects that, as in this verse. The summary is that it has been borrowed from the distance of times to indicate the distance of rank. In my view there is another possibility in this verse and similar ones: that it indicates the continuation of the action it conjoins and the extension of its duration. On this reading it has not departed from implying a distance in time, but its original meaning is the delay in the time of the action's occurrence, while its borrowed meaning is the continuation of the action's existence and the delay in the time of its persistence. On this basis is interpreted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they stood firm﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13], i.e., they persisted in steadfastness with a delayed persistence of extended duration. That steadfastness is the one that is valued, not what is cut off by its opposite, such as deviation toward desires and lusts. Likewise His saying: ﴿then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of generosity or with injury﴾, i.e., they persist in forgetting the favor and in not regarding it or boasting of it, not leaving it at times to injury, and to attaching reminders of favor to it; then they repent. And Allah knows best.

Close to this, or similar to it, is that the *sin* (as in *sa-*) accompanies the verb to indicate the spreading out of the time of its occurrence and its delay. Then there came His saying, exalted is He, narrating about the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. Allah has narrated in a similar verse: ﴿He who created me, and He guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78]. So there is no way to interpret the *sin* as a delay in the time of the occurrence of the guidance for him. It is therefore necessary to interpret it as indicating the spreading out of the continuation of the guidance that he had attained, and the delay of its persistence and the extension of its duration. End.

**The second:** Al-Zamakhshari said: *(If you say)*: What is the difference between His saying ﴿for them is their reward﴾ and His later saying ﴿so for them is their reward﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274]? *(I say)*: The relative construction here did not include the meaning of the condition, whereas it does there. The difference between them in terms of meaning is that the *fa'* (so) in that place indicates that spending earned the reward through it, while omitting it is devoid of that indication.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The omission of the *fa'* from the predicate, which would indicate that what precedes it is the cause of what follows, is to make clear that the arrangement of the reward upon what was mentioned, namely spending and abandoning the following up of reminders of generosity and injury, is an evident matter that does not need an explicit statement of causation.

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He:

[263] ﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾

﴿A kind word﴾ means: a good word and a supplication for a Muslim. ﴿And forgiveness﴾ means: pardoning an injustice, whether verbal or practical. ﴿Better than charity followed by injury﴾ because the charity earns no reward while the sin of injury is incurred. Included in His saying "a kind word" is a gracious response to the one who asks. And "forgiveness" is pardoning the beggar when something from him burdens the one who is asked. ﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the request for charity from His servants, together with injuring them or reminding them of favor: ﴿Forbearing﴾ toward dealing with the one who reminds of favor and injures, by punishment.

**Commentary on His words, exalted is He:**

[264] ﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like a smooth rock with dust upon it; then a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury﴾ That is: do not cause their reward to be voided by either of them. Each of them is a wrong that contradicts the goodness required in charity, and that which contradicts it nullifies it, just as ostentation (riyā') does.

So the one who reproaches and the one who injures become, ﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, in the nullification of his charity. The word (رِئاءَ) is either an object of purpose (مَفْعُولٌ لَهُ) or a circumstantial state (حالٌ). That is, "showing off." The first hamzah in (رِئاءَ) is the root letter of the word, since it derives from (راءى). The last one is a substitute for a yā’ because it occurs at the end of the word after an extra alif, as in (القَضاءِ). It is permissible to lighten the first hamzah by changing it into a yā’, to avoid the heaviness of a hamzah after a kasrah, and it has been read that way. This was said by Abū al-Baqā’.

﴿His example﴾ That is, the example of this one who spends out of ostentation, in that his spending is accompanied by what corrupts it. The example of his expenditure is ﴿like a smooth rock﴾, which is a stone that is slick and smooth, ﴿with dust upon it; then a heavy rain strikes it﴾, that is, abundant rain, ﴿and leaves it bare﴾, that is, stripped and with nothing on it. ﴿They have no power over anything they have earned﴾, that is, the one who shows off, the one who reproaches, and the one who injures, have no power to obtain any of the reward for what they did, because it has been voided. This is like His words: ﴿and We made it scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqān: 23].

So they do not find the reward of their charities, just as dust cannot be found on the rock after the heavy rain has struck it. ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ to goodness and right guidance. In this there is an implicit indication that ostentation, reproach, and injury upon spending are among the attributes of disbelievers, and the believer must avoid them. Hadiths about the threat against reproaching after giving charity have been transmitted through many chains (mutawātir). In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Abū Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three (p) will not be spoken to by Allah on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He look at them, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment: the one who reproaches for what he has given, the one who lets his garment hang down (below the ankles), and the one who sells his merchandise with a false oath." In Sunan al-Nasā'ī, from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The one who is addicted to wine will not enter Paradise, nor will the one who disobeys his parents, nor the one who reproaches."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 2, verse 265:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[265] ﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah and firmly establishing themselves is like a garden on a high elevation: when heavy rain strikes it, it yields its produce twofold; and if heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah﴾ — "seeking" (ibtigha') is a direct object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, object of purpose). "And firmly establishing" (tathbitan) is coordinated with it. It is also permissible that both are circumstantial accusatives (hal, state), meaning: seeking and firmly establishing. ﴿from their own selves﴾: Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permissible that "min" (from) carries the meaning of "li" (for), i.e., firm establishment for their own selves, as you say: "I did that as a breaking of my desire (min shahwati)." It is also permissible that it remain in its original sense, i.e., a firm establishment proceeding from their own selves. Tathbit is the verbal noun of a transitive verb. On the first reading, ﴿from their own selves﴾ is the object of the verbal noun; on the second, the object is omitted. Its estimated sense is: (p-681) "they establish their deeds through sincerity of intention." It is also permissible that tathbit carries the sense of tathabbut (becoming firm), in which case it is intransitive. Verbal nouns may differ and some may take the place of others, and similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], i.e., tabattul (devotion). End. And from al-Sha'bi: "tathbitan" means affirmation and certainty. ﴿Like a garden﴾, i.e., an orchard; ﴿on a high elevation﴾, i.e., a raised place; ﴿heavy rain strikes it﴾, i.e., abundant rain; ﴿it yields its produce﴾, i.e., it brings forth its fruit; ﴿twofold﴾, i.e., in comparison with other gardens. ﴿And if heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain﴾ — "tall" is the weak rain, or the lightest rain, or its weakest, or dew. It is necessary to estimate an omitted noun here, as was mentioned before: either on the side of the compared or on the side of the comparison, i.e., "and the likeness of the expenditure of those who..." etc., or "like the likeness of one who plants a garden" etc., in keeping with the coherence of the passage.

Al-Shihab said: In the comparison there are two aspects:

One of them: it is a compound comparison, and the comparison is of the state of the expenditure to the state of a garden on a height, in that it is growing and multiplying in benefits with Allah, whatever the condition may be.

The second: the comparison of their state to the state of a garden on a height, in that their expenditure, whether abundant or little, is growing and increasing in the goodness of their condition, just as the garden's produce is doubled by strong rain and by weak rain. This too is a compound comparison, except that the resemblance is considered among the individual elements. Its essence is: their state in following little or much is the doubling of reward, like the state of the garden in producing its fruit doubled by heavy rain and light rain.

It may also bear a third aspect, which is a comparison of a single thing to a single thing: their state is likened to a garden raised high in beauty and delight, the abundant and little expenditure is likened to heavy and light rain, and the reward and recompense to the fruits. The letter "ra" in al-rabwa may be vocalized three ways (rabwah, ribwah, rubwah), and ukul (its produce) is read with two dammas, and may be softened by sukun for lightness. It was also read thus. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a warning against showing off and an encouragement toward sincerity.

(p-682) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[266] ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, and in it every kind of fruit, and then old age overtakes him while he has weak offspring, and a fiery whirlwind strikes it and it is burnt?⁠ Thus does Allah make the signs clear to you, that you may reflect.﴾

﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, and in it every kind of fruit, and then old age overtakes him⁠﴾, i.e., the age of decrepitude, for poverty and dependence in old age are harder. ﴿And he has weak offspring⁠﴾, young children who have no ability to earn. ﴿Then a whirlwind strikes it⁠﴾, i.e., a violent wind. ﴿In it is fire, and it is burnt⁠﴾ — that garden. Its owner is left in a state of helplessness, with his weakness, the burden of his dependants, and the scarcity of wealth. The meaning is an illustration of the state of one who performs good deeds but then adds to them what nullifies them, such as showing off and causing harm, so that on the Day of Resurrection he will feel regret and anguish; when his need for them becomes intense, he will find them nullified, in the condition of one whose matter is like this. ﴿Thus⁠﴾, i.e., like this clarification: ﴿Allah makes the signs clear to you, that you may reflect⁠﴾, i.e., upon them, so that you may take warning from them.

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Tafsir, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) once said to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "About what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden…⁠﴾?" They said: "Allah knows best." ʿUmar became angry and said: "Say: we know, or we do not know." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I have something in my mind about it, O Commander of the Faithful." ʿUmar said: "O my nephew, speak, and do not belittle yourself." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It was struck as a parable for a deed." ʿUmar said: "What deed?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "For a deed." ʿUmar said: "It is for a wealthy man who worked in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, then Allah sent Satan to him, and he committed sins, until his deeds were drowned." (Ibn Kathir said: this is among the narrations unique to al-Bukhari.)

(p-683) And Ibn Jarir has, through the route of ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas, a similar meaning: "Would any of you like to spend his life doing deeds of goodness, and then when his life is about to end, it is concluded with the deeds of the people of misery, which corrupt all of that and burn it?"

The Explanation of His Words, exalted is He:

[267] ﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth. And do not aim at the defective therefrom to spend [from it], while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook [its defect] in it. And know that Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾ This is an explanation of the condition of what is spent, following the explanation of the principle of spending and its manner. That is: spend from the choicest of what you have earned, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will not attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 92]. So the requirement of faith is spending from the good, especially that by which the pleasure of Allah is sought and the soul is steadied. And in the command there is an indication that it is what is spent of the good that is likened to a seed that grows seven spikes, or to a garden on a height. ﴿And from what﴾ i.e., and from the good things of what: ﴿We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾ — from grains and fruits. ﴿And do not aim﴾ i.e., do not intend: ﴿the defective﴾ i.e., the inferior ﴿of your wealth to spend from it﴾, ﴿while you would not accept it yourselves﴾ i.e., would not take it, meaning the inferior if it were given to you as a gift, ﴿unless you overlook [its defect] in it﴾ i.e., except by being lenient in accepting it and making allowance for it. From your saying: "Fulan overlooked part of his right" when he lowered his gaze; and it is said to the seller: "Aghmid" (overlook), i.e., do not press for full value, as if you do not see. Thus [it is stated] in al-Kashshaf.

Al-Razi said: al-Ighmad (overlooking) in the language is lowering the gaze and closing one eyelid over the other, and what is meant here is leniency, because when a person sees what he dislikes, he closes his eyes so as not to see it; then this became widespread until every overlooking and leniency in sale or otherwise was called ighmad. So His saying: ﴿while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook [its defect] in it﴾ means: if such things were given to you as a gift, you would not have accepted them except with reluctance and overlooking. So how can you be pleased for Me with what you would not be pleased with for yourselves?! ﴿And know that Allah is Free of need﴾ from your spending, and He only commands it for your benefit. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ — He rewards the doer of good with the best reward. And in the command that they should know this, along with the evidence of their knowledge of it, there is a rebuke for giving the defective, and a notification that this is one of the effects of ignorance of His due regard, exalted is He. And when He, exalted is He, encouraged the spending of the good, He warned against the whisperings of Satan in this matter, so He said:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[268] ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency, but Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾ in spending; ﴿and commands you to indecency﴾, meaning he incites you to stinginess and withholding charity, the incitement of one who commands to one who is commanded. The fāḥish (one who is indecent, base) among the Arabs is the stingy person. Ṭarafa said:

*I see death choosing the noble and taking, as its choice, the treasured wealth of the fāḥish, the stringent one.*

Al-Ḥarālī said: al-faḥshā' is everything upon which the reprehensions of the Sharia converge, and the greatest thing meant by it here is stinginess, which is the most afflicting disease, given the connection with the mention of poverty. Upon it the evil of this world and the Hereafter is built, it is accompanied by greed, followed by envy, and all evil follows one another from it.

﴿And Allah promises you﴾ in return for spending, especially from the good: ﴿forgiveness from Him﴾ of sins; ﴿and bounty﴾, a replacement and reward in the Hereafter. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾ in power and bounty, so He fulfills what He has promised you of forgiveness and the replacement of what you spend; ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your charities, so He will not waste your reward.

(p-685) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[269] ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given abundant good. And none will be reminded except the people of understanding.﴾

﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ Many have said: wisdom (ḥikmah, the perfect mastery of knowledge and action) is, in other words, knowing the truth and acting upon it. Abu Muslim said: "Ḥikmah is an form (fi'lah) derived from ḥukm, and it is like niḥlah from naḥl. A man is ḥakīm when he possesses intellect (ḥijā), understanding (lubb), and soundness of judgment. In this context, it carries the meaning of the agent (al-fā'il). It is also said: amr ḥakīm, meaning muḥkam (firm, well-ordered), and it is fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl." He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿In it every matter of wisdom is made distinct﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 4].

﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given abundant good﴾ Because through it the affairs of both abodes are ordered. The use of the noun in place of the pronoun (al-iẓhār fī maqām al-iḍmār) serves to show care for its importance. The placement of this verse after what precedes it implies that the one who is not deceived by the promise of Satan, and who has certainty in the promise of Allah, is the one whom Allah has granted wisdom. ﴿And none will be reminded﴾ meaning: none takes heed through the parables of the Qur'an and of wisdom. ﴿except the people of understanding﴾ meaning: those endowed with intellects purified from the impurities of desire, and they are the wise. The purpose of this is to urge acting upon what the verses contain regarding spending (al-infāq).

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[270] ﴿And whatever you spend of expenditure or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾

﴿And whatever you spend of expenditure or whatever vow you vow﴾ i.e., it returns to spending: ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, nothing is hidden from Him, and He will recompense you for it. ﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., those who spend to be seen by people, or who place their spending in other than its proper place, or who follow their spending with reproach and harm, or who spend from what is corrupt, (p-686) or who withhold charity, or who spend their wealth in disobedience, or who do not fulfill their vows: ﴿there are no helpers﴾, i.e., no supporters who will defend them from the punishment of Allah.

Al-Harali (al-Ḥarālī) said: In its implication is that Allah takes by the hand the generous and the noble whenever they stumble, so they find a helper for them, while the wrongdoer does not find a helper, by placing compulsion in the place of righteousness.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[271] ﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you, and He will remit from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿If you disclose your charities, then they are excellent﴾ is a kind of detailed explanation of some of what was stated in general in the conditional clause, and an elaboration of it; for this reason the conjunction between them is omitted. That is: if you make your charities apparent, then excellent is the thing that their disclosure accomplishes, for it removes suspicion, and it prompts everyone who hears of it, whether needy or otherwise, and it leads people to follow suit. ﴿But if you conceal them﴾, that is, keep them secret, fearing ostentation (riya') and to shield the poor from shame; ﴿and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾, that is, better than public giving, because it is further from ostentation and closer to sincerity (ikhlas), which is the spirit of acts of worship. ﴿And He will remit from you some of your misdeeds﴾, your sins in proportion to your charities. ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: an encouragement toward secrecy.

In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on the day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a young man who grew up in the worship of his Lord; a man whose heart is attached to the mosques; two men who loved each other for the sake of Allah, gathered together for Him and separated for Him; a man who was called by a woman of rank and beauty and said, 'I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds'; a man who gave charity and concealed it until his left hand does not know what his right hand gives; and a man who remembered Allah in solitude and his eyes overflowed."

Imam Ahmad and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Dharr, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, which charity is best? He said: 'Secret giving to a poor person, or the effort of one of modest means.'"

Subtleties (lata'if):

Abu al-Baqa' said regarding His words, ﴿then they are excellent (fa-ni'imma hiya)﴾: ni'ma is an invariable verb which has no imperfect form; its root is ni'ima, like 'alima, and this pattern has come in poetry; however, they reduced the middle vowel and transferred its vowel to the nun, so as to indicate the original form. Some leave the nun open according to the original form, and some vary it with kasra for both nun and 'ayn by assimilation; all of these have been recited. The subject of ni'ma is an implied pronoun, and "ma" means "thing." Then he said: "And We will remit from you" (nukaffiru 'ankum) may be read with nun, ascribing the verb to Allah, mighty and majestic; it may also be read with ya' on the same reckoning, and on another reckoning in which the subject is the pronoun of concealment. "Wa-tukaffiru" may be read with ta', the verb being ascribed to the pronoun of charity. It may be read with jazm on the ra' as a conjunction with the position of "fa-huwa khayrun," and with raf' by implying a subject, that is: "wa-nahnu" or "wa-hiya." The "min" here is superfluous according to al-Akhfash, so that "sayyi'atikum" is the object; according to Sibawayh, the object is elided, that is, "some of your misdeeds." The word sayyi'ah is of the form fay'alah, and its middle radical is waw, since it derives from sa'a yasu'u; its original form is sayw'ilah, so the waw was changed to ya' and the first was assimilated into it. End of quotation.

In Ghayth al-Naf': Ibn 'Amir (al-Shami) and al-Akhawan read fa-ni'mmā with fatha on the nun, while the rest read it with kasra. Qalun, al-Basri and Shu'bah read with sukun on the 'ayn; many chose for them the hidden kasra (ikhfa'), meaning ikhtilas, to flee from joining two consonants; the rest read with kasra on the 'ayn. They all agreed on shaddah on the mim. Then al-Shatibi objected to his not mentioning for Qalun and those who follow him anything but ikhfa', although sukun pure has also been related from them. Then he said: al-Muhaqqiq has clearly stated in his Nashr that al-Dani related both modes. Then he said: sukun is more transmitted, and ikhfa' is more analogical; it is the reading of Abu Ja'far and al-Hasan. The full extent of the matter is joining two consonants, where the first is not a long vowel letter (madd or lin), and this is permissible both in recitation and in language. No attention is given to one who denies it, even if he were the imam of Basra; and the one who denies it here himself recites it for Hamzah in His words, ﴿fa-ma istata'u﴾ in al-Kahf, where joining two consonants in connected recitation is undoubtedly present, since the sin is quiescent and the ta' is doubled, and this is similar to it. And Allah knows best. Thereby the rejection of what has been said is known: that the transmitter of sukun did not accurately record the recitation because the reciter elided the kasra of the 'ayn and he thought it was sukun. That is a heedlessness regarding its permissibility in language, as Abu 'Ubayd related, and regarding recitation with its parallel in "istata'u." And success is from Allah.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[272] ﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills. And whatever you spend of good, it is for yourselves. And you spend not except seeking the Countenance of Allah. And whatever you spend of good will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾ meaning: it is not obligatory upon you to make them guided to doing what they have been commanded of good deeds and to refraining from what they have been forbidden of the blameworthy matters enumerated, such as reminding of favour and causing harm, spending from what is corrupt, and miserliness. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾ by creating guidance in his heart after your explanation, in accordance with the continuation of His custom (sunnah) of creating things after their causes, not by way of obligation but by way of choice. This was conveyed by al-Mahayimi.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah), brought in by way of varying the address and directing it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), together with a shift to the third person between the addresses relating to the responsible persons, as an intensification in urging them to comply. For the information that it is not obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ) to follow up on their affairs indicates that it is obligatory upon them, as what follows in the conditional clause expresses. ﴿And whatever you spend of good, it is for yourselves﴾ meaning: in reality, because what is spent upon satisfies the recipient's transient need, while for you there is gained by it everlasting reward. So why do you remind of it to people and harm them? Similar examples in the Qur'an are many, such as His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Countenance of Allah﴾ is a negation carrying the sense of a prohibition: that is, do not exalt yourselves over people by it, nor show off by it. ﴿And whatever you spend of good will be repaid to you﴾ its reward multiplied manifold. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾ meaning: you will not be diminished from your good deeds, just as nothing will be added to your evil deeds.

**The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, Verse 273**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[273] ﴿For the poor who have been confined in the way of God, who cannot travel about the land. The ignorant man thinks them wealthy because of their restraint. You shall know them by their mark; they do not beg of people importunately. Whatever good you spend, indeed God knows it.﴾

﴿For the poor﴾ is connected to an omitted element that the context implies. That is: make what you spend be for the poor, or make your charities be for the poor, meaning those in need of expenditure. ﴿who have been confined in the way of God﴾, that is, who have confined themselves to His obedience, exalted is He, whether through jihad or otherwise. ﴿who cannot travel﴾, that is, go about. ﴿in the land﴾, to earn or to trade. ﴿The ignorant man thinks them﴾, concerning their condition, ﴿wealthy because of their restraint﴾, that is, because of their abstaining from asking. Their hinting at their need is contentment with what their Master has given them, satisfaction with Him, and nobility of soul. ﴿You shall know them by their mark﴾, through the characteristics that appear to people of understanding. As He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their mark is on their faces﴾ [al-Fath: 29], and He said: ﴿And you shall surely know them by the tone of their speech﴾ [Muhammad: 30]. In the hadith recorded in the Sunan (p-690): "Beware of the discernment (firasa) of the believer, for he sees by the light of God." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern﴾ [al-Hijr: 75]. This is related by Ibn Kathir.

Al-Ghazali said: It is appropriate that one should search out, in every neighborhood, the people of religion, and investigate the inner states of people of goodness and dignity, among those who are concealed, hiding their need, who do not repeatedly complain or lay out their troubles, or who are from among the people of honor whose wealth has gone but whose customs remain, so that they live in the cloak of dignified appearance. The reward for directing kindness to them is many times what is given to those who openly beg. Likewise, one should seek out for one's charity those whom charity makes grow, such as people of knowledge, for that is a help to them in knowledge, and knowledge is the most noble of acts of worship, provided the intention in it is sound. Ibn al-Mubarak used to restrict his kindness to the people of knowledge. It was said to him: "Would you not extend it more broadly?" He said: "I do not know, after the station of prophethood, of a station more excellent than the station of the scholars. When the heart of one of them is occupied with his need, he does not free himself for knowledge, and does not turn to learning. So freeing them for knowledge is more excellent."

A subtle point:

The word al-sima (السيما) is maqsur (with no final long vowel), like al-simah (السيمة), and al-sima' (السيماء) and al-simiya' (السيمياء), both with the long vowel (mamdudayn) with their vowels kasra. Al-suma (السومة), with a damma, means a mark. Abu Bakr ibn Duraid said: Their saying "upon him is a good sima" means a mark, and it is derived from wasamtu, asimu. The original in (sima) is wasma, so the waw was moved from the position of the first radical to the position of the middle radical, as they said ma atyabahu and aytabahu, and it became suma. The waw was changed to ya' because it is quiescent and the letter before it is kasra. Al-Samin said: So the pattern of sima is 'afla. When it is lengthened, the hamza in it is converted from an added letter used for assimilation (ilhaq), either waw or ya', so it is like 'ilba' (علباء), assimilated to sirdah (سرداح). The hamza is for assimilation, not for feminine marking, and it is therefore declinable. End of quotation.

﴿do not beg of people importunately﴾: (إلْحافًا) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative, meaning insistently. It is said: alhafa 'alayhi, etc. Al-Zamakhshari said: Al-ilhaf is al-ilhah, which is persistence, and not leaving until one is given something, from their saying: lahafani min fadli lihafihi, meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had. It has been said that the meaning of the verse is: if they ask, they ask gently and do not press, so the negation applies only to the qualifier. The correct view is that it negates both asking and insistence together, so the negation returns to the qualifier and what it qualifies, as in His saying: ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. In this there is a warning against the bad way of one who asks people importunately, and a claim to praise and honor for the one who refrains from that. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The poor man is not the one who is turned away by a date or two dates, nor by a morsel or two morsels. Rather, the poor man is the one who refrains. Recite, if you wish: ﴿They do not beg of people importunately﴾." Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A man's asking will not cease until he meets God with no piece of flesh on his face." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban related from Samurah ibn Jundub that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Asking is like a scratch that a man scratches on his face. Whoever wishes, leaves it; whoever wishes, abandons it, except one who asks a ruler, or in a matter he cannot avoid." Ahmad related from Ibn Umar, (p-692), who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Asking is like a scratch on the face of its owner on the Day of Resurrection, so whoever wishes, let him preserve his face." Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim and Ibn Majah related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever asks people for their wealth to increase it, he is only asking for embers, so let him reduce it or increase it." Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Khuzaymah related from Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyyah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever asks for something while he has what suffices him, he is only accumulating embers of Hell." They said: "O Messenger of God, what suffices him?" He said: "What feeds him at morning or evening." Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, who said: We were nine, or eight, or seven, and he said: "Will you not pledge allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?" We said: "On what shall we pledge allegiance to you?" He said: "That you worship God and do not associate anything with Him, and the five prayers, and that you obey, and that you do not ask people." I have seen some of those men whose whip fell, and not one of them asked anyone to hand it to him.

Malik, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "For one of you to gather a bundle of firewood on his back is better for him than to ask someone, who then gives him or refuses him." al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "God loves the believer who earns his living by a craft." Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever seeks independence, God will make him independent; whoever seeks chastity, God will make him chaste; whoever seeks sufficiency, God will suffice him; and whoever asks while he has the value of an ounce, he has indeed pressed the matter." al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i related from Ibn Umar that Umar said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to give me a gift, and I would say: 'Give it to one who is needier than me.' He said: 'Take it. When something of this wealth comes to you while you are neither seeking it eagerly nor asking, take it and make it your property. If you wish, eat it, and if you wish, give it in charity. And what does not come to you, do not let your soul pursue it.'"

Salim ibn Abd Allah said: For this reason Abd Allah would not ask anyone for anything, nor would he refuse anything that was given to him. ﴿And whatever good you spend﴾, that is, even on those who press their requests, and on those whose poverty is not verified or whose need is not severe. ﴿indeed God knows it﴾, that is, that this spending is for Him or for others, and He will reward according to it. Then, exalted is He, indicated that spending is not restricted to a particular time or state, by His saying:

The Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 2, Verse 274:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[274] ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, will have their reward with their Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, will have their reward with their Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ In mentioning the night before the day, and the secret before the open, there is an indication of the superiority of concealment over display.

Al-Harali said: The most excellent of them is the one who spends by night in secret, and the lowest of them is the one who spends by day openly. Thus they are four categories.

Subtleties:

It is not hidden that in His, the Exalted, urging to spending in this abundant verse, and His striking of examples of kindness to His creation, both as encouragement and warning, is what calls every believer to purify himself by the excess of his wealth.

[p. 694] Imam al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, said in *al-Ihya'* (*The Revival of the Religious Sciences*), and his words are: Regarding the aspect of the trial through charities, there are three meanings. The first: uttering the two words of testimony (the shahadah) is a commitment to monotheism (tawhid) and a testimony to the singling out of the One worshipped. A condition for the complete fulfilment of this is that no beloved remains for the monotheist other than the One, the Unique, for love does not accept partnership. Monotheism by the tongue alone is of little benefit, and the degree of love is tested only through separation from the beloved. Wealth is beloved to creatures because it is an instrument that provides them enjoyment in this world, and through it they find comfort in this world and recoil from death, although in death is the meeting with the beloved. So they are tested in the truthfulness of their claim of love, and they are brought down from wealth, which is their object of regard and their object of passion. For this reason God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and that is through jihad, which is the giving of one's life, out of longing for meeting God, Mighty and Majestic. Giving of wealth is easier. Since this meaning was understood in the spending of wealth, people were divided into three categories. One category were truthful in monotheism, fulfilled their covenant, and relinquished all their wealth, so they did not store up a dinar or a dirham. A second category, whose rank is below those before them, are those who keep their wealth, watching for the times of needs and the seasons of good deeds. Their intention in saving is to spend according to the need without indulgence, and to direct the surplus beyond need to the paths of righteousness, however many they may be. These do not limit themselves to the measure of zakat (obligatory almsgiving). A group of the Successors (tabi'un) held that there are rights in wealth beyond zakat, such as al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, 'Ata' and Mujahid. Al-Sha'bi said, (after he was asked: Is there a right in wealth beyond zakat?) he said: Yes. Have you not heard His, Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And gave wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and the verse. They cited His, Mighty and Majestic, saying [p. 695]: ﴿And from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Anfal: 3], and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254]. They claimed that this is not abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of zakat, but rather it falls under the right of a Muslim over a Muslim, meaning that it is obligatory upon the wealthy, whenever he finds a needy person, to remove his need, let alone the zakat wealth. A third category limit themselves to fulfilling the obligation, neither adding to it nor reducing from it. This is the lowest rank, and all the common people have confined themselves to it, due to their miserliness with wealth, their inclination toward it, and the weakness of their love for the Hereafter. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿If He should ask you for it and press you, you would be miserly, and He would bring out your malice﴾ [Muhammad: 37]. "Yuhfikum" means: He would press you. So how great is the difference between a servant from whom God has purchased his wealth and his self in exchange for Paradise, and a servant from whom He does not press for it because of his miserliness. This is one of the meanings of God's command to His servants to give up wealth.

The second meaning: purification from the attribute of miserliness, for it is among the destructive things. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Three things destroy: a miserliness that is obeyed, a desire that is followed, and a man's self-admiration." And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul – it is those who are successful﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16]. The attribute of miserliness is removed only by accustoming oneself [p. 696] to giving up wealth, for love of a thing is not severed except by forcing the self to part with it until it becomes a habit. Zakat, in this sense, is a purification, meaning it purifies its giver from the filth of destructive miserliness. Its purity is in proportion to his giving and in proportion to his joy in paying it out and his delight in dispensing it for God, the Exalted.

The third meaning: thankfulness for blessing. God, Mighty and Majestic, has a blessing upon His servant in his self and in his wealth. Acts of worship of the body are thanks for the blessing of the body, and financial acts are thanks for the blessing of wealth. How base is one who looks at the poor man whose provision has been constricted and who has been brought to need, and yet his self does not allow him to render thanks to God, the Exalted, for enriching him so that he is spared from asking, and for making others need him.

Section

Al-Ghazali, may God have mercy on him, also has a discussion on the reproach and harm mentioned earlier. It is worth mentioning here, because of its benefits for the seeker of the Hereafter.

He, may God have mercy on him, said: The fifth duty (meaning of the duties of one who desires the path of the Hereafter through his charity) is not to spoil his charity with reproach (mann) and harm (adha). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do not invalidate your charities with reproach and harm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. They differed regarding the reality of reproach and harm. It was said: reproach is to mention it, and harm is to make it public. Sufyan said: Whoever reproaches, his charity is spoiled. It was said to him: How is reproach? He said: That he mentions it and speaks of it. It was said: reproach is that he makes the recipient a servant through the gift, and harm is that he reproaches him for his poverty. It was said: reproach is that he acts arrogantly toward him on account of his gift, and harm is that he scolds him or rebukes him for asking. The Prophet ﷺ said: "God does not accept the charity of one who reproaches." In my view, reproach has a root and a seedbed, and it is one of the states and attributes of the heart. From it branch out outward states on the tongue and the limbs. Its root is that he sees himself as doing good to the recipient and bestowing a favour upon him. The right is that he should see the poor man as doing good to him by accepting God's right from him, which is his purification and his salvation from the Fire, and that had he not accepted it, he would have remained held in pledge by it. So the right is that he should bear the obligation of the poor man's favour, since he has made his hand a deputy of God, Mighty and Majestic, in taking God's right, Mighty and Majestic. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed, charity falls into the hand of God, Mighty and Majestic, before it falls into the hand of the beggar." Let him realise that he is handing over his right to God, Mighty and Majestic, and that the poor man is taking his provision from God, the Exalted, after it has reached God, Mighty and Majestic.
